As has been mentioned, EU countries are migrating away from Microsoft systems; that was mainly driven by the President of the US claiming that he was going to activate the kill switch for Microsoft, which worried a lot of countries. Can the Minister be clear about how we are planning to migrate away from US-based systems and invest a lot more in British-based systems, so that we can have more data sovereignty?

There are a number of answers to that question, and I am grateful to my hon. Friend for raising it. First, let me go through again what this incident involved. We are working very closely with Microsoft, and it has confirmed that this was not an attack on its systems. One of its servers went down due to a defect that had been found; there was a surge in load that brought that bug—that defect—to the fore. There was another completely unrelated issue, which was that a server that accounts for 14% of capacity was also down for maintenance at the time. This outage was caused by the volume of traffic choking the servers that were left, which produced a backlog and brought the servers down. Microsoft resolved the problem relatively quickly. By 2 pm on Friday, services were coming back online. My hon. Friend asked what we are doing to diversify away from US suppliers and the big international suppliers. I have already mentioned the £500 million sovereign AI fund, which is there to back British businesses and promote that sovereignty; the £1.1 billion AI hardware plan; and the £500 million to try to resolve some of these issues that was in this year’s Budget. We have a tech stack that is dominated by US tech companies. We want more AI sovereignty in the United Kingdom; we are willing to fund that, and we are funding it. That is how we will make sure we have the most resilient services, but also the most technologically advanced services, in the UK.

I am grateful to the Minister for making this important statement. Those of us with rural constituencies represent many people who are very worried about the copper switch-off that is coming as we move to fibre. Fibre is an energy-intensive system, unlike the copper system, and it seems to be coming without a delay being considered. Donald Rumsfeld once talked about the known unknowns. We know that an attack will happen somewhere. The Minister has outlined that this outage was a specific issue, but it shows how reliant we are on these systems. The hon. Member for Rotherham (Sarah Champion) talked about the switching off of terrestrial television. These things are of great concern. I urge the Minister to take away what happened on Friday and look at the broader picture. When the known unknown happens and everything gets closed down, the proven and tried systems of copper connections and terrestrial radio and television should be there as a back-up system on which people can rely.

This is an issue for all of us in this Chamber, because we rely on that technology. Similar discussions about whether we are over-reliant on technology probably happened, if we check Hansard , with the invention of the personal computer and the internet. Technology makes us a better economy and makes it easier for businesses to operate. It makes it easier for us all to stay connected and informed. Resilience is a key part of what we are trying to do in government, whether through our cyber action plan or all the other initiatives that I have mentioned from this Dispatch Box. That cyber action plan has £210 million in funding to better utilise cyber-skills and to deliver once and for all, at scale, a co-ordinated approach across Government to tackle all those critical risks that the right hon. Gentleman mentions. The right hon. Gentleman talks about power and national power outages. We know that telecoms networks have substantial power back-ups at core network sites. We have a resilient electricity system, but we cannot plan for every eventuality. It would be wrong for a Minister of any colour to stand at this Dispatch Box and say that we will not have any other cyber-attacks or any other outages such as this. What we need to do is minimise them, minimise the risk and make sure that the Government are in the best place, including in terms of the wider economy.

I declare an interest, as I have a close relative who is working on the regulation of Microsoft. I thank the Minister for his statement. Will he update the House more broadly on how the UK is planning to be more resilient in this field, particularly given that a relatively small number of suppliers have such a critical role in the economy?

As I have said, we recognise that relying on a small number of suppliers can create risks for resilience, competition and value for money. Those suppliers provide us with the very best technology, and we are not trying to swap one dependency for another, but alongside the large global providers, which bring skills, security and capability, we must ensure that we have our own sovereignty in this country in the areas of the tech stack that we are good at. We have put taxpayers’ money where our mouth is to develop that tech stack and that sovereignty, so that we have resilience.

The statement raises the issues of resilience and preparedness in the public and private sectors. Can the Minister and his team do more to support businesses, both small and large—including through the known communication channels, such as the Federation of Small Businesses, Prosper and others—by more widely distributing advice and messages about digital preparedness tools? This has been a significant enough incident to warrant a ministerial statement, but there are rural and remote businesses and public services that tackle digital challenges every single day of the week due to lack of fibre broadband and other issues. Can more be done to roll out fibre broadband even faster?

There was a lot in that question, and I will try to run through it in order. Building Digital UK has Project Gigabit, which is trying to get to 99% of all premises by 2032. Many of those who are most affected and are the hardest to reach will be in the hon. Gentleman’s constituency in the highlands of Scotland. For that 1%, there will be additional technologies—they are evolving all the time—to make sure that everyone is connected. As I have said at the Dispatch Box many times, we cannot have growth in every postcode without connectivity, and the more rural somewhere is, the more difficult it is to have that connection. From the point view of the wider economy and business, the only thing that I can continue to emphasise from this Dispatch Box is that people should use the National Cyber Security Centre’s free tools on cyber-security. That should be on the lips of every board member sitting around the boardroom table. We will have a much more resilient economy with much more resilient businesses only if everybody plays their part.

West London is part of a cluster of data centres where, if there is a problem with one centre, data can be backed up in another. In my constituency, two data centres have recently been agreed by Ealing council, which has taken the position that only data centres with the highest environmental standards will be allowed. Does the Minister agree that clustering data centres in this way is the right approach to digital resilience, along with the Government’s new data centre covenant, which will ensure that we meet our climate commitments?

I could not have put it better myself. We do need data centres for this. If we are talking about AI sovereignty and tech sovereignty, it is best for them to be onshore here in the United Kingdom. That is a big challenge, but we must ensure that it is done correctly, and I pay tribute to Ealing council for the way in which it has done it in its area.

The Cyber Security and Resilience (Network and Information Systems) Bill is in its final stages of parliamentary scrutiny, and in this context I particularly note the role of resilience in ensuring our national economic security. What assessment have the Government made of the potential impact in future outages on critical national infrastructure—including communications and supply chains—on which essential services depend, and what further amendments to the Bill might be needed?

The Bill will return to this House relatively soon. It updates the Network and Information Systems Regulations 2018 to bring some of these companies into scope, including data centres, and contains a provision to extend the scope, if necessary, to include more organisations and more sectors of the economy. It will be back in this House before the end of the year, and we will be able to debate these matters in more detail then, but its purpose is to ensure that we have greater resilience and to update the regulations.

I thank the Minister for coming to the House in such a timely fashion. I know he will have been disappointed to learn today that the new James Bond is not a Scotsman. The Microsoft outage had a huge impact on residents and businesses in my constituency of Harlow, and I was reassured to hear when I contacted my local hospital that it had not been hugely impacted, but will the Minister reassure the House that he will do everything he can to hold Microsoft to account and ensure that there is no spectre of future outages?

I am glad that my hon. Friend managed to talk to his NHS trust and resolve that issue over the weekend. Only two NHS trusts stood up an incident response unit, but it was no longer required so they stood it back down relatively quickly. That shows that the system does work. The co-ordination of the Department for Digital, Culture, Media and Sport and the National Cyber Security Centre to bring together the Government Cyber Co-ordination Centre meant that the information was filtered from Microsoft through the Government to trusts and local government so that they could stand up incident responses if they needed to do so, but they did not need to do so in this particular case.

I thank the Minister for his statement, and for his welcome comments about backing more British suppliers that are small and medium-sized enterprises. May I ask him to extend that review and look into not only alternative suppliers of the solutions, but the decision to have software as a service as the default choice every time, so that we can improve the resilience of the services here and possibly even copy the French by developing our own open-source solution?

I can only re-emphasise what I have said already. The Government are backing our work on the tech stack with taxpayers’ money to see how we can seed good businesses in this country that wish to grow and enter these marketplaces. It is difficult for the Government to do that, because the big suppliers are there for us to secure value for money for the taxpayer. However, the current procurement process through the national cloud infrastructure programme is about ensuring that we not only secure the best value for money but have some tech sovereignty on British soil by seeding those companies to make them grow.

Given the Microsoft 365 outage, the Vodafone outage last year and Storm Éowyn, which prevented my constituents from receiving communications, does the Minister agree that sometimes the older ways are the best? In my constituency, we have a 90-year-old transmitter that still transmits analogue. I worry that if the Government go ahead with their plan to switch off analogue, it will cut off people in a way that we know will happen again. What can the Minister tell my constituents to assure them that old technologies will still be considered critical national infrastructure?

The media Green Paper lays out that the Government have already made the choice that we will switch off digital terrestrial television and move to internet protocol television at some point in the future, but the date has not yet been determined—it could be 2034 or 2044. We are examining the consultation to work out the best way forward. The hon. Lady’s constituents can be assured that no decision has been made, and we will take into account the issues that she raises when making that decision.

The Microsoft outage was, of course, a shock—indeed, it was a wake-up call to us all—but it may be that we got away lightly. Imagine if it lasted for a week or a fortnight, enhanced by bad actors. The Minister and other Members have referred to the need for open-source alternatives. Will he commit to coming back within three to six months on plans and progress for such alternatives?

The rhetoric from the hon. Gentleman is not necessarily helpful, because it was an isolated incident at Microsoft. There have been incidents in the past, which he referred to, and there will be incidents in the future. Our job is to make the Government as resilient as possible, and to put in place the tools and legislation to make sure that the economy is as resilient as possible, so that the UK can stand when these kinds of incidents happen.

I am pleased that the Minister has spoken about the steps that this Government will take in relation to digital resilience, because for weeks I have been pointing out a fault in the General Register Office’s new electronic register for births, deaths and stillbirths in England and Wales, which went live earlier this month. Over 70 senior council officials from around 50 local authorities wrote to the Home Office and told it that when the system fails, it is impossible to issue the death certificates needed for the deceased to be repatriated and buried overseas—something that is very important for many religious communities. In response, the Home Office has simply ignored warnings and continued regardless. Does the Minister agree that the lessons of the Microsoft outage should be learned by the Government as well as corporations, and will he agree to raise this matter with his counterparts in the Home Office so that we can prevent a disaster from happening?

I am not aware of that incident, but I will raise it with Ministers in the Home Office to find out what has happened. The hon. Gentleman asks us to learn the lessons from the Microsoft outage, which we and Microsoft will learn, but we were learning lessons before the Microsoft incident, because this Government want to be much more resilient. The Government’s cyber action plan, which was published at the start of this year, is part of that project, and is backed by £210 million of taxpayers’ money. That is about central direction, co-ordination, pace, consistency and clarity when it comes to the resilience of Government, and it is also about making sure that the wider economy has resilience.

I thank the Minister for his very comprehensive answers and for his interest in this matter. When Microsoft goes down, the country grinds to a halt—“IP meltdown” is how we refer to it. In my constituency last week, problems were not only financial. We saw NHS staff forced to use pen and paper, courts forced to adjourn, and councils and schools left scrambling to function. The IT system in my office, and in Government offices, was down until 1.40 pm on Friday, and my constituents and others were disadvantaged as a result. It raises serious questions about our over-reliance on a single system. What steps are being taken to ensure that every Government Department has proper contingency plans and offline back-ups, so that a technical failure never again paralyses our public services?

The hon. Gentleman talks about people reverting to pen and paper and other systems kicking in. The whole point of having a resilience plan is that when things happen across the tech stack or any of the systems, other systems kick in. That is why we did not see widespread disruption across the whole public sector. Yes, it was an inconvenience. My own emails went down until about 2 o’clock on Friday. I know that because the test email I sent myself on Thursday night arrived at about 2 pm on Friday, and the acknowledgment that it had arrived bounced back. The backlog has been cleared, and Microsoft resolved the problem as quickly as it could, but the whole point of the Government’s cyber action plan is to make sure that all Government Departments, local government and our public sector have resilience, and that the private sector also has resilience.

On a point of order, Madam Deputy Speaker. There are about 300,000 jobs in tech and telecoms in Berkshire—Reading lies in that county and is the county town—and there are many more thousands of those jobs across the country, yet we only occasionally discuss issues related to this very important area of employment. Could there be a debate in the House on the contribution of tech and telecoms to the British economy?

I thank the hon. Gentleman for his point of order. As he will know, that is not a matter for the Chair, but he has put on record the great extent of businesses in his constituency that are reliant on tech.

On a point of order, Madam Deputy Speaker. We have lots of tech companies in Harlow, but my point of order refers to a mistake I made, and as a former maths teacher, I apologise for getting my numbers wrong. Last Thursday, when I spoke in the Backbench Business debate about the battle of the Somme, I referred to Private Thomas Lewis—he lived in my constituency and, sadly, died in the Somme—but I stated his age incorrectly. I said he was 19 when, sadly, he was killed at the battle of the Somme, but he was actually 21. I am taking this opportunity to set the record straight. —[ Official Report , 12 November 2026; Vol. 793, c. 403.]
I thank the hon. Gentleman for his point of order. He has sought to correct the record at the earliest possible opportunity, although I am far from convinced that that was actually a point of order.

On a point of order, Madam Deputy Speaker. I would like to correct the record of the debate on Friday on the private Member’s Bill promoted by the hon. Member for St Ives (Andrew George). I incorrectly said: “We also build the infrastructure first. We are extending the grid roads, our famous roundabouts and our redways, which means that bicycles and pedestrians do not have to interact with the roads. Those provisions are set out in our council planning.” —[ Official Report , 13 November 2026; Vol. 793, c. 468.] What I meant to say was “in the local plan”, because as you will know, the council plan has everything in it that the council does, whereas the local plan has statutory standing in planning guidance. Thank you for allowing me to correct the record at the earliest opportunity.
I thank the hon. Member for her point of order. She has indeed done well to correct the record about the difference between a local plan and a council plan, and I am sure we thank her for that.

On a point of order, Madam Deputy Speaker. Thank you for allowing me to raise this point of order. In fact, it is the first point of order I have raised, so please bear with me. On 4 November, I spoke in the Adjournment debate on the strategic licensing regulations for London, and I am afraid that, as I am still a newbie to this place, I neglected to state an interest in that my partner is the manager of the trading standards and licensing department at Brent council. I believe I should have raised that at the time. A little time has gone by since then, but I am afraid I did not realise that I should have raised the issue until my partner mentioned it to me over the weekend, having noticed that I had spoken in the debate. I apologise for raising this so late. I hope you can assist me in correcting the record, and I will make sure not to make the same mistake again. —[ Official Report , 4 November 2026; Vol. 792, c. 969.]
I thank the hon. Member for what I think may actually have been a point of order. She has indeed corrected the record, and I thank her for that.

With permission, I would like to make a statement on digital capability for health and care. This Government are determined to give patients access to technology that supports their care while improving productivity. We want to give the health and care system more choice, greater resilience and less dependence on any single supplier, as well as the ability to adapt and evolve as new technologies emerge in future, with better value for taxpayers through time. These objectives require a new approach: one that will stimulate a more diverse and innovative supplier market, including greater use of sovereign AI as well as internationally developed capabilities, building on the shift from analogue to digital set out in the 10-year health plan. As we have just been learning, the global outage of certain Microsoft systems on Friday brought home the importance of avoiding overdependence. Our future capability should avoid being locked into any single technology. We need a new approach—one that will boost competition, demand interoperability and diversify NHS technology within a safe and modern regulatory framework. That approach has three parts: investing in strategic technologies; changing how future technology capabilities are procured; and developing open standards and our safety regime. In the Budget, my right hon. Friend the Chancellor confirmed a further £140 million for sovereign AI. The NHS will work with sovereign AI on speeding up clinical trials, monitoring medicines safety and scaling proven AI products across the NHS, such as cancer cell detection. The Government have committed to using public procurement as a strategic lever to back British industry and ensure communities benefit from growth and good jobs. We will evolve NHS procurement processes in line with that aim. Within a fair and open competition framework, we will use our purchasing power to create routes to market for innovative companies, giving British start-ups a fair crack at NHS contracts. Rather than the NHS simply buying the technology of the future, we want it to help create the market for it. That is where the federated data platform comes in. Fragmented information stops the NHS from providing patients with effective and emotionally intelligent care. A hospital can have beds available, but struggle to match them with patients waiting to be admitted. A clinical team can waste valuable time trying to understand where patients are on a waiting list, rather than treating them. Different parts of the NHS can hold pieces of the same operational jigsaw without being able to see the whole picture. Those are just some of the problems the FDP is helping the NHS to solve. Technology and Government priorities have moved on since the original FDP procurement in 2023 and our procurement model needs to move with them, so today I can update the House: we will begin a new procurement process along different lines from the current contract. From January, the NHS will begin this vital work with patients, our partners and the market. Formal procurement will begin in the second half of next year and we expect the full process, from engagement to completion, to take around 18 months. This is about the NHS building on what works, while opening the next generation of FDP to the best technologies. Interoperability, resilience and trusted common standards can and must be baked into the next generation of FDP. We will also start work, alongside the new procurement, to work with different providers on developing new capabilities and expertise starting with systems used in maternity care. Innovative providers will be invited to help address the data and digital fragmentation in this important area of care, and to test how health priorities can create routes to build UK AI capability. We will announce further details within the next few weeks. A process this important must command public trust as well as clinical confidence. Public trust is won through clear rules, transparency, inde

I am grateful to the Minister for advance sight of the statement. AI and tech have huge potential in health, from drug discovery to diagnostic imaging and personalised medicine, and for more preventive care, better efficacy in treatment and more time free to be with the patient. The UK is uniquely placed because of our universities and our life sciences and tech sectors—and perhaps most of all because of the national health service and its rich data. The Health Data Research Service has been called a once-in-a-generation chance to lead the world, and in the NHS the federated data platform that the Minister spoke about is already helping to run healthcare services more effectively for the good of patients. AI will turbocharge both. However, success in delivering those better outcomes will depend on how well the service can leverage that unique NHS data resource. Public trust and confidence are critical, as is the confidence of clinicians. We need effective principles and protocols around data security and privacy. We have the Caldicott principles, GDPR and the Data Protection Act 2018, the digital technology assessment criteria within NHS England and the NHS data security and protection standards. If there is something deficient with one of them, the right thing to do is to change it. The procurement process is the right way to evaluate one supplier against another within the principles and protocols. It should be about delivering the right spec at the right price for optimal patient care. We cannot have the selection of a supplier of an IT contract being a matter of politics or a matter of Labour MPs’ tastes or distastes. I ask the Minister: what is actually different here? Interoperability and not being tied into a single supplier agreement are not bad principles to have in a procurement, and they can be written into a procurement specification. I think they already feature in procurement—the Minister will correct me if I am wrong—such as on the single patient record. Will he confirm that it will still be the case that any qualified supplier will be able to bid? Could the Minister tell us what this line from his statement means: “Within a fair and open competition framework, we will use our purchasing power to create routes to market for innovative companies”? What is different between the old and the new federated data platforms? If there is a difference, how will he ensure that we do not get a drop-off in FDP participation and use if people in the system expect it to be a materially different system in two years’ time, rather than an evolution or upgrade? On related matters of data privacy and public confidence, following the appalling cases where families who had already been through the most unimaginable pain in the Southport and Nottingham attacks found that their loved ones’ records had then been snooped on—there are many hundreds more instances of unauthorised access—what are the Minister and his colleagues doing to ensure that there are consistent penalties sufficient to act as a proper deterrent against that abuse, or, better still, mechanisms to block it happening at all? Can the Minister also tell us what is happening with the frontline productivity programme? How much of that funding has now been released, and for what? Finally, the entire system has been plunged into disturbance and distraction by the Minister and his boss’s top-down reorganisation of the NHS, so where— [ Laughter. ] Before they laugh, they should talk to people in their local ICBs. Where in the new set-up will responsibility lie for the federated data platform and the single patient record? These clearly do not belong in a regional management layer structure, and instead belong firmly in the national health service at a national level.

I thank the right hon. Gentleman for his customary selection of very strong questions. It is good to be across the Dispatch Box from him today. I will start with the issue of trust. This is fundamental, because innovation can move only at the speed of trust. I take that incredibly seriously. We are today announcing a new procurement for the next iteration of the FDP programme, which builds on an increased appetite for additional capabilities. In my statement, I used the example of maternity services, but there will be others. It is fundamental, therefore, that in the ongoing use of the FDP, and of any new procurement process, my colleagues and I take every opportunity to remake the case for trusted systems, particularly on the issue of data. If data is accessed and misused, the full force of the law will fall down on those people, as has been the case. If the law is broken, they will face the consequences. People in the NHS and elsewhere should be in no doubt of that fact. The benefits of the new FDP iteration will be a procurement process that welcomes international and UK capability alike—whether that is UK small and medium-sized enterprises that want a crack at NHS contracts, sovereign AI-backed capability in the UK or any international provider worth merit, they should be encouraged to take part in this. This should stir interest in the future capability. The point is this: the principle of the FDP and the benefits of the FDP are not what is being ignored. The merits are being remade, and the case for it is being remade. The additional appetite for new capabilities, potentially backed by UK sovereign capabilities, is what we are talking about today, as well as international counterparts. On interoperability, I agree wholly with the right hon. Gentleman’s instincts that it must be baked in from the get-go. That framework still exists.

At the outset, I declare that before I came to this place I previously worked with the NHS AI and digital regulations service, so I am a little bit chuffed about this statement, particularly the recommendation for a life cycle model after a project is deployed. I thank the Minister for that. I want to raise the issue of Palantir. NHS England and Palantir claim that the current £330 million platform contributed to over 110,000 additional operations and a reduction in long-stay discharge delays of 12% to 15%. However, independent investigations by the likes of the Financial Times, the Health Foundation and digital rights groups found that that headline number was heavily skewed by a tiny minority of trusts. Additional freedom of information data and reports by the Guardian revealed that nearly a third of trusts performed fewer procedures after adoption and 29 trusts reported little or no actual use of the platforms. May I ask for the Minister’s assurance that any future contracts and future iteration of the platform will have independent oversight and auditing to ensure the platform’s efficiency and value for money, so that we do not see such exaggerated claims of performance again?

I assure my hon. Friend that scrutiny of performance is vital, both in the platform’s current and future form, and any overstated benefits should be subject to correction. The opportunity here is in launching a new procurement process for the next generation of the FDP that builds on what works now—from the metrics of the 137 of our trusts that are actively realising those benefits today. Away from any grandstanding or overstatement, it is those measures that I care about, as well as taking the responsible decision to commission new procurement and next-generation FDP while maintaining patient continuity of care as we do so.

We are glad that pressure from the Liberal Democrats, especially my hon. Friend the Member for Newton Abbot (Martin Wrigley) and the Chair of the Health and Social Care Committee, my hon. Friend the Member for Oxford West and Abingdon (Layla Moran), has helped bring about this statement. We have long been sounding the alarm about the dangerous Palantir contract, which has been shrouded in secrecy, and the need for digital sovereignty for the NHS. The Liberal Democrats are clear that we need to get Palantir out of the NHS. A Trump-aligned tech giant should be nowhere near the data of millions of NHS patients and a piece of important national infrastructure. The whole Palantir story has been mired in secrecy and controversy. The Conservatives were wrong to sign this contract and showed a disregard for our sovereignty and security. We have two primary objections: first, the lack of transparency surrounding the whole deal, including the opaque procurement process; secondly, the national security implications of offshoring our whole nation’s health data to a company with an appalling human rights record, run by an ally of Donald Trump. Lack of trust in Palantir has led to doctors and patients voting with their feet, opting out of sharing their data and undermining the fundamental effectiveness of the FDP system. Will the Minister accept the core principles that the Liberal Democrats believe should underpin NHS digital transformation and, as reflected in the amendments we tabled to the Health Bill, consider our proposals for a risk assessment for all non-UK tech and data suppliers, an NHS digital sovereignty strategy and the prioritisation of domestic suppliers? The reality is that over the next two years this platform will become a lame duck, and we need to use that time to best effect.

The hon. Member and I agree on the opportunity given to us by a new FDP procurement process. I repeat that part of the opportunity is about fully articulating additional capabilities to realise the productivity benefits and efficiency savings that the FDP, as it exists, is already proving. The decision taken today is based on independent measures of use by 137 trusts. This is not about the politics of executives of suppliers, nor is it about the territories or customers of one company or one supplier. To repeat what I said in response to the opposition spokesperson, the right hon. Member for East Hampshire (Damian Hinds), the procurement process will be open, fair and transparent, with UK sovereign capability—SMEs in constituencies across the land—encouraged to tender, and any international capability also invited to tender.

I am grateful for the thought that the Government have given to an obviously difficult situation. I am still concerned that we may be locked into Palantir. May I ask the Minister to assure us that, within a year, he will ask Palantir to prove that is not the case by moving at least one application off Foundry or another platform so we can see that we are not dependent on it anymore? I am delighted to hear that we are moving towards a common data platform based on common standards, because, as the Minister said, that will enable the involvement of lots of British companies, creating a sovereign data offering here in the UK and helping patient care. Does the Minister therefore intend to carry on with and grow the FDP or to work on developing the common data standards—I gather Nesta is doing that at the moment, and that work could be completed in six months—and have a completely different data platform so that we can fully get rid of the albatross of Palantir hanging around the NHS’s neck once and for all?

I thank my hon. Friend not just for his engagement and questions to me today but for his counsel throughout, which has often been in corridors as we pass each other as well as formally. I look forward to further engagement with him and the Health and Social Care Committee on which he serves. We are both excited about the prospect of Government policies improving and enhancing UK sovereign capability. We recognise that the next iteration of the FDP, while including all possible suppliers and providers from the UK and internationally through an open and transparent process, brings with it new, exciting prospects for UK-based companies. I do not need to wait a year: I can confirm today that we are not locked in.

I thank the Minister for his statement. I want to probe him a little on ensuring that trust is established and maintained as other research areas, such as those from higher education, and sovereign companies may come in. Will measures be in place to stop infiltration by foreign countries buying into those companies or having research students at universities who could take data away for their own ends?

In the common standards framework, we would expect there to be an explicit appreciation of the lineage or ownership of any particular company. The point is that the product—the FDP—is NHS-owned, as is the intellectual property and the data. Who provides the product is subject to open, robust, free procurement processes. The distinction we are making is that we recognise—not least through the appetite of those using the FDP—that the FDP can do more. I will be making the case as to why—not just now in this period of continuity of care, but in the future iteration—more trusts should sign up and take it up, and why those using it should do so fully. I look forward to using their voices to ensure that the case is made to their peers.

I thank the Minister for his statement. I believe that something as important as NHS data should be managed by a trusted British provider, and that we should not pass up the capability to develop our own AI capability. Can he tell me what role public trust will play in the final decision? I hope he agrees that we should not give the contract to a company that the British public do not trust with their data.

My hon. Friend is absolutely right. Trust will either undermine a system or underpin it, and innovation can only move as fast as the trust therein. The opportunity today, in launching the procurement for a new iteration and next generation of the FDP, is an opportunity to remake and restate the Government’s commitment to trust in the use of data in such a system.

I thank the Minister for his statement and for delivering quite so comprehensively what I and many colleagues across the House have been searching for for some while, particularly with the emphasis on interoperability, common standards and a new approach, which I hope will also apply to the single patient record. May I request him to specify that we stop the funding of new development on the existing Palantir system, and to investigate preventing further expansion into new trusts? May I also request him to recognise Palantir as a US supplier—rather than, as it claims, a British supplier, which it is clearly not—and to look into clarifying the actual benefits that have been delivered through the system that we have today, based on the others? And may I further congratulate him on responding to my debate tomorrow evening, before it has even taken place?

This is the first time I have been thanked for a performance I have yet to make, so I appreciate the hon. Gentleman’s remarks. The benefits are clear. In Greater Manchester, hospital teams book cancer tests, so patients can choose to be tested sooner at another hospital. In the midlands, we are testing regional systems and monitoring for winter performances as we head from autumn to winter. In Northampton, transfers between hospitals cut surgery waits. These are the benefits that we should be judging the system on. On the hon. Gentleman’s point about the SPR, I can confirm that interoperability will be baked in by design. The system will be secure by design and interoperable by design, in line with the new codes that he has rightly championed for so long with colleagues across the House. As to the funding, it will be at the current annual rate for the duration of the extension.

I thank the Minister for what he has said about open data standards, but I am extremely disappointed by his decision with regard to the Palantir contract. Palantir exhibits three of the four barriers to effective digital transformation that my Committee identified in its recent report, “Rewiring the state”: hype, vendor lock-in, and a lack of digital sovereignty. If a break clause cannot be exercised because of continuity of care, it is not a break clause; it is a lock-in. In correspondence with my Committee, the Minister assured me that there were already contractual requirements that smooth continuity of care should continue. Were those assurances made in error? I was the first person to mention Palantir in this Chamber and in Hansard , and I did so because of my concerns about how it had leveraged a £1 covid contract into a £330 million NHS contract. It has made it clear that it intends to use the next two years to embed itself even more deeply in our public services. What steps is my hon. Friend taking to ensure that other companies will have equal access, with Palantir, to the federated data platform, its existing architecture and its users? Finally, as I have mentioned to the Digital Minister, France and Germany are using open source to move away from proprietary vendors such as Palantir. What is my hon. Friend’s approach to open source in the NHS?

I thank my hon. Friend for her distinguished contribution, for the work that she leads as Chair of the Science, Innovation and Technology Committee, and for her questions, as well as for the exchange of letters that we are, ourselves, locked into. I can confirm that the contracts we are talking about include exit and transition provisions, that migration is possible in principle, and that NHS-funded IP and supplier background IP are distinct. However, given the requirement for a new iteration, given performance and the benefits already in play, and given the opportunity to add new capability, including maternity services, to a next generation of FDP, an 18 to 24-month period for commission and procurement is a reasonable assessment.

The Minister has referred many times to trust and confidence, which are at the very heart of the whole problem with Palantir—or at least one of the problems. Trust and confidence are also important when it comes to the figures that the Minister quotes. He told us in his statement that 142 trusts were live on the FDP. In response to questions, he used the figure 137. That figure is very dubious: in the past few weeks, NHS England deleted that figure from its platform, because 29 trusts that were included as being live said that they were not live. I therefore make the figure 108. First, can we please be accurate about the number? Secondly, if the Minister cannot give us an assurance that the break clause will be implemented, can he confirm that Palantir’s involvement in the contract will end for good in 2029?

I can confirm that the contract will end in March 2029. I appreciate the distinction that the hon. Gentleman makes on the matter of numbers of trusts. Of the 170 trusts that are signed up, 142 are live—that effectively means they have activated it. Of the 142, 137 are realising benefits. I am happy to write to him with any follow-up data or metrics on which he seeks assurance. I repeat the point that we have the opportunity to restate and remake the case based on trust, and that we cannot expect to underpin our next generation of the FDP if we do not bring trust with us for everyone, whether they are patients or NHS workers.

I thank the Minister for his statement. Trust is absolutely fundamental, as is the patient journey through the NHS. Although the different fragmented systems were cumbersome, they added a bit of friction, which meant that there was more security for patient data. Whoever has this contract, we need to make sure that patient data is paramount and safe. Can the Minister confirm that any data Palantir holds will be transferred wholly to a new system, and that it will have no control over any data it has had access to?

I thank my hon. Friend for her excellent question. I can confirm exactly that: the data will be transferred, and the exit and transition provisions are part of the contract. In getting my head around the issue of a federated data platform and speaking to others about it, it has helped to think of it as fetching. It fetches data, presents it to the user, and then puts it back where it was. It is, by its design as a federated model, a safer option than having one honeypot, as it were, where information and data are kept. As with the FDP as it is now, the design of any future iteration is about ensuring that that data is stored. [ Interruption. ] And I can see that Madam Deputy Speaker wishes for me to fetch myself and sit down!

I am sure the Minister will agree that this is not just about open, transparent and fair procedures in procurement; it is about trust and the ethics of the suppliers. Given Palantir’s relationship with Israel, and its destruction of Gaza’s healthcare, why should Palantir have anything to do with ours?

We are announcing new procurement for the next generation of FDP. That is the responsible thing to do for continuity of care for patients who are benefiting from the FDP as is. That is the judgment and the announcement that we are making today. This is not, as I said earlier, about the territories in which a company has customer products, or the views of a company’s executives and their politics.

I thank the Minister for his statement. Several constituents in Erewash have raised concerns with me regarding Palantir, covering several different matters, and the ongoing contracts. I am pleased that the Minister confirmed just a minute ago that the current contract with Palantir will end in just two years. Can he elaborate on the opportunities that will arise from that contract ending?

I do not want to second-guess what additional capabilities there could be. Use of the platform now is not compulsory, but it should be compelling. On the additional scope for the next generation of the FDP and the procurement, we have committed to engaging with staff, the workforce, patients, the data guardian and, of course, the House and my fellow MPs, on articulating what should come next. I look forward to those conversations.

On the concerns raised by Members of this House about Palantir, the Minister has said that this is not about the views of executives or Palantir’s political views. I would challenge that; I would say, on behalf of my constituents in Lagan Valley, that the British people want to know that whenever we trust our most sensitive data to this company, we do it in a way that the vast majority of the public are happy with. I do not think they are happy with it. Would the Minister agree?

As I have said—this is an opportunity to remake the point—we either undermine or underpin, when it comes to data systems and products in this space that the Government are providing to trusts across the country. We should not expect innovation to move faster than trust. I continue to make the case for the highest possible trust standards, and will have that conversation with patient groups, NHS staff, trusts, integrated care boards, and the range of people that we have to bring with us in this rebuild of FDP for the next generation, if we are to truly fulfil its potential.

I thank the Minister for setting out so clearly the process that will be followed as we move towards the new FDP contract. He will be aware that many people are concerned about the security of their records and how they may be used. Can he reassure patients and families that NHS organisations remain in control of their data, and that safeguards must be in place to ensure that suppliers operate only within the legal, contractual and information governance safeguards set by the NHS?

My hon. Friend has my full assurance that that is now the case in contractual terms. I will take every opportunity to repeat our commitment to security, and to the appropriate and contractual use of data.

I thank the Minister for his statement and answers, and I very much welcome efforts to modernise our health and care systems with digital transformation. I am asking not about which system we use, but about how it will work practically for people on the ground, including the elderly, and the rural and vulnerable patients left behind. This must never leave Northern Ireland on the sidelines. In my Strangford constituency, many older residents and those in rural areas struggle with poor broadband, or simply cannot navigate online portals to book a GP appointment or access care. Under the new system, will the Minister ensure that traditional phone and face-to-face routes are permanently protected, alongside digital tools? Will he work with the Department of Health in Northern Ireland, so that patients across all four nations can share this?

I can give the hon. Gentleman that commitment and my full attention to that issue. One benefit of adopting tech, and the roll-out of safely deployed AI in primary care settings, is that doctors are now able to turn and face their patients. They will not sit side-on, tapping away and administering their records; they will be giving their full attention, which will allow them to understand body language or any cues that they need to understand. One challenge we have is the fragmented system, and one answer that the FDP gives is that it brings together the fetching principle of that fragmented system, to ensure a whole view, whether that is a rural setting, a city, a coastal area, or anywhere else.

The Minister has my full support in trying to find a new digital system that makes the patient experience better, whether that be through the single patient record or the federated data platform. However, I worry about places like Stoke-on-Trent; Royal Stoke hospital and the University Hospitals of North Midlands NHS trust struggled just to get up to date with the electronic patient record system. How will the Government ensure that those operating on legacy systems are not left behind, and that we do not end up with a two-tier function system? Will the Minister ask his officials to take up the request from me and my hon. Friend the Member for Stafford (Leigh Ingham) for a meeting in which to discuss funding that would unlock potential savings in our trusts?

Yes, of course I will do my bit to champion that meeting. On realising the benefits of using AI with legacy systems, or indeed a federated platform, the point is that this sits on top of legacy systems. It is provided centrally, so that the regions my hon. Friend describes do not have to commission systems for themselves; it is made available for them to benefit from. We will make sure that there is much stronger peer-to-peer advocacy for those trusts using the FDP, so that they can fully realise its benefits. My hon. Friend rightly describes a fragmented system, and the challenge is to ensure that the data is drawn together, so that a whole view can be taken, wherever someone is in the country.

As Member of Parliament for Bournemouth East, it is my democratic duty to represent the concerns of my constituents about Palantir’s involvement in our national health service. The Minister says that excellence and continuity of care is uppermost in his mind. Fast-forward the tape two years. It is clear that the Government want competition, tech sovereignty, and to back British. Britain has the skills, so will the Minister set out how, over the next two years, the Government will support British alternatives?

The Government are ensuring, whether through the statement from my right hon. Friend the Chancellor, or through commitments made in the House, that their spending goes a long way, and that there is a first-customer principle in our economy. I look forward to that, and I appeal to businesses in my hon. Friend’s constituency, and across the country, because this should spark interest from small and medium-sized enterprises, start-ups, innovators, entrepreneurs, and established businesses that want to scale up across the country. I encourage them to apply for the next iteration of the FDP in due course.

It is crucial that we establish an evidential base, not least as many of the providers listed as live have only logged on to the system once, if at all. We know that the poor capability of the current Palantir contract is slowing clinical practice, and clinicians say that it is inoperable. Will the Minister ensure that there is no further extension of the Palantir contract, and that it has no ability to ratchet and draw on further data, and will he operate the break clause in February 2027 to stop the extension and expansion of the use of Palantir?

I welcome my hon. Friend’s question. It is absolutely right that we continue to recognise the need for trust in the system to come. Correspondence from Palantir to me and the Secretary of State says that exit arrangements are clear, and that the NHS has all the rights and support that it needs to transition to a new supplier when the contract ends.

The Minister has announced that he is extending Palantir’s contract by two years, but he presents this as a transition to find a replacement. An extension of that length is not a transition, and why should it take another two years to find an alternative when a break clause is available? How can the Minister justify that extension, when serious concerns remain about patient data, as set out by colleagues, and given the company’s role in Israel’s genocide in Gaza? Surely the Minister should have been announcing a rejection of the extension, and that we are finally kicking Palantir out of our NHS.

The judgment that I have made begins a procurement process that will see the contract end in March 2029, and I have just given an indication of the current supplier’s acknowledgement of that fact. I am measuring the performance, and am making a judgment based on the thousands of patients who will continue to benefit from the FDP as a product in principle—not based on the supplier, or on the politics of the executives or the territories in which the company has other customers.

As my hon. Friend the Member for Bournemouth East (Tom Hayes) said, our responsibility is to represent our constituents. My constituents have made it clear that they do not want their NHS associated with a company like Palantir because of its human rights abuses, and they expect the contract to be ended. If that does not happen, and we go through this two-year period before rebidding takes place, can we ensure that we build into the criteria a good humanitarian track record? On that basis, we could then say to Palantir, “No need to apply.”

My right hon. Friend speaks to the sensitivity of some of the issues discussed today. Procurement starts today. Meetings are happening this week relating to new provider possibilities. There will be market engagement from January, to describe what the next iteration of FDP needs to include. The terms for that procurement will be issued in the coming weeks. I note my right hon. Friend’s request on what those terms should include, and thank him for it.

Unfortunately, as I live in Scotland, I do not have access to an NHS app, so I have to call the GP practice at 8 am and I have to call to order certain repeat prescriptions. Does the Minister agree that the SNP Government in Scotland could learn from some of the new technologies that are being adopted in England? Will he reach out to his counterpart in Scotland to discuss this with her?

I would be delighted to do that. I commit to my hon. Friend that I will reach out to my counterpart, and I am sure that there are things that I can learn from listening to the Scots. We do not intend to make the new technologies she mentions mandatory, but I hope that we can compel all areas of the United Kingdom to recognise the benefits of those systems to people, not least the Scottish people, and that the decision not to take up the NHS app—the example that she gave—is not repeated.

I thank the Minister and his team for engaging with me about my concerns on this issue. Data, particularly NHS data, is one of the most important things. Current US laws mean that data can be requested from any US AI company, which can then be shared. Does the Minister agree that the best way to avoid any potential transfer of copies of our data outside this country is to support British innovation and British businesses to win these contracts in the future?

I thank my hon. Friend for her championing of our UK sector. She has my full support in those efforts. As I have made clear today, I hope that this decision sparks and stirs interest in new provision and new uptake to be involved in the next iteration of the FDP model. The storing of data is a trust issue. With the current provision, just as with the next, UK storage of that data is fundamental and baked in by design.

I know that people in Ipswich will want me to be direct with the Minister and say that when it comes to their data, especially their sensitive healthcare records, trust, transparency and accountability are paramount. What assurances can the Minister give in that regard, and how will those values influence future procurement decisions?

I thank my hon. Friend for his question and his typically excellent representation of his constituency. As I have said, we cannot expect to underpin trust unless we move at the speed of trust. That is about remaking the case, and giving assurances on data protection and the security by design of the system that we commission, which will be securely built. The federated nature of the platform makes the data more secure. I fully appreciate the concerns that some of his constituents have raised, and I will ensure that we continue to make the case, as we need to bring everybody with us if we are to fully realise the benefits of digital capability in our healthcare system.
No statement is complete without hearing from Harlow, so I call Chris Vince.

Harlow, as we heard previously in an ill-timed point of order, is home to some of the world’s leading tech companies, which is no real surprise considering that Harlow is the birthplace of the fibre optic cable. Will the Minister assure me that future procurement for the FDP will give British firms, like those in Harlow, a fair opportunity to compete, contribute their expertise and provide that trusted data collection that many colleagues have talked about?

I thank my hon. Friend, the heavyweight champion for Harlow, for his point, on which he has my full assurance. I hope that he will help me to communicate to the businesses in his constituency the opportunity that the new procurement process announced today will present to businesses and employers across the country.
I call Sammy Wilson on a point of order in connection with the code of conduct to rectify a failure to declare.

On a point of order, Madam Deputy Speaker. I wish to apologise to the House for my failure to declare an interest when participating in a Westminster Hall debate on 22 June 2026 on the topic of pro-Israel influence on UK politics and democracy. When I spoke during the debate, I inadvertently failed to declare a relevant interest, which is that I visited Israel between 23 and 30 October on a trip funded by the embassy of Israel. This was in breach of the rules and I apologise to the House for that error.
I thank the right hon. Member for his point of order. There will be no further points of order on that issue.

On a point of order, Madam Deputy Speaker. I have seen an email, circulated at 10.12 this morning, from Lord Watson of Wyre Forest, the senior vice-president of Palantir Technologies, to some MPs, referring to the two-year extension of Palantir UK’s contract for the NHS federated data platform not as a proposal but as a certainty, and setting out how Palantir UK would use that time to better position itself for future contracts. Madam Deputy Speaker, Mr. Speaker and yourself are rightly jealous of the Chamber’s rights, in particular that policy announcements should be made here in the House to MPs. While the email went to some MPs, it did not go to all MPs—it did not go to me—it was not from the Minister responsible, and it did not have your authority, Madam Deputy Speaker, to make it orderly, so can you advise me whether it is orderly for company executives, no matter how noble, to be announcing policy via email to selected MPs? What steps can I take to ensure that this issue is addressed by the Department of Health and Social Care?

I thank the hon. Member for her point of her order and for notice of it. She will know that as Chair, I am certainly not responsible for the actions of private companies or indeed Members of the House of Lords. She has placed her concerns on the record, and I am sure Ministers will wish to reflect on them and perhaps respond shortly. As always, my expectation and that of Mr Speaker is that policy announcements will be made in this House by Ministers.

Further to that point of order, Madam Deputy Speaker. I thank my hon. Friend the Member for Newcastle upon Tyne Central and West (Dame Chi Onwurah) for her point of order. The communication that she refers to is a direct breach of agreed conditions and we are pursuing our serious concerns directly with the company.

Further to that point of order, Madam Deputy Speaker. I have no skin this particular game, but for accuracy of the record, it has been well publicised that Lord Watson of Wyre Forest has taken a leave of absence from the House of Lords since he was appointed.
I thank the hon. Member for that clarification, about which he is correct.
The Speaker has not selected any of the reasoned amendments.

I beg to move, That the Bill be now read a Second time. This Government are committed to good growth in every postcode, not just as a matter of fairness but because Britain is at its best when every area of the country can play its part. The Visitor Levy (England) Bill is the next major step towards that, and will give strategic authorities new powers to raise money and invest in their area. Every mayor will soon be able to choose whether an overnight visitor levy is right for their region. If they do implement one, they will be able to use what they raise to invest in local priorities, which will improve the visitor experience and support wider economic growth. This country’s mayors have huge ambitions for the future of tourism in their regions: Kim McGuinness aims to double the scale of her region’s tourist economy, and building on Bradford’s year as UK city of culture, Tracy Brabin wants to bring more gigs, performances, art and sport to world-recognised venues. The new powers in the Bill and the investment it generates will mean that they can do exactly that. All visitor levies will be set as a percentage of the cost of the accommodation, meaning that low-cost holidays will stay at a low cost, and revenues raised can be used to support new projects in the local area to make places better to both live in and visit. Tourism brings significant benefits to an area, but it can put pressure on transport, public services and local services. The levy means that visitors can contribute directly to the places that they enjoy. It is a major milestone in fiscal devolution and our plans to completely rewire the state. Most importantly, it means more investment in Britain’s future and the change that people want to see.

May I pose a question to the Secretary of State that has come to the attention of those of us from Northern Ireland who have to travel by plane? Tomorrow morning I have a meeting with a Minister. The people who are coming here to deal with the fishers issue flew over tonight to stay in the mainland United Kingdom, because it is not practical for them to stay at home if they are to be here in time for the meeting. While this legislation is oriented towards England, it will impact directly on us in Northern Ireland in a greater way. Has any consideration been given to those from Northern Ireland who have to travel here and have to have overnight accommodation, as they will be disadvantaged right away?

A national mechanism and framework for the overnight visitor levy will be available to local mayors, but they will have discretion in looking at how it affects their area. We want to see this Government’s clear theory of growth—to retake control and devolve power to places—realised, and this Bill in action will fundamentally shift where and how decisions are made.

I very much welcome the overnight visitor levy, which is the next step in devolution. However, the Secretary of State will know that London has a different form of devolution to the rest of the country, as we do not have a combined authority, and there is no requirement to include local authorities in decisions. While we can be sure that the current Mayor of London has the best interests of London at heart, that might not always be the case with future mayors—perhaps they will be from the Conservative party. Will the Secretary of State consider whether we need a formal role for London boroughs in the design and governance of this funding to future-proof London governance?

As my hon. Friend acknowledges, the Greater London Authority has its own set of governance arrangements. The Bill gives London Assembly members a formal scrutiny role and a vote on the mayor’s proposals at the approval stage, while the final decision on whether to proceed with the levy rests with the mayor. We are bringing forward this Bill because we believe that this country needs a new model of government.

If a future mayor of Hampshire—if we eventually get there—is ever mad enough to introduce this levy, because they wanted fewer tourists in the New Forest, what would happen to pubs with rooms in my constituency, which is an hour away? They currently struggle to make a living because of things that the Government have done, but they face becoming even more expensive than they are at the moment. Surely the Secretary of State can see that this tax will do what lots of taxes do: deter activity and visitors from my part of the county.

The Conservatives raised the burden of tax to its highest level since the second world war, so I will take no lectures from them. Mayors can decide on the overnight visitor levy; it will go through a formal consultation period, and any money raised will go back into the local area. We know that tourism can have an impact on transport and some other services, so that money can be directly invested, which will help local people and businesses.

I do not personally think that an overnight visitor levy is right for Hartlepool and the wider region, and I am confident that we will not end up with one for that reason. However, does the Secretary of State agree that we cannot preach about empowering local communities and leaders and not give them any powers?

I agree. That is why we are rewiring the state, devolving power and giving it to those who have skin in the game and want to do this. We are not imposing this measure on areas; areas have asked us for the powers, and we are coming forward with them. The powers have to go through a full consultation period before they are implemented. We are bringing forward this Bill to better serve people and place by moving powers closer to them. Entire regions have choices that are imposed on them because they do not have the power to make choices for themselves. To fix that, we need to rewire the state so that places have control over their own tax revenue. In every part of this country, we have a tourism industry that we can all take pride in. In the west of England, visitors spend billions of pounds each year, drawn by attractions such as the Roman baths, the Clifton suspension bridge and the Bristol Zoo Project. More than 100 million people come to see world-class events in the east and west midlands, and millions come to see two of the UK’s best national parks in York and North Yorkshire.

The Secretary of State mentioned the Roman baths. Bath welcomes 6 million visitors a year. My council and I have long supported a visitor levy, but it is not clear that the city will directly benefit from it, so the levy must be ringfenced for my community, businesses and residents. Does she agree?

Again, this is about mayors working with local authorities to ensure that investment from the levy goes back to where it is needed the most. Hopefully the hon. Lady will be able to see that as we go through the passage of the Bill. This Bill means that we can improve the visitor experience and make it even better. It will allow Mayor Godwin, Mayor Ward, Mayor Parker and Mayor Skaith to reinvest money right back into transport and tourism improvements, helping communities to see and feel a difference from devolution.

The Secretary of State spoke about the power of fiscal devolution. Can she explain how this tax will interplay with other tax-raising powers that may come from strategic authorities as part of her proposals on wider devolution and rewiring the state? Importantly, what fiscal impact assessments will take place?

If the right hon. Lady means business rates and the ability to maintain them, this levy does not interact with those. This is about being able to have an overnight visitor levy and for investments to come back into local areas. It will be for strategic authorities and mayoral areas to decide how best they want to implement this measure with the national framework that oversees it.

We have talked about impact assessments, but I want to talk about coastal towns, which suffered disproportionately under austerity. Bournemouth lost its tourism team and, as a result, we have not been able to resurrect our tourism industry to the extent that we should have done. Will my right hon. Friend confirm for me and my constituents that through an overnight visitor levy we will be able to ringfence funding raised locally to reinvest in our hospitality scene and get our tourism back to where it should be, so that coastal towns such as Bournemouth have a brighter future ahead of them?

That is precisely why local areas will be able to decide on the percentage of the levy and how they will reinvest it. We believe that people with skin in the game in their local area will understand the issues that affect their local towns, whether they are in coastal areas or other areas, and they will be able to implement the levy appropriately. We need to shift power so that local leaders can collect and spend tax revenue on what the region wants; mayors such as Oliver Coppard in South Yorkshire can decide whether to implement the levy and spend that tax revenue on what the region wants. Regional government knows what local priorities are. This is about a partnership in which we as a Government support regional government to deliver what is needed. We are therefore overhauling how regional government is funded, starting with a new power to introduce the overnight visitor levy. That will mean that if local leaders can grow their tourism economy, they will have more to spend on local priorities. It brings us in line with many of the world’s major cities for tourism, including New York and Paris, where evidence shows that the levy works.

Along with New York and Paris, my right hon. Friend could have mentioned Edinburgh. Will she join me in congratulating Jane Meagher and Margaret Graham, who are both Labour councillors? They introduced the UK’s first tourist tax—as it is called in Edinburgh—or transit visitor levy. It is going to raise £50 million a year, and through consulting with local people, that money is going to get spent on parks, homes, public toilets and city centre policing.

My hon. Friend is absolutely right. This is not something new; it happens around the world. I congratulate those who have come forward with schemes earlier, because this levy will have a profound effect on local areas, enabling them to do the things they want to do.

When making international comparisons, will the Secretary of State also take levels of VAT into account? Some of the countries she has mentioned have a much lower sales tax than we do, and adding a holiday tax to that is going to put holidaymaking in the UK out of the reach of many UK families.

I dispute that—I do not think the levy will make holidaymaking out of reach for many people locally. It is for mayors to decide the percentage rate, and because it is a percentage rate, people will pay a lower amount for lower-cost holidays. As my hon. Friend the Member for Edinburgh South West (Dr Arthur) mentioned, parts of the UK have introduced these levies, including through voluntary schemes. They have been able to invest in their local services, in contrast to the scaremongering about how the levy is going to impact industries locally. The main provision of the Bill is a new power for every strategic authority to introduce, administer and collect the levy. It is on those strategic authorities to decide whether to use that power; if they choose to do so, the levy can be delivered in line with the nationally consistent levy framework created by the Bill. That framework means that the levy can be charged as a percentage of accommodation costs at a local rate determined by the strategic authority. Using a percentage, rather than a fixed amount, means that low-cost stays will stay low-cost while giving certainty to business, and allowing local leaders to choose their own rate means that they can do what is best for their area. A percentage rate model also accounts for inflation and adjusts according to price changes, such as seasonal peaks. To protect the smallest providers from disproportionate burdens, the Government will also introduce a minimum threshold. Any provider below that threshold will not be liable for the levy, and strategic authorities will have the power to set a higher threshold, as long as they consult. We are also confirming the scope of the levy, and as part of that we are providing for national exclusions and limited local accommodation-type exemptions. The levy will apply to most visitor accommodation, such as hotels and short-term lets, as well as to hostels, campsites and caravan parks where local leaders do not choose to exempt them. The national framework includes national exclusions, including for shelter and refuge and for temporary accommodation. We know that devolution cannot just be the transfer of power from one set of leaders to another; communities must get a say directly. The Bill therefore also contains provisions requiring local consultation before a levy can be introduced, including on the percentage chosen and how it will be spent.

Communities in my constituency know all about the impact of tourism—in fact, we are really proud of the visitor economy we have locally. I am a strong supporter of the Bill; I think devolution of fiscal matters is really important. I agree with my hon. Friend the Member for Ealing Southall (Deirdre Costigan) about the role of local authorities and communities in the consultation. Will the Secretary of State talk about how we might consult local authorities, which—particularly in the City and in Westminster—provide many of the services that mitigate the impact of tourism, whether that is cleansing or the additional information requests locally?

The mayor and the GLA can support the boroughs’ activities through visitor levy funds if they choose to do so. I was pleased to hear that the mayor and the boroughs have already committed to working collaboratively on the mayor’s plans for a visitor levy once the power is conferred on them. As a devolved power, it is fundamental that decisions on spending are made by local leaders who know their areas best, and are not mandated by Westminster or Whitehall.
The Secretary of State mentioned the west midlands earlier, and she is talking about local leaders. Has she spoken to the Mayor of the West Midlands, and is he for this levy?

The Bill gives mayors powers, which they can use if they wish. It is not for me as Secretary of State to decide whether a mayor wants the levy or not; the powers will exist, and if a mayor wants to take advantage of them, that is up to them locally. That is the whole point of devolution—I do not understand why Members do not understand that point. It is not for me to dictate; it is for me to work with local leaders to provide the framework for productivity in their local area.

I agree about the need to ensure that local authorities have a meaningful say in how the levy is spent. However, given the pressure that lots of hotels are under, does the Secretary of State agree that it is a good thing that the Mayor of London has said that the levy will be no more than 5% of room rates?

I agree with my hon. Friend that mayors know their area best. I think 10 mayoral areas have confirmed that they would not go above 5%, because they know their areas and are working with their local hospitality industry and other local businesses. The consultation I have described forms part of a broader process that means strategic authorities must publish a prospectus and an impact assessment before proceeding. The public will expect that these decisions are not made off the cuff. We are also introducing key aspects of the administrative framework for the levy through this Bill, including annual reporting requirements and information-sharing provisions. Together, these mechanisms will allow for transparency and local scrutiny while also minimising administrative burdens on businesses.

The Secretary of State has rightly pointed out that any authority would have to conduct impact assessments before introducing a levy. I have searched for the impact assessment for this Bill, and could not find it. More importantly, last week, I raised with the Lord Chancellor the justice impact test. This Bill creates a slew of new offences that could see people jailed for up to 14 years, but we do not know how that would impact the courts and the prisons. Can the Secretary of State elaborate on that?

The penalty systems are broadly similar, with the common features of civil penalties for failures such as late returns and non-payment, escalating for continued non-compliance. It will be for strategic authorities to carry out their impact assessments on the basis of what they decide their levy will be.

In this place, we talk much about the cost of living, and we are particularly conscious of the cost borne by families. Could the Secretary of State therefore say whether children can be exempt when families have to pay the levy, in order to support family finances?

Again, we have been looking at a national framework, but local levies can contain exemptions. That will be for local areas to determine. Through the Bill, we are also bringing forward provisions on enforcement, appeals and anti-avoidance powers. These include tax-style compliance and inspection powers, civil penalties, rights of appeal to tribunals, and offences for fraudulent evasion or deliberate misstatement. Subject to the passage of the Bill, local leaders will be able to set out plans by March 2028for how levy revenues will be invested, and then introduce a levy before the end of this Parliament.

Further to the point made by my hon. Friend the Member for York Central (Rachael Maskell), the Secretary of State will undoubtedly say that it is for mayors to decide, but surely the Government have an opinion on whether children should be exempt. I cannot imagine that it is the Government’s intention that in places such as Staffordshire, where we are home to the Kibblestone Scout camp, the visitor levy should mean Cubs, Squirrels and Scouts having to pay to stay in the tents they pitch on the Scout camp where they have gone for years.

Again, I gently say that areas will be able to make exemptions. We expect local leaders to factor various needs into the decision-making process, including those of medical visitors, disabled visitors and children, as well as the need for simplicity for business. The new powers contained in this Bill are just the start. Our plan for good growth in every postcode means that regions will benefit from increased receipts when they grow their tax base.
