We need to explore the issue of packaged experiences that include not just an overnight stay, but an experience, such as pe

The British seaside holiday is part of the fabric of Bognor Regis and Littlehampton. Wherever anyone goes in my constituency in the summer, they will find families enjoying the seaside holiday they have spent all year looking forward to. I could give credit to the West Sussex sunshine, but our local businesses would rightly have something to say about that. An undeniable attraction of the British seaside holiday is that it is fantastic value for money. From the guest houses and hotels that welcome the same families back every year, to the fish and chip shops that stay open late on a summer evening, as well as the seafront attractions that give children so much joy, people choose to holiday in Bognor Regis and Littlehampton not only because it is wonderful, but because it is affordable. Our businesses make that possible. From independents such as the East Beach guest house, the Navigator hotel and Bailiffscourt hotel and spa, to household names such as Butlin’s and Premier Inn, businesses work so hard to ensure that families can enjoy a great British holiday at a price they can afford. However, this Government have so far spent their time in office making it harder for such businesses to survive. They have hiked employer national insurance, pushed up business rates by an average of more than 30% and piled on red tape. As one local business owner put it to me recently: “This Government has made it harder to run a business than ever before.” Not content with adding layer upon layer of cost on businesses, the Government now want to make it more expensive for families to holiday in seaside towns such as Bognor Regis and Littlehampton. Nationally, Oxford Economics estimates that this 5% levy could result in 12 million fewer overnight stays and £1.7 billion less visitor spending, and put 33,000 jobs at risk. In local terms, for a family of four holidaying for a week in Littlehampton, that could add more than £100 to the bill. For many, that is simply unaffordable; even if they could afford it, that is money that will no longer be spent in other local businesses. There are no two ways about it: higher accommodation prices will reduce occupancy rates in hotels and B&Bs in our seaside towns. Some families will cut their holiday short; others will look abroad or decide that they cannot afford to go away at all. That is the real fear for Richard and Mark Groome, the proprietors of East Beach guest house in Littlehampton. They know that people cannot afford to spend any more, and they worry that they will choose to stay away instead. What will that force them to do? They have already cut back on costs, and are desperate not to put up prices for their customers, but they are now worried that the Government are making that decision for them. The levy will deter tourists and lead to less custom for the businesses around their lovely hotel. That means less spending on the locally roasted coffee at Edge by the Sea, Mewsbrook Park café or East Beach café in Littlehampton; on the delicious food at Chez Moi in Aldwick, which has been recommended in The Sunday Times , at Fino in Felpham, or at Lemongrass in Rustington; or on a well deserved holiday beverage at the Waverley in Bognor Regis, the Maypole in Yapton or any number of outstanding venues across my constituency. For businesses that rely on a good summer to get through the winter, the levy will force them to push up prices, cut staff and, in some cases, close their doors for the last time. At a roundtable with local hospitality businesses in July, I heard genuine fear about the impact of this holiday tax. Iain Brown, the director of Sussex Inns, hit the nail on the head when he called it out for what it is: an “absolute killer blow” for our hospitality sector. He is right. There will be a further damaging knock-on effect of this tax. Tomorrow we expect the Milburn review. It will rightly say that we need to get more young people off welfare and into work. I will speak in support of the Bill, but I believe that we need to bring some amendment to it. The quality of York’s tourism offer is exceptional. Right now, the streets are buzzing. We have the Christmas market, the nutcracker trail and numerous attractions, such as the railway museum, the castle museum, Clifford’s tower, the art gallery and Yorkshire museum. The retail offer is exceptional because of its independence, but also because the people in tourism, hospitality and retail work exceptionally hard to make it a success. We are on the tentative list to become a world heritage site, and that in itself incurs a cost. If we invest, we will gain the benefit from that and save, but we need the resource in our city. Occupancy remains high in our city, and yet cuts to our council’s budget have meant that improvements have not been forthcoming at the rate we would want to see. The visitor levy provides an opportunity to invest in that infrastructure and improve the offer we can make to residents and visitors, and therefore see a greater boom in the hospitality sector—not what the naysayers on the Opposition Benches are saying. However, we need to recognise that when people come to our city, they draw on its infrastructure, whether that is street cleaning, bin collections, A&E—especially for those who like to party at night—or the police who ensure that our city is a safe place. We are an incredibly safe city. We have 9.1 million visitors to our small and perfectly formed city and 1.7 million overnight stays, so that has a real bearing on what happens across York. That is why a visitor levy would be a way for people who come to our city to give back, not only through the tourism offer, but to the residents of York to show their gratitude for the enjoyment they have gained. When I first advocated for a tourism tax, as we called it back in the day, we favoured a flat rate because of its clarity and simplicity. I said it should be pinned to the price of a cup of coffee, which nobody these days bats an eyelid at. I acknowledge that the Government have put in a more progressive model of a percentage levied on the cost of accommodation, and I support that approach, but we need to recognise that it will have a bearing on those providers. I have heard from hospitality providers in my city that are struggling at the moment, and we have to recognise that what they pin that on is not necessarily the visitor levy, but the national insurance contributions, which took their toll. Providers say that VAT is a problem and they want to see the Government take action on that. If we are introducing a visitor levy, there must be some trade-offs for the industry. Perhaps looking at VAT again for the hospitality sector would be an encouraging step forward. In other European countries where VAT is lower and there is a levy, tourism has boomed as a result. I ask the Government to publish an impact assessment of the proposals as we travel into Committee stage, so that we can see the impacts while acknowledging that mayors will have to put together their own impact assessments. The way the hospitality sector operates is important, and the detail of the legislation needs tightening up in some areas. In York, we believe the revenue should be hypothecated to York, not wider North Yorkshire, because of the hospitality work our city does as a unit. We believe that if money is raised in our city, it should be spent in our city for the benefit of our residents, as well as for the tourists.

Research from the Labour Rural Research Group emphasises exactly that point. Its latest report on “The Future of the Rural Economy” found that if the levy were introduced, stakeholders would want to see it ringfenced for the area raising that money. That is just as important to rural areas as it is to more urban areas such as my hon. Friend’s, because they want to see the direct benefit that comes from people visiting their area. Does she agree that it would be great for the Minister to look at how that could be mandated?

I am grateful to my hon. Friend for that intervention because, as I have heard from other Members across the House today, it would be an important amendment in Committee to enable hypothecation and resource well spent in the locality. Also, it would mean that there is a direct relationship between the tourism sector and residents. I have heard too many times residents in York say to me, “It all goes to the visitors and tourists.” This is about accountability within the locality, and surely that is the piece that is often missing in our politics. Spending determination should not be the domain of the mayor alone. That offer should be developed with the hospitality sector—again, that co-production which is so important. Our hospitality sector would welcome that engagement to ensure that its voice on where the money is spent is threaded through. Hospitality businesses have said that if the levy is used for the promotion of tourism, the locality and services, they would absolutely understand the need for it and the benefit of charging that levy. I believe a proportion should be dedicated to local projects, so that residents can get the benefit of that for community spaces, and a proportion should be spent on services such as street cleaning, and the additional demands on health, policing and other services; there is data to show that that demand comes from outside of our area when tourism comes to our city. It is also right to think about which accommodation is included and which is excluded. As hon. Members know, I have long called for short-term holiday lets to be properly licensed—it is appropriate to ensure that there is a levy on them. However, I would exclude hostel accommodation, like youth hostels and local provision. We have heard about tents; those low-budget options should automatically be removed from the levy. I recognise that new types of accommodation are on the scene. I do not know where these pods fit in, or yurts—maybe the glamping world would not be exempt. It would make for a good debate in Committee, so that we get this right. Paragraph 2(1)(b) of schedule 1 states that a strategic authority should “consult such persons as the authority considers appropriate on the initial prospectus and visitor levy proposal”. I am afraid that is far too vague. The strategic authority must be obliged to consult local authority leaders, MPs, the hospitality sector, and the wider tourism and retail sectors. It should also consult residents and local service providers. Mayors are already far too unaccountable for the decisions they make. I know that is something the Government want to address, but we need to be able to bring in that accountability when introducing a new form of taxation. It is therefore crucial that those stakeholders are listed on the face of the Bill as statutory consultees. The consequential report that the mayor must produce should also reflect the findings of the consultation, not just have “regard” to those responses as set out in paragraph 2(3) of schedule 1. I ask for the Minister to further consider those points. As I have said, family budgets are tight and we need to consider an exemption for children. That option is not in the Bill, but I ask that such a measure is considered. It would be a popular move, and it would enable families to ensure affordability. We have also heard about carers and people on hospital stays, including for treatment—there should be proper exclusions in those cases too. With inflation currently running at 4%, to introduce a 5% charge could mean a 9% increase in the cost of holidays. I therefore ask the Government to consider introducing a levy with a 1% per year increase, so that there is a phasing-in stage and a more gradual approach. Finally, will there be consideration for neighbouring authorities? If there are cliff edges, there could be challenges, and that needs to be debated and considered by the Government. Order. There is a speaking limit of 10 minutes. I call Robert Jenrick.

Thank you, Madam Deputy Speaker. “Most people won’t even notice a tiny little bit extra”. That is what the Secretary of State for Housing, Communities and Local Government said earlier today. A “couple of quid”, someone said; “don’t shed crocodile tears” said another. Those comments are completely out of touch. We are living through an affordability crisis where people are finding life very, very tough in the real world. Bills are going up—food bills in particular—rents are rising, and mortgages are going to go up next year. The cost of taking a family away on holiday is going up and up and up, and many people are worried and concerned about whether they will be able to afford just a few nights away. We are not talking about staying in four or five-star hotels, or about international business travellers staying in corporate hotels. We are talking about whether a family from Nottinghamshire can go on a caravan holiday in Cleethorpes. Can they go camping? Can they go to a small B&B in the Peak district or the Derbyshire dales? Can a school party go to a youth hostel? Is that too much to ask? No, of course it isn’t. But at the moment it is hard. Why in these circumstances, why at this time, would anyone consider making it more difficult to take the kids away on holiday? It is not a crime to go on holiday with your family, yet this policy is going to make it just that little bit harder. On top of that, the change comes at a time when the hospitality sector is being battered by rising energy bills, employer national insurance and changes to the minimum wage, with thousands of jobs being lost, predominantly among the young. Why would anyone make the business of hospitality more difficult at a time like this, when it is facing probably the greatest crisis in modern times? Pubs are closing. Hotels are shutting. This is a tough time—we all know it—so why are we doing this? There is rising unemployment—next year, unemployment is set to increase. What are we most concerned about with unemployment? It is youth unemployment, and yet which sector of our economy is both most labour intensive and employs the most young people proportionally? It is hospitality. Why are we doing this at this time, of any? It does not make any sense. This is not just a “tiny little bit extra”, as the Secretary of State said. UKHospitality estimates that this move will add £100 to a typical family break. Well, maybe £100 does not mean that much to us in this place, but it means a hell of a lot to millions of families out there in the real world. Why are we doing this to everyone? If we are going to go down this road, why do we not just do it to those coming from overseas—to foreign visitors to this country—rather than to Brits, who just want to have a holiday in our own country and support the domestic economy? It does not make any sense. The truth is that the holiday tax has always been a bad idea. It has been knocking around for years. Its two principal proponents were the Conservative former Mayor of the West Midlands, Andy Street, and the now Prime Minister when he was the Labour Mayor of Greater Manchester. It was knocked back time and again by a succession of Chancellors as a bad, out-of-touch idea, but this Prime Minister and this Chancellor have decided to go ahead with it. It will pummel hospitality, it will increase unemployment, it will increase youth unemployment, and it will harm the cost of living, at the worst possible moment. The holiday tax will be an administrative nightmare. There are 260,000 short-stay hosts, just to give an example of one aspect of the hospitality sector. Each of them, in one form or another, will be responsible for paying the tax. Imagine what that means for someone who owns an Airbnb: most of the bookings are done through website, but perhaps there are a few repeat direct bookings over the telephone or by email. That person will suddenly have to sign up with His Majesty’s Revenue and Customs to pay the tax. And if they forg

I am sure the hospitality businesses in Newark want the local authority to do more to attract people to that economy—to spend money there and support those businesses. Does the right hon. Gentleman accept that if the proceeds of a well-run tourist tax are invested in the local tourist economy in Newark, it could actually help those businesses? That is the model in Edinburgh. It is about people coming more often, staying longer and spending more money because there is more to do in the city.

No, I just want my businesses to be competitive, and I want working people to be able to afford to go on holiday. Is that too much to ask for? Maybe that is the big divide across this Chamber. Some of the suggestions that we have heard today are obviously ridiculous. “Let’s employ a ‘visitor economy consultant.’” Just imagine how much that would cost! Sadiq Khan, the Mayor of London, seems to be a specialist in those. Remember Amy Lamé, his night-time economy adviser, who earned hundreds of thousands of pounds and managed to crush the night-time economy, closing nightclubs and bars in central London? We do not need more quangos. We do not need more bureaucrats. We just need to be able to take our kids on holiday. This money will obviously be spent on mayors’ vanity projects. The former Mayor of the West of England, Dan Norris, spent £10,000 on bus decorations featuring himself and his dog, and he offered people a free bus journey on their birthday. Sadiq Khan spent £200,000 on Pride last year. Boris Johnson spent £43 million on the garden bridge, which was never built. There was the £340,000 that the Greater Manchester combined authority spent on EY3 Media—mysteriously, the same publicity agents who worked for our now Prime Minister’s election campaign in Makerfield. We all know that this money will be wasted. It will be robbed from the pockets of working people just trying to take their kids away on holiday. We in Reform will oppose this measure every step of the way. We will vote against it tonight. Reform mayors have vowed never to implement it in our areas, so if people want to avoid this tax, they should go on holiday to a Reform area. They should go to Skegness or Cleethorpes: their holidays will be cheaper and better. If we are lucky enough to form the next Government, we will scrap the tax altogether.

When the right hon. Member was a Conservative Government Minister, he opened hundreds of asylum hotels—he opened three in Bournemouth. Replacing the guests in those hotels with asylum seekers rather than holidaymakers was not good for my town’s hospitality industry or tourism. Will he apologise to the people of Bournemouth for doing that? Will he explain to them why he is suddenly apparently on the side of hospitality?

That has nothing to do with this debate, but let me answer the hon. Gentleman directly. I was disgusted by the increase in the illegal migration of people coming to this country at the end of the last Conservative Government. And do you know what I did? I resigned. I resigned when I could not persuade the then Conservative Prime Minister to do what was necessary, which was to leave the European convention on human rights, to detain and deport every single illegal migrant, and to free this country from the scourge of illegal migration. Let me close on this point. The problem with this Government is that they only ever want to increase taxes. Remember the remarks of the Secretary of State for Work and Pensions under the last Prime Minister? He said: “Every meeting I have is ‘who can we tax in order to pay benefits to others’”. Well, it seems that the present Prime Minister has exactly the same approach. The Office for Budget Responsibility estimates that £95 billion more will come in tax revenue by the end of this Parliament—and it is still not enough. There have been increases in taxes on everything under the sun: employer national insurance contributions; income tax and national insurance threshold changes; capital gains tax; entrepreneurs’ taxes; inheritance taxes; private school; stamp duty; savings income tax; landlords’ income tax; dividends tax; pensions taxation; the mansion tax; the bank tax; energy taxes; vaping taxes; taxes on taking our kids on air travel; and now even a tax on holidays. When will this nightmare end? The Labour party just wants to tax, tax, tax, and its latest tax is on taking our kids away on holiday. That is a disgrace, and we will oppose it every step of the way.

I would like to draw the attention of Members to my position on the Digital, Culture, Media and Sport Committee and as the chair of the all-party parliamentary group for coastal communities. “All I Want for Christmas Is You” is once again playing everywhere as we head into the festive season, but if people actually want to see the diva behind the song live in concert, they should head to sunny Scarborough next summer. Along with the Kaiser Chiefs, Alfie Boe, Robert Plant and many more, Mariah Carey will be performing at Scarborough’s own Open Air Theatre, no doubt helping to smash the venue’s 2026 record of 180,000 tickets sold and £18 million generated for the local economy. Most of those music lovers will travel from across the UK, booking out local, family-run hotels, B&Bs and short-term lets for a night or two, and boosting the tourism and hospitality sector. Despite our successes, the tourism economy on the beautiful part of the coast that I represent is fragile, due to years of under-investment in coastal towns under the Conservatives, as well as seasonality, the high cost of energy, the cost of employing staff and the price sensitivity of domestic tourists. International visitors will not think twice about a 5% charge on a stay in a four or five-star hotel in York, but domestic visitors will definitely look at the cost of a holiday at one caravan park near Filey and compare it with the cost of a stay at another caravan park a few miles away in Bridlington, which might not be charging the levy. I support the Bill, and I am not against the overnight visitor levy in principle. I believe it works well in cities and will do well in York, but before it is rolled out to coastal towns like Scarborough and Whitby, we need to see the nitty-gritty of an economic impact assessment. I welcome the provisions in the Bill that ensure that local businesses will have to be consulted before any levy is introduced, because at a recent roundtable in Whitby, several operators reported to me that visitor numbers and occupancy rates are already under pressure; some noted that occupancy levels are at their lowest in a decade. The idea of the overnight visitor levy is that the money raised stays in the area, helping to attract more visitors, support local businesses and improve places for the people who live there. I support that idea, but when the area is 3,000 square miles, what does “local” really look like? Will the money raised in Scarborough, Whitby and the villages stay in Scarborough, Whitby and the villages, or will it disappear into a big pot? In 2025, North Yorkshire welcomed 31.2 million visitors, generating an economic impact of £4.3 billion. The stakes are high. I could come up with a wish list of investments that the mayor could make with the proceeds of an overnight visitor levy, including in the Whitby cliff lift, the Capitol theatre, and toilets in Danby and Hinderwell—indeed, some in Scarborough town centre would be nice. However, before we dream, we must be clear-eyed about the regional and patchwork nature of uptake of the levy. If the mayors either side of us do not impose it, might we push our incredibly price-sensitive small hotels and caravan parks metaphorically over the cliff, as holidaymakers book where there is no levy?

The hon. Lady is making a very good speech. Does she agree that a £2.50-per-head tourist tax on a family of four takes £70 away from that family and gives it to the mayor? That is £70 that they otherwise would have spent in Scarborough or Whitby on drinks, a meal, or treats for the children. Is the real danger not that the tourist tax undermines the purchasing power of tourists with modest means who choose to holiday in England?

On this occasion, I agree with the hon. Gentleman. Under these proposals, a family staying at the Blue Dolphin holiday park for two weeks in the summer could pay an extra £152. At a time when households are already feeling the squeeze, that is a significant extra cost, and one we need to think about carefully. Scarborough and Whitby will always be destinations in their own right, but what about families seeking the humble bucket-and-spade holiday, for whom the object of the holiday is not necessarily the destination, but the ingredients—sea, sand, fish and chips, ice cream and, if you are lucky, sun? Will holidaymakers navigate to towns that offer all this, but without the extra charge? In polling of around 10,000 adults by Stack Data Strategy for UKHospitality, 18% said that any increase in cost would stop them booking a holiday, and 85% said that they would be deterred by a £100 increase. What about corporate travel, business, tourism and conference-related visits? Will people book rooms in the Tees Valley and Greater Lincolnshire to avoid the North Yorkshire tourist levy? The impact of lost bookings would be felt not just by accommodation providers, but by pubs, restaurants, cafés, attractions and other businesses that depend on visitors. I welcome the Government’s move to devolve decisions to local leaders who best understand their region, allowing them to tailor investment towards growing the local economy and making their area better for people to visit and enjoy. I very much look forward to working with Mayor Skaith as he consults the communities we both represent. As Mariah Carey might say to Mayor Skaith, “I don’t want a lot for Christmas; there is just one thing I need. Visit Scarborough and Whitby, so we can bring you up to speed.”

This has been an interesting debate. I genuinely believe that the House should view with caution any provision that grants tax-raising powers that, to be blunt, will harm businesses in all our constituencies across the United Kingdom. In my constituency and throughout Essex, we are alarmed by these plans. The tourism, leisure and hospitality sector is worth an estimated £3.75 billion to the Essex economy. It supports approximately 77,000 jobs; about 57,000 are directly in leisure, hospitality and tourism, and a further 20,000 are throughout other industries. We are worried about what this levy will mean for those jobs, and this sector is already under pressure. It is estimated that more than 52 million visits are made to Essex’s attractions every single year, around 2.4 million of which are overnight stays. Those will clearly be impacted and affected by this tax. We have heard Government Members almost trivialise the impact of this tax on households and families. They have said that it will cost just a couple more quid for working families, but every additional tax and burden that Labour imposes puts jobs and investment at risk and puts pressure on household budgets. These are families who love travelling around the country, and we should back them and support their taking staycations. We have had many representations already from Government Members talking about their constituencies —beautiful parts of the country where we want to encourage tourism and hospitality, as we do in Essex—but families and jobs in this important sector will be under strain from this Bill. As you will know, Madam Deputy Speaker, Essex has many incredible attractions, and I never tire of speaking of Essex in this House. We have Colchester zoo, which is in my constituency, Langford Museum of Power, Layer Marney Tower, Cressing Temple Barns, Markshall Estate and Abberton reservoir, just to name a few. We are the home of Rossi’s ice cream, which is a great landmark in Essex. In the Maldon district, we have the promenade and the Combined Military Services Museum. We are on the Blackwater estuary, and of course we have a very famous county cricket club, Essex, which is based in Chelmsford. We host wedding venues, hotels and resorts such as Five Lakes, Prested Hall and Braxted Park. We are strategically placed for inward tourism, because we have Stansted airport and Southend airport. Essex is competing, if I can politely say it, not just with the rest of the United Kingdom, but globally and internationally. We attract tourists who have the option of travelling across the world, but they choose to come to Essex. We want more people to come and enjoy our fabulous county, and to stay overnight in our wonderful hotels. While those businesses face significant pressures and challenges—we have heard about many of those challenges already—they are still fighting to invest. They want to invest; they want to create more jobs; and they want to promote Essex. They want to promote their sector and give young people the opportunity of a job, which we should all back and support in this House. Given rising prices and uncertainty, the wider economic climate is tough enough, but we have a Labour Government who are anti-business and obsessed with treating business—and this particular sector—like a piggy-bank to be robbed. We have had job taxes imposed on us, and new planning policies that make it easier for speculative developers to concrete over our countryside, as a result of inappropriate housing targets, than for hospitality venues to undertake modest extensions. We have experienced the burdens of the Employment Rights Act 2025 and the changes in business rates, which, even with new multipliers and reliefs, have caused venues to face higher costs. On top of that, the tourism sector in Essex has been hit hard by Labour’s axing of investment in the A12 widening scheme and stopping work on the A120 dualling scheme. This levy—the tourism tax—is just another imposition and bu
Order. Back-Bench speeches will now be limited to eight minutes.

Let me start by apologising to my colleagues and the rest of Staffordshire, because I will be appropriating a number of their attractions for the purposes of my speech. However, we are one big happy family most of the time. When you think of places to visit in the UK, Madam Deputy Speaker, you may not think immediately of Stoke-on-Trent or Staffordshire, but that is because most people do not appreciate the depth and wealth of opportunities and experiences that we have. We are home to Alton Towers, which generates about one third of the visitor overnight stays for our entire county. We are home to the World of Wedgwood. The historic roots of our ceramics industry often draw people to explore parts of Staffordshire. We are home to—depending on how we count them—between three and eight different castle settings, because of our rich history that stretches back through the ages. We have Uttoxeter racecourse, the New Vic theatre, the Regent theatre, the Lichfield Garrick theatre and Lichfield cathedral. We have a host of anchor institutions that bring people to Staffordshire and Stoke-on-Trent. Currently, what we do not have is a mayor. I am told that we are getting one in 2028, and my fear about some of the Bill’s provisions is that that mayor will have at their disposal a series of opportunities to raise money through the attractions that we have in the county, but the money will ultimately be used to fund their mayoral priorities. I happen to agree with a number of Members from across the House that there needs to be a legislative ringfence to make sure that, if we are to progress with this levy on visitors, it is used solely for the purpose of boosting the tourism offer. Across my city, we have a host of wonderful things to visit, which are mainly linked to our ceramics industry. People can visit the Spitfire at the Potteries Museum & Art Gallery. They can visit Middleport, Emma Bridgewater and the Gladstone Museum, where “The Great Pottery Throw Down” is filmed, but the strategy that unites all of that does not really exist at the moment. The work being done by the local visitor economic partnership is getting there, but it is not there yet. Any revenue raised from the levy should go towards delivering a strategy, but the Government’s explanatory notes to the Bill state: “Levy receipts may be used for purposes connected with a strategic authority’s areas of competence. The policy does not impose a legislative national ringfence within those areas, allowing authorities to determine local priorities”. My fear is that that will mean that newly created mayors who lack revenue income sources from other areas will be encouraged to maximise income from the overnight visitor levy to pay for the other strategic priorities in the county, such as adult education and skills, highways infrastructure and land assembly for urban regeneration—things that do not immediately deliver on the tourism strategy. I ask the Minister to genuinely consider how we can offer at least some statutory guidance, if not legislative protection, to make sure that it is local areas that determine what will be of benefit to tourism, rather than allowing mayors to fund projects that they may wish to claim are tangentially related to tourism. I also suggest to the Minister that she read a copy of last week’s The Sentinel , in which there is a wonderful article by local author Paul Williams, who has been leading on the heritage, culture and tourism conversations in our city. He points out that if we are to introduce the levy, we have to consider where the money comes from and where it goes. As I have pointed out, a third of the overnight visitor stays in Staffordshire are linked to Alton Towers in Staffordshire Moorlands, yet we have a population of 1.1 million, covering everything from the Wolverhampton border to Chesire. How can we make sure that the money raised goes back into the areas where it is raised, where the immediate effects of tourism, as welcome as it i

I struggle with this Bill. On the face of it, I really agree with the principle of introducing a visitor levy. It would be very helpful to areas such as mine in Harrogate and Knaresborough that have a tourist and visitor economy, but are often put under strain by the number of people coming to the area to see our fantastic offering. In Harrogate alone, we have the convention centre, which brings many trades to the town, the international festivals, the Great Yorkshire Show—the largest agricultural show in England—and the literature festival.

I am being heckled about Bettys. It would of course be remiss of me not to mention Bettys. We have one of the world’s largest crime writing festivals, and it is clear to see why so many people want to come to Harrogate. Next door in Knaresborough, we have the world famous Knaresborough bed race and FEVA—the festival of visual arts and entertainment. The local area is quite often called the jewel in the crown of North Yorkshire, and understanding what makes it so special is key. I have engaged extensively with local business on this matter. For two years in a row, I have run a post-Budget business breakfast with the hospitality sector, and over the summer I held a hospitality roundtable. Those involved say that they agree with the principle of a visitor levy, but they struggle with the idea that a far-off, distant mayor from York and North Yorkshire will get his hands on their money. As we have heard from so many Members, we need that money to be ringfenced for local priorities. The idea that Harrogate would once again be used as a cash cow to pump money and investment into other areas and for the pet projects of a mayor—he was only elected, on a turnout of under 30%, with 35% of the vote—is jarring for a lot of people. This really matters because that same mayor has said in the local press today that he is not content with the potential of a tourism tax, which he has said he wants to levy, and is now talking about a transport levy. It would be yet another tax on working people and anyone who comes to Harrogate and Knaresborough, or to North Yorkshire more broadly. That brings me to the Secretary of State’s point about how the visitor levy could be used to invest in transport. If we will already be getting that money through a transport levy, that prompts the question: where will it really go? It feels to me as though this is just another way for the Labour Government to tax people yet again, and that simply will not do. For me, when we talk about what investment we need to facilitate, embolden and empower Harrogate’s tourism offer, we need the dualling of the line between Knaresborough and York, and investment in our pothole-riddled roads, particularly at a time when the Mayor of York and North Yorkshire has cut North Yorkshire’s funding and allocation for road repairs for potholes. That really prompts the question of whether we are going to end up worse off if this levy comes in. I know that local authority leaders can object and recommend, but the final say remains with the mayor alone. That is not devolution; it is a bit of a con, quite frankly. We have not seen any impact assessments or justice impact assessments. Time and again, we hear Ministers and others who support the Bill compare it to similar schemes in France, Italy, Spain and across the world. In France, a hotel that accidentally or deliberately evades the tourist tax gets a fine. In Spain, people only get a jail sentence if it is over €120,000. In Italy, where they used to lock people up for dodging the tourist tax, it has been changed to just a fine. I strongly suggest to the Minister that if the Government seriously want to start giving out maximum sentences of 14 years for the evasion of this tax, they should publish the justice impact test to say what the consequences will be for the justice system, the court system and prison places. That is the bare minimum we should expect if this is a serious and credible punitive measure that they wish to hand out to those who evade the levy. That is not to say that people should be allowed to get off scot-free—absolutely not—but it is about proportionality. Anyone who is watching this debate or reading it will think that locking up Mrs McGinn who runs a B&B in Scarborough might be a little bit much. The other issue that has been mentioned time and again throughout the debate is that any authority would have to bring forward those same impact assessments—something the Government themselves have not done. This has been an interesting debate. The Bill is important and I support it, but having listened to Members—the ones who are honest—I think that there are areas that will need amending, ringfencing and safeguarding. However, in principle, a visitor levy is something we should definitely implement. London is the most visited city in Europe and tourism brings in about £41 billion to the capital’s economy. London Pride was mentioned earlier in a negative way. Actually, London Pride, one of the biggest and the best in the world, brought in a lot of money to the London economy.

My hon. Friend is referring to the comments made by the right hon. Member for Newark (Robert Jenrick) about the Mayor of London’s spending on Pride. An article by the deputy chief executive of the Heart of London Business Alliance refers to £26 million of benefit to the local economy from London Pride. Does she not agree that that seems like a very good idea for our businesses?

Absolutely. It is a huge investment in our businesses, and that is what this debate is about. London is the engine of the UK economy and we should not shy away from that. London puts in more than it takes out—it gave £49 billion more to the Treasury in 2024-25. A modest visitor levy of 5%—I agree it should be ringfenced at a maximum of 5%—will be used to bring jobs, businesses and investment into the economy. Every week, I post a list of free things to do in London. I was at an event and a young man said to me, “I normally don’t go out very much, but I saw the free things to do. I went out, made some friends and had a really good time.” The visitor levy could be used to put on more things like that, making the experience of visitors to our country better and more enjoyable, but also making local people enjoy what is on offer, too. The Mayor of London spent £7 million on an international tourism and investment campaign to promote London, fighting against the disinformation that is out there about our wonderful city. The visitor levy would help to do more good things in London and help to promote us even more. I am the MP for Brent East, where we have Butler stadium—also known as Wembley stadium—which is very well visited. We also have the OVO arena. We have thousands of visitors every year who enjoy lots of things around the area, but we could do more if we had a percentage of the visitor levy. I also think that local councils should have a say in how at least 50% of the money is spent—that should be in the Bill—and it should be a meaningful say. I am also in favour of implementing citizens’ assemblies so that local people can have a stake and a say in how the money is spent. That is how we build communities in those areas. In lots of areas where there is an overseas visitor levy, they also have a local rate. That could also be implemented —I do not know whether the Minister has thought about that. For example, I would have a Londoner’s levy, which might be set at zero in some cases. That is something that we can consider as part of the Bill. Overall, a visitor levy—especially an overseas visitor levy—will bring a lot of welcome money into areas that need boosting. Local mayors will have a say on how that money is spent, and it can be used to boost the area in whatever way they see fit.

Thank you, Madam Deputy Speaker, for allowing me to catch your eye as a late entrant to this debate. As I made a late entrance, I will put only a few brief comments on the record. I will disappoint the Minister by not offering her any free hotel rooms to encourage her to come to my area. The Cotswolds are one of the most important leisure, tourism and hospitality areas in the country. Everybody knows the beautiful countryside, the hospitality and the various attractions of the Cotswolds—they do not need to be reminded of them. I view this proposal as a tax—it is not a levy; it is a tax—and the sad thing about it is that it is going to tax some of the poorest people in the country. A family of four going to a modest bed and breakfast for seven days are likely to pay £150, which is probably the difference between going on holiday and not, because they are so squeezed on their cost of living. It is a very unfortunate tax, I have to say. I have heard arguments from Labour Members, one after the other, who say that they need this tourist tax to be able to improve their areas so that more tourists will come. Actually, the local authority should want to improve the area without a tourist tax. It should be devoting sufficient tax to make the area litter-free, make the lights attractive and cut the verges—all the things that attract tourists to the Cotswolds—without a tourist levy.

Too often, local authorities do not have the resources to deal with the extra impact of mass tourism. I do not know about the hon. Gentleman’s constituency, but many do not have the resources and do not benefit economically from tourists coming into the area. The tourist tax will help them make their places even better for tourists to come, so that people can be proud to welcome them to litter-free streets—and perhaps pothole-free roads as well.

The logical impact of what the hon. Gentleman suggests is that we clobber poor people and discourage foreign visitors from coming to this country by imposing a tax on them. The reverse should be the case. We should want businesses to thrive and make a profit, but they have been clobbered by this Government: they have been clobbered by extra taxes on jobs, by inheritance taxes on their businesses and by employment regulations. They have been clobbered by all sorts of things by this Government. The tourism, leisure and hospitality sector is internationally sensitive. Whether people come to an area is very price-sensitive, and if we start making our hospitality more expensive, foreign visitors at the margin will simply not come and our tourist business will go down and down—it is happening already.

My hon. Friend makes an important point—this is a tax on working people. Nine out of 10 visitors in the west midlands are day visitors. This tax will discourage those day visitors from staying overnight and spending more and bringing more money to our local economy. Furthermore, there are no safeguards that tax revenue raised in Walsall will actually come into Walsall to benefit our local area.

My right hon. Friend makes a good point. As has been reiterated across the debate, it has been estimated that a 5% levy will cost 30,000 jobs. Many of those jobs will have been held by school leavers; they will be unskilled jobs in hospitality businesses in my constituency. We saw youth unemployment go up in one month last year from 14% to 16%, and yet the Government want to impose a tax to discourage employment among youngsters even more. I return to the theme about international cost-sensitivity. Instead of taxing foreign visitors and discouraging them from coming to this country, why not reintroduce a scheme to reclaim tax? This was proposed by my party in 2021. It would bring in more foreign visitors and bring more money into this country. I have been lobbying on this for at least the past 10 years. Oxford Economics, which conducted a detailed study of the measure, reckoned that by reimposing a VAT reclaim scheme on shopping the country would gain £4 billion. That simple policy could be introduced by which the country would gain money and jobs and it would benefit businesses. I think the Government should seriously consider it. I turn to the proposed tax. If this Government are determined to introduce this levy, let us for goodness’ sake make it more business friendly by properly consulting businesses. It should be hypothecated for measures that would benefit businesses in the area in which it is levied. It must also be an additional tax, not a substitute for any other tax that a local authority might want to spend anyway. Finally, let us ensure that if the levy is imposed, a future local authority can take it away if it wants to do so. My great fear is that once it is imposed in any area, it will never, ever be abolished. One speaker from the Government Benches today proposed a 1% increase in the levy every year, which means that it would go up from 5% to 15% in the first 10 years and then to 25% in the second 10 years. That is a bonkers proposal. Another said that this tax will have no effect on tourism. How is it that organisations such as UKHospitality reckon that it would cost 30,000 jobs? I am opposed to this tax. However, I say to the Minister on the Front Bench in the friendliest way I can, let us for goodness’ sake make it as business friendly as it can be. Give businesses a say in it and ensure that it is spent properly in the local area. As Chairman of the Public Accounts Committee, I add that we must ensure that at the end of the day, we all get proper value for money from it.

Tourism and hospitality are vital to the whole of the UK. The sector employs millions of people and sustains communities in every corner of our country. It is particularly important in Somerset, where we welcome thousands of tourists every year. The sector is having a tough time at the moment. It has at last recovered from the devastating effects of the pandemic, and visitor numbers have returned to pre-covid levels, but it is now weighed down by the many additional burdens that this Government have placed on them. Many hospitality businesses already pay VAT, business rates, corporation tax and national insurance contributions, as well as struggling with rising food and energy costs. Instead of providing help, the Government now propose a new tax on holidays, tourism and business travel. This tourist tax comes on top of Labour’s unemployment rights Act, Labour’s jobs tax and increases to the minimum wage by substantially more than the rate of inflation. It threatens to put people off visiting beautiful seaside areas such as Burnham-on-Sea, Berrow and Brean in my constituency. The breadth of opposition to this tax is striking. UKHospitality, ABTA, Premier Inn, Choice Hotels and the Country Land and Business Association have all raised concerns. UKHospitality warned that a 5% overnight visitor levy could place 33,000 jobs at risk and deliver a £2 billion hit to the economy. The owner of Premier Inn has described the proposal as hugely damaging. Choice Hotels has said that operators feel that they are being strangled by additional costs. Yet again, this Government think they know better than businesses. Their guiding policy towards the economy seems to be, “If it moves, tax it. If it continues to move, regulate it.” Only when it stops moving do they wish to nationalise it. This is a lesson in how not to grow a crucial sector in our economy. The Government’s stated ambition is to grow visitor numbers to 50 million by 2030, yet at the very same time they are making visits to England more expensive. Perhaps the Minister could explain how she intends to reconcile those two objectives. I am particularly concerned about the impact on domestic tourism. Families already face difficult financial decisions. A tourism levy may appear modest in Whitehall, but for a family of four enjoying a week’s holiday, it can quickly become a significant additional expense. In many parts of the country, this may not have a huge impact. We have heard the hon. Member for Bath (Wera Hobhouse) say that she wants a levy on her city, and the hon. Member for Cities of London and Westminster (Rachel Blake) said that she welcomes the levy. Large cities attracting wealthy foreign tourists may be all right, but has the Minister assessed the risk on those people looking to take domestic holidays—families with modest incomes who go to seaside towns like those in my constituency? A tax of £2.50 per person per night will add £70 to the cost of a week’s holiday for a family of four. That is £70 that will not be spent on drinks or a meal or treats for children. It will reduce the spending impact of that tourist family on the whole economy. I have another serious concern about the concept of this tax. This tourist tax will not be ringfenced to support the areas in which it is collected. The Government claim that the levy will support growth and improve destinations, yet there is no requirement in the Bill for the proceeds to be spent on tourism infrastructure, destination marketing, visitor facilities or local attractions. Businesses will be asked to collect this tax. They will become another army under the control of HMRC, and they will be fined if they get it wrong—or perhaps put in prison for 14 years. Visitors will be asked to pay it, yet the revenue could ultimately be diverted elsewhere entirely. In Somerset, that means that money raised in Burnham-on-Sea, Berrow and Brean will most probably be spent by the Liberal Democrats on management consultants in Taunton, bec

Earlier, we heard proposals that a portion of proceeds could be diverted to organisations or groups, such as town or parish councils, that are responsible for putting on events, managing toilets and sorting out flowers and flower beds. Does the hon. Member agree that is sensible and that the Government should bring it forward?

I would much rather not have the tax at all, but if it is going to happen and, as the Government say, it is for the benefit of tourism areas, my question is: why not ringfence it? I suspect the honest answer is that the Government intend for it to become a general form of revenue for mayors and councils that will have nothing to do with tourists at all.

Does my hon. Friend share the suspicion of many of us that the Government’s view is that this additional revenue will simply be netted off the grants provided to local authorities? Certainly, the feedback from the consultation undertaken by the Local Government Association was that the levy would likely result in zero additional revenue to those local authorities because, in effect, the money would be then deducted from other sources, so nobody except the Treasury would be better off as a consequence.

My hon. Friend makes a wise point. That is precisely what will happen. Over time, the tourism levy will rise and the Government will restrict the amount of money going to those local authorities that have particularly high numbers of tourists. I thought it was naive of the hon. Member for Cities of London and Westminster to welcome the tax because all the money would be spent on her constituents. She is not in her place, but I tell her that that money will be spent on the Mayor of London’s pet projects, and none of those will be in the Cities of London and Westminster. Most worryingly of all, the Bill contains no statutory cap on the levy; perhaps today’s modest charge will become tomorrow’s significant burden. Tourism is not a problem to be taxed; it is a success to be encouraged. The Bill will undermine growth, make staycations less attractive, increase costs for business and families, and raise revenue that will not be spent on the communities generating it. That is why I shall vote against the Bill tonight.

It is a pleasure to follow my hon. Friend the Member for Bridgwater (Sir Ashley Fox) and to respond to the debate on behalf of His Majesty’s Opposition. The hon. Member for South Shields (Emma Lewell) began the debate from the Back Benches with a stark warning about the impact that such a tax could have when imposed on an area and the damage it could do to a sector. In contrast, the hon. Member for Crawley (Peter Lamb) said that the concerns being raised were a storm in a tea cup. That complacency does not reflect the threat to what the Chair of the Digital, Culture, Media and Sport Committee, my hon. Friend the Member for Gosport (Dame Caroline Dinenage), pointed out is a key part of our GDP and economy. As my right hon. Friend the Member for Skipton and Ripon (Sir Julian Smith) said, businesses in the sector are only just surviving. As my right hon. Friend the Member for Witham (Priti Patel) put it, we should be encouraging more visitors to create more opportunities in the sector. As an MP for a coastal area who grew up on the North Norfolk coast, I enjoyed the speech from my hon. Friend the Member for Bognor Regis and Littlehampton (Alison Griffiths) about seaside holidays. My hon. Friend the Member for North Dorset (Simon Hoare) posed the key question: what is the problem that this tax seeks to address? This Labour Government, like all Labour Governments, like to tax. In their first two Budgets, they increased taxes by £66 billion, hitting businesses, farmers, savers, investors, pensioners and working people. Our hospitality and leisure sectors have been hammered by the jobs tax and by the significant increase in business rates imposed by the Government, with over 100,000 job losses since the election. What is the response of a Prime Minister who said he wants to give households struggling with the cost of living some “breathing space”? This new holiday tax—a tax on family breaks, a tax that hits businesses, a tax that will damage our economy, and a tax that the Conservatives will vote against this evening. The visitor economy is worth about £147 billion a year, supporting 3 million jobs. Every year, as we have heard, there are 43 million international visits to the UK, and this new tax has been sold by the Government as a way to raise money from those international visitors. Ministers claim that it will simply bring us in line with other European countries, but they ignore that we have higher VAT rates and higher business rates on hospitality than many other countries. Let us not be hoodwinked into believing that this is primarily a tax on foreign visitors. It has been estimated that over 60% of the revenue will be paid by British people taking trips, so—despite what the Government might claim—this is a tax on hard-working British families. Weekends away, a family holiday or a few nights by the seaside will all cost more. This is a tax on staycations. According to the Housing Secretary, who I am pleased to see in her place, “most people won’t even notice a tiny little bit extra”. Frankly, that shows how out of touch she is, when this could see over £100 added to a family’s bill for a typical week-long break, making many trips unaffordable for many of my constituents, and perhaps for hers and for others across the country. Every pound that is taken in tax is a pound not spent in the local economy. As UKHospitality, the Country Land and Business Association and others have said, those meals will not be had in the pub, and those visits to the local attraction and those taxi rides with local businesses will not happen. This Government do not seem to understand that if you tax something, you get less of it.

Can my hon. Friend confirm, for those who wish to dismiss the significance of this tax, that, like me, he has received emails from constituents on this? I have received one that says: “My husband and I both already work, but we struggle to afford family holidays. Another tax will price me and all working families out of British holidays.”

I have indeed had similar representations, and I would be amazed if hon. Members on the Government Benches have not had similar ones. Some of them have spoken up on behalf of those constituents, but others have chosen to put their head in the sand and pretend that this is not happening. Oxford Economics has warned that a 5% levy could cost 33,000 jobs and cut visitor spending by £1.7 billion. Ministers can challenge those figures if they like, but the Government have not published an impact assessment. Why such a lack of candour about the impact on jobs and the economy, I wonder. Did they listen to the representations to their own consultation, which concluded that “a visitor levy could reduce holiday affordability, deter overnight stays or encourage UK travellers to choose destinations abroad”? When all tourism areas are trying to extend day trips and encourage more overnight stays and visitors all year round, that is a damning verdict on Labour’s holiday tax.

We have to be honest: one place where the tourist tax has failed is Amsterdam. It introduced a 12.5% charge with the aim of reducing tourism, but instead tourism has continued to increase. What does the hon. Gentleman think of that?

I think I will return to the point that has been made by the shadow Secretary of State and other hon. Members: we need to look at the other tax rates within those countries, including the higher VAT and business rates. Importantly, this tax is not just going to hit people going on holiday. Research for Airbnb has found that British patients and families spend over 600,000 nights a year away from home in private accommodation for medical reasons. How can the Government justify this tax being faced by people travelling for medical treatment or to care for their sick child or family member? Businesses will also face higher costs, through the 5 million business trips a year. Why are Labour Mayors so keen to hit the electricians, the plumbers, the fit-out engineers and the sales reps who typically stay overnight mid-week in budget accommodation? Far from cutting the cost of business, the Chancellor is loading on more costs, just like his predecessor did. He is loading more costs on to hard-working families, just like his predecessor did—and the people working in the hospitality and tourism sector, particularly those young people wanting that first opportunity in rural and coastal areas, will suffer the most. A repeated theme of the debate has been which types of accommodation will be covered. As it stands, the Bill includes all short-term visitor overnight accommodation: hotels, B&Bs, campsites, campervan pitches and self-catering cottages. It could even include scout camps, despite the Scout Association pointing out these are “being run for charitable purposes by volunteers, on minimal budgets”. Even tents at music festivals are covered. So what is actually excluded from the legislation? The Government have selected three national exemptions, one of which is Traveller sites. There is a power to exempt more categories, but that is discretionary, so scout camps and other sites are liable by default. The Secretary of State did not have a view on scout camps, but we do and other Labour Members have a view. Scout camps should be exempt, and we will be bringing forward amendments to that effect. This should not be left to the whims of mayors. This House should set the framework. Extraordinarily, or perhaps not, the Government want this to be an uncapped power to charge an unlimited amount. Although Labour mayors, who cannot wait to introduce this tax, say that they will limit it to 5%, there is nothing in the Bill to prevent higher rates. The Government are even adding VAT to the levy, pushing it up even further. It will apply to 28 days of a stay, not five days, as in Scotland. Frankly, it does not take much imagination to see those Labour mayors breaking promises on tax, just like their Front Benchers did after the election. The Government have said that whether to have a cap is a finely balanced issue. No, it is not. It is very straightforward: there should be a cap to protect the public. If the Bill passes, we will seek to amend it to limit the tax to 5%.

We have a Labour Mayor of the West Midlands. Does my hon. Friend agree that the Bill gives local people in my constituency no reassurance whatsoever that the levy will be 5%, let alone that it will actually benefit the residents of my constituency and the Walsall borough? This is not devolution at all.

In many ways, this is taxation without representation or any benefit for my right hon. Friend’s constituents. A number of Members made that point. The Housing Secretary has not been here for much of the debate; otherwise, she would have heard those points. She can read them in Hansard tomorrow if she wishes. What will these uncapped tax rises be used for? This is called a visitor levy—that is the name of the Bill—but nothing in the legislation states that the proceeds must be reinvested in supporting the visitor economy. The Bill does not mention tourism at all, unlike the equivalent Scottish legislation, which states that money must benefit the objectives of the scheme and the tourism economy. If a new tax is to benefit tourism, it must be ringfenced in the legislation for that purpose. The Minister will have heard many calls for that. We all know that the Government are itching to impose these new tax-raising powers. In Scotland, there must be an 18-month gap between a decision to impose the levy and its taking effect. The Government proposed a 12-month gap for businesses in their consultation, and three quarters of people agreed with them that that was a good idea. What did they do? They ditched that idea. Why might they have done that? Removing that gap and protection shows a motivation simply to get these tax-raising powers in place as rapidly as possible. Businesses will have to collect this tax, but, again, there is no specific provision in the legislation to cover the costs of their collecting those taxes, unlike the approach taken in Scotland. That burden will fall on the smallest businesses and owner-operators. We know that they are working people—it is the Chief Secretary to the Treasury who does not consider them to be. The strategic authorities will take on local tax administration, and get HMRC-style information, inspection powers, and the ability to charge interest and penalties. Small wonder that businesses are concerned there will be a potential proliferation of systems and registers, rather than a simple collection system. This Government have already hammered our tourism and leisure sectors. Now they are coming back for more—with attacks not just on holidays, but on people working away to provide for their families, people staying to support friends and family in hospital, and even on scout camps. That will mean higher prices for families, fewer opportunities for young people to get jobs and lower growth in the economy. Rather than hiking taxes, Conservatives are backing hospitality and the visitor economy with our plans to cut business rates for 250,000 businesses in the sector, to encourage more international visitors by reintroducing VAT-free shopping, and to make it easier and cheaper to hire people. As the hospitality sector has said, the public want their holidays kept “relaxing, not taxing”. That is our approach, and we reject the calls for this new tax.

I thank hon. Members from across the House for their thoughtful contributions to today’s debate. I am pleased to speak to this Bill, which is something that mayors and local leaders have long called for. I thank the Secretary of State and the Minister for Local Government, Devolution and Regional Growth for introducing the Bill. The Devolution Minister sends his apologies for being unable to attend the debate, but I know that he strongly believes in these measures and would thank Members for their time and contributions this evening. I also thank the Financial Secretary to the Treasury. This Bill has been a joint endeavour between the Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government and His Majesty’s Treasury, and I am grateful for his support in bringing it forward. I turn to points raised by Members. As many have said, many people have paid a levy of this kind on holidays and travels in other countries, and it is right that our cities, seaside towns and areas of natural beauty have the option to introduce such a levy to support their local economy and tourism industry, and to improve the visitor experience in their area. We have heard from my hon. Friend the Member for Edinburgh South West (Dr Arthur), who gave an excellent explanation of how the levy has worked in his city, and I hope that Members have listened to that. The levy will be a local decision, made by mayors and local leaders, in consultation with local businesses and residents. It is our job in this House to ensure that the levy can be delivered and works for the hospitality industry, which is the backbone of so many local economies, while recognising that local leaders know what is best for their area. That is why this power will be devolved, and why the decision of whether to introduce a levy will be made locally.

We made a commitment in the Labour manifesto to having a wide programme of devolution, and this is about devolving power to local areas. Those who choose to introduce a levy will be able to invest the proceeds in what makes their area special, in improving the visitor experience, and in driving economic growth and local growth. That could mean building new infrastructure, holding and supporting cultural events, security, promoting the area as a destination, or working with local authorities to improve the destination, with cleaner streets and better looked-after parks. Crucially, it will be for local leaders in collaboration with their local authorities to determine how that investment can best support local economies and the visitor economy.

I will make progress, because there is limited time left. A percentage levy ensures that the cost of the levy is proportionate to the cost of the stay. Liability sits with the accommodation provider. However, where the levy is passed on to the consumer, a percentage levy ensures that a lower charge will apply to families going away on lower-cost holidays. A wide range of issues have been raised. I have listened carefully to Members from across the House and will seek to respond to as many points as possible in the time available. I therefore turn to the main themes and issues raised. This country has a proud and successful visitor economy. Devolving the visitor levy gives mayors and local leaders the power to improve their area, and makes them accountable for doing so. All other G7 countries have some form of tourism or overnight accommodation levy, and local leaders will decide whether introducing this levy is right for their area.

I will not be giving way. Members have had the opportunity to speak in this debate. Local leaders will need to consider the appropriate balance between supporting local economic priorities and ensuring that the levy is affordable. The UK is already one of the most competitive destinations in the world, ranking seventh on the World Economic Forum’s travel and tourism development index. Last year alone, overseas visitors made more than 40 million trips to the UK, bringing almost £30 billion to our economy. Flexibility in how revenue can be used will be matched by local accountability and transparency. Before introducing a levy, strategic authorities will set out their spending plans and consult locally, giving businesses and communities the opportunity to shape them. Once the levy is in place, authorities will report annually on revenue raised, expenditure and future spending plans. Businesses, residents and visitors will be able to see how the revenue is used and hold local leaders to account. To be clear—this was raised by some hon. Members—the levy will not replace Government grants. That is the right balance for a genuinely devolved levy, which empowers local leaders to invest in the visitor experience and support local growth while ensuring that decisions are shaped locally and are transparent and accountable. I have to say that some Opposition Members have failed to understand the concept of devolution—
On a point of order, Madam Deputy Speaker. I wished to raise an issue about sick children, but the Minister seems unwilling to take interventions, claiming that you will cut her short—
Ms Kearns, you have a great deal of experience, and that is not an appropriate point of order. It is up to the Minister whether to accept or decline an intervention.

Thank you, Madam Deputy Speaker. Members across the House have had the opportunity to speak in this debate, and some have chosen not to. Some Opposition Members have demonstrated that they have failed to understand the concept of devolution. We are unashamedly devolving power to strategic authorities, because for too long, power and resource have been held in Whitehall, and decisions made have not reflected the needs of the communities we serve. Most strategic authorities are headed by mayors who, as democratically elected representatives for their regions, will be accountable to local residents, businesses and voters when making revenue-raising and spending decisions. Empowering strategic authorities prioritises scale and efficiency by reducing the number of levy regimes that would otherwise become complex and burdensome to navigate. The Government already took steps through the English Devolution and Community Empowerment Act 2026 to strengthen the powers of strategic authorities, including on economic regeneration and boosting tourism, as well as other powers that support the visitor economy, such as adult skills, transport, housing, strategic planning, the environment and climate change.

I will not give way again to the hon. Member. Local authorities will have the opportunity to feed into local consultation and decision-making processes. Local authorities will also see the benefits of revenues being invested locally. I am sure that mayors up and down the country will ensure that voices of MPs and council leaders are heard in the process. Consultants have been raised by some hon. Members. There is no expectation that consultants will be employed, and the Minister is working closely with strategic authorities on the delivery of the levy. As part of the “Rewiring the State” delivery plan, we are looking at capacity in strategic authorities, and ensuring that they have the people and resource that they need to take on additional devolution. We recognise that visitor economies differ from place to place, so strategic authorities will have flexibility to exempt particular types of accommodation, such as camping pitches or dormitory-style accommodation, where that is right for their area. For example, strategic authorities may exempt lower-cost accommodation that is commonly used for educational trips and groups such as scouts and squirrels—that point was raised by my hon. Friend the Member for Stoke-on-Trent Central (Gareth Snell).

Calm yourselves down. Will the Minister be clear that although that might be the decision of a mayor, the Government do not want Scout camps to be taxed by mayors under this regime? We may not have the power to stop them doing that, but it is not what we want to see.

I thank my hon. Friend. I have now taken an intervention from both sides of the Chamber, and will continue with my remarks. It is right that strategic authorities and mayors get to decide what is right for their areas. We specifically included in the Bill the fact that mayors have power to exclude educational trips and groups such as scouts and squirrels, and they will use that as an indication of what is right for their area. Motorhomes will fall under the same arrangements as campsites, and there is the option for strategic authorities to exempt caravan pitches. My hon. Friend the Member for Chester North and Neston (Samantha Dixon) mentioned package holidays, and it would be just and reasonable to attribute this measure only to the cost of the accommodation element of the stay. Where visitors purchase accommodation as part of a package, the Bill gives providers significant flexibility to apply the cost only to the accommodation. This also applies to festivals, which were mentioned by the hon. Member for Gosport (Dame Caroline Dinenage). As the levy should be based on accommodation costs only, festival operators who are offering accommodation as only part of the ticket price will not need to apply that levy to the full price of the ticket. While the power to introduce a visitor levy is devolved to strategic authorities, the Bill provides a clear and consistent framework for its administration. The Bill sets out the core requirements on accommodation providers. These include notifying the relevant strategic authorities when they become liable, making returns and payments, and keeping records. We want those requirements to be proportionate and straightforward. We will continue to work closely with strategic authorities and industry on the plans for implementation to minimise administrative burdens, while ensuring that the levy can be administered effectively. London was mentioned by my hon. Friends the Members for Kensington and Bayswater (Joe Powell), for Cities of London and Westminster (Rachel Blake) and for Brent East (Dawn Butler). The Greater London Authority has its own set of governance arrangements that are different from those for mayoral strategic authorities. The Bill gives London Assembly members a formal scrutiny role and a vote on the Mayor’s proposals at approval stage. While the final decision on whether to proceed with the levy rests with the Mayor, boroughs will be encouraged to work closely with the Mayor of London to advocate for where revenue will be spent. I am sure that the Mayor of London will hear representations from hon. Members, as well as from leaders of the borough councils, and he will work closely with them to ensure their voices are heard and representations are made. On short-term lets, the Bill provides that each levying authority must publish a notice setting out the information that levy-liable accommodation providers are required to include with their quarterly returns. This is deliberately a local decision, rather than something prescribed nationally, and we are working closely with strategic authorities on the delivery of the visitor levy, and on how the framework can support other functions and priorities. We will keep under review whether and how information collected through the levy returns can support the enforcement of the 90-day short-term let limit. Local leaders will be empowered to invest levy revenues and improve the visitor experience in their region, including through projects related to economic development, transport and infrastructure. It is for them to decide how that is spent and not Ministers. In relation to concerns raised by the hon. Member for Harrogate and Knaresborough (Tom Gordon), accommodation providers will not face imprisonment for honest mistakes or minor breaches. Ordinary errors and failures are dealt with through the civil compliance regime and, where necessary, penalties; there are review and appeal rights. Criminal sanctions are reserved for the most s

No. I will continue to work collaboratively and constructively to ensure that the levy delivers for our local areas, visitor economy and businesses that support it. The Government are delivering on their commitment to shift power out of Whitehall and into the hands of local leaders. The Bill is an important part of that commitment. Crucially, this is about local choice. It will be for local leaders, working with businesses and residents, to decide whether the levy is right for their area and how the proceeds will be used to support their local economy. I am grateful to Members from all parties who have contributed to the debate today, and to those who have given their support to the Bill. I look forward to continuing the constructive debate and scrutiny as the Bill progresses through the House, and I commend the Bill to the House. Question put, That the Bill be now read a Second time.

On a point of order, Madam Deputy Speaker. The self-described race realist Nathan Cofnas will speak at Oriel College, Oxford tomorrow. He has written that in a meritocracy, black people “would disappear from almost all high-profile positions outside of sports and entertainment”. He has also said: “After the revolution, I’ll be the head of the department of eugenics and race science at Harvard.” In 2026, Oxford University will give a platform to a eugenicist. Hope Not Hate has written to the Home Secretary setting out why his presence is not conducive to the public good. This power has been used repeatedly, often unprompted, and many feel that the inaction now shows how little priority is given to anti-black racism. Free speech sits alongside equality law, not above it, and little thought seems to have been given to Oxford’s black students. Madam Deputy Speaker, can you advise me how to best raise such matters urgently when tens of thousands of members of the public feel that they are being ignored?

I thank the hon. Member for giving me notice of the point of order. It is not a matter for the Chair, but she has put her concerns on the record and no doubt will have been heard by those on the Treasury Front Bench, and those concerns will no doubt be passed on.

With the leave of the House, I will put motions 3 to 5 together. title: High-control Religious Groups:  Support for Victims

items.txt: In recent weeks we have seen a number of powerful men held to account for hideous abuse, particularly towards women, and I pay tribute to those victims who have fought for too long to be heard and taken seriously.
