However, I have initiated this debate to speak on behalf of another group of victims who often face significant barriers to being heard and believed, because society struggles to understand what has happened to them. I refer to victims of cults and high-control religious groups. These are organisations that go far beyond the acceptable boundaries of a mainstream religion and take over people’s lives, using fear, shame, isolation and authoritarian power to control and coerce their members. Most people are not aware of the extent to which groups like this can operate in the UK, because by their very nature they are often quite secretive or seem benign to the outside world. That is one of the primary reasons why the victims of such organisations so often struggle to be believed: people simply do not accept that this can be going on in modern society. Let me take a moment to comment on the attendance in the Chamber tonight. It is rare for more than three or four Members to be present for an Adjournment debate, but the breadth of those who have come to show support demonstrates that people care about this issue, which affects our constituents. I am very grateful to them all. I will focus on religious groups, but it is important to recognise that cults do not have to be religious in nature. There can be cults in all sorts of areas—any areas in which an “us versus them” narrative can be built. Victims from those backgrounds also deserve be heard.

I commend the hon. Gentleman for bringing this issue to the House, as he has in the past. It is important to mark the concerns of local parents for their children and the need to protect ordinary parenting for those who believe in religious freedoms. It is the high-control religious groups who use intimidation and manipulation to control individuals. Does the hon. Gentleman agree that such behaviour must be distinguished from ordinary religious teaching and genuine pastoral care, and that genuinely coercive harmful practices are more carefully targeted by legislation?

I thank the hon. Gentleman for making that point. I entirely agree with him about the importance of making that distinction clear, as I will later in my speech. We all have many fantastic religious organisations in our communities, and they do brilliant work. The types of abuse that I will discuss tonight, and the organisations that I will use to exemplify each one, are varied, but together they are often termed “spiritual and ritual abuse”, when spirituality or culture are weaponised to inflict harm.

I entirely accept the hon. Gentleman’s point about religious groups, but having thought about it earlier today and with the help of some of the casework that I have received, I have established that also included are spiritual enlightenment groups, multi-level marketing, group awareness training, internet-based psychotherapy groups and personal growth organisations. What they have in common, of course, is coercive control. Does the hon. Gentleman agree that coercive control must cover all sorts of cults and belief systems, and that that needs to be included in the regulations that are currently going through Parliament?

I am grateful to the hon. Lady, with whom I have worked on this issue for some time, for making those points. I will respond to some of them later in my speech. I want to tell a victim’s story—that of Rachael Reign, who escaped from the Universal Church of the Kingdom of God and now runs a survivor advocacy group, Surviving Universal UK. Rachael joined the organisation when she was 13, and before long she was warned that the devil would use people close to her to tell her bad things about the Church and encourage her to leave. That was made out to be a test of faith, but in reality, it was the beginning of coercive control and psychological subjection to create a dependency in her mind on the Church, and to shut down her critical thinking. Each Friday, she had to attend an exorcism service, with intense prayers involving physical contact and telling her that she had demons within her. Later, she was made to perform exorcisms herself, including on traumatised people, and she was told that if she ever left, all the demons that she had cast out of herself and others would be waiting for her. A BBC “Panorama” documentary in 2023 secretly filmed the Church doing this to a 16-year-old, and reported how a gay ex-member said that he was subjected to similar “strong prayers” at 13 years old to try to change his sexuality.

I thank my hon. Friend for securing this really important debate. The Government’s recent report tells the story of a gay man whose parents used emotional blackmail and manipulation, including making him attend group prayers in an attempt to “pray away the gay”. Does my hon. Friend agree that we must get the conversion practices draft Bill across the line and passed into an Act as soon as possible?

I absolutely agree with my hon. Friend. I am really pleased that she has raised that, because a significant amount of that abuse is going on, disguised as therapy or some other helpful practice, when it absolutely is not that. It is entirely relevant to the abuse I am discussing, and I appreciate her raising that. In an article in The Guardian earlier this year, other victims spoke of the Universal Church of the Kingdom of God’s financial exploitation of its members through “prosperity gospel” teachings. A victim, referred to in the article as Jennifer, was coerced into handing over £15,000, despite the Fundraising Regulator later finding that the church breached the fundraising code. The church was aware of her previous mental health issues when it took a large donation from her, and did not have policies in place regarding vulnerable donors. Other victims named in the article, including Rachael, corroborate the constant, extreme pressure placed on people to give huge sums. Rachael was coerced into giving regular tithes from the age of 13, and she was taught that she would otherwise have a “devouring spirit” descend upon her life and that she would be “robbing from God”. This group is a cult, and it is spreading through London at pace, particularly targeting black people. It is also legally classified as a charity, meaning that it receives tax exemptions and significant public money through gift aid. With a donation and legacy income of over £13 million in the year to March 2025, in theory up to £2.5 million of that could be direct public gift aid subsidy. I have called before in this House for fundamental changes to charity law that would stop that, and I hope the Government will take that on board. I also urge the Government to look at putting the Fundraising Regulator on a statutory footing, so that it can be empowered to hold organisations accountable for failures. The clear threads in these stories are coercive control through financial exploitation, threatening horrific consequences for leaving, and shutting off critical thinking. Such coercive tactics are commonplace in high-control groups. Another is mandated shunning, whereby adherents are ordered to ostracise former believers who have left, even if they are close family. In my previous Adjournment debate in March, I spoke about how the Jehovah’s Witnesses, the group I was raised in, do that. It happens when people leave of their own accord, or when the religion forces them out for doing something it considers sinful—being gay, for example, as we have just discussed. There are also cases where someone has been sexually abused within the Witnesses. When they have reported it, their abuser has faced no consequences but they, as the victim, have faced shunning, which may lead to homelessness—for example, if someone’s parents shun them and force them out of the home. Similar shunning occurs within Scientology, which retains a significant presence in the UK. Scientologists are required to adhere to a strict system of internal ethics. Reporting another Scientologist to the police is considered a “crime” and will result in expulsion and forced disconnection, so someone can lose everybody and everything they have ever known, even if they are a child—a clear sign, once again, that it a cult. Over the summer, The Times published the results of an undercover investigation into Scientology. Children as young as 13 are being taken out of school and made to work full time for a pittance, having signed so-called “staff contracts”. One 15-year-old girl was found to be administering massages to adult male staff. I cannot see how that is not modern slavery, yet the church insists that these children are “religious volunteers”, and nothing has been done to put an end to the practice since the article came out. Indeed, as far as I and the survivors I work with are aware, pretty much every case where an ex-Scientologist has reported abuse, modern slavery, human trafficking or harassment

I am very grateful to my hon. Friend for securing this important debate. A mother recently came to see me with concerns about her adult daughter’s involvement with a religious organisation locally. She described how her daughter was once very close to the family, but became increasingly isolated. Concerns were also raised about financial contributions she made while she was a student and struggling to pay everyday basic costs. Of course, freedom of religion is a fundamental right, but does my hon. Friend agree that there may be a gap in the support available to families when concerns arise about undue influence, social isolation or financial pressure in organisations that fall outside the scope of existing legislation on coercive and controlling behaviour?

My hon. Friend’s intervention lets me make a really important point. Stopping psychological subjection in high-control religious groups is not anti-freedom of religion; it is pro-freedom of religion. People who are trapped do not have free choice, and creating true free choice means making sure that people are free to change their religion or leave a religion. I will shortly come to her point about support.

Coercive control is wrong in any context, but does my hon. Friend agree that there is something particularly insidious about religious and faith-based abuse, because it preys on something as intensely personal as someone’s faith?

I agree entirely, and it is a very deep perversion of what religion is meant to be. I speak as someone who is not religious but who recognises how much value religion and faith can add to people’s lives. To distort and twist that in such a way is deeply wrong. When people in these cults and high-control groups take the extraordinarily brave step of leaving, despite the immense barriers to doing so both physically and psychologically, who is there to support them and what help can they find? The answer is very little. There is a deep lack of awareness among therapists and care professionals about this deep-reaching type of abuse and harm.

I thank my hon. Friend for securing what, as others have said, is a really important debate. For someone to leave their high-control religious group or cult can mean losing their family, friends and community all in one go. Would he join me in paying tribute to the volunteers and organisations who support people at what can be an extremely lonely and difficult time, including Faith to Faithless run by the Humanists UK?

I am grateful to my hon. Friend, and I will shortly sing those volunteers praises, because it is very much right that we thank them. People just cannot understand why victims in these groups do not leave early, or why they stayed. The themes of thought control, financial exploitation, isolation from family and friends, and threats against leaving should sound familiar, because they are exactly the things that characterise domestic abuse and coercive relationships. Indeed, the Government’s statutory guidance on what could constitute criminal coercive behaviour puts it as “a range of acts designed to make a person subordinate and/or dependent by isolating them from sources of support, exploiting their resources and capacities for personal gain, depriving them of the means needed for independence, resistance and escape and regulating their everyday behaviour.” That is a very good definition, but there is a catch. Under the current law, coercive control can take place only in a family or in a romantic relationship, so when religious leaders or cultic groups do exactly the same thing, it is not covered. The Family Survival Trust has been campaigning to change that. It is one of the few organisations that specifically aims to support cult survivors, and one to which I often refer cult survivors who write to me, alongside the excellent Faith to Faithless service operated by Humanists UK, which supports people leaving a range of different religions and the consequences that can bring. May I ask the Minister and officials to look at the Family Survival Trust’s extensive report on coercive control and cultic groups in the UK, published in 2022, which sets out the scale of the problem far more than I can in the time I have available? Would she agree to meet me and the Family Survival Trust to explore options for legislative reform? That could mean a change to the existing coercive control law through the Serious Crime Act 2015 to remove the requirement for a family or romantic connection, or it could mean a new offence. Governments around the world are waking up to the reality of what people are being subjected to. France has had legislation in place since 2001, focusing not on particular organisations but on the psychological subjection tactics they use. It strengthened that in 2024. Belgium passed an abuse-of-weakness law in 2011, and Luxembourg passed a similar law in 2013. Several proposals aimed at combating psychological manipulation, particularly in relation to high-control groups, are under consideration in the Italian Senate, and the Government of the Netherlands consulted earlier this year on a proposed Bill, too. In the Australian state of Victoria, a parliamentary committee published an extensive report in July this year, specifically on the recruitment methods and impacts of cults and organised fringe groups. It concluded that there was “a clear case for legislative reform” to capture “group-based coercion as a distinct criminal offence”. So there are a range of options available to us. I urge the Government to work with me to consider them in detail, and to bring forward measures to combat the very real phenomenon of psychological subjection in high-control groups in the UK. Let me turn briefly to what else we can do to support victims right now. In 2023, the Bloom review was published, an independent review of how Government engage with faith. There are some things in there that I do not agree with, but on the whole, I think it is a very valuable report that made important recommendations around countering extremism and supporting victims of high-control groups. True to form, the previous Conservative Government welcomed the report, said that they would consider the recommendations carefully, and then proceeded not to lift a finger on them. I want to cite recommendation 19: “Government should fund a programme that supports vulnerable people to leave high-demand groups, high-control movements (often referred to as cults) or

My hon. Friend is giving a powerful speech and deserves immense credit for bringing forward this debate. Allegations against members of the Ahmadi Religion of Peace and Light, headquartered in my constituency, are a matter of public record. Local children’s services and Cheshire police are, unfortunately, shouldering the burden of carrying out due process in that case. Does my hon. Friend agree with me that in the aftermath of such cases, we really need cross-Government co-ordination and resourcing to ensure that local communities do not pay the price?

I remember seeing that case earlier this year, and I was very sorry to hear what happened, when I learned more of the details. That is exactly why we need the Government to take high-control groups seriously at policy level. We need to create the powers and offences to deal with cases like the one in my hon. Friend’s constituency before they become catastrophic and create more victims who need more immediate support, so that this harm is prevented. I am coming towards my conclusion. Perhaps the Minister could consider picking up once again the recommendations in chapters 6 to 8 of the Bloom review and providing a substantive response to it; the Conservative Government who commissioned it failed to do so. One of the major issues, in my view, is that supporting victims who are leaving high-control groups does not fit neatly into any Government Department. There are safeguarding and crime concerns for the Home Office; implications for faith, on which the Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government leads; links to healthcare, as I have just outlined; and I highlighted earlier the problems that a lack of education can create for employment. There are also implications for charity law and regulation, which comes under the Department for Digital, Culture, Media and Sport. This is truly cross-cutting. What steps can the Government take to create ownership of this issue? Could they set up a dedicated unit of some sort against spiritual, ritual and cultic abuse, or give a named Minister responsibility for co-ordinating across Government in this space? Until Government and Parliament take this issue seriously, people will continue to suffer, and I know that all of us want to ensure that is not the case. So let us have the courage to do what Governments have shied away from for too long: call this out and put an end to it.

I congratulate my hon. Friend the Member for North West Cambridgeshire (Sam Carling) on securing this important debate and shining a light on the experiences of people who have suffered abuse in high-control religious groups. He is right to say that the issue does not fit neatly in one Government Department. It is on all of us to do better, to be aware of the issues faced by vulnerable individuals fleeing those organisations, and to recognise that what they are suffering is abuse, and that they are victims. For someone who has spent their life in one of those environments, finding the courage to leave can mean, as my hon. Friend the Member for Spen Valley (Kim Leadbeater) said, risking everything they have ever known: their family, friends community, and the support networks they rely on. Nobody should have to choose between their freedom and the people they love. But for too many people in our country, that is sadly their reality. Freedom of faith and belief is, of course, a fundamental right, and this Government and I will always defend it, but that freedom must never be used as a shield for coercion, exploitation or abuse. The right to practise one’s faith must go hand in hand with the right, if one so chooses, to leave it. We know, however, that leaving a high-control group rarely means simply walking out of a door. It often means someone leaving behind their entire world, facing profound trauma and complete social isolation. Even after someone has escaped, their ordeal may be far from over. The trauma of what they have experienced can remain with them for years, and finding the right support can be another enormous challenge. We know that those experiences do not always fit neatly into the categories that support services are designed around. That means that victims struggle to find the help they need at precisely the moment they need it most. We must do better at recognising those experiences and making sure that survivors can access appropriate support. As my hon. Friend the Member for North West Cambridgeshire will be aware, this Government have proudly committed over £550 million for victim and witness support services over the next three years. That is the largest investment in victim support to date. At a local level, police and crime commissioners are able to allocate funding based on their assessment of need, including funding for specialist organisations and therapeutic support. We are also providing a 2% uplift, year on year, to reflect the fact that it sadly now costs more to deliver support services. We cannot stand still; we must continue listening closely to survivors, victims, frontline charities—some of which have been mentioned in this debate—and Members across this House to ensure that the system truly captures every victim and survivor. Let me be clear: where criminal behaviour is suspected, it must be reported to the police, and it is never too late for a survivor to come forward. We must be alive to the fact that high-control religious settings can sadly be a gateway to other forms of abuse. It is deeply harrowing to hear affected victims’ accounts of modern slavery and exploitation. High-control religious settings and isolated communities can create acute vulnerabilities to trafficking, forced labour, domestic servitude and even sexual exploitation. For some survivors, escaping those environments is sadly only the beginning. They may need immediate protection from even further exploitation, violence or harm. When someone has been subject to modern slavery, specialist support is available through the national referral mechanism. Frontline responders, whether the police, local councils, or specialist charities, have a clear duty to identify victims, ensure their cases are referred to the police, and connect them with vital support. For adults, including those carrying the trauma of childhood exploitation, the modern slavery victim care contract can also provide dedicated, specialist recovery support. F
1. What assessment she has made of the potential impact of reductions in funding for the warm homes plan on delivery of the programme.

The Government are committed to delivering the warm homes plan. We are investing billions of pounds to support households to upgrade their homes with technologies to lower bills, cut fuel poverty and create skilled jobs. We have taken difficult decisions to fund the defence investment plan, but the vast majority of funding for low-income and social housing will be protected.

The autumn Budget confirmed a £1 billion reduction in capital grant funding for the warm homes plan. While the Government insist the majority of funding for low-income households and social housing is protected, the cuts suggest otherwise. The £25 million pilot scheme, which would have given free plug-in solar panels to low-income households, has been scrapped, while the 0% VAT rate on solar panels, batteries and heat pumps is also due to end. As the roll-out of the warm homes plan is already significantly behind the Government’s own ambitions, with fewer than 6,000 homes receiving upgrades, what assessment has the Minister made of the impact of these cuts on the delivery of the programme?

Tens of thousands of homes have received upgrades through Government-funded schemes in recent years. Our ambition for the warm homes plan remains: we will upgrade 5 million homes by the end of this Parliament and, while difficult decisions have been made as part of the defence investment plan, we still have many billions of pounds of spending for home upgrades. We also have the future homes standard and the minimum energy efficiency standards, which will come into play and create upgrades across the housing sector.
I call the Chair of the Energy Security and Net Zero Committee.

As the Minister knows, not every home is suitable for a heat pump, solar or battery. I encourage him to look at the work in this space of York University, which has identified significant savings for people in fuel poverty through the adoption of appliances including air fryers, dehumidifiers and clothing racks, and indeed heated wearables and electric blankets. Alongside the warm homes plan, this is a great way of enabling people to take advantage of electrification, which is consistent with the Government’s agenda.

I thank the Chair of the Select Committee for his question, and I look forward to speaking to his Committee tomorrow. I will look closely at that proposal from York University. The Department will soon launch a new advice tool to provide consumers across the country with advice not just on the grants on offer for heat pumps, solar and batteries, but on the small, everyday fixes that people can make to their homes, like the ones my hon. Friend has just mentioned, so that people can save money on their energy bills this winter.

We have heard compellingly from my hon. Friends on the Liberal Democrat Benches about the impact of the £1 billion cut to the warm homes plan, but it was not the only cut to the plan. In the Budget, the Government managed simultaneously to launch and to raid the warm homes loan scheme fund. The original £5 billion fund was meant to help drive electrification, enabling households across the country to do their bit by overcoming the up-front costs of installing heat pumps, batteries and solar panels through zero-interest and low-interest loans. I have asked repeatedly for transparency: how much of the financial transactions part of that £5 billion is now being diverted, and how much will actually remain available to help households to cut their energy bills and get off fossil fuels?

I would say to the hon. Lady not to talk down the warm homes fund. We have already seen significant demand for the warm homes loan scheme. The Money Co-op, which is one of the providers, has already suspended its applications because the demand was so overwhelming in the first couple of days. There are still lots of other lenders— [ Interruption. ] I say to the Lib Dems who are chuntering from a sedentary position that people can still apply to the eight other lenders that are still open. The warm homes loan scheme is fully funded, and we remain totally committed to it. The scheme will provide significant amounts of funding for people to upgrade their homes with heat pumps, solar and batteries.
2. What assessment she has made of the impact of environmental and social levies on domestic electricity bills.

We are focused on driving down every element of energy bills. We have a strong record of removing levies. We have already moved 75% of the cost of the renewables obligation to the Exchequer and are funding hydrogen projects through public spending rather than consumer bills. No new policy costs will be put on bills until a comprehensive cost control framework is put in place at the spending review in 2027.

That is all well and good, but some 1.5 million households across the UK, including many homes in my constituency, rely on heating oil. They have had no price cap on their heating fuel, yet still face environmental levies on their electricity bills. Why will the Minister not adopt the Conservatives’ cheap power plan to help bring down energy costs for these rural households?

I mean, honestly! The cheap power plan would add over £1,000 in a homes tax by abandoning the future homes standard. The cheap power plan assumes that the price of gas will be stable and low rather than volatile and high, which would be the reality. The Tories are quite literally gaslighting the British people into thinking that higher bills are the result of clean power policies, when what the Tories would do would end up putting up people’s bills.

I was going to say, “Finally a dose of reality from the Department for P45s”, with the Secretary of State admitting in an interview on Friday that clean power 2030 was unachievable—a “stretch target” as she put it. That is some stretch. Given that Government now agree with the Conservatives on this and given that the wholesale cost of electricity only contributes 29% of the average electricity bill, why not go the whole hog and, as my hon. Friend the Member for South West Devon (Rebecca Smith) said, adopt the Conservatives’ cheap power plan, and scrap the unfair and damaging net zero taxes and levies that make up so much of people’s energy bills?

The hon. Gentleman needs to be clear about the fact that we are exposed to global fossil fuel prices and are dependent on gas. Greater dependency on gas would make things worse. That is why we are shifting to home-grown, clean, reliable—and therefore cheaper—energy made in this country. That will create jobs and stability, and increase resilience—all the things that the British public are looking for.
3. What steps she is taking to support off-grid homes using oil-fired heating systems.
21. What steps she is taking to support off-grid homes using oil-fired heating systems.

Off-grid homes in council tax bands A to D are eligible for the £100 household energy payment and will also benefit from the zero rate of VAT on electricity bills that we have extended to July 2027. In the Glastonbury and Somerton constituency, around 33,000 households will receive the energy payment. In the Chichester constituency, around 37,000 households will receive payment. This is on top of the £53 million of targeted support for low-income heating oil users via the crisis and resilience fund, announced in March.

One Henstridge household now pays more than double for 500 litres of heating oil compared with this time last year. They are not alone. The way off of oil is by switching to a heat pump, powered by clean, home-grown renewables, but some older homes are harder to switch. The off-grid grant uplift ends in March, adding around £2,200 to the cost of switching. Will the Minister extend the uplift and back alternatives for homes where heat pumps will not work?

We have talked at length in this place and elsewhere about the challenges around heating oil. I am keen to make sure that the maximum number of people possible take up the £9,000 boiler upgrade scheme. We have already seen a 120% increase in the number of people applying to that scheme since the outbreak of the war in Iran. That is precisely because, unlike the Tories, those people understand that the best thing to do is wean themselves off the exposure to global fossil fuel prices.

More than 8,000 households in my constituency, because of their reliance on heating oil, have been left exposed to the price volatility that the Minister talks about. A specific issue is the minimum order requirement, which currently stands at 500 litres. It means that households are having to stump up hundreds of pounds at a time when they cannot afford to, especially those that do not receive financial support. The Competition and Markets Authority report into the heating oil market recognised this specific issue and called for a review. Will the Minister outline what steps the Government are taking to reduce the required minimum order volume?

The hon. Lady is right. I am delighted that the Government decided to respond to the Competition and Markets Authority recommendations and to finally regulate the heating oil market. It is appalling that people have been so exposed to those prices and that behaviour for so long. We will explore how minimum payments will fit into regulation. In the interim—we need to ensure that regulation is right—I am talking to the UK and Ireland Fuel Distributors Association and other trade bodies to ensure that the voluntary standards and codes of conduct are enforced and upheld this winter, including on minimum payments. I am concerned about people ending up out of pocket. It is also worth while pointing out that heating oil users in council tax bands A to D will benefit from the household energy payment, which will give people some of the breathing space they are looking for.

In Scotland, the SNP Government run the heating oil fund centrally, but despite boasting that they would double the fund to £10 million, only 7,028 households out of 169,000 in Scotland that rely on heating oil have had approval from the heating oil fund. Of over 12,000 households in my constituency, half of which use heating oil, only 324 have been able to claim the £300. Will the Minister meet Scottish Ministers and urge them to get that money out the door, take the rurality and insularity of islands into account, and widen the eligibility so that more people can get support?

I am disappointed to see that the Scottish Government, despite claiming they have allocated more money, are not managing to get that money out the door. I am really determined to ensure that anybody who has allocations given to them—be they local authorities in England, the Welsh Government or the Scottish Government—gets the money to the people who really need it as fast as possible.

With Government support for those struggling with the cost of liquefied petroleum gas and heating oil heavily reliant on councils distributing the money quickly and fairly, would the Minister consider instructing the Department to publish performance data for councils allocated money, so that, where needed, local Members and councillors could hold underperforming local authorities to account?

I know that my hon. Friend has been diligent in pursuing issues around the crisis and resilience fund. I and the Under-Secretary of State for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs, my hon. Friend the Member for Suffolk Coastal (Jenny Riddell-Carpenter), met Baroness Sherlock from the Department for Work and Pensions to understand what more can be done to ensure that support reaches those households that need it. Indeed, although the crisis and resilience fund was the choice back when the war broke out—it was pretty much the only option we had—with the household energy payment, we will be looking at a new discretionary fund with better ways of targeting the people who really need help.

The Liberal Democrats welcome the Minister’s work in this area and her recognition that rural households off the gas grid that rely on expensive heating oil and LPG are already particularly exposed to volatile fossil fuel prices. However, from next April, they face a double blow: the end of the enhanced boiler upgrade scheme grant and the reintroduction of VAT on energy-saving materials such as heat pumps, batteries and solar panels. Our analysis shows that a household installing a heat pump, 4 kW solar array and battery could face an additional £1,530 in costs. It seems bonkers that the Government are reintroducing a solar and heat pump tax at the same time as paying households to adopt the technology. Does the Minister agree with the Liberal Democrats that, to help rural off-gas-grid homes to get off volatile fossil fuel prices, we should reverse those measures?

The hon. Lady will be aware that the key means of improving the fabric of people’s homes—not only in rural areas—will be delivered through our warm homes plan and in particular the warm homes loan that the Under-Secretary of State for Energy Security and Net Zero, my hon. Friend the Member for Inverclyde and Renfrewshire West (Martin McCluskey), outlined earlier. Funding for the boiler upgrade scheme will also continue. We are working with the heat pump industry to drive down costs, ensure consumer protections, and reduce as much as possible the regulatory barriers so that people can get what they need installed.
4. What steps her Department is taking to support the development of emerging renewable technology.

We will need a range of technologies to build the clean power system that will get us off fossil fuels. We are backing emerging renewable technology through innovation and investments via our publicly owned energy company, Great British Energy, which will create skilled jobs and strengthen domestic supply chains. That includes investing in floating offshore wind projects including Pentland in Scotland and Erebus in the Celtic sea.

The success of offshore wind is proof that early Government investment in emerging technologies can achieve cost reductions, create viable technology for energy generation and help to reindustrialise the UK. Recent comments suggest that future contracts for difference rounds will be focused on the lowest cost possible, which is understandable, but will my hon. Friend confirm that the Government will continue to support all emerging technologies, and will he commit to using money from the new North sea energy wealth fund for that purpose?

My hon. Friend is right to say that affordability will be absolutely central to the decisions that we make in allocation round 8 and to other decisions we make when it comes to investing in technologies. We have also said that through the National Wealth Fund and Great British Energy, we will continue to support the deployment of clean energy, because it is the only answer that will get us off fossil fuels, and protect bill payers in the long term and the industrialisation that is so important in communities across the country. By taking that funding alongside our continued commitment to deploy clean power, we will make sure that we have jobs in every single part of the country and the power that will get us off fossil fuels.

The east of England has a strong record in delivering renewable energy projects; the Minister will be very familiar with the offshore programmes and turbines. Will he review the merits of developing an offshore grid to get the electricity generated into the grid without the need for more than 100 miles of pylons, which would devastate the east of England, the constituencies of Essex and our countryside?

I am really glad to hear Conservative Members championing renewables; it is really good to hear that. I hope that we can rebuild that consensus across the House. I agree with the right hon. Lady that renewables are hugely important. Of course, the great grid upgrade was started by the Conservatives, including the important transmission infrastructure that we need. The problem was that they left it too late, and that is why important projects off the east of England are not connected and delivering cheaper power to homes and businesses across the country. I am really interested in the idea of offshore co-ordinated assets. We agreed with European neighbours to look at much more offshore co-ordination—I think it is the long-term answer—but we also have to build the grid here in the UK to get the power to where it is needed.

In my constituency, there is so much innovation going on in floating offshore wind in the Celtic sea that could add to the energy mix and provide security. However, our offshore wind projects are all in the east of the country. Developers and investors are ripe to invest in the Celtic sea, but they need certainty to do so, because emerging technology needs to be tested. The contracts for difference AR8 will be crucial to supporting those test and demonstration models for offshore wind in the Celtic sea. Will the Minister commit to floating offshore wind in the Celtic sea as part of AR8 and future auction rounds?

My hon. Friend is a great champion for her constituency and for the Celtic sea more generally, as she is for the important role that technologies will play in reindustrialisation and in the energy mix. I will not be drawn on what will or will not come in AR8. We will say more on the budget later this week and then the process will have to run its course. Of course, in AR7 we got the first Welsh project through in more than decade. The Erebus project is also one of the first test and demo projects of floating offshore wind in the country, and it is in the Celtic sea. We remain committed to deploying those technologies, but I will say what I have said frequently before: that technology has to come at an affordable price to make sure that we are also bringing down bills for consumers.

Last week, the Prime Minister responded to me from the Dispatch Box, saying that £1 billion was being invested in a project off the east coast of Scotland. That was backed up later in the day by the Under-Secretary of State for Energy Security and Net Zero, the hon. Member for Inverclyde and Renfrewshire West (Martin McCluskey), who stated it in a post on X. Will the Minister confirm exactly which project off the east coast of Scotland is getting that £1 billion?

I am disappointed that the hon. Gentleman has not come here to welcome the investment decision in Berwick Bank, off the coast of Scotland, with £33 billion going to SSE across the next five years, including investment in Berwick Bank—a hugely important project. We are driving forward investment not just in building those projects but in the supply chains and industrialisation in Scotland. If the Scottish Government moved forward faster with some of the consenting decisions, we might see even more being built.
5. What steps she is taking with Cabinet colleagues to support growth in Forth Valley.

We are working across Departments and closely with the Government in Edinburgh to support growth and secure a prosperous industrial future for Forth valley. In addition to the substantial funding already deployed at Grangemouth, the National Wealth Fund stands ready with £200 million to support new opportunities, alongside private investment, while our investment agencies are working hard to bring forward investors.

If we are to deliver good growth in the FK postcodes, Grangemouth must remain a priority. The Government’s welcome National Wealth Fund commitment should have delivered more quality new projects by now, so with land remediation identified as the primary barrier to new investment, what will the Minister do, alongside colleagues, to ensure that projects at Grangemouth can secure access to the strategic sites accelerator?

Both my hon. Friends the Members for Falkirk (Euan Stainbank) and for Alloa and Grangemouth (Brian Leishman) are constant advocates for Grangemouth and have already won the investment to protect 500 jobs at Ineos, for example. My hon. Friend the Member for Falkirk is right to point to ground remediation as a significant barrier to deploying the £200 million allocated to the site, and we are working with the Government in Edinburgh to encourage faster action on this. On the strategic sites accelerator, we are of course happy to explore possibilities with him, within the scheme’s criteria.

In February 2025, the Government promised the £200 million of funding for Grangemouth. The Prime Minister at the time called it a “generational opportunity”, but 22 months on, the money has still not appeared. The Government said that this money would lever in £600 million of private investment, but if the promised funds are nowhere to be seen, that investment will not follow. The private investment at Grangemouth will go elsewhere if the Government keep delaying. Can the Minister confirm that the £200 million commitment still stands and say when it will be made available?

For a year before the election, the Conservatives knew that Grangemouth was going to close and they had absolutely no plan for it. The technologies that we are working on—through Project Willow, for example—involve complex, often unproven technology, so this will take time. As I have just said in response to my hon. Friend the Member for Falkirk (Euan Stainbank), we are working at pace to ensure that ground remediation, for example, is done at pace so that we can begin to deploy that £200 million. This is co-investment, so it will rest on investors coming forward, but we are working hard to make sure that that happens.

title: Energy Costs: Newcastle upon Tyne Central and West

items.txt: 6. What steps her Department is taking to help reduce energy costs in Newcastle upon Tyne Central and West constituency.

The Prime Minister has committed to bring down energy costs so that they are in line Europe within 10 years. Measures announced in the Budget will give families breathing space this winter. In the short term, households in council tax bands A to D are eligible for the £100 household energy payment, and all households will benefit from the zero rate of VAT on electricity bills, which we have extended to July 2027. For constituents in Newcastle upon Tyne Central and West, around 59,000 households will benefit from the energy payment and 17,400 from the warm home discount.

The £100 off energy bills is incredibly welcome in Newcastle upon Tyne Central and West, but families are still being hammered by the rising petrol and diesel prices caused by the war in Iran. We cannot control President Trump, but we can control and grow our local energy capability—our North sea wind is much more consistent than President Trump is—so will the Minister meet me to discuss how we can ensure that local businesses and communities take part in and benefit from GB Energy’s investment in the North sea?

My hon. Friend is right: there is an enormous amount of opportunity and consistency in the reliable energy that we can generate, from North sea offshore wind in particular. The National Wealth Fund last week announced two £500 million commitments for each of RWE and KKR’s Vanguard West and Vanguard East wind farms off the coast of Norfolk. That is not in Newcastle, admittedly, but it is another vote of confidence in British home-grown clean energy. The projects combined will deliver 2.8 GW of capacity, which is enough to supply the equivalent of about 3 million UK homes. Of course I am happy to have a meeting with my hon. Friend, particularly to focus on how the local power plan will increase the community benefits and improve the quality of things in her constituency.
7. What steps she is taking to help reduce the cost of energy for businesses.

We recognise the pressure that energy costs place on businesses. We will bring down those costs as part of our 10-year plan, but more immediately, our supercharger and our British industrial competitiveness scheme to support thousands of businesses are cutting energy costs by up to £40 per megawatt-hour.

Whether it is heavy industry or high street shops, businesses are being hammered and electricity bills are set to rise between 2025 and 2030 by 25% on average. In their manifesto, the Government said that energy bills were going to come down. We are now hearing from the Minister that they are going to come down within 10 years. When will the Government abandon ideology and actually take some steps to get on the side of businesses so that they can keep their doors open?

Renewables are the solution to the energy crisis. [ Interruption. ] The hon. Gentleman shakes his head from a sedentary position, but I was quoting him—how things have changed. He was absolutely right. In addition to making the big structural changes that will bring down wholesale prices over the long term, we are taking action through the supercharger and the British industrial competitiveness scheme—help that was not available under his Government.

Yesterday, I held a roundtable in my constituency with a Treasury Minister and businesses large and small, and one issue that was raised consistently by those businesses was the cost of energy. BICS is very welcome for the large organisations involved in big industrial processes, but there is little available for small and medium-sized enterprises. What more will the Government do to help those small businesses survive?

My hon. Friend makes an important point. BICS will support lots of small businesses as well, but we are clear—the Prime Minister has said this—that as part of the 10-year plan, we want to get to a situation in which all businesses’ energy bills are much more comparable to European averages. As well as subsidising energy bills, we need to move faster to support small businesses with, for example, electrification, so that they can become more energy efficient and reduce costs in the first place.

We are sorry not to see the Secretary of State here, but the Under-Secretary of State for Energy Security and Net Zero, the hon. Member for East Thanet (Ms Billington), just let the cat out of the bag. She said that energy bills are not going to come down for 10 years—a decade. Does that mean she admits that the Labour party misled the British people when it said at the election that bills would come down by £300 in this Parliament?

We just saw, at the Budget, a vote in which we made a choice to ask banks to pay a bit more in order to reduce energy prices for domestic customers. On industrial energy costs, we want to see more interventions—like the solar panels that I understand the hon. Gentleman’s business has on its roof. He knows that such investments are the future of sustainable industry in this country.

Further to the question from my hon. Friend the Member for Great Grimsby and Cleethorpes (Melanie Onn), the Minister will know that electrification is all well and good, but that there is not the grid capacity in places such as Stoke-on-Trent and the current cost of industrial electricity is too high to make it profitable. Outside of BICS and the supercharger, lots of companies in Stoke-on-Trent get no help at all, so what would the Minister have me say to them about what help they can access? Currently, they feel abandoned.

My hon. Friend is right to raise the challenge of electrification. As he will have seen, the Prime Minister this week set out the course towards that for the country. In the meantime, my hon. Friend will be aware—because he was one of the driving forces in achieving it—of the ceramics fund, which helps some of the harder-to-abate industries to invest in novel technologies that will help them deal with the high energy prices that currently make them uncompetitive.

The Government have said that they wish to join the EU’s internal energy market, which will involve a payment to the EU for the privilege. Will the Minister tell us whether that cost will be paid through higher energy bills for businesses, by taxpayers or through a combination of the two?

Unsurprisingly, the hon. Gentleman is viewing this issue through a slightly broken lens; there are also huge opportunities to make savings for industry through those negotiations. I am not going to negotiate at the Dispatch Box, but we will work incredibly hard to ensure that we get the best possible deal for UK industry.

I think that answer means that the Minister knows there is going to be a big bill, but he does not want to tell us. The emissions trading scheme is a costly burden on businesses’ energy bills, and it is a cost that the Conservatives would abolish. If the Government sign up to the EU’s emissions trading system, they will further increase the price that British businesses have to pay. Will the Minister explain why he is pursuing a policy of increasing energy prices further?

Again, there are huge opportunities to reduce costs for businesses through negotiating with our European partners. I know the Conservatives take the view—I would have to use unparliamentary language to say what the former Conservative Prime Minister said about business—that it does not matter what we negotiate in terms of costs for business. We will work to get a better deal for business, including on energy costs.
Colchester Institute has been made— [ Interruption. ] Sorry, Mr Speaker. I shall ask Question 8.
8. What steps she is taking to increase public control and community ownership of clean energy projects.

Through the local power plan, the Government are delivering the biggest expansion of community and local energy ownership in a generation. In September, Great British Energy launched £30 million of funding to support community group and local authority projects. That is a down payment on the £1 billion this Government will invest in community energy.

I got ahead of myself, so keen was I to celebrate Colchester Institute! Colchester Institute has been made a clean energy technical excellence college. It is one of just five CETECs in the country. The institute will train our clean energy workforce, help to bring down energy bills and work with our local authority. Will the Minister—any Minister— join us at a reception I am hosting for CETEC students not just in Colchester but around the country next spring?

My ministerial colleagues and I can argue over the invite, but I would be delighted to accept my hon. Friend’s invitation. It is wonderful to hear about Colchester Institute, and I pay tribute to it and to her for raising it.

On public and community control over energy projects, will the Minister note the strong public and community antipathy towards so-called energy from waste projects, and follow Scotland’s lead in banning any future waste incinerators in England?

Energy from waste has an important role to play in generating electricity across the country, and I have seen for myself a number of different projects that have powered heat networks and provided either low-cost heat or low-cost electricity across the country. Obviously, any decision has to be contingent on a planning application, and that would be for local authorities to determine.
9. What assessment she has made of the potential impact of the Chatteris wind farm on local communities in Cambridgeshire.

The project is at pre-application stage with the Planning Inspectorate, with submissions expected in July 2027. The Secretary of State will then make her assessment in the usual way once she has received the report of the Planning Inspectorate’s examination.

I thank the Minister for his recent clarification on my questions on this topic. My concern is that of scale. We have existing wind farms in the local area that use the MM82 turbines, which are around 100 metres tall, so roughly the same height as Big Ben. The proposed Chatteris wind farm would use wind turbines that are 220 metres high, which is just about as tall as any of the buildings in central London, more than twice the height of Big Ben and two thirds the height of the Shard. This is on some of the flattest countryside in the country and the turbines would be much taller—three times the size—than nearby Ely cathedral. What assessment have the Government made of the likely impact of the scale and of the peatland that may see subsidence, as we see with roads in that part of Cambridgeshire?

I am always disappointed when I open my box and there are no written questions from the hon. Gentleman to answer, so I appreciate that he is diligent on these matters and on many others. I appreciate the various comparisons he squeezed into that question as well. The national policy statements are clear that national need for infrastructure does not negate the need for an assessment of local impacts. All those considerations about scale but also about cumulative impact will be taken into account. I hope he will appreciate that I cannot comment on the particular application, but that is what the planning system exists to do.
10. What assessment she has made of the potential impact of reductions in funding for the warm homes plan on households.

The Government remain committed to delivering the warm homes plan and upgrading up to 5 million homes by 2030. We have prioritised the protection of funding for low-income households and social housing, and are pushing ahead with delivering the plan.

Energy bills have been skyrocketing for the last few years across the whole country and are putting real pressure on households in Winchester. Now that the Chancellor has confirmed the £1 billion cut in capital grant funding for the warm homes plan, thousands of people will struggle to make the adaptations they need—for example, installing heat pumps, solar panels and batteries. That seems fairly short-sighted at a time when were are looking to reduce energy bills and our carbon output, and even in respect of our national security. What impact assessment or review has been done on the impact of the cut in this grant?

Let me say to the hon. Member what I said to his Front-Bench colleagues: we are committed to delivering the 5 million upgrades that were promised in the warm homes plan, and I am confident we can achieve that, because we have the future homes standards, minimum energy efficiency standards and the warm homes loan scheme, all of which will be supporting people across the country to upgrade their homes this winter. I am confident we can meet that ambition of the warm homes plan, and I am always happy to work with him and his colleagues on achieving it.
11. What steps she is taking to involve civil society and young people in climate and energy policymaking.

I thank my hon. Friend for asking this incredibly important question. Young people should be involved in the issue of climate change because the window of opportunity to act is now; we cannot kick the can down the road. That is why I launched the youth climate and nature panel. It is why I have engaged with campaigners like Ava Langridge and Unjaded Jade. Last week at COP, I was lucky enough to meet the UK Youth Climate Coalition and the Department for Education’s youth sustainability champions.

I thank the Minister for her answer. My young constituents in Wolverhampton West are most active on climate change and energy issues. While I really welcome the Government’s initiatives in creating the youth climate and nature panel and “Young Voices for Climate and Nature”, how can we ensure that our young people are not simply consulted but can have a meaningful influence on the policy decisions we make on climate and energy?

I totally agree with my hon. Friend, who made this point eloquently in the Westminster Hall debate yesterday. We cannot act with our youth campaigners in a tokenistic way; we need to ensure that they are fully involved. That is why, when I met the final 25 of the 1,000 applicants we had, we agreed that we would co-create the process that we will work on over the next two years. That is really important. We are also exploring how we can involve youth campaigners throughout our G20 presidency. I want to give them the space to do it in their own way, so that they can flourish and bring their best ideas to the forefront.

A key thing that young people and wider civil society are calling for is the “polluter pays” principle—in other words, that those who make a mess should pay to clean it up. Can the Minister tell me whether the Government have been championing the “polluter pays” principle at COP31? Will the Government use the remaining days to ensure that there is strong language on “polluter pays” levies in the cover decision?

We obviously pursue various elements of the “polluter pays” principle through the energy profits levy. The COP negotiations are live, and the hon. Lady will have seen that the UK has been at the forefront of those. I was hugely proud that the Prime Minister was out there with the Foreign Secretary, and the Secretary of State is out there this week. She is pursuing a range of issues, including clean electricity, the Tropical Forest Forever Facility and various other issues. I am happy to keep the hon. Member updated on those.
12. What steps she is taking to support grassroots sports clubs with their energy bills.

We recognise the pressure that higher energy costs put on organisations that provide vital local services. That is why we have to create clean home-grown energy that we control, bringing down bills for good, and why we are seeing the largest expansion of community and local energy ownership in a generation.

We have many brilliant sports clubs across Spen Valley, but like many organisations they have felt the impact of rising energy bills. Clubs have taken innovative action themselves, such as Mirfield Parish cricket club fundraising for solar panels and many others in Battyeford, Scholes, Birstall, Cleckheaton and East Bierley working hard to bring costs down. However, given that these clubs are at the heart of all our communities, what are the Government doing to support them with rising costs? Will the Minister visit Spen Valley to see for himself the invaluable role that sport plays in my constituency and why it is so important?

I know that my hon. Friend is a former personal trainer, so she clearly recognises a natural athlete when she sees him. [ Laughter. ] I welcome the opportunity to visit her sports clubs to show them what physical excellence looks like, and I will take her up on that when the diary allows. Our drive on community and local energy ownership is a huge opportunity for sports clubs like the ones in my hon. Friend’s constituency, backed, as the Minister for Energy said a moment ago, by £1 billion from GB Energy to support more than 1,000 such projects around the country. I am also delighted to see community-owned organisations like Energy for Communities Kirklees in my hon. Friend’s constituency, which are running at this opportunity to ensure that we make the most of it.

Obesity among young people has been a problem for many years, and many of the academies and youth clubs that try to get those young people doing more exercise need support. Will the Minister double down on giving those clubs support so that they can do more to combat the obesity problem?

The hon. Gentleman is right. We often talk about the industrial cost of high energy prices and the opportunities lost through that, but it is important that we also talk about the opportunities lost because of the cost to sports clubs. A lot of national sports bodies that distribute lottery funds and Government funding also recognise that challenge, and they have schemes in place to support more energy efficient lights, solar panels on roofs, and that sort of intervention.
13. What assessment she has made of the potential merits of introducing a social tariff for energy for people with a terminal illness.

I welcome the hon. Member’s advocacy for people living with a terminal illness. No one facing a terminal illness should have to worry about their energy bills. I have seen reports in the media about Marie Curie and its campaign on fuel poverty and people who are experiencing a terminal illness. One of the first things I did when I took this job was to invite representatives from disability and age-related health charities—including Scope, Mencap, Sense, Age UK, Fair by Design—along with Citizens Advice and Martin Lewis, to speak to me about how we tackle fuel poverty among those people, given their exposure to high energy bills. I will meet Marie Curie in a couple of weeks to hear directly about those pressures, and discuss how we can best support those in need.

I thank the Minister for that reply. Energy costs for people with a terminal illness often increase after diagnosis because of an increased need for heating or to run medical devices. As the Minister said, research from Marie Curie has found that since 2023 nearly 400,000 people have died in fuel poverty, which equates to about one person every four minutes. Will the Minister consider introducing a social tariff for energy, specifically for people living with terminal illness, to provide at least a 50% reduction in their energy bill to help them meet the extra cost? We could, for example, use the recently published Energy Independence Bill.

It is extremely important for us to consider that issue, and how we want to reform the overall energy retail market. There is consensus, particularly on the Labour Benches, that the energy retail market is broken, and that is why we are looking to reform gas standing charges, and electricity standing charges over time. As we do that, we will increasingly need to work out how we target help for people who have unavoidably high energy usage because of medical need and so on. We must ensure that support for one group does not increase costs on others, which is why we are looking carefully at who should be supported, how that support should be funded, and how it can be delivered fairly. I would welcome support from across the House for us to establish proper data matching, so that we can get people the help they need without them having to apply for it.
T1. If she will make a statement on her departmental responsibilities.

The climate crisis is a threat to our national security, our economic stability, and the safety of people in Britain and around the world. That is why this week the Secretary of State for Energy Security and Net Zero is leading negotiations in Turkey at COP31. That comes alongside the Prime Minister’s announcement of two major offshore wind projects, creating hundreds of jobs in the east of England, and securing our energy future. Britain has also agreed to increase electricity’s share of global energy consumption to 35% by 2035, accelerating the global shift to clean electricity and appointing a new special representative for climate security. Every step we take to tackle the climate crisis is a step towards greater energy independence, stronger national security, and hope for future generations.

In September I asked the Prime Minister to review the Government’s approach to solar development on agricultural land, particularly when my constituency has so many warehouses without a single solar panel on them, so that we safeguard both our food and our energy security. He said it was a “good suggestion” that he would take up, but just five weeks later the Government approved a major huge solar farm in my constituency on prime agricultural land. What discussions have taken place across Government since the Prime Minister gave me that commitment?

In all our proposals solar will take up only 1% of our land. It is one of the cheapest forms of renewable energy—I know that Conservative Members like to use that adjective on a number of occasions. We are pursuing rooftop solar and land-based solar at the same time, and with our colleagues in the Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs, we are working across Government on the land-use framework to ensure that we prioritise areas of land.

T2. Ofgem’s debt relief scheme could help clear energy crisis debts for up to 2.4 million households. Sadly, that scheme does not start until the spring, after this winter, by which time we will likely have seen a further increase in energy debt, and Ofgem has limited information about households in Scotland that are in energy debt. Will the Minister do everything that she can do to work with Ofgem and others to reduce energy debt, so that we can tackle that as quickly as possible and help people keep their bills under control?

My hon. Friend will be aware of the new debt strategy, which was announced in the Budget, that will act as a circuit breaker. That strategy is expected to save a typical household almost £30 by 2030. At the moment, on average everyone is paying roughly £60 a year to service the debt in the energy system. That needs to be broken and that is what the energy circuit breaker will do.
What is more important to Ministers—the lives and livelihoods of thousands of oil and gas workers, or the views of 75 Labour Back Benchers?

In the past two and a half years, we have been very clear that oil and gas will remain a hugely important part of our energy mix, and it is critical that we put in place a credible plan to support that workforce into the jobs of the future, while supporting oil and gas in the short term. The answer is to invest as heavily as we possibly can in renewables, carbon capture, hydrogen and other technologies in order to support them. That is what we have been doing—it is what pragmatism means—and why we made the decision on Jackdaw, as well as announcing record investment in renewables. We have to do both and I hope the hon. Gentleman will support that.

Thanks to The Times today, we know that the Minister has signed off the Government’s impact assessment that showed £2.5 billion being lost to the British economy as a result of their ban on licences. We know that impact assessment showed that jobs are being lost because of their ban on licences. The Minister signed off a plan to ban licences knowing the pain and damage that would cause, but he had a chance to redeem himself by making a positive case for Rosebank and taking on the ignorance of a minority of Labour MPs, whose sole reason for coming into politics seems to be to make Britain poorer and weaker.

The hon. Gentleman’s last comment demeans him and I will not respond to it. In the interest of everyone concerned, I will not risk the process that is under way with Rosebank from the Dispatch Box or anywhere else, and we will stand up our decision on that in due course. He is wrong to take one side of the impact assessment and, as his party is increasingly doing, completely ignore the other side, which is the significant cost—up to 3.3% of GDP by 2050—of the impact of climate change if we do not act now. It is important that we do both parts of this.

T7. I congratulate the Government on the major announcement on offshore wind off the Norfolk coast, which has the potential to benefit 3 million households. Will the Minister update us on the accompanying work on the grid? How are we investing in it and ensuring grid connections can speed up, so that clean and green power can start flowing to households in the east of England and across the country as fast as possible?

My hon. Friend is absolutely right that we are making a £12 billion investment in offshore wind, one of the biggest investments in clean energy in this country’s history, creating jobs across the east of England and the UK. He is right to say that we have to fix years of under-investment in the grid to remove barriers for network connections, so that the clean power can flow to homes and businesses and we can bring down bills as a result. We are reforming the connections queue, building the grid that is necessary for the future, and making up for decades of under-investment by the Conservatives.

T3. In my constituency, 86% of households are already experiencing fuel poverty, so it is no surprise that families, not just in my constituency but up and down the country, will be deciding between heating and eating. I welcome the Government’s initiatives, including the crisis and resilience support as well as £100 for certain households, but that will simply not be enough when energy bills rocket up by more than £500 later this year. Will the Minister meet me and leaders of Birmingham city council to see how we can assist local residents in Birmingham?

We are aware how appalling the situation is in relation to global energy prices, and that is one reason that we have created the household energy payment, taken the VAT off electricity, and put the crisis and resilience support aside, particularly for people who use heating oil. We also have the warm homes plan, on which the Minister for Energy worked very hard, to improve the quality of people’s homes, which will be vital in the hon. Gentleman’s constituency. I am happy to meet him. That stuff will happen through devolution, the warm homes plan and the warm homes agency, but to get where we need to be, profound retail-market reform will be required as well.

T8. Like many others, I welcome the announcement of the Vanguard wind farm off the East Anglian coast, which will further boost the pivotal place that the east of England plays in our energy security. Can Ministers confirm the Government’s commitment to renewables, clean energy and fighting climate change?

Yes, I absolutely can. I welcome my hon. Friend emphasising the historic investment in Vanguard East and West off the East Anglian coast, and we remain absolutely committed to the deployment of clean energy as the route to get us off fossil fuels and protect households. That is a hugely important example of what is now more than £110 billion of private investment flowing into the UK, with jobs and opportunities in every single part of this country to build the clean power system of the future, and we will continue to back it.

T4. Following a summer of wildfires and many community screenings of the national emergency briefing across North East Hampshire, constituents have told me that they want faster action on climate change. What further steps is the Secretary of State taking to accelerate investment in renewable energy and ensure that local communities feel the benefit where it is built?

I believe the hon. Lady was at the debate yesterday in Westminster Hall, which was absolutely packed. That is a testament to the campaigners, who have been working in constituencies up and down the country. It was great to be able to announce that we are meeting next week with the national emergency briefing to see what next steps we can take. Through our Energy Independence Bill, we are introducing community benefit—an ownership scheme that will be a great way for communities to see the direct, positive implications of the transition.

Biomethane is great for farmers, households and businesses, but it is sometimes dismissed as a niche form of energy that has peaked. The National Energy System Operator has said that the sector could grow tenfold, and there is more than £1 billion-worth of pent-up investment in the Ofgem queue. Will the Minister look at getting the future biomethane framework out the door so that we can back this sector to reach its full potential?

I am getting quite a reputation for my interest in biomethane; I had an excellent visit most recently to the Severn Trent Green Power facility in east Birmingham. My hon. Friend is right to highlight the contribution that biomethane can make in decarbonisation and energy security. The Government recognise the importance of providing greater certainty, and we will do that as soon as possible.

T5. Under the smart export guarantee, a supplier can pay a household just a penny for every unit of solar exported to the grid. Many of my constituents are doing their bit for energy resilience through home domestic solar. If the Government want more domestic solar, will the Minister look at a fairer pricing model for it?
I thank the hon. Member’s constituents who are interested in exporting to the grid. We are reviewing the smart energy guarantee, and we will come forward with proposals in due course.

Many households in rural areas such as South West Norfolk are already paying a rural premium, with increased costs linked to rurality. Will the Minister commit to considering what more can be done to tackle the combined risk of poorly insulated homes, low wages and high running costs impacting on rural households?

As my hon. Friend knows, tackling affordability is the No. 1 priority of this Government. Fuel poverty affects 13.8% of rural households, compared with 9.4% of households overall. That is one reason we have made commitments through the household energy payment, the warm homes plan, abolishing gas standing charges and so on, as well as the £9,000 for the boiler upgrade scheme. We know that that is important, but we also know that local authorities have a responsibility to use the crisis and resilience fund properly. I am aware that the Reform council in Norfolk is not doing that, and we would like it to do so as fast as possible.

T6. On 8 and 9 November, wind supplied just 2% of Britain’s electricity, with gas accounting for 63%. The grid operator warned publicly that spare capacity was thin. Ofgem says that without the Belgian interconnector deal, we could face a negative gas supply margin in very rare stress conditions; in a gas emergency, it assumes that three quarters of the shortfall is managed by switching off gas power stations, just when cold weather drives up electricity demand and puts the grid at risk. Has NESO costed the electricity consequences, up to and including—

I think I can probably guess the rest of that tirade. The hon. Gentleman is wrong on all counts. We rightly have as the highest priority of this Government our security of supply for both gas and electricity. We have published the winter outlooks, which show exactly how we will meet the supply requirements. We take this issue very seriously, and he is absolutely wrong to come to this place and scaremonger about something as important as that. We have resilient supplies in this country, and we are seeking to make them even more resilient through the exact investment that he opposes.

Reindustrialising our communities is incredibly important to my constituency, which has a proud industrial heritage that continues today. What steps is the Minister taking to ensure that the green power revolution will bring new manufacturing investment, skilled jobs and apprenticeship opportunities to Smethwick?

My hon. Friend is exactly right: the task for this Government in reindustrialising is to build on the deep heritage in communities such as his, and to bring it up to date through investment in clean power. To that end, there are now 1.1 million jobs in net zero, with more than £1 billion of gross value added, and there is now more than £110 billion of private investment, all of which is connected to jobs in constituencies such as his.

T9. Solar farm developers are currently trying to blanket my constituency with 10,800 acres of panels—an area the size of Oxford under black plastic. Because they are classed as nationally significant infrastructure projects, the plans bypass local democracy. The Minister has talked about this being 1% of the country, but that 1% is concentrated in small areas, so will he work with the Minister for Housing and Planning to urgently review the planning framework in order to ensure that the cumulative impact is taken into account before these projects are approved?

Cumulative impact is already taken into account—it is a key part of the nationally significant infrastructure project programme process—and even in our most ambitious scenarios, if solar is deployed at the scale we hope it will be, it will take up to 0.6% of total agricultural land, so it is a small amount of land. I appreciate the right hon. Gentleman’s point about concentration, but that is exactly what the planning process is there to assess.

There are over 4,000 businesses in my constituency of Stevenage and the villages, most of which are small and medium-sized enterprises. They are really feeling the pressure from the conflict and stand-off with Iran, so what can my hon. Friend do to help relieve some of that pressure?

My hon. Friend is absolutely right. At the moment, for example, applications are open for the British industrial competitiveness scheme, which will particularly help smaller manufacturing businesses. As the Prime Minister has set out, we as a Government also need to move quickly on electrification, to help businesses such as those in my hon. Friend’s constituency cut their costs and become more efficient.

T10. National Grid is planning a huge substation in North Shropshire, and the process of community engagement has been really poor—I only found out by looking on NESO’s website, despite having explicitly and repeatedly asked it about scale, and the local community are largely in the dark about what is proposed. The Minister has already agreed to meet me to discuss the appropriateness of the site. Will he please expedite that meeting and add the community engagement process to the agenda?

When I meet the hon. Lady, she will be in charge of the agenda, and I will be very happy to have that conversation. I expect everyone who is building infrastructure in the UK, including National Grid, to take community engagement seriously—it is a critical part of the planning process. The planning system only works if communities have a chance to voice their views, but I am not directly responsible for the siting of infrastructure. I am happy to pick that up with the hon. Lady during our meeting.

Yesterday, alongside many MPs from across the House, I took part in the Westminster Hall debate about the national emergency briefing, and I am very grateful to the Minister for her time.
