In my constituency the loved one of a family with ties with Iran was detained in an immigration centre and taken to the airport to be sent abroad, only to be returned to the detention centre. I wrote to the Home Office asking for his removal, but the Home Office has not responded.

I am grateful to the hon. Gentleman for raising that issue on the Floor of the House. That is exactly what this Chamber is for, and I should be more than happy to discuss the issue with him after the debate. As I was saying, those who are in detention and fall in the late claims process may have their appeals expedited, but that is on the basis that they have not ignored the requirements of the claim notice. New clause 12 streamlines the immigration and asylum appeals process by removing the power of the first-tier tribunal to give permissions to appeal to the upper tribunal. Applications for permission can be made directly to the upper tribunal instead. As the House knows, the first-tier tribunal immigration and asylum chamber is currently facing significant pressures, with an outstanding caseload of 156,000 cases as of June 2026.

I entirely agree with the intention of the Minister and the Government to stop people taking our immigration system for a ride, and to identify fraudulent claims and take appropriate steps to remove those people, but can the Minister reassure the House and my constituents that when genuine errors are made in the application process or in following the rules, people will not be inadvertently thrown out—that the baby will not be thrown out with the bathwater?

The hon. Gentleman has gone to the heart of what we are trying to do with this process—that is, to ensure that those who have a genuine claim will receive the proper support and due notice for not only their claim itself, but the rights to appeal. The new immigration and appeals authority will ensure that people have the opportunity of a clear and rapid appeal process which will help us get to the truth of the appeals that are submitted. New clause 12 streamlines the immigration and appeals process by removing the power of the first-tier tribunal to give permission to appeal to the upper tribunal. By removing this duplicative stage, the new clause will allow judicial resource in the first-tier tribunal to be directed towards deciding substantive appeals, improving efficiency while maintaining access to justice through a right to seek permission directly from the upper tribunal. The Bill addresses the wider systemic challenges within the appeal system. However, the Government will continue to pursue every available mechanism to ensure that cases in the existing appeal system can be dealt with as quickly as possible, to provide certainty for appellants and ensure that the Government can swiftly remove those with no right to be in the UK. Government amendments 4, 5, 6 and 25, and amendment 8 to clause 7, concern the review and onward appeal arrangements for decisions of the independent immigration appeals authority. Together, they seek to make the process more efficient and avoid unnecessary delay, while preserving the important safeguard of appeal to the upper tribunal. As I have said, we do not want to replicate the duplicative process that we are removing through new clause 12. The amendments to clauses 6 and 7 therefore provide for permission to appeal to be sought only from the upper tribunal, and preserve the authority’s ability to correct its own decisions. Amendments 4, 5, 6 and 25 therefore leave more of the review framework to the authority procedure rules, allowing the circumstances in which review is available and the powers exercisable following a review to be tailored appropriately. Amendments 7 and 3 concern the routes through which decisions of the authority may be challenged. Together, they clarify which decisions may be appealed against to the upper tribunal, and the position on judicial review for decisions excluded from that appeal route. Amendment 7, to clause 7, specifies the categories of the authority’s decisions that are excluded from onward appeal to the upper tribunal. These exclusions closely align with those applying to the first-tier tribunal under section 11 of the Tribunals, Courts and Enforcement Act 2007. Amendment 3 is consequential on those exclusions. It clarifies that clause 1(8) applies to decisions that may be appealed against under clause 7, and does not prohibit excluded decisions from being challenged by way of judicial review, subject to the usual requirements. New clause 9 sets out that the IIAA will fall under the remit of the Parliamentary Commissioner for Administration, which operates under the title of the Public Services Ombudsman. If the hon. Member for Dewsbury and Batley (Iqbal Mohamed) has any concerns about any individual cases, the ombudsman will provide that route of access for hon. Members in this place. This will provide an independent route of redress for matters relating to administrative functions. That is separate from any internal complaints process. To be clear, that will not create an additional route of appeal against the authority’s decisions. The ombudsman will not be able to reconsider adjudicator reasoning or overturn a decision. New clause 10 sets out a new removals process for individuals who have the right to bring an appeal to the new IIAA. It also sets out our process for expediting late claims within the IIAA.

I wonder whether the Minister has had an opportunity to consult the relevant Scottish Minister about some of the slavery measures in the Bill. As she will know, we have devolved responsibilities for a swathe of provisions relating to this, and there is a concern that this will have an impact on our ability to meet those obligations.

My officials have worked very closely with the Scottish Government in developing these measures, and I know that there is a lot that we can learn from some of the modern slavery provisions over the border, so I am keen to continue that conversation.
Can the Minister outline how the Government’s proposals relating to modern slavery make their provisions compatible with article 4 of the European convention on human rights?

We have made it very clear that every amendment being made to the Bill is completely compatible with the European convention. In this country we are proud of the leadership that we have shown in respect of modern slavery in particular, and we will continue to show leadership in that regard. We refer more people to our national referral mechanism than every other European country combined.

I am going to make some progress, if that is okay. New clause 11 and amendments 21 and 29 are related to asylum reforms and linked to wider core protection proposals. The Government are committed to bringing order and fairness to our asylum system, and that is underpinned by our international obligations. Article 31 of the refugee convention states: “The Contracting States shall not impose penalties, on account of their illegal entry or presence, on refugees who, coming directly from a territory where their life or freedom was threatened in the sense of article 1, enter or are present in their territory without authorization, provided they present themselves without delay to the authorities and show good cause for their illegal entry or presence.” The UK has incorporated this principle into domestic legislation through section 31 of the Immigration and Asylum Act 1999 and section 37 of the Nationality and Borders Act 2022. New clause 11 will ensure that only those who have come directly from a country where their life or freedom was threatened, or who have good cause for their illegal entry or presence, benefit from the statutory defence in section 31 of the 1999 Act. As a result of our amendments, a person who is at risk of persecution or serious harm in their country of origin, but who has stopped in a safe country—defined as one where their life or freedom is not threatened—will not be treated as having come directly to the UK. EU member states, European economic area member states and Switzerland will automatically be treated as safe countries in which a person’s life or freedom was not threatened. It is our position that those choosing to travel through countries where their life and freedom are not threatened should not benefit from the article 31 defence. We are also amending the legislation so that individuals with protection status may be eligible to benefit from the section 31 defence, not just refugees. It is right that anyone who comes directly to the UK when fleeing persecution or serious harm, whether for a specific convention reason or for reasons such as war and indiscriminate violence, can seek to rely on the section 31 defence where applicable. Amendments 30, 14 and 22 relate to the Home Office’s ability to designate claims from nationals of certain countries as inadmissible. Under the current legal framework, asylum claims made by EU nationals must be declared inadmissible, other than in exceptional circumstances. Where a claim is declared inadmissible, it will not be considered substantively and the decision will not generate a right of appeal. Section 59 of the Illegal Migration Act 2023 would extend that regime to all human rights claims, as well as protection claims in non-EU states. This provision, however, remains uncommenced. As set out in section 40A(4) of the Act, if there are exceptional circumstances why the protection claim should be admitted to the asylum system, the merits of the claim will be considered substantively. That includes an assessment of any protection and human rights claims raised. Through this Bill, the Government are expanding section 80A of the 2023 Act so that all protection claims will be included in the inadmissibility framework, including those related to serious harm. However, the uncommenced provisions in section 59 expand that to include any human rights claim. This includes any claims made on article 8 family or private life grounds. In reality, the safety of a person’s country of origin has little to no bearing on the strength of their article 8 claim, and we do not consider it appropriate to treat article 8 claims as inadmissible based on nationality. It is for this reason that Government amendment 30 proposes removing human rights claims from section 59. Instead, article 8 claims that are clearly unfounded can continue to be refused and certified under existing powers. Amendment 30 will therefore mean that if section 59 of the 2023 Act were to be commenced, protectio

I appreciate that many Members want to contribute to this debate, so I shall not take too much time. I will speak to the new clauses, including those in the name of my right hon. Friend the Member for Croydon South (Chris Philp), particularly clauses 50 and 54. I start by thanking right hon. and hon. Members from across the House for their thoughtful contributions and the measured debate that we had in Committee, and I thank the Minister for detailing the Government’s new clauses and amendments. I congratulate her on taking the Bill through Committee and Report, which I think is the first time she has done so as a Minister. I expect that she and her team will be very relieved to pass this legislation to the other place for its detailed consideration. The British public, including my constituents in Mid Bedfordshire, expect us to do whatever it takes to strengthen our borders and to strengthen our country. We must be honest with them: there is no silver bullet and the solutions are not simple. Securing our borders and strengthening our country will take honesty with the public, tough choices and hard, detailed work. Today I ask right hon. and hon. Members to consider the Conservatives’ amendments, which we have tabled in good faith to strengthen the Bill by properly controlling our borders and restoring trust in our immigration and asylum system—a system that defines who gets to share with us these incredible islands we call home and, importantly, who does not. However, the system does not currently strike the right balance and has not done so for some time. We all know that, and our constituents know it too. Too often the response to short-term need has been to invite more people to our shores, and too often our instinct for generosity as a people has been taken advantage of. The Conservatives’ amendments to the Bill seek to reset that balance. Settlement and citizenship are the greatest privileges that this country can give. Our new clauses 50 and 54 ask the House a simple question: should they be earned, or should British citizenship be able to go to someone who broke our laws in order to get here? Members do not need to guess where each party stands—it is on the amendment paper in black and white.

New clause 54 appears to exclude Hongkongers on British national overseas visas and Afghan interpreters from ever being able to earn indefinite leave to remain. Is that the shadow Minister’s understanding, and can he confirm that that is the intention of the new clause?

The intention of new clause 54 is to set the principle. Of course, we would not seek to remove the rights that have already been committed to, including for Hongkongers and Afghan interpreters, and subsection (6) would allow the Home Secretary to issue regulations to that effect. The hon. Member can be assured that we would not use the new clause to deny the rights of those to whom we have provided safety. The Conservatives have tabled a suite of amendments to implement our borders plan. They include new clause 54, which would put into law a 10-year qualifying period for settlement. New clause 50 says that anyone who enters this country illegally should never become a British citizen. In Committee, we pressed such proposals to over 50 Divisions in an attempt to improve the Bill, and I have tabled dozens of written questions on the Bill and the system it governs, which thus far have mainly been unanswered. Serious policy is built on evidence and, despite commitments to do so, the Government did not provide it before Report. Reform UK has tabled seven new clauses, but not one of them deals with settlement or citizenship. Having tabled no amendments to this Bill in Committee, these last-minute new clauses are seeking headlines, not a better immigration system. Anyone can write a slogan. Securing our borders requires detailed plans that survive contact with reality, the courts and the facts. I may disagree with them, but the Greens were at least clear in Committee that they did not want this Bill at all. Today they would strike out the asylum support repayment clauses and stop the police sharing information with immigration enforcement. On settlement, all five Green Members have signed up to the left-wing new clause 62, which I am sure we will hear about during the course of this debate. It would allow more and more people to qualify for indefinite leave to remain in the coming years. The Liberal Democrats tell their constituents they are standing up to the large asylum camps. The hon. Member for Bicester and Woodstock (Calum Miller) has rightly tabled new clauses on large sites and asked questions about MOD Bicester, which Piddington residents strongly oppose. We backed their site clause in Committee. In contrast, they voted against every one of our new clauses to secure our borders, against a duty to remove, against a removals force and against deporting foreign offenders. Today, the Liberal Democrats will be pushing to a vote new clause 18, which seeks to secure our borders by outsourcing security to the European Union. In our opinion, this is not a serious policy. One cannot vote for more people to come and fewer to leave, and then oppose every site where they will be housed. The asylum camps are a consequence of the system the Liberal Democrats are voting to protect in this Bill. Then there is the Government. On 2 November, the Home Secretary announced that settlement would take 10 years. The very next day, every Labour Member present in Committee voted against our new clause to do exactly that. Today, the Government are restricting onward appeals, which the Minister voted down when we proposed it, and are tightening late claims, which she voted down too, but we welcome both. However, the British public should know that the Government are moving because our arguments were right in Committee, not because they had a plan or found the will on their own.

I often hear Conservative Members talk about the well founded concerns of individuals now that sites are being proposed in the home counties. However, Stoke-on-Trent has for decades been home to well over 1,000 people who are getting support from the state through an asylum process, and not once have I heard Conservative Members say anything about my constituents and their concerns. Why is it that when such proposals come forward that affect their constituencies, it is a matter of immediate concern, but when it was affecting constituencies in the north of England and the midlands under their Government, they were silent?

Communities up and down the country are affected, and certainly those in Piddington are affected now, as are those in Crowborough and around the country. It is right that Members come to this House and raise the concerns of their constituents. If people housed in these sites are granted leave to remain in the UK, the cost does not stop there. Migrants granted visas in-country due to an article 8 claim cost the taxpayer £141,000 per person. For the 2025 cohort alone, that cost is estimated at £4.9 billion. Although this Bill makes some progress which I welcome, it will still leave open article 8 claims and does almost nothing on other human rights claims. That is indicative of what is lacking in the Bill. The Government have no clear plan to end the legal framework that puts the interests of people entering the country illegally ahead of the interests of the hard-working, rule-abiding people already here. That is why the Government should consider the range of new clauses on a removals duty, a removals force and foreign national criminals. The Opposition recognise that Home Office Ministers have diagnosed some of the ills in the system, but they have failed to prescribe the appropriate medicine. When faced with a choice between securing our borders and securing its own majority, Labour would prefer its majority. It has failed to confront those who oppose the changes we know are needed to secure our country. The Liberal Democrats would prefer that we delay, even as thousands more people every day become permanent residents of our country, to wait for independent assessments to confirm what we already know: that the cost of inaction is far too high and borne unfairly by the British people. The Green party, of course, would prefer that we did not secure our borders at all, while the Reform party would prefer to talk about securing our borders while not actually doing any of the hard work to secure them. Reform claims to care about immigration, but it failed to submit a single amendment for consideration in Committee. The Conservative party is willing this Government on to fix our borders and build a stronger country. We have not attempted to wreck this Bill, but we are clear that it does not go far enough to meet the expectations of the British public. Our amendments are necessary to implement key elements of our detailed borders plan and restore trust in our immigration system. I encourage the Government to accept them, and, in doing so, secure our borders properly and build a stronger country. If this Government cannot or will not, we Conservatives certainly will.

I have come today in part to speak to new clause 7, in the name of my hon. Friend the Member for Hackney South and Shoreditch (Dame Meg Hillier). The new clause is, in part, a continuation of the debate that she and I had almost a decade ago on the Public Accounts Committee about the benefits and operability of some elements of the Modern Slavery Act 2015, in particular whether the required reporting mechanisms are at a level that makes the data useful. The Minister spoke a little about this matter, and the Government have tabled amendments to try to ensure that that data is published. However, she will know that over the past decade or so of the operation of the Modern Slavery Act, the section 54 requirements have been, shall we say, hit and miss in some places. Some organisations take them very seriously; they publish the full depth of their supply chain and make clear the actions they are taking to ensure that they are buying their products and importing things from places that are free from modern slavery. As she will also know, some people put up a modern slavery statement, at the bottom of a website, normally, that just says that they comply with modern slavery recruitment rules. It was not until recently that all this was compiled and looked at exclusively by third party organisations, after which the contravention of section 54 was met with a shrug and an instruction to try to do better. My hon. Friend the Member for Hackney South and Shoreditch has tabled new clause 7, which I have signed, along with many Members across the House. It simply seeks a greater step towards enforcing the requirements under section 54 of the Modern Slavery Act, and repercussions for the organisations that fail to meet not just the letter of the law, but the spirit under which it was proposed, which was meant to ensure that we in this country are not knowingly using products that have been produced, supported or enhanced by slave labour, whether in the UK or overseas. The way in which my hon. Friend wishes to do that, which I support, would be through a statutory duty on relevant commercial organisations, sticking to an annual turnover of £36 million or more, and on relevant public authorities, excluding courts and tribunals, to take the appropriate steps as specified by the Secretary of State to identify, mitigate, remediate and prevent slavery and human trafficking in their supply chains. If they fail to do that, organisations and public authorities could be fined up to 5% of their annual global turnover, bringing UK enforcement into line with comparable EU legislation. New clause 7 is based on some of the discussions with the Independent Anti-Slavery Commissioner. It basically seeks to make clear that, where we have expectations on industry and their commercial operations, organisations are doing more than simply publishing statements for which there is no consequence. When I served on the Public Accounts Committee almost 10 years ago, we saw examples of organisations that published statements that categorically said that they were not complying with the spirit of the section 54 requirements but that because they were publishing that statement they were meeting the requirements of section 54. The statements exposed the challenges that they were not dealing with and allowed them to say that they were compliant even though they were doing nothing tangible to help to deal with the modern slavery that they were in part funding. We know that the British public are good people. When they go into a shop or to an organisation to buy a service, they want to make sure that what they are buying aligns ethically with their values. They want to make sure that they are not buying things that perpetrate and force the modern slavery that we know happens around the world. There is public support for what my hon. Friend the Member for Hackney South and Shoreditch is trying to achieve through new clause 7. We all know—I certainly know from my own casework—t

I do not think there is much anyone can disagree with in the point the hon. Gentleman has just made about slavery, but there are Members of this House who have been sanctioned by China for raising the issue that slave labour is being used in the processing of renewable materials, and the Chinese process 90% of renewable materials. In terms of transparency, does the hon. Gentleman feel that the Government should be robust and say that we cannot be buying those renewable materials? Should it not apply across the board rather than only in some areas?

As is customary, the right hon. Gentleman hits the point exactly. There is always a challenge between what we aspire to do and the reality of the circumstances in which we seek to deliver it. New clause 7 seeks a much more rigorous system for companies to declare what they are doing as well as how they are mitigating modern slavery activities. He will almost certainly be of the opinion, as I am, that there are supply chains coming into the UK that are being underwritten and underpinned by modern slavery activities. We should be doing everything we can to remove that element from the supply chain or to remove ourselves from those supply chains. In some cases, as with the materials that he talks about, that will mean an incredibly difficult set of conversations that we need to have with international partners, but we should not shy away from doing that, because it is the right thing to do. It is not going to be easy, and neither is it going to happen overnight, but part of the way in which we can drive change is by consumers in the UK having a better understanding of where the products they buy come from and the labour that is being used to construct the products. That would then drive the Government to think, “We are going to have to find a way of making this that does not rely on slave labour, mainly coming out of China.”

Does not the hon. Member think there might be an opportunity in this broad sweep of legislation to put more consequence on businesses using slave-labour goods? He is arguing that we should do more encouragement, while I would argue that we need to take a firm stance and ensure that action is applied.

I agree with the right hon. Gentleman. New clause 7 would provide for a fine, potentially of 5% of annual turnover. I appreciate that he has tabled new clauses that would allow the Secretary of State to designate some companies as being completely outside what we consider acceptable, to prohibit them from importing things. We probably need to construct a suite of consequences, with multiple levers available for us to pull, to ensure that the supply chains of goods and services coming into the UK are devoid of any element of modern slavery. But I will not stand here and kid the House that we can do that easily overnight. Elements of modern slavery are probably coming into the country through supply chains that we know about and do not yet have an alternative to, and, unpleasantly, we suck that up, against our values as a nation. Modern slavery also probably exists undiscovered in other supply chains, but we will undoubtedly discover it as the world looks towards it. I will speak briefly in support of some of the Government amendments. It is right that we put a legislative and parliamentary lock on what we believe the article 8 rights of the ECHR say, so we can say what they mean for people coming into the UK and how we operate. The Government have been right in previous announcements to say that citizenship in the UK is a privilege that we get to control, and we get to say how we operate it. It is important that every Government should have that ability. I turn briefly to new clause 1, tabled by the hon. Member for Bicester and Woodstock (Calum Miller), about the site near his constituency. I understand why he comes to this place, rightly, to stand up for his constituents and say that decisions made in government have impacts that affect constituencies, but I will re-argue the point I made previously. For the best part of a decade, Stoke-on-Trent has been a national dispersal city for the Home Office. Routinely, 1,000 people in my city are waiting for an asylum claim to be dealt with. We had two hotels opened by the previous Government—they have been closed by this Government—but still 1,000 people are in that city in dispersed accommodation. I genuinely understand why the hon. Gentleman is concerned about having a large site in his constituency. The uproar when we have one large site is loud. However, and I heard my hon. Friend the Member for Hartlepool (Mr Brash) agreeing with me on this, towns and cities in constituencies like mine have long borne the burden—I use that word in its technical sense, not in its pejorative sense—of the asylum failures of the previous Government, yet little was said. We were told to get on with it.

Does my hon. Friend agree that, in the previous situation, when hotels were opened in constituencies like his and mine, nobody was told? Whether it was the police or the council, nobody knew. The difference is that we are telling communities and working with them as we establish these new sites. That is a completely different way to do it.

I agree with my hon. Friend. The hotel opened in my constituency by the right hon. Member for Newark (Robert Jenrick), the former Conservative Immigration Minister who is no longer either a Minister or a Conservative, was directly opposite the railway station—it has been closed now and is functioning normally—and we did not find out about that. There was no consideration of conversations about existing community tensions and what that hotel might do to them.

We are a decade on from the Jomast red door scandal in Middlesbrough when the housing association occupied huge numbers of terraced houses with bright red doors, and everyone in the town knew exactly who was being housed in them. That was incredibly difficult for community cohesion. Does my hon. Friend agree that the Government’s approach is about fairness across our country and supporting working-class communities?

I agree with that. I also want to make clear that the way in which Stoke-on-Trent has risen up over the last decade to support the communities that were moved there should be celebrated. The organisations that stepped up to do that did the right thing and the contributions that asylum seekers have made to my city has been enormous and welcomed in most cases. I will note—more to the Conservative party than to the hon. Member for Bicester and Woodstock—the hypocrisy of saying that having 1,000 people in one place is a terrible thing because it is happening in their areas. I had 1,000 people in my constituency and not once did they say anything.

The hon. Gentleman is making a powerful case for why local communities should be given advance warning of both the justification and the likely costs of any large group of people being moved into their community. I have great sympathy for him and other colleagues who suffered that under the last Government, who did not provide them with that notice. He is not, however, providing evidence as to why Opposition Members and the Government will not accept my amendment, which simply asks for that information to be provided. It is not about advocating for one location or another; it simply says that when the Government seek to put more than 300 people into a site, they should have the courtesy to let the local community know what their intentions are.

I look forward to hearing the hon. Gentleman’s argument for that later on. I commend to the House new clause 7 in the name of my hon. Friend the Member for Hackney South and Shoreditch, and I look forward to the rest of the debate.
Order. I inform Members that there will be a five-minute limit on Back-Bench speeches. I call the Liberal Democrat spokesperson.

I speak first to new clause 18 in my name. Britain has a long and proud history of responding with compassion to those fleeing unimaginable horrors. That must continue, but in a system that is controlled and fair and which works with our international partners in the EU. Alas, while the Prime Minister tells us that he is starting a big discussion about our relationship with Europe, the Home Office does not appear to be 100% on board and the splits could not be more obvious. The Prime Minister is right to say that Brexit is like the emperor’s new clothes, but his position on Brexit, and that of the Government, could not be more like the emperor’s new clothes. His policy on Europe has not moved a single inch since the days of his predecessor and that is most obvious in the area of migration and asylum. I wonder whether that is because he knows that his Home Secretary, who used to be pro-European, is now a born-again blue Labour hard Brexiteer. The asylum system was left in total disarray by the previous Conservative Government, and it is still in a mess. They told us that borders would be controlled after their Brexit plan, but the opposite happened, and they are in denial about the problems that they have caused—we heard that again today. Their main policy on immigration is to team up with the Reform party to give us Brexit 2.0 and to follow Russia and leave the European convention on human rights. That would not only further isolate this country on the international stage, but it would trash the Brexit deal they negotiated and which they insist must be sacrosanct for ever. Do Conservative Members truly understand the consequences of the policy that they keep voting for and telling this House is the one thing that will solve this country’s asylum problems? They have clearly learned nothing from the last decade. Every undecided case fails the taxpayer, and asylum seekers too. Faster decisions mean we would not need large asylum accommodation sites, as referenced in the amendments in the name of my hon. Friend the Member for Bicester and Woodstock (Calum Miller). People who need protection must be given it; they must be supported in their integration and allowed to work so they can pay their way. Those who have no right to stay must be returned and the same logic applies to appeals. However, the appeals backlog has doubled under this Government. The Bill will not fix any of those problems. Instead, it will create a new bureaucracy that will continue to fail us all, and asylum seekers too. New clause 18 seeks to address that. Before the 2016 referendum, there were very few small boat crossings, but since the Conservative party’s Brexit, delivered in cahoots with the hon. Member for Clacton (Nigel Farage), more than 200,000 people have crossed the channel in small boats. Time and again they point at the mess that they have created.

The hon. Gentleman just said that we have the boat crossings because of Brexit. Does he have the figures to hand on the number of crossings in lorries through the channel tunnel back in 2002, when we were full members of the European Union?

I do not, but I know that they were lower than those who now arrive by small boats. [ Interruption. ] They were in the hundreds rather than the thousands, as I understand it, but I am willing to come back to the House and correct—and the right hon. Member might be here to take part in the discussion with me. This week, we saw the ludicrous spectacle of the shadow Home Secretary and some angry bloke from Reform shouting at each other in Piddington. It is, apparently, all about them. Given that they have effectively the same message on immigration and asylum and so much else, we can only conclude that that was little more than performative nonsense. They must collectively take responsibility for their contribution to the mess that has been created.

Touching on that performative point, new clause 66 is headed: “Criminal offence for legal professionals knowingly assisting illegal immigration”. That is a proposition put forward by Reform. In actual fact, the 1971 Immigration Act already covers that and the punishment is life imprisonment, whereas the new clause proposed by Reform seems to provide only for a simple fine for such lawyers.

I thank the hon. Member for his intervention. I wonder whether he is implying that the Reform party might be going soft on immigration, crime and law and order at the same time? Who knows? It is a good point, well made. I too was surprised to see that among the new clauses. The Conservative party and Reform told us that Brexit would let the UK take back control of borders, but the reality is that being outside the EU is a huge factor driving this crisis. According to research by the Oxford Migration Observatory, asylum seekers themselves tell interviewers that they are heading to the UK because we no longer have agreements with the EU. Those whose claims have failed in EU countries know that the UK offers a second bite at the cherry. We have become the de facto court of final appeal for every asylum seeker whose claim has failed in the European Union. Without access to the EU’s Eurodac database, we have no idea who they are or whether they have already been refused asylum by our neighbours and on what grounds. Without a watertight EU-wide agreement, we cannot hope to reassert control. The shadow Home Secretary knows this better than anyone, because a leaked audio recording has him admitting that, just before the end of the transition period in December 2020, the then Government realised that Brexit meant losing the Dublin agreement and that they could no longer, in his words, “rely on sending people back to the place where they first claimed asylum”. That is why the Liberal Democrats are calling for Members to back new clause 18, which would see the UK join the EU’s new migration and asylum pact. I have a sneaking suspicion that Labour MPs know this makes sense and, based on his comments, so does the Prime Minister. It is just a shame that the Home Secretary is lagging behind. Joining the pact would remove the incentive to come here. Indeed, under the rules of the pact, asylum seekers are obliged to seek help in the first country they arrive in and are safely processed onward. The Government are reportedly already negotiating access to the biometric database as part of the UK-EU reset. Why not just cut out the middleman and join the pact instead? It would be cheaper than the series of deals the Government are negotiating, and it would likely reduce the number of asylum seekers arriving. This is the only reasonable proposal for tackling small boat crossings. If Ministers will not countenance joining the pact, they should surely at least be able to support new clause 20, which simply asks for an assessment of Brexit’s impacts on migration—something that the Prime Minister has already started his big discussion about. On the topic of monitoring, why can Ministers not support an independent assessment of the economic impact of changes to earned settlement, as recommended in our new clause 21? On the point about impacts, may I briefly speak to the new clause tabled in the name of my hon. Friend the Member for Harrogate and Knaresborough (Tom Gordon)? When the Prime Minister arrived in Downing Street, he pledged to end homelessness. That is a laudable aim that everyone in this House would agree with, but sadly it is obvious that the measures in this Bill risk increasing the number of homeless people on our streets. New clause 6 seeks to unpick this problem. Other new clauses before us today arrive from the Conservative party and include even more extreme limits on grants of ILR than those put forward by the Home Secretary. Following on from the intervention by my hon. Friend the Member for Sutton and Cheam (Luke Taylor), Hongkongers in this country will wonder whether the Conservative party has decided they are no longer welcome here, because that is what the Tory amendments today suggest. If their intention is not to tell British national overseas visa holders that they are unwelcome, why not name them in the amendments specifically? What is required is a fair system that aligns grants of ILR for refugees broadly with the time peri

The Conservatives’ new clause 46 would introduce a £38,700 threshold, meaning that newly qualified nurses or serving British soldiers would be unable to bring their spouses here. To me, people who are serving our country deserve to have a right to family life. Does my hon. Friend agree that the Conservatives are so far off the mark and have completely abandoned British values?

My hon. Friend is right. That just goes to show how far away the Conservative party is from its traditional values, and how far they have drifted to the right as they seek to catch up with the hon. Member for Clacton (Nigel Farage). The party would be better off electorally if it took the advice of the Liberal Democrats and showed a bit more moderation.

I draw hon. Members’ attention to my entry in the Register of Members’ Financial Interests, which includes the support provided to my office by the RAMP—Refugee, Asylum and Migration Policy—Project. I thank the Minister and her colleagues for their engagement with me on part 1, which is where I focus my remarks, particularly in relation to amendments 55 to 59 and 66, tabled by my right hon. Friend the Member for Hayes and Harlington (John McDonnell). In Bill Committee, the Minister stated that the Government’s intention is to deliver a swift and fair decision-making body. I completely agree with that. Long, drawn-out appeals serve no one, and nor does poor-quality initial decision making. Many of us made that point on Second Reading. With nearly 40% of asylum appeals granted in the first quarter of this year and many more withdrawn, there is still some way to go, and it is the initial decision-making quality that most directly affects the appeals backlog. The appeals backlog is, of course, unenviable, but it is not clear that it is a permanent crisis. The Government have been successful in boosting judicial capacity in the first-tier tribunal, and the most recent tribunal statistics show receipts down and disposals up 30% on the same period last year. That should be celebrated. Before we go down the IIAA route, will the Minister produce an updated impact assessment that confirms whether the new appeals body will do a better job than the existing system, properly resourced, in clearing the backlog? If the proposed new appeal body is established, ensuring its independence, competence and fairness is paramount. Several amendments have been tabled in this vein. I welcome the introduction of an access to legal representation provision in clause 12. That is an area that the Justice Committee has recently investigated. Amendments 56 to 58, which I support, would strengthen that clause. The objective must be that everybody served with an appealable decision gets legal advice and representation, so will the Minister guarantee that that will be secured? That would be quicker in the long run. In her statement in November, I think the Home Secretary accepted that early legal advice was key to enabling all claims to be advanced in one go, which saves time in the long run. Let me dwell a bit longer on competence, which is addressed in amendments 55, 59 and 66. We are talking about individuals who are affected by often traumatising situations: people fleeing conflict and persecution, and people who may have been trafficked and be at risk of modern slavery. Appeal decisions are not only highly consequential, but hugely complex, requiring an in-depth understanding of the law and how it is applied. This extract from Lord Justice Underhill, in a case called Khan from the Court of Appeal in 2017, helps us to understand the complexity of the law that we are dealing with: “I have great sympathy for applicants trying to find their way through the maze of immigration and asylum procedure (quite apart from the shameful complexities of the substantive law)”. That makes good this truth: even a simple factual case will involve the application of complex law. That is why rigorous training will be required, and why minimum knowledge standards should be stated in the Bill. It makes no sense that, to represent an asylum seeker at appeal, someone must have passed a rigorous knowledge assessment, as they have to do under the Immigration and Asylum Act 1999, while there is no minimum requirement for the person deciding the case to have any immigration knowledge at all. It seems that supervision by legally qualified senior adjudicators of executive adjudicators will be a key feature of the system, but the senior adjudicators, who do have to be legally qualified, will, on the current wording, have far less experience than anyone working in a supervisory capacity elsewhere in the legal profession. I wish to raise two points. The first is an omission and the second is what I will describe in shorthand as the 10-year rule. First, on the omission, some 180,000 Ukrainian refugees who are resident in the United Kingdom are not covered by the Bill’s provisions and, sadly, nor are they covered by any of the amendments. Their status is uncertain—effectively, they are stateless. I hope that when the Minister replies, she will be able to clarify their position. In many cases, they have already been here for the best part of five years. Children who were in primary school are now in secondary school and will go on to further and higher education. People have established businesses and have jobs. Some will certainly, if the opportunity presents itself, wish to return to Ukraine; others regard themselves as British and wish to remain here. I hope the Minister will be able to explain when she replies that any accumulated years of residency in the United Kingdom will go towards a pathway to ensure they are able to remain here if they so choose. My second point is on the 10-year rule. Retrospective legislation, in my fairly long experience, almost invariably ends in tears, and I will not support it. I have no problem whatever with the Government or the Opposition formulating a proposal that the pathway to residency should be 10 years; I do have a problem with that being applied to those who are resident already, who have come to the United Kingdom in good faith, have established businesses, have jobs and families here, and have bought homes here in the expectation they will be on a five-year pathway. I believe that that retrospection is entirely wrong. The shadow Minister, my hon. Friend the Member for Mid Bedfordshire (Blake Stephenson), is the epitome of courtesy, and I hope that when he sums up, he will confirm that the proposal supported by the Opposition will not be retrospective, but will apply going forward.

This Bill is harmful on many fronts. It makes it harder for refugees to get settled status and reunite with their families. It significantly weakens our response to trafficking and modern slavery. It replaces the first-tier tribunal with an appeals body staffed by adjudicators who are not legally qualified. However, in the short time I have to speak, I will focus on its impact in relation to violence against women and girls. VAWG sector organisations describe the Bill as “far-reaching and devastating, particularly on those who are already vulnerable and who face severe marginalisation and discrimination.” Under its proposals, a migrant woman who is a victim-survivor of gender-based violence can lose her right to stay in the country due to the consequences of the abuse she has faced. The Bill’s public interest considerations will count against migrant women who are not financially independent, and it will heavily penalise those with criminal convictions. These proposals will punish women who have experienced economic abuse and exclusions from education or employment, women who have convictions relating to acts they were coerced or pressured into committing to meet their own basic needs, and women who have been criminalised for behaviour resulting from their own experiences of abuse or exploitation, exacerbated by the rise in perpetrator counter-allegations. For example, if a migrant woman retaliates after years of abuse by her British husband, and despite reporting the abuse to the police, is convicted and spends time in prison, this Bill would put her at high risk of deportation and being left with no route to settlement. The Bill also proposes that “no weight” should be given to family or private life formed when a person did not have leave to enter or remain, and that little weight be given to family life formed when someone’s immigration status was precarious. But many migrant survivors of male violence face immigration abuse from their perpetrators and therefore have no control and often no awareness of their immigration status. Coupled with the new earned settlement plans, a woman who has been a lawful resident of the UK for 10 years or more could be told she has no right to respect for the family and private life she has built here. That is so clearly wrong and so clearly at odds with the Government’s mission to halve violence against women and girls. If that mission is to mean anything, it must apply to all women, including migrant women. My amendment 42 would require a court or tribunal to take into consideration the effects of violence against women and girls when deciding whether an interference with a person’s article 8 rights is justified. In Committee, the Government argued against including a public interest consideration relating to VAWG in the Bill, since courts can already consider relevant circumstances. However, campaign groups such as Hibiscus Initiatives and Rights of Women make clear that a statutory requirement is needed to ensure that courts give VAWG appropriate consideration, which, in their experience, all too often does not happen. I fear that without amendments to the Bill, this Government will unwittingly punish many women twice for their own abuse and exploitation. Surely none of us can live with such a legacy. I urge the Government to reconsider.

Although I have recently assumed the role of my party’s immigration and asylum spokesperson, I am speaking today as a member of the Home Affairs Committee. Although I am not speaking on behalf of the Committee, I am, in the unavoidable absence of the Chair, offering reflections based on the Committee’s work in the areas covered by the Bill, rather than focusing on my party’s policy priorities. The creation of the independent immigration appeals authority under part 1 of the Bill risks perpetuating and almost certainly exacerbating the very problem it seeks to resolve. Staffing a first-tier tribunal with people from non-judicial backgrounds runs the risk of simply moving the backlog to the upper tribunal, as they discovered in Australia, where they had to abandon such an approach. Professor Richard Ekins of Oxford University warned of the very same thing in his evidence to the Bill Committee, and it is a point that the judicial head of the Danish Immigration Appeals Board also made when the Select Committee visited Denmark to observe its approach to asylum. The Select Committee learnt a large amount relevant to the Bill from its trip to Denmark, where the immigration system is often simplistically characterised as being hard-line on asylum. The reality is in fact far more nuanced and, in some respects, far more enlightened than the UK approach. In Denmark, accommodation is run mostly by non-governmental organisations, notably the Red Cross. It is an approach that changes the whole tone of the debate. Rather than making millions for “Asylum King” Graham King, the Danish Government award accommodation contracts on a not-for-profit basis. That contrasts with the UK, where such contracts are awarded on a cost-plus basis that incentivises commercial providers to spend more money, thereby increasing profits. The Prime Minister tells us he wants to roll back the tide of neoliberalism. Is there any more egregious example of its excesses than outsourcing for private profit the provision of substandard asylum accommodation, as seen on occasion by our Committee and as highlighted in last Sunday’s ITV documentary “Inside the Asylum Camp”, which highlighted deficiencies in the Crowborough camp in East Sussex, run by Graham King’s Clearsprings Ready Homes? That programme, which I urge all Members to watch, told a depressing story of inadequate safeguarding and considerable local hostility. The Danish approach, in contrast, takes a great deal of heat out of the issue, with local people volunteering to help inside the asylum accommodation, rather than protesting outside. The Committee was also told about one example of an asylum centre that the Danish Government sought to close but local people campaigned to keep open. Retrospective changes to the earned settlement rules were also considered by the Select Committee, which were of great concern to a number of its members. Indeed, I tabled an amendment articulating my concern that extending the length of time required for indefinite leave to remain for migrants who had played by the rules and already embarked on that path would cause “injustice, unintended consequences…damaging the UK’s reputation in the international labour market.” It is noteworthy that although my amendment was not accepted, some Labour Members either voted with me or abstained on the vote in Committee.

When I last spoke about the Bill, I highlighted the progress that we are already making in reforming our immigration system, including the return of 5,962 foreign national offenders in the past year, which is a 12% increase on the previous year. Those figures matter. They demonstrate that we can have an immigration system that is firm, effective and protects the public, while remaining fair and consistent with our international obligations, and that is precisely what the Bill seeks to deliver. For my South Norfolk constituents, the expectation is straightforward: a rules-based immigration system in which the rules are clear, the public interest is properly recognised, and those who have no right to remain here are dealt with fairly and effectively. Importantly, we can achieve that while maintaining our valuable membership of the European convention on human rights. I have no desire to see Britain abandon our principles and the protections that underpin that convention. However, membership must not mean that we cannot address the way that provisions have been interpreted, and in particular we must end the juridification of our politics, where an increasingly expansive and unfair interpretation of article 8 has sometimes allowed individual claims to frustrate the wider public interest. We need to restore a proper balance. Compassion and human rights matter, but so do public safety, the integrity of our borders and public confidence in the immigration system. Although it might sound reasonable to require the Government to negotiate our entry into the European Union’s pact on migration and asylum, there is a fundamental problem with new clause 18, because it seeks to compel the UK Government to commence negotiations with another sovereign body that is entirely free to reject those negotiations or their outcome. The last time I checked, Parliament could not force another country or institution to fulfil an action that it is perfectly entitled to reject, so my question would be this: what happens if the EU says no? The Government have then supposedly failed to meet a statutory obligation, despite having no power to deliver that outcome. That is not serious policy making; it is political theatre dressed up as legislation.
Is the hon. Member saying that we should never negotiate with any other country because it might say no? Is that not the whole point about negotiation?

No, I am saying that the new clause proposed by the Liberal Democrats is unenforceable. We must be serious about legislation that we try to pass in this House. If we try to pass legislation that finds us in the wrong, while also not being able to do the grown-up politics of international negotiations, we will look ridiculous in the eyes of our constituents. That brings me to the amendments tabled by His Majesty’s loyal Opposition. My constituents know exactly where the approach of performative politics gets us. We saw it with the Brook hotel, where asylum accommodation was placed just 500 yards down the road from residents, without proper consultation. People were left feeling ignored and taken for granted. That is what happens when politics becomes about headlines rather than delivering workable solutions and engaging with communities. The Bill seeks to take a different approach. It is compassionate but firm, protects our international commitments while restoring common sense, and it puts in place a rules-based system that the public can have confidence in. That is what South Norfolk residents expect Parliament to deliver, and it is time that we got on and passed the Bill. Another aspect of the Bill that is important to reiterate, and vital for my constituents, is the provision that allows the Secretary of State to require payment from people who have received asylum support. That is welcomed by my constituents, but it is vital to reiterate that there is a carve-out to ensure that minors, under the age of 18, who receive asylum support are not liable for those costs later on, which underlines the fact that the Bill is firm but fair. As the Bill goes forward for consideration in the other place, I hope we can show that we take these matters seriously. I thank the Bill Committee members from across the House for discussing the issue in a grown-up way. We need to take the heat out of the debate, so that we consider things that benefit our constituents and do not divide our communities.

There is much in the Bill that I agree with and support. However, there is a danger that it presents a missed opportunity to deliver a greater and better good, so most of my comments will address new clauses 4, 5 and 7. I thank the Independent Anti-Slavery Commissioner, Eleanor Lyons, the charities Hope for Justice, Unseen and the Human Trafficking Foundation, and, of course, the brilliant Clerks for the drafting of new clauses 4 and 5—I hope that will get me further assistance in future. The scope of the Bill is broad and it covers many aspects of the subject. When I was Chief Whip, I would probably have described it as something of a Christmas tree, as it both offers opportunities and presents problems for the Government. It touches on human trafficking, but it does not really seek to do anything. In this country we should be rightly proud of the historical role that this House played in tackling slavery right around the world, including the actions of the West Africa Squadron. We have led the way, not just in words and ideals but, just as importantly, with actions. Like many Members of the House, I feel proud of my small role—of course your role was much larger than mine, Madam Deputy Speaker—in the Modern Slavery Act, which all Members voted for when it was passed in 2015. In reality, that Act went some way towards making the moral arguments, but it did not go far enough on enforcement—there was no West Africa Squadron as a result of that Act. We talked a good talk, but we did not do enough to follow up, which is what I seek to amend through new clauses 4 and 5. The Bill should be about more than just a good argument and good deeds; it should be about actions flowing from those moral arguments. As was articulately put by the hon. Member for Stoke-on-Trent Central (Gareth Snell), the Modern Slavery Act went some way but does not have the enforcement element. I would be bolder than him and say that we have to go further than what is proposed in new clause 7. We know that there are certain parts of the world that produce goods under slave labour, so we can designate those areas, which is what new clauses 4 and 5 aim to do. The Minister for Border Security and Asylum is an incredibly thoughtful and passionate woman, who came into politics to make a difference, in common with so many of us in this House. The Bill tackles many issues, but it leaves that question open and it could do more. The issue of goods produced under slave labour is impacting our businesses in the United Kingdom. The Government say that they want to build more houses, but we do not want those houses to be built from bricks that are produced by slave labour in other countries. This is not a marginal thing—we are talking about almost 50 million people across the globe who are either in slave labour or indentured labour, almost the same number as the population of Spain. I beseech the Minister to work with me, the other organisations I mentioned and the Independent Anti-Slavery Commissioner to do everything we can do to ensure the Bill tackles those issues.

I very much support what the right hon. Gentleman is saying. Does he share my concern that, as these rules are crafted, victims of slavery and trafficking in our communities who might have found safe harbour in this country will be unable to get citizenship because of the good character requirement that we are introducing into law? Will he consider my amendment 75, which would support those victims of trafficking?

I thank the hon. Lady for drawing attention to amendment 75. I am afraid that I cannot read through it all at the moment, but I am very happy to look at it. She makes an important point. We have a duty to the victims of slavery, but we also have a duty to ensure that the legislation we already have on our statute book has teeth, with the ability to have an effect and an impact. As we go through this process, I urge the Minister to look at how we can improve this legislation and make it something that the whole House is able to support.

Today, across our country, hundreds of thousands of children were sitting in classrooms, eager to learn, laughing with their friends and planning for their futures. Those children are not strangers or a threat; they are simply children, and they deserve the opportunity and protection that our great nation offers. I will today speak to my amendments, which are designed to help ensure that is the case. Let me turn to my new clause 71. This Government have important ambitions to drive down child poverty and give every child in this country the best start in life. My new clause asks them to demonstrate how they will protect those commitments. The Women and Equalities Committee heard compelling evidence earlier this month about the impact of longer routes to settlement on children, and I have written to the Home Secretary from the Committee asking for greater clarity on pathways for children. In addition to commenting on the substance of my amendments, will the Minister provide that clarity and set out how this Government will protect the rights of children with these reforms? Let me turn to my amendment 76. Clause 41 of the Bill requires well-known indicators of child abuse to be damaging to a child’s credibility when determining whether they are a victim of modern slavery. The independent inquiry into child sexual abuse found that children frequently delay disclosing abuse because of fear, shame, threats and a lack of trust in adults. The Home Office’s own guidance explicitly recognises that conflicting accounts from children can be a common indicator of trafficking. Child victims often do not recognise themselves as victims and cannot consent to their own exploitation. I urge Ministers to amend the clause to ensure that recognised signs of child abuse are not used as reasons to fail to protect a victim of modern slavery. Amendment 77 would also extend protections for vulnerable young people who are at risk of exploitation by extending the child trafficking guardian measures to the age of 25 for looked-after children. Let me turn to my new clause 70. There is no more important responsibility than looking after children in care, providing those children who have already experienced significant trauma and pain with stability and opportunity, and helping those children to resolve their immigration status, but our current system is not working for children in care. Coram shared with me the story of Aisha, who lived in the UK from the age of six and was taken into care when she had just turned 13 years old. Aisha did not know that she had been brought to the UK on a temporary visa as a child. No one in children’s services knew how to resolve that, and no action was taken. Aisha still had no immigration status when she turned 18, which meant that she could not work, get a student loan or claim benefits, and she was barred in every practical way from leading an independent life. By that time, it was too late for any of the simpler and quicker routes to immigration status or citizenship that had been available to Aisha as a looked-after child. Coram’s research shows that at the end of 2021 there were 19,000 children and care leavers with an immigration or citizenship issue in England. For all those children, the lack of status or citizenship has a huge impact on their mental health, sense of belonging and ability to plan. As such, I welcome the Government’s commitment in their May 2025 White Paper to solve that problem—to establish a clear pathway to settlement for children in care who reach adulthood without having secured their immigration status, and to ensure that children who turn 18 and discover they do not have status are supported and able quickly to regularise their status and settle. That commitment was repeated in the November 2025 earned settlement consultation, but in the Government’s response to that consultation earlier this month, it seems to have changed. I wish to speak in favour of new clauses 1 and 2, which stand in my name. Both concern basic Government accountability—demonstrating that any proposed large asylum accommodation site is suitable, and explaining what the site will cost the taxpayer. Ministers justify moving to large sites on the grounds that they will reduce both the cost of hotels and the pressures their use creates in communities. The Government must demonstrate that their chosen approach will address those problems, because decisions taken in Whitehall have lasting consequences for the communities that are expected to accommodate these sites, and those communities deserve to see the evidence behind those decisions. The experience of my constituents in Bicester and its surrounding villages is that the Government have not provided this information for their proposed asylum centre at MOD Bicester. They have delayed publication, chosen an urgent planning route that reduces scrutiny, and cited vague security and commercial concerns as grounds not to publish key information or to redact it. New clause 1 would require a published suitability assessment before a site accommodates 300 or more people, including consultation with the relevant local authorities—something that did not happen in my constituency’s case. That assessment would cover accessibility, public services, infrastructure, environmental constraints and the impact on the surrounding community. MOD Bicester demonstrates why that is necessary, because even after a planning application, fundamental questions remain about transport, utilities, local services and the practical implications of developing the site. Cherwell district council’s objection to the planning proposal identified insufficient information across those areas. There is no supply of electricity, water, or sewage removal to a site that has never had accommodation before; there is, however, a Ministry of Defence training site still used as part of the £100 million bomb disposal training facility at MOD Bicester. As a result of the Government’s not providing that information, an incredible army of local volunteers has devoted hours to examining the application, working through redacted documents and identifying gaps. Those volunteers have brought information to light that was not previously public, showing that Ministers have not fully considered the implications of this proposal. New clause 1 would require Ministers to explain publicly why they consider a site suitable—if the evidence supports their decision, they should be willing to publish it. New clause 2 would require publication of the expected acquisition, construction, annual running and total costs before a site opens, alongside comparisons with alternatives and the assumptions behind the figures. Material changes before opening would require an updated assessment. The Government’s estimates of nightly costs are very inaccurate. Yesterday, in response to an urgent question I posed, the Minister claimed that large-scale asylum centres would be cheaper than hotels. However, due to the huge set-up costs associated with MOD Bicester, the Wrong Plan Wrong Site group estimates that the cost per bed per night will be nearly £235, fully £100 more than the cost at some other sites and over 60% higher than occupying similar hotel beds. It is especially important to see the Government’s statement of total expenditure, because the Home Office has a frankly terrible record of managing the cost of large asylum sites. It wasted £60 million on the Scampton site before abandoning it in 2024. Back in 2005, it wasted £28 million at the site at MOD Bicester, before rightly abandoning those plans. In March 2024, the National Audit Office reported that four large sites were forecast to cost £46 million more than hotels and fully £140 million more than the original estimate. The hon. Member for Stoke-on-Trent Central (Gareth Snell), along with other Members, rightly criticised the Government for not info

I support this legislation as someone who represents a proud working-class coastal town—a town that understands the importance of secure borders, fair rules, properly controlled immigration and a functioning asylum system, and also a town founded on compassion, decency and tolerance. No matter how hard some politicians try, those two things must never be considered contradictory. We can be a welcoming country and a country that controls its borders. We can uphold our international obligations while insisting that those who have no right to remain here leave. We can treat people humanely while being uncompromising about those who abuse our immigration system. Let me be absolutely clear that illegal immigration is unacceptable. People smugglers are criminals who exploit human misery for profit. Small boat crossings in the channel are not an acceptable immigration route, and I welcome the 40% fall that we have seen this year. No matter how many times politicians try to spin it, that 40% reduction is in individuals, not in boats. It is not about bigger boats; it is about the number of people coming across the channel. Our borders must be secure, our rules must be enforced, and those with no legal right to remain must be removed. The public are entitled to expect nothing less. We also need an asylum system that makes decisions quickly, prevents endless appeals and repeated claims that frustrate removal, and stops leaving people languishing in hotels at enormous expense to the taxpayer. That is why this Bill matters. It establishes an independent immigration appeals authority, tackles abuse of late and repeated claims, reforms the application of article 8 and the modern slavery framework, simplifies the protection system and introduces a mechanism for those with the financial means to contribute towards the cost of their support. These are important reforms to restore order, fairness and confidence, because compassion without control is not a sustainable immigration policy, but neither is control without compassion. We need to do both. There is a wider point, because whenever immigration is debated, particularly by some politicians on the right, we hear an increasingly familiar argument that immigration is responsible for everything that has gone wrong in our country. We must challenge that narrative, not because concerns about immigration are illegitimate—they are not—and not because population pressures have no consequences for housing, schools, healthcare and local services, because they absolutely do; we must challenge it because there is a fundamental dishonesty in blaming immigration for problems created or made considerably worse by political decisions and, may I say, the 40 years of neoliberalism that this country has experienced. Nowhere is it more important to challenge that narrative than in towns like mine. Immigration did not close our shipyards. It did not close our steelworks or dismantle the industries that once provided generations of Hartlepool families with skilled, secure, well paid employment. It did not cause the financial crash. It did not introduce austerity or make decisions to cut local government budgets or leave councils struggling to maintain essential services. Immigration did not sell off public housing, undermine our high streets or cause the decline of our public services. Those are the consequences of economic choices, inadequate investment and political neglect. Many of the politicians who are arguing today that immigration is the cause of all our problems are the same politicians who made the decisions to rip the heart out of towns such as mine. They presided over austerity, they oversaw deindustrialisation, they failed to invest in communities like mine, and now they want to tell working people that their problems can be explained by immigration. It is wrong, and it is an insult to the intelligence of working people. The people of Hartlepool know the difference between someone who is identifying

My name is attached to new clauses 4 and 5, tabled by my right hon. Friend the Member for Stone, Great Wyrley and Penkridge (Sir Gavin Williamson). As I said earlier, I have concerns about how the slavery prevention system will be applied to countries that we know are exploiting slavery, and I am sure that the Minister will respond to them. However, I now want to focus on new clauses 1 and 2, tabled by the hon. Member for Bicester and Woodstock (Calum Miller). I added my name to them in Committee, and I still support them. They make important points about transparency, and the ability to work out why things are happening. I am grateful to the immigration Minister for the letter that she sent me last week, and I am grateful for the offer that she made yesterday to meet me, but I should like to extend that. I am writing to her today to ask whether she will come to my constituency and meet me, and others, to see what is going on. New clause 1(3)(a) requires the Secretary of State to work with authorities, such as North Yorkshire council, on planning permission, because some local issues of this kind are best dealt with through a planning authority. New clause 1(2)(h) refers to “the likely impact of the proposed use of the site on the local community.” That is important. As the Minister knows, because I have mentioned it several times, I am talking about a quiet rural community consisting of 600 adults, where children play in the streets. A site with no sewerage, water or electricity that could be serviced would on its own create a huge number of HGV movements, along with coach movements. It would fundamentally change the nature of the village, and, as the Minister knows—I reiterated it again yesterday—personal safety is an issue. The village of Linton-on-Ouse is integrated into the site. I feel that new clause 1 would make it obvious to those doing the feasibility study, which will be given to the Minister, that the boundaries of the site were moved back and the housing that was inside it was brought into the village. One of the consequences was the building of a new playground, which is within yards of the accommodation where the illegal migrants will be held, and it will not be a secure site. New clause 1(2)(e) refers to “environmental, planning or infrastructure constraints”, and, as I have already said, there are huge constraints. The sewerage system cannot cope with a further 1,200 to 1,500 adults in a community of 600. I have received letters from Yorkshire Water saying that it cannot increase the supply because it does not think that the system would be able to cope with that increased pressure, and the local electricity grid has confirmed that it would take a decade to be able to supply the electricity that would be needed. Those are all important points, which is why I keep urging the Minister to come to the constituency and see what is happening for herself. What worries me is that when it comes to the feasibility study, it may just be necessary for these problems to be heard, so we will present to the Minister what we think. We can get round these problems, and the new clauses require the commitment that would have to be made. New clause 2(2)(d) makes an important point about the “estimated total expenditure over the period for which the site is expected to be used”. We in Linton-on-Ouse have been led to believe that the site will be in place for only three years, until 2029. That timeframe is getting smaller and smaller, so any estimates on costings are getting higher and higher, and becoming more economically unreasonable. I support new clauses 1 and 2, in the name of the hon. Member for Bicester and Woodstock. I also support new clauses 4 and 5, in the name of my right hon. Friend the Member for Stone, Great Wyrley and Penkridge, because I have concerns about slavery in our supply chains.

I voted against this Bill on Second Reading, and everything that has happened since has strengthened my opposition, both to what is in it and to the ill-advised speed at which it has been pushed through. I welcomed the Home Secretary’s decision to keep the five-year route to settlement for care workers, who came here in good faith on a promise, but if it is wrong to change the rules halfway through for care workers, why is it right to do so for everyone else who came here on the same understanding? For almost everyone earning under £50,000, the wait for indefinite leave to remain will double from five years to 10, but someone earning over £125,000 will wait only three years. Settlement is not being earned; it is being bought and flogged to the highest bidder. I am old enough to remember the global pandemic, when low-paid workers were essential. Refugees will now wait 20 years, or thirty if they arrived by small boat. That punishes people for how they were forced to flee, which is exactly what the refugee convention was designed to stop. These changes will hit people who are already here and who are part of our communities, and we will not even have a full impact assessment until after the policy has been implemented, when it will be too late to stop it. That is why I am pleased to support new clause 62, in the name of my hon. Friend the Member for Poole (Neil Duncan-Jordan). Nowhere is the injustice of wealth deciding someone’s status clearer than in the case of the children I discuss in my new clause 56. It would make sure that children pay only what it actually costs the Home Office to process their applications, not the inflated fee charged now, and it would make registration free for children born here. Their parents are living here legally, and these children are not migrants but are being treated as if they were. The law recognises that, and many of them have British birth certificates. This country is the only home they have ever known. They already have the legal right to be British, and we are simply charging them £1,000 for a right that the law says they already have. Neither these children nor their parents are what anyone in this House would call “illegal migrants”, and Members of different parties agree on that. Even the last Conservative Government agreed.
