They implemented a fee waiver and an end to the charge for looked-after children. Just a few years ago, wards of the state were being charged full price to register as British citizens, as my hon. Friend the Member for Reading West and Mid Berkshire (Olivia Bailey) mentioned. The fee waiver that was put in place is not working, as at one point more than half the people applying for it were being rejected. The Supreme Court has said that the level of the fee is a matter for Parliament. We are Parliament, and that decision is ours. The Conservatives accepted that these children are not migrants and should not be held back. The Liberal Democrats, the Greens, Your Party, Plaid Cymru, the SDLP and the SNP have gone further, and in the nearly seven years in which I have been arguing for the provisions in new clause 56, they have lent their signatures to the idea that the fee should be scrapped or cut to cost. Labour backed this in opposition and assured me that it would be resolved in government, so why am I still saying the same thing nearly seven years later? I withdrew the last amendment I tabled, because the Government assured me that they would fix this issue. Well, fool me once, because nothing has changed. I am back again, and I will keep coming back until someone with the power to change something actually does so. Are we so obsessed with proving how tough we are on migrants that we are willing to put at risk the safety and future of children who we all agree are not migrants? Did we learn anything from the Windrush scandal? Are we not ashamed? I am ashamed of us. With so much in this Bill to object to, I had hoped that we could at least get one thing done on
Order. I will reduce the time limit to four minutes after the next speaker.

I will speak in support of the Reform party’s new clauses 63 to 65. This Government’s open borders policy is having a profound effect on our culture, our freedoms and our safety. The lack of will in this Government and the last to secure our borders and defend this country from invasion is a dereliction of duty. The principal function of any Government—

No. I am going to make some progress. The principal function of any Government is to defend their people from a hostile threat, yet the Government are doing the opposite. The progressive liberal elite needs to wake up and see what is happening to this country. If we do not stop the invasion of the UK, we will not recognise this country in years to come. From Bradford to the Edgware Road, there are already places that we will never get back and that would be unrecognisable to our forefathers. It is the duty of Government to protect our culture, our values and our laws for our children and their children. I have just had my first grandchild, and when I hold that beautiful little baby girl in my arms, I wonder what the future holds if we do not stand up for our family values and our communities. We need to protect the British way of life. The social contract in this country is broken. British citizens need to be able to defend our history, be proud of our achievements and teach our children to be proud of this country, without fear of a backlash from those with an alternative agenda. We need to stop apologising for our past; we need to celebrate our past. This Government are more interested in entertaining reparations to countries for things that happened 200 years ago than imposing sanctions on those same countries when their citizens are still doing us harm. For example, why are this Government not demanding reparations from Pakistan for the victims of grooming gangs? That is why we have tabled new clause 63. The way things are going, our schools, our police and our Parliament will be so full of toxic ideology that we will not recognise them any more. Indeed, in some instances it is too late, with schools that do not speak English, and police who automatically assume the white guy is racist and leave him to die on the ground. Furthermore, we are enabling the establishment of a parallel legal system in this country, one that operates in the shadows and allows the subjugation of women. Both this Government and the last have been so obsessed with not being labelled racist that they are prepared to sacrifice the safety of women on the altar of inclusion. Just look at the grooming gangs scandal. They refuse to publish available data revealing the ethnicity of those who commit sexual assault crimes against women. We know that immigrants from countries such as Afghanistan, Sudan, Eritrea and Somalia are 20 times more likely to commit a sexual offence, yet we still let them in and grant them asylum. This could be solved by Reform’s new clause 65. Not only that, but we are housing 1,500 foreign national offenders at taxpayers’ expense, 900 of whom are failed asylum seekers, and there I refer to new clause 64. Unless we leave the ECHR—removing article 8, which is so abused by asylum seekers and their human rights lawyers—unless we repeal the Human Rights Act 1998 and unless we vote against this Bill today, we will be powerless to stop the hostile invasion of this country.

New clause 62, tabled by my hon. Friend the Member for Poole (Neil Duncan-Jordan), would prevent the Home Secretary from retrospectively changing the qualifying period for ILR for skilled worker visa holders already in the UK. While there has been something of a concession for care workers, the change affects remaining workers, and the Bill proposes that the language, income, residence or other settlement requirements will be made harder once someone holds the visa itself. People made lifechanging decisions and came to the UK under one set of rules, only for the goalposts to be moved. This situation in the Bill is not just a breach of faith, but, from the perspective of many of my constituents and myself, an utter betrayal. I am concerned about the Government proceeding in this manner today because I believe it will result in a judicial review. In fact, I think that the proposals to narrow article 8 will result in challenges at the European Court. I simply cannot look my constituents in the eye—many of whom have been in touch once again over the past two weeks—and support this Bill. I opposed it on Second Reading, and I will continue to oppose it. I want to place on the record my support for other amendments tabled by my hon. Friends the Members for Clapham and Brixton Hill (Bell Ribeiro-Addy), for Nottingham East (Nadia Whittome) and my right hon. Friend the Member for Hayes and Harlington (John McDonnell). I also wish to speak to new clause 3, tabled in my name. Nobody should be forced to choose between leaving an abusive situation or remaining in it out of fear of immigration enforcement, but that is the reality faced by migrant survivors in this country. We know that hundreds of migrants who report domestic abuse have their details shared with immigration enforcement every year. These routine referrals allow perpetrators to weaponise immigration status against victims, providing abusers with a tool of coercive control and a means to evade justice. It prevents victims and survivors from accessing statutory services, including healthcare and/or social services, or from receiving the support that they deserve. This harms not only the Government’s violence against women and girls agenda, but their ability to tackle other abhorrent crimes in relation to modern slavery, labour exploitation, sexual offences and more. There is a clear, unacceptable harm to women and other victim-survivors that cannot be ignored any longer. My new clause would create a statutory firewall that would prevent the personal data of victims, witnesses or reporters of offences being used for immigration investigation or enforcement. I am pleased that the new clause has received the backing of Members across this House, along with specialist organisations and charities. Successive Governments have also recognised the public harm that is created by the interface between immigration enforcement and our essential public services, but they have shamefully refused to take the action that would resolve it. Indeed, as has been made clear by the Step Up Migrant Women campaign, a statutory firewall is the only way to protect migrant victims of abuse. The campaign states: “If the amendment is not introduced, this Bill risks facilitating the abuse and exploitation of migrant people in the UK”. I hope that Ministers have listened to my remarks and that they will seriously consider this new clause and meet me and members of the campaign to discuss how they will ensure that our laws do not cause further and greater harm to migrant victims of crime, including survivors of domestic abuse.

Before I begin my remarks, I want to address the speech by the hon. Member for Runcorn and Helsby (Sarah Pochin), which was, in my opinion, one of the most disgusting and obnoxious speeches I have ever heard in this House. She castigates whole cultures and communities as deviant and not welcome in this country—the sheer quasi-racism at the heart of all her remarks should shame her. This is why it is so important that Reform never gets within a whiff of power in this country. As we get to the end of another Bill on immigration and asylum, I am trying to think of all the immigration Bills that I have been involved in over the past 25 years; I think I can probably compete with the right hon. Member for Hayes and Harlington (John McDonnell) on being a veteran of these particular debates. These immigration Bills have two things at their heart: the first is making it as difficult as possible for people to come to these shores; the second—and probably more important—thing it has to do is making life miserable for the poor souls who actually make it here. This Bill does that absolutely perfectly. The Government say that they are trying to achieve a fair, efficient and sustainable asylum system. The Bill achieves none of those seemingly noble objectives. Instead, it introduces certain reforms that risk weakening safeguards fundamental to fair asylum procedures, and it could undermine the very conditions needed for successful integration.

My hon. Friend is making his usual excellent speech, and I agree with everything he has already said. Does he agree that this relentless focus on controlling immigration and asylum applications is having serious unintended consequences? In my constituency, there is an existential threat to many parts of the fishing industry, particularly in the processing side. Does he further agree that new clause 36 has some merit in this regard, and that the Government should rethink their approach in this area as it affects the fishing industry?

I am grateful to my hon. Friend, who is a doughty champion for the Scottish fishing industry. He gets up and defends his constituents’ interests in a way that is an exemplar for this House. He is absolutely spot on. Let me turn to what this Bill does not do. It will not improve decision making, reduce reliance on expensive and unsuitable accommodation or create the safe legal routes that we really require in order to undermine the business model of the people smugglers. Instead, it will introduce further complex and bureaucratic systems with no clear benefit. One thing that is heartening about the Bill is the sheer number of amendments that have been tabled to it—that is pretty unusual. I will support the amendment from the hon. Member for Poole (Neil Duncan-Jordan). I believe that there is a real opportunity to press it to a Division, so I encourage Labour Members who are concerned about the rightward drift of immigration policy to get solidly behind us and ensure that we at least do something to improve this Bill on the basis of so many of the constituents that we are here to represent.

I rise to support new clause 62, which is in my name. Not only does it have the support of a number of MPs from a wide range of parties, but it has the backing of 10 of the country’s trade unions. That is because it goes to the heart of their understanding of what a fair and decent society looks like. I begin by welcoming the recent announcement by the Home Secretary that many of those working in the care sector and other health and educational settings will continue to be eligible for the five-year route to settled status. I pay tribute to Unison and its general secretary Andrea Egan for the campaign they have been running on this issue. This decision recognises the importance of this group of workers, but I believe that the same arguments that are used for this group can quite easily be applied to those currently on the skilled worker visa as well.

I represent Ealing Southall, where many people came from Punjab in the ’60s and ’70s to work. They learned English and integrated into this country. Is my hon. Friend aware that the 1.1 million skilled workers due to settle in this country shortly would not need to be able to speak English to a good standard under his amendment? Surely he does not think that we should overturn the Government’s sensible proposal that people who want to stay in this country on a skilled worker visa should be able to speak English well, not least as these workers may well not be able to understand their rights at work without it?

I do not accept my hon. Friend’s analysis of what my new clause would do. For many of those affected, it is not just about waiting longer for settlement. They have made significant career, financial and family decisions based on the existing immigration rules. The plan to double the qualifying period for settled status risks alienating skilled workers who benefit the UK every single day. Retrospection is wrong, and my new clause would give voice to that. I urge every hon. Member across the House who disagrees with retrospection to back it.

My hon. Friend is making a typically eloquent speech. If I have read his new clause correctly, it would overturn the Government’s tightening of settled status eligibility for people who have committed crimes and had a custodial sentence of less than 12 months. That could include those convicted of domestic abuse. I am sure that is not his intention, but that does appear to be his new clause’s effect. Surely he cannot expect us to vote for that.

My hon. Friend has obviously been briefed extremely well. I do not accept that analysis. I will come to that point in my closing remarks. The Government have described settlement as a privilege to be earned, but that ignores the valuable contribution that these workers have already made to our country, the economy and their local communities. They pay their taxes, they pay the immigration health surcharge and they pay their visa fees; now, we are effectively saying “You haven’t paid enough.” Not only that, but constituents of mine working in the NHS, such as scientists and IT staff, see medical staff retaining a five-year route while they will have to wait 10 years to claim settled status. Both groups of workers are contributing to the public sector—they may even be on similar wages and working in the same building—but one group has better treatment than the other. That cannot be right. We need to recognise not just the contribution that migrant workers make but the real consequences of driving them away. According to the Migration Advisory Committee, individuals on the skilled worker visa are projected to make a net positive fiscal contribution over their lifetimes, with a total impact of £5.9 billion on our public services. I will now deal with the question asked by my hon. Friend the Member for Hartlepool (Mr Brash). Let us be clear about this: the new clause would in no way constitute a free pass for people with persistent criminal records. The Government already have wide powers to deport foreign national offenders, and rules allow for leave applications to be refused or cancelled due to various criminal activities. So let us not go down that dead end. I offer the Government this olive branch before the Division on new clause 62. They could consider starting the proposals from a later date, such as 2028. They could offer a five-year qualifying route to those who have already completed over half their stay. They could reduce the qualifying salary to the skilled worker visa threshold of £41,000, which is similar to that in Scotland, or they could broaden out the list of roles covered in annex C of “A Fairer Pathway to Settlement” to include the very NHS workers I have been talking about. Our values reflect the country we are. I urge the Government to apply those values to this issue and rethink their stance on skilled workers.

The Bill will do so much harm to people who have faced torture or political oppression, who feared for their lives in war and who need their human right to leave their country and be given asylum to be fully respected. It will do harm to children and families, whose family life human rights will be eroded, and to victims and survivors of abuse, violence and exploitation. Justice will be curtailed under the Bill, processes will be made more discriminatory and unfair, and the tax on successful refugees will push people who are trying to build a new life into desperate poverty. It will not bring communities together, but will further divide them. The shadow Minister was right to note that Green Members oppose the Bill, and we will continue to do so. The amendments that I will talk about relate to the refugee tax—the payment proposals in part 4 of the Bill. Amendment 1 to clause 28 changes the words “without becoming destitute” in the requirements for regulations to prevent harm being done by demanding payments from refugees who have needed support while claiming asylum, instead ensuring that we prevent them or their households from becoming impoverished. Without that amendment, the Bill will push into ongoing poverty people who have successfully claimed asylum and are just trying to rebuild their shattered lives. Amendment 2 to the same clause would extend exemptions from the refugee tax to victims of modern slavery, survivors of sexual or gender-based violence or domestic abuse, as well as survivors of torture. Support organisations point out that the Government’s violence against women and girls strategy says of survivors: “financial insecurity should never force them back to an abusive partner.” Yet, without the amendment, the Bill risks doing exactly that. Why not give people the right to work to support themselves while they are waiting for Government decisions, which are taking too long and are wrong in far too many cases? I have tabled several other amendments and, as I argued in Committee, I want all of part 1, which creates the appeals authority and reduces access to justice, removed and clause 41 struck out completely, because it cruelly seeks to doubt the testimony of survivors of modern slavery who already face so many barriers to speaking up. I have also tabled new clauses 16 and 17 to remove the current uses of artificial intelligence from Home Office systems for summarising asylum information and to prevent its use in any part of decision making in future. I do not need lots of time, because I spent hours in Committee arguing against the cruelty, discrimination and neglect of our international duties in the Bill, which the Government have continued to ignore. The new Prime Minister has pressed on with the Bill, proposed under the previous Administration, which plays into the hands of the far right’s narratives, instead of doing what is right, standing up for the right to asylum and making sure our processes are without errors, fair, efficient and just. A hostile environment, a tax on rights and the enforced disbelief of people’s experiences will not stop the boats, but will create more harm and more opportunities for criminals. I hope we can amend some humanity back into the Bill and if not, we should vote it down.

I rise to support a number of new clauses tabled by colleagues. There were the points made by my hon. and learned Friend the Member for Folkestone and Hythe (Tony Vaughan) on new clause 71 and the points made by my hon. Friend the Member for Reading West and Mid Berkshire (Olivia Bailey). There is new clause 62, discussed in the cracking speech just made by my hon. Friend the Member for Poole (Neil Duncan-Jordan), and new clause 56 tabled by my hon. Friend the Member for Clapham and Brixton Hill (Bell Ribeiro-Addy). I rise also to put forward amendments 43 and 75 tabled in my name. I do that because I want to speak up for the taxpayers in this nation; because I want us to have a fair and well-managed asylum and immigration system. I do not want open borders, and I recognise that every claim needs to be properly checked and that not everyone will meet our threshold. But many do. Many people coming to this country make an important contribution to our economy and to our society, and it saddens me that we have to say that so clearly in this Chamber. After all, that is why we gave those people a visa in the first place. If you shop at Marks and Spencer; if you have ever looked to the Bank of England, set up by the Huguenots, who share a surname with myself and the hon. Member for Clacton (Nigel Farage), who is not in his place; if you have ever thanked the Afghans who helped keep our soldiers safe when they were in Afghanistan; and if you have ever cheered on most premiership football teams, sung songs from “Les Miserables” by Victor Hugo who fled to the UK for safety, been served coffee, taken medicines that have been invented by immigrants and refugees, lived in houses built by them, or fallen in love with one—or, indeed, your family members have—you will know that we would be lost as a nation without the immigration and refugees that we have taken in. Somebody needs to say that on the record because then, when we look at a managed immigration system, we will ensure that it is not a hostile one, but a fair one. The amendments that I have put forward today reflect a truism that the great Tony Benn used to say: Governments treat refugees how they would like to treat the public if they could get away with it. The dysfunction of the Home Office should not fall on those people who are fleeing persecution, yet many of us will have told constituents in good faith that the rules that came in just last November around settled status for refugees would not apply to those who had not sought status before 5 March. It was in a footnote in the earned settlement proposals that the Government chose to swipe away that protection, having told this House that they would not do that.

It is no surprise that there are no Reform MPs in the Chamber. They are not serious about immigration. They are more serious about causing divisions in society. I want to talk about a constituent of mine, Faraz. He went to university and fought through depression to find work in a local accounting firm. Faraz received his refugee status in November 2022. He would have been eligible for indefinite leave to remain in a year’s time, but now, thanks to the proposed changes to earned settlement, he has been told that he is not contributing enough to deserve indefinite leave to remain after five years. Faraz came to this country as a refugee, but he did not come here to claim benefits or leech off the state. All he wants is the status he deserves: the recognition that his contribution to our country warrants a permanent place among its people—the status that our country promised him in 2022. He pays his taxes, he pays his health surcharge to fund NHS care that he never uses, and he works for a local enterprise that helps people every day. Now he has been left shellshocked by the changes. He has been left to ask: what did he do wrong? What more could he do to show that he belongs? The answer to that question is simple. There is nothing he could have done, because this Government have had it in for legal, hard-working migrants ever since the far right came to prominence. The changes to earned settlement are nothing but a cynical appeal to the interests of people who think that any amount of immigration, no matter how small, is wrong. Just because the Government have softened the rules for carers, it does not make it any less cruel to retrospectively change the rules for everyone else. Hundreds of thousands of people came to this country on the clear promise of settlement after five years. They trusted the system, and that system is letting them down.
Many of my constituents in Stratford-on-Avon have made long-term decisions about careers, housing, education and employment, relying on the rules that were in place—
Order. The hon. Lady should address her comments through the Chair, not facing the back of the Chamber.

I apologise, Madam Deputy Speaker. Many of my constituents have made their home here. They came here through established pathways years ago, and now they find that the ground under their feet has moved. Retrospective changes risk breaking the trust between the state and the individual, so does the hon. Gentleman agree that we should have meaningful transitional pathways for people who are already on the established settlement route?

I wholeheartedly agree with the hon. Member. It cannot be fair or just to apply the rules retrospectively. People have come to this country, paid their taxes, worked hard and contributed to society on a promise that they would get their indefinite status within five years. Pulling the rug from beneath their feet cannot be right. It is not serious policy to make coming to this country impossible or unattractive. It is not moral to turn back on our promises and ruin the lives of hard-working people in order to serve selfish political interests. The hon. Member for Runcorn and Helsby (Sarah Pochin) did not mention the Reform party’s new clauses 65 to 67. That is no surprise, because they show that Reform is not in touch with reality. The party is not really interested in driving forward sensible policies around immigration, because if it had done its homework, it would have realised that these measures are already incorporated in section 25 of the Immigration Act 1971, which covers facilitating or assisting illegal migration. In fact, the 1971 Act provides for a harsher penalty: after a recent amendment in 2022, people can go to prison for life. However, Reform’s new clauses suggested that people would get a simple fine. That shows that the party is just performative and wants to capture headlines. I hope that the country sees it for what it is. I will vote against the Bill. We need an immigration system that upholds our legal obligations to refugees and asylum seekers while valuing the contributions of those who form the bedrock of our economy, public services and society. I urge others to do the same.

I draw hon. Members’ attention to my entry of the Register of Members’ Financial Interests, as I am a board member of the Human Trafficking Foundation. I am pleased to see some strong and robust measures in the Bill, which, after 15 years working on immigration policy, I think will make a tangible difference. First, I strongly welcome the creation of safe routes. We are not living in the world of 70 years ago. With mass international travel, successive global conflicts and migration pressures, a combination of safe routes and core protection is a good balance if we want to preserve and reform a refugee system so that it survives. I completely condemn the comments of the hon. Member for Runcorn and Helsby (Sarah Pochin) in her vile characterisation of the immigration system, but I also strongly believe that we cannot say that any reform of immigration is somehow a drift to the far right. We must keep reforming the system so that it is manageable in the future. I am pleased that some of the concerns I set out on Second Reading are addressed in the clauses on the reform of the appeals process, particularly measures on prioritising public interest cases and expanding or contracting the system dynamically. That will make the system effective while addressing the concerns of the public, whose trust has been eroded by the legacy system. As always with immigration policy, the issue is not just the principles, but state capacity—that is, can the Home Office adequately grip the system? That brings me to the issue of asylum costs. I agree that refugees should contribute if they are able to pay, but the structural and systemic flaw in the costs of asylum lies in the asylum accommodation contracts. The Prime Minister has spoken passionately and powerfully about the impact of decades of centralisation and privatisation, the outsourcing state and HMO Britain. I absolutely agree, and nowhere is that more pertinent than the asylum accommodation system. I have been sounding the alarm on this for two years and have been approached by multiple people speaking privately about egregious failures—allegations of data manipulated to mislead the Government, failure of the Government to conduct basic audits, glaring flaws in supply chain oversight and an extraordinarily opaque network of interconnected companies and directorships allowing individuals based in tax havens to extract substantial sums of public money while our poorest communities bear the consequences. On top of that, there are safeguarding failures. It is a scam and it is wrong. I want to be clear that I welcome the Government’s progress and many of the Bill’s measures, alongside a reduction in small boat crossings and hotel use, faster decisions, increasing returns and upstream work with our international partners. These are practical, substantial measures in contrast with the gimmicks and, frankly, ridiculous moves of the last Government. But I say to Ministers that we will not radically restore public confidence unless we grip these contracts at the heart of the system. I hope the Minister can reassure the House that the pilots proposed last year are continuing and that they do not require primary legislation to have an impact on the system. While I wait for that, and I assure the Minister that I will keep asking, I strongly welcome the measures in the Bill.

There is agreement across the House that our asylum system needs reform, and it is right that the Government are bringing order to it, but it should not be at the expense of compassion and fairness. Ask any parent what safety means and they will say it means the safety of their family, which is why I support amendment 78, tabled by my hon. Friend the Member for Westmorland and Lonsdale (Tim Farron), which would ensure that refugees granted protection here can be reunited with close family without fees or financial barriers. Family reunion was one of few safe and legal routes used overwhelmingly by women and children. Keeping families together allows refugees to rebuild their lives. Where amendment 78 would bring fairness for families kept apart, new clause 21, tabled by my hon. Friend the Member for Cheltenham (Max Wilkinson), would bring fairness to families kept waiting, preventing changes to indefinite leave to remain until an independent economic assessment is laid before Parliament. Doubling the qualifying period from five years to 10 years and applying it retrospectively is deeply unfair on people who have built their lives here under the rules as they stood. My constituency of Eastleigh has a proud history of welcoming refugees. On Friday, I met a constituent from Afghanistan—a transport engineer keeping our roads running, whose wife makes covers for military aircraft for the Ministry of Defence. They pay their taxes, own their own home and were due settlement in December 2028, but they now face waiting years longer. A working, tax-paying family supporting our infrastructure and armed forces is potentially being left in limbo—how can that be right? Although I welcome the Government keeping the five-year British national overseas route, a constituent who worked hard to pass their B1 English exam after the Government confirmed that this was the standard then saw the bar raised to B2. That is a breach of good faith. Will the Minister commit to honouring B1 qualifications already obtained? Those who have shown this country nothing but good faith deserve a system that treats them with humanity and dignity.

I have 18 amendments down on the amendment paper, so I am relieved that we are not down to a three-minute time limit—this is no way to legislate. This will affect hundreds of thousands of people. It will affect nearly 1,000 at the detention centre in my constituency, the 2,000 in hotels and maybe another 2,000 in the constituency. We need to think about programme motions in future, because this is little short of a disgrace, and I hope that it is taken into account in the other place when they look at some of these issues. I will zip through some of the amendments I have tabled. On new clause 15, 40 years ago I met a group called Kalayaan, which was trying to organise overseas domestic workers—some of the most exploited workers in our country. These are the people who care for the children of rich people, who wash up and clean and so on. They have no rights. We campaigned and secured a work visa for them. We have tried to improve it at different times so that they can change employers if they continue to be abused, but the work visa arrangements that we have at the moment mean there is no time for them to even get through another application to find an alternative employer. My new clause would simply give them more time and enable them to change to a new visa, so that they can protect themselves. Otherwise, they will continue to be exploited. I do not think it is much to ask, and it is supported by the Independent Anti-Slavery Commissioner, whom I thank for her support. I have tabled amendments 64 and 55 to clause 2. My hon. and learned Friend the Member for Folkestone and Hythe (Tony Vaughan) has raised some of the issues, but let us be clear: in the adjudication system at the moment, no one will be legally qualified or have sufficient experience in this field. We have been told that they will have adequate training, but we do not know what that training will consist of, and there have been no pilots and no experimentation. Adjudicators will be deciding on the application of article 3 and article 8, and these will inevitably be contested hearings, because as we all know, this is one of the most complex areas of law. All I am asking is that they should have at least five years of legal experience.
With an immediate three-minute time limit, I call Iqbal Mohamed.

I do not think this has been raised so far. The UK fertility rate in 2014 was 1.81 children per woman. It had dropped to 1.41 children per woman in 2024. To maintain the population of the UK as it is today without immigration, the fertility rate needs to be about 2.1 children per woman—so just to maintain our population, we need immigration. I welcome that the Government are retaining the five-year route for healthcare workers and care workers, including those who are exploited and did not have a role here, to allow them to find work elsewhere. That is extremely appreciated by my constituents in Dewsbury and Batley, where we have hundreds of immigrant healthcare workers and carers, so I thank the Government for that. I support new clause 62, tabled by the hon. Member for Poole (Neil Duncan-Jordan), which would protect existing skilled worker visa holders. Recently I have been inundated with emails—like other Members, I am sure—from constituents who are concerned about what this change will mean for them and their loved ones, especially for skilled worker visa holders. Skilled worker visa holders are people such as my constituent, Ali, who entered the UK lawfully with his family and spent two years waiting for a decision on his asylum claim, followed by another four years under protection. During that time, Ali obtained a PhD at his own expense and worked, paid taxes and contributed to our country. He has invested considerable time, money and effort in developing his qualifications and contributing to British society, while building a stable future for himself and his family. It is deeply unfair that, after these years of lawful residence, employment, education and contribution, Ali may now face up to 20 years before settlement or be required to restart a completely new qualifying period. Another constituent of mine, James, has written to me because he is worried about his partner, who moved here from Vietnam six years ago. Since then, she has studied, worked and built her future in the UK. She has invested over £150,000 in her British education, tuition fees, NHS surcharges and visa fees. My appeal to the Government, to echo many other Members across the House, is that this retrospective extension—

I support the Bill, as I do new clause 10 and Government amendments 7, 8 and 24, which seek to improve decision making, and ensure that appeals are dealt with swiftly. I listened with interest to the hon. Member for Mid Bedfordshire (Blake Stephenson) who said that the Bill fails to prescribe the appropriate medicine, but I am afraid I do not accept that from the party that created the system that they now call broken. I also wish to address another Conservative idea. Conservative Members often make the case for small government—indeed, I remember a debate last year in which the hon. Gentleman decried huge Government spending and the rapid establishment of new quangos. They had that libertarian zeal in government when the Home Office budget was slashed by a quarter in real terms in the decade from 2010, when funding specifically allocated for immigration enforcement fell every year between 2013 and 2020, and when the National Crime Agency was made to operate with around one in 10 empty posts. To me there is a fundamental contradiction, because a small state cannot be a secure state. If we make sustained cuts to public services, as the Conservatives did, we cannot expect to become safer.

Another legacy of the previous Government was their privatisation of the asylum system, which resulted in the profit motive becoming part of that system and in companies targeting constituencies such as mine, and that of my hon. Friend, because of our low-cost housing. The damage that did was intolerable. Is that another legacy of the broken Government who we got rid of in July 2024?

I agree, and the broken system we are talking about today is a free market system that an active Government need to address. That is why we passed the Border Security, Asylum and Immigration Act 2025, and increased investment in illegal working arrests and visits to the highest level on record. It is why we have put in more staff and sped-up asylum decision making to a 24-year high, and why the reforms in the Bill are necessary, including Government new clause 10. The British people are fair-minded and do not resent those who genuinely need protection, but they cannot understand why decisions take years, why appeals drag on endlessly, and why people with no right to be here can stay in limbo while costs continue to rise. It is right that the appeals authority is established to speed up decision making, and common sense that we address the obvious abuse of the legal system with a single appeal route to prevent last-minute claims. It is reasonable to tighten our interpretation of article 8, particularly in the case of serious offenders—I echo the comments of my hon. Friend the Member for South Norfolk (Ben Goldsborough) in that regard, as well as about the holes in new clause 18. Ultimately this is about a progressive Government intervening in an uncontrolled market, as we would in so many others, to ensure that working-class communities are protected. The Bill is in that Labour tradition. It will strengthen our asylum system and our response to border security.

Amendment 78 would return to the default position for refugee family reunion visas. The Home Secretary’s statement on 2 November means that refugee family reunion is now available only to those on the protection, work and study route, and not to refugees who have core protection status. It will therefore be out of reach for most newly recognised refugees. It means that any refugee who has a disability, long-term health issue or caring responsibilities and is therefore unable to work or study, will be unable to reunite with their family. That is cruel and it is shameful. It is estimated that 20,000 people have been denied access since that change was introduced. In the past, 93% of those using the visa were women and children. As was the case in Australia when a similar change happened, we can now expect there to be an increase in the number of women and children seeking irregular and more dangerous routes to the UK. Again, that is cruel and shameful. Research by the British Red Cross highlights how family separation can undermine refugees’ integration. Red Cross ambassador Hamed Amiri, a refugee from Afghanistan, said: “That separation doesn’t just hurt emotionally; it stops people from being able to rebuild their lives. You can’t really settle into a new community, learn, work, or heal when part of you is still elsewhere, still unsafe. I know what a difference it makes to feel safe with the people you love most by your side.” Why would we want to prevent that? However, that is the Home Secretary’s intention. Surely family reunion should remain an entitlement for those who we have recognised already as being in need of protection, and therefore unable to return to their country of origin, rather than being wrongly treated as a reward for economic contribution. The Home Secretary has said that the Home Office wants to apply the same rules to everyone, yet the UNHCR advises that refugees are in a very different position to other households. Of course they are, and their needs and experiences need to be respected in a separate visa. Earlier on, I heard the hon. Member for Runcorn and Helsby (Sarah Pochin) make her speech, which was shameful. She talked about British values. There is often a conflation of British values and Christian values, and people will talk about those Christian values very often not understanding what on earth they are talking about. My Christian values tell me that families belong together, and that people who have fled war or persecution are my neighbour and need the support of their loved ones. They need protection—they should not have to earn stability and happiness. This policy will make things harder for recognised refugees who have already experienced war or persecution. It will penalise the most vulnerable women and children, and push people into the hands of people smugglers. We should be responding with compassion and humanity, not with shameful cruelty. Being with family should not be a luxury—it is a very basic human need. Every family deserves the chance to be safe.

I wish to speak to new clause 62 in the name of my hon. Friend the Member for Poole (Neil Duncan-Jordan). The new clause would prevent the Secretary of State from retrospectively changing the qualifying period for indefinite leave to remain for skilled worker visa holders already in the UK. The Government have, quite rightly, made a concession for care workers, but many other workers remain affected if that settlement pathway changes. Regarding the Bill and how we have ended up here, the media that platform the extreme views of certain politicians are almost as responsible as those right-wing parties in creating a toxic and hateful atmosphere against refugees, migrants and minority groups. I want to be clear: I do not think that people who have voted for Reform UK or Restore Britain are racists, but people should realise that by voting for either of them they are voting for a party with racists in it. We have seen those parties promote racism—they have contributed to the actions and disturbances that we saw on the streets of Portsmouth and Dover, for example. The language of some elected Reform politicians in how they describe asylum seekers, immigrants and other races is frankly disgusting. The hon. Member for Runcorn and Helsby (Sarah Pochin) is not in her place. I can only hope that she is in front of a television somewhere in Parliament and she is getting annoyed by black faces being on it, which is making light of a rather dreadful sentiment. The truth is that the rising attitude of inhumanity is the real threat to our communities across the UK.

I am really sad to report that a councillor in Kirklees who belongs to Reform UK posted recently and referred to immigrants as “third world animals”. Using that kind of language against any human being is absolutely disgusting, and it does not pay anybody’s bills, it does not repair the roads and it does not fund our schools—it does not contribute anything positive to our country. Does the hon. Gentleman agree with me that anybody in elected office who uses language like that should be appropriately sanctioned?

In short, I wholeheartedly agree with the hon. Member. That is utterly deplorable, but I want to draw a line under that subject because I have spent more than enough time talking about Reform UK. In all honesty, it breaks my heart that this Bill is a product of some people in my party who are chasing right-wing votes. This Bill is the grimmest hangover from the Keir Starmer days. I did not join the Labour party for us to present a Bill such as this, which will create an underclass of people and, make no mistake, this Bill is classist at its dark heart. If somebody earns £50,000 or more, they are deemed to be more worthy of staying in this country than someone who still performs an important job for society but possibly earns the minimum wage. Let us call that what it is: inequality. As the hon. Member for Perth and Kinross-shire (Pete Wishart) touched on earlier, this Bill will have a larger impact in Scotland than it will in England. In fact, it will have more of an impact on people who do not live in London, because wages in this town are usually higher. There is no getting away from it: that is creating a hierarchy of humanity, and it does not say anything about that on my Labour party membership card—quite the opposite, in fact. It says that we should “live together, freely, in a spirit of solidarity, tolerance and respect.” That is not prevalent in this Bill, and I cannot and will not support it.

I will speak to new clause 14, which is tabled in my name. I believe that people granted asylum for a 30-month period under the new rules should be able to transfer to the new work and study route prior to the expiry of the 30-month period. I have been assured that that is being considered by His Majesty’s Government. I also wish to say something about language. I do not think I am the only MP who has been appalled by the way in which some hon. Members have used language in this space to demonise asylum claimants and instil fear in the hearts of some of our citizens. A person seeking asylum and awaiting a determination is not an illegal migrant or an “illegal”, as some have referred to these people. They are not dangerous criminals, rapists or invaders, as a previous Secretary of State disgracefully described them. While it is against the law to arrive in our country on a small boat, that offence is stayed if such a person claims asylum within a reasonable time limit. That is a long-standing rule. It is not illegal to claim asylum, so can we stop calling people who are seeking asylum criminals, illegal migrants or simply illegals? We are all better than that.

With the leave of the House, in the time that remains, I will do my best to respond to the many thoughtful and heartfelt contributions that we have heard this afternoon. Let me start by turning to new clause 62, which is in the name of my hon. Friend the Member for Poole (Neil Duncan-Jordan). A number of other Members have spoken in support of it, including the hon. Member for Birmingham Perry Barr (Ayoub Khan), my hon. Friend the Member for Poplar and Limehouse (Apsana Begum), my right hon. Friend the Member for Hayes and Harlington (John McDonnell) and my hon. Friend the Member for Alloa and Grangemouth (Brian Leishman). I know that my hon. Friend the Member for Poole is a tireless campaigner for workers, and I appreciate the intent behind his new clause, but I profoundly disagree with it and with the use of the word “retrospective” in this debate, for reasons that I will come on to explain. As my right hon. Friend the Home Secretary has said in the House and in discussions throughout recent weeks, including in conversations with my hon. Friend the Member for Poole, settlement has always been determined at the point of application, not at entry, and that principle has been upheld in the courts. Being in the United Kingdom does not give someone the right to settle under the rules that happened to exist when they first arrived. Settlement in this country is a great privilege, and it comes with indefinite access to great institutions, such as the NHS, our schools and the welfare state. People should not have a sense of entitlement to that when they come to this country under visas or other short-term rights. We believe that people should have the time to demonstrate contribution in order to receive the status of settlement.

The Minister is making a profound point. This is about citizenship. For citizenship to mean anything, it must confer certain entitlements that non-citizens do not enjoy. That is not a complicated idea; it is a time-honoured principle, and I support any Member of this House who upholds it.

I sincerely appreciate the right hon. Gentleman’s contribution. He is right; the whole purpose of our reforms is to recognise the privilege that comes with settlement in this country—the rights and the responsibilities, and the contribution we expect people to make when they are here. As all Members know, we have created a targeted exemption for care workers and other non-degree-level public sector roles in health and education. This is exceptional and has been done in view of their service during covid and during our recovery since, when we asked them to come to this country and support us in looking after some of our most vulnerable people. Some 300,000 skilled workers expected to settle at 10 years will not fall into that category. As my right hon. Friend the Home Secretary has said, this policy is about fairness, both to those who are here now and those who have come recently. Where exceptional conditions do not apply as they do for care workers, I do not think it is fair to allow permanent access to our great institutions if a contribution has not been proved; as my right hon. Friend has said, the impact would be billions in welfare costs and a huge number of people becoming eligible for social housing. Many of these workers came to this country when the salary threshold was £25,000, a threshold set by the previous Government, and vast numbers now remain on very low wages, so we know that the likely impact on things like social housing would be profound. We do not think it would be fair—either to those who have contributed more, including in public services, or to the British people—if demands on the welfare state go up. This is not a question of removing people. No one is being asked to leave. It is about people who do not yet have permanent status and the conditions for accessing it. We expect them to be able to settle after a further period of contribution.

I am going to make some progress, because I only have nine minutes, and a huge number of points have arisen in this debate for me to respond to. Those are not my only concerns about the amendment tabled by my hon. Friend the Member for Poole. I know he said that this was not the intention of his amendment and has disputed it today, but I am afraid that the amendment as it stands would not only change the time periods, but exempt all skilled workers who are yet to settle from our English language and criminality settlement conditions—that is 1.1 million people who would be exempted from those criminality conditions. If the amendment were to pass, it would take us back to the previous situation, with only those who receive a custodial sentence of 12 months or more barred from settling. I do not accept that the country has a duty to let domestic abusers, shoplifters and sex offenders settle, nor do I believe that was my hon. Friend’s intention in tabling his amendment, so I am afraid that we cannot accept it.

The Minister is absolutely right. It was never my intention to give a free pass to criminals, and I made that quite clear in my speech. However, does she not agree that the Government already have the power to deport those people if they choose to do so?

I am afraid that I cannot agree with my hon. Friend. The Government’s scope to use that discretionary power is heavily constrained by a wide range of litigation. That is exactly why we have introduced the more robust mandatory criminality requirements, so that it is absolutely clear that no criminal can ever settle. To side with the old system is to accept that criminals can and will continue to settle. That would be the effect of my hon. Friend’s amendment, and I am afraid that the Government could never accept that. The right hon. Member for Herne Bay and Sandwich (Sir Roger Gale) asked about Ukrainian settlement in this context. The Ukrainian schemes were established to provide temporary sanctuary in response to the war; they were not devised as routes to permanent settlement. Like him, we recognise the contribution that those individuals have made to our country, but as I have said, the Ukrainian Government have a desire for their citizens to return to Ukraine after the war to assist with the rebuilding of their country. We will continue to keep the scheme under consideration and monitor it in line with the ongoing war, but when that war is over—we all hope it will be soon—we could not wish to drain Ukraine of its talent. I know that the right hon. Member will also bear that in mind. Turning to my right hon. Friend the Member for Hayes and Harlington (John McDonnell), I am sorry that he did not get the chance to speak to many of the amendments he has tabled, reflecting the effort he has put into his work on this Bill. However, I will address the workplace justice visa that he proposes in new clause 15. Earlier this year, the Government launched the Fair Work Agency, which brings together existing labour market enforcement functions—including the Gangmasters and Labour Abuse Authority and His Majesty’s Revenue and Customs national minimum wage team—in one place. Bringing the functions of the labour market enforcement bodies together supports both British and migrant workers by ensuring a more cohesive and streamlined response to workplace exploitation. We recognise that there is always more we can do, which is why we have taken steps to tighten up the sponsorship system, such as by preventing employers from passing immigration-related costs on to workers. We are committed to exploring further options to support sponsored workers to change employers. The effect of these amendments would be to commit us to a course of action before we have established what the best mechanism would be. I look forward to engaging further with my right hon. Friend.

The Government are undertaking a review and consultation, which we believe will end at the end of this year. Will the Minister write to me about the terms of reference, that review and the exact date when it will be completed?

I would be more than happy to do that and to meet my right hon. Friend to discuss it in more detail. I appreciate all his work. My hon. Friend the Member for Walthamstow (Ms Creasy) asked important questions about refugees. We are applying the new rules to refugees across the board to make the rules consistent. I am afraid that I disagree with her if she is advocating that those who have come in small boats should settle in five years, which is faster than some of our skilled workers who have come and contributed. That would not be fair on our constituents, who are rightly outraged by the levels of illegal entry we have seen since the Conservatives were in government— [ Interruption. ] I appreciate the clarification—the levels that we saw while the Conservatives were in government. One of the things I have been keen to emphasise throughout my discussions on this Bill, and in my speech opening this debate, is that we have to rebuild the consent of the British people for the asylum system. The system is broken, and we must recognise that we have to have a fair system.

I will make some progress; I have a huge amount to get through. The hon. Member for Westmorland and Lonsdale (Tim Farron) tabled amendment 78, which relates to refugee family reunion. The Government recognise the importance of family unity, but we have a duty to ensure that communities are not placed under unsustainable pressure. As the House will know, the refugee family reunion route, which had minimal requirements, was suspended in September 2025 in response to the severe pressures on local authorities. The amendment would pre-empt our ongoing work on the future framework, with further details to be announced in due course. I am afraid we cannot support an amendment that would prescribe the fundamental features of future refugee family reunion measures in primary legislation, as it would remove the flexibility needed to maintain a coherent immigration system. [ Interruption. ] I would be happy to meet the hon. Gentleman to discuss it further. The shadow Minister raised the Opposition’s new clause 54, tabled by the right hon. Member for Croydon South (Chris Philp), which would increase the period for indefinite leave to remain to 10 years. The shadow Minister may not have noticed, but we have just set out in the last week that our baseline period for leave or settlement will be 10 years. We welcome the Opposition’s support for that announcement through their new clause, but their blanket 10-year provision fails to recognise contribution. It is important for us that contribution is at the heart of settlement rights that people gain in this country. We want to recognise those who have made a sustained contribution to this country, either financially or by public service. As the Home Secretary has said, this is a fair balance—fair for those who have come and those who are here. It is much fairer than the Opposition’s one-size-fits-all provision, and it has a huge impact on our economy and public services, too. The shadow Minister also talked about removing citizenship for those who arrived in small boats. That is a reheat of what the Conservative Government tried and failed to do when they were in government. They last introduced measures in 2023 to try to deter people coming in small boats. What happened? Small boat crossings remained high—far higher than they are today. Crossings are down by around 40% under this Government. This year, we are on track to have the fewest arrivals through small boats since covid. We agree with the principle that there should be an impact on settlement for those who have come here illegally, which is why those who have come on small boats and who do not work or study will wait at least 30 years for settlement. I have already set out how that privilege works in my response. We want to encourage those who are in this country to integrate, and that means joining our work and study routes. If they are genuinely fleeing war and persecution, we want to support them to integrate. I am proud of the modern slavery amendments in this Bill. We are doing a huge amount to support victims of modern slavery, and how far we have come and the leadership this country shows should be recognised. Through this Bill, we are creating a power to devolve national referral mechanism decision making for children so that the Home Secretary can name a public authority as a decision maker on a case-by-case basis. That has been asked for by lots of people in the sector who recognise that local authorities, which are the corporate parent for many of these children and young people, are the best placed authority to fight for their wellbeing. We have also placed the independent child trafficking guardians on a statutory footing, which strengthens specialist advocacy and embeds support for exploited children across England and Wales. We have strengthened expectations for businesses and public sector organisations to report on modern slavery in their supply chains, with stronger penalties for non-compliance. I say that in response

I beg to move, That the Bill be now read the Third time. This is a significant moment, and one that we have reached thanks to the support and scrutiny of Members across the House. Exactly a year ago, I stood at this Dispatch Box and set out the most significant migration reforms of modern times. It was a plan to restore order and control to our borders by bearing down on illegal entry and swiftly removing those with no right to be here, while at the same time opening safe and legal routes for genuine refugees. The inheritance that we received from the last Conservative Government was far from that ideal. They lost control of our borders and criminal gangs, not the previous Government, decided who could come to this country. The small boats crisis led to regular tragic deaths in the channel, and the cost borne by the taxpayer was unprecedented, reaching £5 billion a year. Since then, we have been restoring order. Small boat arrivals are down significantly, returns of those here illegally are at a decades-long high, and the cost to the taxpayer has fallen by £1 billion. We are also on track to close every asylum hotel by the end of this Parliament. Clearly, we must go further, and that is what the Bill does in three ways. First, it makes asylum decisions swifter, with a new independent immigration appeals authority and single appeals process. That will ensure that genuine refugees will receive protection, while those here illegally are rapidly removed. Secondly, it closes loopholes that have been exploited in our legal system, namely by tightening the application of article 8 of the ECHR, and refining our modern slavery laws to sustain genuine protections while bearing down on abuse. Thirdly, the Bill asks those who have benefited from our support to pay a portion back when they can. In doing so, we reduce the burden on taxpayers and communities, and thereby sustain support for the very concept of refugee protection. The House has passed further amendments today, including measures to speed up the removal of those who have exhausted all their appeal rights, and tightening our application of article 31 of the refugee convention. The Bill restores control and fairness to our asylum system. Labour Members know that Britain is an open, tolerant and generous country, and we are proud to offer sanctuary to those fleeing peril. I am proud to have opened new capped safe and legal routes for genuine refugees, but I also know that that generosity is not unconditional. It depends on public consent which demands that we control who comes here, that those who have no right to be in this country are swiftly removed, and that the burden borne by local communities is reduced. We have already made significant steps forward. Our system is fairer and more controlled but there is more to do. This Bill is the vital next step, and for that reason I commend it to the House.

There is not much I can say in a minute, Madam Deputy Speaker. The Home Secretary was congratulating herself on swiftly removing people who were here illegally, but I gently remind her that since this Labour Government came to office, 88,000 people have illegally crossed the channel, and only about 6,000 have been removed. Over 90% have been allowed to stay. When it comes to foreign criminals, almost none of those from some nations outside Europe are removed. For example, there are 161 dangerous, serious foreign criminals from the Democratic Republic of the Congo, but only one was removed last year, and there are 775 from Jamaica, but only 24 were removed, so the Home Secretary’s complacency is not well founded. The Bill makes some small steps in the right direction and it is a commendable attempt, but until we leave the ECHR and completely dismantle the legal system around illegal migration and foreign criminals, we will never succeed in controlling our country’s borders. Tinkering at the edges does not work—it has been tried before, it failed before and it will fail again under this Home Secretary.

With the leave of the House, I will put motions 3 to 8 together. Motion made, and Question put forthwith (Standing Order No. 118(6)), International Development That the draft African Development Bank (Seventeenth Replenishment of the African Development Fund) Order 2026, which was laid before this House on 13 October, be approved. That the draft African Development Fund (Multilateral Debt Relief Initiative) (Amendment) Order 2026, which was laid before this House on 13 October, be approved. That the draft International Fund for Agricultural Development (Thirteenth Replenishment) Order 2026, which was laid before this House on 13 October, be approved. That the draft International Development Association (Multilateral Debt Relief Initiative) (Amendment) Order 2026, which was laid before this House on 13 October, be approved. Environmental Protection That the draft Persistent Organic Pollutants (Amendment) Regulations 2026, which were laid before this House on 14 October, be approved. Dangerous Drugs That the draft Misuse of Drugs Act 1971 (Amendment) Order 2026, which was laid before this House on 27 October, be approved. —( Rachel Hopkins .) Question agreed to .

On a point of order, Madam Deputy Speaker. In the statement of changes that was issued with the immigration rules, there was an explanatory memorandum on 5 March that made it clear that anybody who had been granted leave as of 1 March 2026 would remain eligible for a five-year route to settlement in this country. The Government then confirmed that in a written answer in the other place on 19 March, and on 23 June, repeated again in a written statement that adults and children would be eligible for earned settlement if they had had asylum granted as of 1 March 2026. In today’s debate, the Minister has confirmed that the footnote in the earned settlement proposals that were published on 2 November removes the exemption for this group of people. That is 200,000 refugees, including 35,000 children, for whom the exemption no longer exists. Many of us will have constituents whom we may have pointed towards that explanatory memorandum and told in good faith—because it was reported to the House—that they would be exempt from these requirements. That is no longer the case, so how can we correct the record to ensure that our constituents get the correct legal advice as a result of today’s U-turn?

I thank the hon. Member for her point of order. While it is not a matter for the Chair, she has made her point and put the matter on the record. I am sure that those on the Treasury Bench will have heard it and will make the Department aware.

I start with a declaration of my interests, as I chair the all-party parliamentary group for UK innovation startups and SMEs. I thank the Minister for his statement yesterday, which answered so many of the asks I made in my April debate in Westminster Hall, but this is still an important issue that we have to discuss. It is not simply a question about one NHS contract, but a test of whether the Government are serious about cleaning up politics, fixing public procurement and building UK sovereign capability. The Government have spoken repeatedly about using procurement to support British innovation, British businesses and national capability, and this is an opportunity to demonstrate that those commitments mean something in practice. I previously received public assurances that the NHS medium-term planning framework would not be used to force the continued roll-out of Palantir’s federated data platform across the NHS. At yesterday’s statement, I welcomed the investment being directed towards interoperability, common standards and future NHS digital capability, rather than simply extending the life of what increasingly appears to be Palantir’s lame duck FDP. When I first started examining this issue, I genuinely was not sure whether the FDP had become so embedded that it could no longer be switched off. My conclusion now is that it can be switched off. In fact, I suspect that outside a relatively small number of trusts, with Chelsea and Westminster perhaps being an example, most clinicians and patients would barely notice. If that assessment is wrong, it should be independently proven, and I would like the Minister to commit to commissioning an independent audit of the FDP’s actual usage, its genuine operational dependency and the transaction options available. Crucially, that audit must be conducted independently of NHS England, which has been closely associated with the programme and its delivery. The FDP has been deeply problematic from the start. The original political pitch was essentially for software as a service, with flashy dashboards sold to Boris Johnson for just £1. We saw a political climate in which the likes of Peter Thiel, Donald Trump and Dominic Cummings were all part of a wider ecosystem promoting this approach to Government technology. Software as a service does not work for this kind of contract. It is not how we build sovereign capabilities. We are paying Palantir to develop intellectual property and know-how, which it then owns and can sell to others, while the NHS just gets the use of it.

I see the Minister shake his head, but it is in the contract. Palantir owns intellectual property rights that are not brought in by the NHS. In fact, this is the worst contract I have ever seen in my commercial life. It is a monument to the previous Government’s financial incompetence. UK procurement needs to move away from software as a service and start building its sovereign capabilities.

I congratulate my hon. Friend not only on securing this debate, but on the manner in which he has conducted himself in investigating these matters. He will know that we have been investigating them on the Health and Social Care Committee, too. In relation to all the weaknesses, and in particular in relation to the procurement that he describes, does he not agree that the Government should be maximising the opportunity of the break clause next year, so that this matter can be properly investigated as soon as possible?
My first point is that we could switch the system off tomorrow, and it would not impact the NHS. In fact, the NHS should not be dependent upon a single supplier for its future data architecture.

My hon. Friend has been a doughty campaigner on this issue and has gone about it in an exemplary way. He has already mentioned that data sovereignty will be key looking forward, but does he agree that we should ensure that no such contracts are handed out in future across all Departments?

I agree entirely with my hon. Friend. In fact, I will go one stage further and say that trust is as important as data sovereignty, and right now we do not have a system that people trust. Recent events only reinforce concerns. Yesterday, Tom Watson circulated a letter that appears to many observers to be another example of highly aggressive lobbying. I would appreciate clarification regarding communications and briefings between Palantir and the Government immediately before and after yesterday’s statement. Recent public commentary from Lord Watson has given the impression that the continuation of the contract is somehow guaranteed, but that decision has not yet been made. The Government must be seen to act independently, and the revolving door between the Government and Palantir must be challenged.

I really appreciate the hon. Member’s work in this area. I, too, have been following this contract very closely since my time on the Health Committee and the awarding of the contract. Does he share my concern that the two-year extension enables Palantir to embed itself further into those systems, and thus place itself in a privileged position to win contracts from 2029, perhaps as Palantir UK?

I agree entirely, and that power of incumbency is what I am about to speak about. The public need to be confident that procurement decisions are being made on the basis of value, capability and public interest, not relationships or incumbency. Following yesterday’s statement, will the Minister serve the contractual termination assistance notice, and if so, when? And—an equally important question—how will the Government ensure that Palantir’s incumbency advantage does not distort future competition?

I congratulate the hon. Member on initiating the debate. He exhibits the same tenacity, expertise and determination in pursuing this issue as he does on the Committee of which we are both proud to be members. He has raised the issue of incumbency. As he has said, Palantir turned a £1 contract during covid into a £350 million contract now. Now it will have two years in which to exercise that incumbency. Does he think it is possible to create a level playing field for the next tender, given that Palantir will have access to all the data, all the systems, all the architecture and those who are designing the tender?

I greatly enjoy serving on the Select Committee with the hon. Lady, and I fully agree with her. That is the challenge that we need to set the Minister: to prove that this can be done. There is another issue that should not be ignored: how Palantir continuously undermines people’s trust. Its leadership has repeatedly made political and ideological statements, which would attract substantial scrutiny if they came from a major British supplier or a company on the Cabinet Office strategic suppliers list, which, curiously, they have not. Why are we willing to apply a different standard simply because Palantir is some weird foreign company?

I thank the hon. Member for securing the debate, and for his tireless work on this topic. Does he agree that British procurement rules should be founded on human rights and ethics, and that ethical procurement should be the foundation of any public sector procurement that we make? Palantir has been used in violations of international human rights in Palestine—in Gaza—and it has been used to enforce illegal searches and violence by ICE in the United States. Statements made by its executives clearly demonstrate that it is a company that cannot be trusted, and that it lacks ethics and morality. Is that not one more reason for us to sever all ties with it?

I do agree, but I think that Palantir actually causes a bigger problem, which is that it is not actually very good at what it claims to be able to do. That is the reason why we should not be renewing its contract, but we should be pursuing ethical procurement as well.

Data is the new oil, and the NHS data on patients and research is so valuable. Is there a risk that Palantir, through this contract, will have unauthorised access or will siphon off data without permission?

We have seen that Palantir has been authorised to access such data, which was previously unknown and undeclared. My point is not that Palantir’s political opinions should determine procurement outcomes, but that scrutiny should be applied consistently. To replace the current approach, I believe that we need an independent NHS design authority to control the architecture of the future FDP, rather than it being controlled by the supplier; multiple suppliers, rather than a single controlling company; and open, common standards—which the Minister talked about in his statement on Monday, and which I fully support—that should be interoperable by design, so that we can take out pieces and plug in another company to replace them.

My hon. Friend is suggesting a very helpful and well-thought-through solution to some of these problems, and what he is suggesting is very important for public trust in future. Does he agree that we have enough problems with totally wild conspiracy theories out there, let alone things like Palantir, which looks like a genuine conspiracy, so what he is recommending and asking the Minister to comment on are all the more important?
I did laugh at Palantir’s comments. In fact, its manifesto was referred to as “the ramblings of a comic book villain”.

I thank the hon. Gentleman for securing this debate, and for inviting experts from the NHS’s analytical and data community into Parliament to meet us last week. Does he agree that there is already sufficient capability and innovation in the NHS to build the data systems, and that the need for Palantir’s federated data platform is largely redundant because of that expertise? It would be better to put those resources into supporting innovation in the NHS, with some of our great small and medium-sized enterprises working as partners.

Yes, it was shown very clearly by the people who are delivering for the NHS right now that Palantir is not capable of delivering the sorts of results that we can already get from bodies such as Manchester’s integrated care board, which is delivering innovation in advance and more quickly than Palantir can. The final thing we need in my list, after interoperability by design, is a competitive process that allows British SMEs and start-ups to participate without the usual level of bureaucracy. The future should be an ecosystem, not a monopoly. Unfortunately, it comes back to procurement reform. The Government have spoken about a new procurement strategy, about using public procurement to support British innovation and business, and about building domestic capability, rather than reinforcing dependency and vulnerability. The Palantir contract is a real-world test of those principles. It is a test for the Government to see if they will truly implement “using public procurement to back British business”, as stated in the Budget. Finally, there is substantial expertise across this House. There are Members with wide experience in health, digital transformation, technology, procurement and business growth. I therefore invite the Minister to engage regularly with interested Members as this process develops—not to influence contract awards, because that would be entirely inappropriate, but to ensure that the principles underpinning the procurement process are transparent, competitive, fair and firmly aligned with the public interest. This is about more than Palantir messing up our NHS; it is about whether the Government want to build our sovereign capabilities, or whether we will continue down a path of dependence on a single, failing foreign provider.

I thank the hon. Member for Newton Abbot (Martin Wrigley) for raising this important issue. It has been a pleasure exchanging with him, in corridors and more formal settings, on areas where we definitely agree as well as others where we are yet to agree, which I will come on to. It is a pleasure to have the opportunity to build on my extensive statement and questions from Members yesterday, and to explain the Government’s approach to the NHS federated data platform. As I said yesterday, after a period of review, the Government are launching a new procurement to end the contract in March 2029.
