This will give us the opportunity to build the next generation of the FDP with new capability. While we prepare for the next generation of the FDP, the current supplier will remain in place. This will provide the necessary continuity of care, preserving the benefits to patients and the healthcare system that we have already achieved, while providing time to run a fair and rigorous procurement process, which it is important to get right.

Is the Minister aware that the “Today” programme on the BBC this morning talked about a brief it had from Palantir saying that it had been awarded the contract as a continuation to show how good it was. Will he ensure that Palantir understands the message he is giving?

This contract—a seven-year contract—was awarded in 2023. This is year 3, and we have announced that the contract will end in March 2029. A letter from Palantir to me and Secretary of State confirms in its third paragraph: “The FDP programme team has done a tremendous job of ensuring that exit arrangements are clear, and that the NHS has all the rights and all the support it needs to transition to a new supplier when the contract ends. We will ramp up exit preparation over the next two years and work with the NHS to ensure that the public and the industry understand that there is no lock-in.” Through engagement with the market under the new procurement we have launched, we can bring forward innovative solutions that build on today’s capabilities and meet the needs of tomorrow in ambition and appetite as well as in capability. This decision is driven by the Government’s aim to secure for patients the technology that supports their care, while improving productivity to give the NHS and social care more choice, greater resilience and less dependence on any one single supplier.

I have two very quick questions. First, what are the obstacles in the way of exercising the break clause next year? Secondly, can the Minister assure all our constituents that no NHS data will have been given to or taken by Palantir if and when it leaves?

The data remains NHS, as does the intellectual property, and there is no lock-in. In the announcement yesterday, I confirmed to the House that we are beginning a new procurement process, and I will come on to confirm more details of that. I will now try to make a bit of progress. In making this decision, we deliver on two objectives: continuing the use of technology to transform the NHS and supporting the Government’s strategy to build UK AI technology capabilities. We want a more diverse and innovative supply market, including greater use of sovereign AI, as well as any internationally developed capabilities. The NHS FDP has the power to transform and is transforming how services co-ordinate care. It gives the NHS the tools to bring together information from disparate NHS systems, and manage and analyse it in one place. This is a system that trusts and integrated care boards need and are using. It is an important part of our objective to secure the best digital data and tech to deliver the health and care system we need. This requires us to draw on innovative solutions both locally and nationally. As I said yesterday, 137 trusts are already delivering benefits. In Greater Manchester, which the hon. Member for Newton Abbot references, hospital teams book cancer tests so that patients can choose to be tested sooner at another hospital. This requires us to draw on innovative solutions locally and nationally. In making better use of operating theatres, planning discharges, reducing list sizes and supporting vaccine supply, the benefits of the FDP are being relied on by our trusts. In North Tees and Hartlepool, the FDP tracks discharge actions so that nothing blocks a patient from getting home, and, importantly, frees up beds for admission. As I stated yesterday, alongside the new procurement, we will work with a range of providers to develop new capabilities and expertise, beginning with maternity care. This will bring together innovative providers to help to tackle fragmentation in data and digital systems, while exploring how NHS priorities can support the growth of UK AI capability. We do not want to sacrifice these gains; we want to encourage the full realisation of this capability so that more people receive the care they need. That means spending the time to deliver a fair procurement process that engages with the very stakeholders the hon. Gentleman encourages, as well as industry and the market, and supports opportunities for UK companies. This is not a quick process, but a methodical one that will ensure interoperability and the common standards announced yesterday in agreement with the work by the hon. Gentleman and colleagues from Select Committees. This relates to the second objective: how we change the procurement of future technology to benefit not just the NHS, but industry, delivering growth and employment opportunities. We want to do more to build UK AI and tech capability, and the new procurement of the NHS FDP will be a flagship for this. We want to invite, stir, spark interest and inspire innovative providers, UK and international alike, to tackle the data and digital fragmentation in this area of care and test how health priorities can create routes to build UK AI capability and resilience.

I agree with the points the Minister is making. However, the issue is that the same points around interoperability and supporting UK procurement were also part of the original tender for the federated data platform, which led to it being awarded to Palantir and a consortium. Will he set out how this differs from the original tender that was followed some years ago? Secondly, in this case, Palantir will be the incumbent. How will the Minister ensure that other companies, small and large, have the same kind of access to the existing FDP architecture, knowledge, information and users as Palantir?

I thank my hon. Friend, the Chair of the Science, Innovation and Technology Committee, for her questions. I heard her concerns both in yesterday’s contribution and in the subsequent conversation that we had. This has my full attention, because incumbency cannot be allowed to be an advantage by design. I will ensure that the Procurement Act of 2023, which requires equal treatment, has my full attention in the drafting of the procurement. More details on that will follow, as I said in my statement yesterday. I refer Members to that statement for further information.

I am grateful for what the Minister is saying, but could he explain to the House how the two-year extension beyond the break clause aligns with what is coming from the Foreign Office with regards to our obligations under our sanctions regime and to the relationship of Palantir with the Israeli Government?

I thank my hon. Friend for her question. This is a decision to procure anew. It is not about other territories or one supplier and their executives holding a political view. It is a decision that is being taken to go to market for a new version—the next generation of FDP. That process began yesterday in earnest. It is not, as I have said, about where else Palantir supplies or who else it has as customers. It is about maintaining what the NHS makes possible—being able to check in sooner for cancer care, other hospital care or social care. We will build on the successes of the FDP to date. We will procure anew the next generation and ensure exit and transition for March 2029. Throughout this period, trusts and ICBs can and should make full use of the capabilities of the NHS FDP to improve their performance and productivity, including those yet to sign up to or realise the full potential of the FDP. In this time, we will create an environment in which new technologies and suppliers can contribute new solutions to protect the capabilities that the NHS relies on today. For those who need reassurance on the security of their data, I can say that security and data protection are a core principle of the FDP in the NHS. That will not change. As I said repeatedly yesterday, innovation adoption moves at the speed of trust. People should be reassured that the NHS FDP is a federated network of systems, each controlled by the relevant hospital or ICB. The use of the FDP and its different products is driven by the local NHS and the data is under their control, just as in the national instance it is controlled by NHS England. Data access is tightly governed. Access to data is for authorised users only and for approved purposes only, with access logged and audited. There is no overseas processing of any type of data by the NHS FDP programme. Data is held in UK data centres and does not leave the UK. I believe that this decision strikes the right balance between maintaining the needs of patients today while confirming that the contract will end in March 2029, when we will have a new-generation FDP in our NHS. That is a process that I am happy to report begins today. Question put and agreed to.

title: Violence against Women and Girls: Prosecution Rates

items.txt: 1. What steps she is taking with Cabinet colleagues to help improve prosecution rates for crimes of violence against women and girls.
4. What steps she is taking with Cabinet colleagues to help improve prosecution rates for crimes of violence against women and girls.

This Government are committed to halving violence against women and girls. Since becoming a Law Officer, I have delivered the early victims’ right to review, giving rape victims a second chance of justice, as well as dedicated victim liaison officers for domestic abuse victims, supporting them from charge to trial, and pre-trial meetings with the prosecution for rape victims, which is now being piloted for domestic abuse victims. This Government are getting on with the job.

I thank the Minister for her answer. While improving prosecution rates and bringing perpetrators to justice as soon as possible must remain a priority, what more can this Government do to support community-led initiatives, such as the Orange Wolves campaign for tackling violence against women and girls in my constituency that I will be taking part in shortly, to ensure that prevention, early intervention and challenging misogynistic and harmful attitudes are given equal priority so that we can stop these crimes happening in the first place?

I thank my hon. Friend for his work through the Orange Wolves campaign. This Government are investing £15 million in the misogyny prevention taskforce to challenge misogynistic attitudes across society, including in schools. I will continue to work with colleagues across Government to ensure that prevention goes hand in hand with a robust criminal justice response. I welcome the vital role that communities like his are playing.

As we approach this year’s 16 days of activism against gender-based violence, what discussions is the Attorney General having with the Crown Prosecution Service to ensure that victims of tech-related violence against women and girls get justice?

The Government are proud to be supporting the 16 days of activism against gender-based violence. We have banned nudification apps and criminalised non-consensual intimate images. The CPS will shortly publish its tech-facilitated VAWG strategy to make sure that it is fully equipped to prosecute these evolving crimes.

Crimes of violence and sexual harassment against women and girls also happen in the workplace, but as it stands the law does not consider this to be a workplace hazard, with legislation such as the Worker Protection (Amendment of Equality Act 2010) Act 2023 yet to drive real cultural change in work practices. Does the Attorney General agree that this should be a health and safety issue for workers and that the law should treat it as such?

I thank the right hon. Lady for that question. It is an issue close to my heart, because I was an employment rights lawyer for over a decade before entering this place, particularly representing women facing discrimination in the workplace. The Employment Rights Act 2025 adds new protections, and we have outlawed non-disclosure agreements in the workplace, but we will always look to see where we can go further to protect women and girls.

Abuse rarely ends with the separation of a couple, with non-molestation orders ignored all the time. One of my constituents secured a restraining order against her ex-partner, but it took her 12-and-a-half years to fully extract herself. One of the biggest issues she faced was being economically attached to him and unable to leave their mortgage. Surviving Economic Abuse, which I have been working with on this, has made it clear that without a legal definition, prosecution of these behaviours is only achievable as a sub-category of coercive behaviour, so judges lack precedent and know-how to deal with it. Will the Attorney General take steps with Cabinet colleagues to produce a legal definition and training on how to prosecute this type of crime?

The hon. Lady makes a really important point about economic abuse being used as a form of violence against women and girls. I will be happy to speak to my colleagues in the Ministry of Justice about what more we might be able to do. We have introduced domestic abuse protection orders and stalking protection orders to make sure that we have the right tools to go after perpetrators, but I will discuss the points she raises with colleagues.
Last week, the Justice Secretary wrote to the Bar Standards Board to demand changes to defence advocacy in rape trials. Was the Attorney General consulted before he did so?

I agree with the Lord Chancellor that rape myths have no place in our courts or our society, and advocacy must not perpetrate myths that have been repeatedly shown to distort understanding of sexual violence. Judges can already give directions to counter rape myths. We are going further in the Courts and Tribunals Bill to stop irrelevant sexual history and previous allegations from being weaponised against victims.

I am not sure whether that was a yes, a no or a maybe. If the Justice Secretary did so as a result of advice from the Attorney General, the Lady Chief Justice has something to say to both of them as she felt compelled to respond publicly to this intervention from the Justice Secretary and others. Last weekend, she told the Bar Council’s annual conference that the debate on the conduct of rape trials is “not fully informed” and risks undermining public confidence in the justice system —ouch. Does the Attorney General agree with the Lady Chief Justice? If not, where is she in error?

The hon. Gentleman will be well aware of the Law Officers’ convention in relation to disclosing what advice may or may not have been given. But I will say this: the Government are determined to tackle violence against women and girls. When it comes to rape, we have announced specialist rape courtrooms in every court in the country, making sure that victims who bravely come forward get the support they need from the criminal justice system.

With your permission, Mr Speaker, I would like to pay tribute to John Pardoe, my predecessor as North Cornwall’s MP between 1966 and 1979. John, who was a Liberal hero and a true servant to the Cornish people, sadly passed away on Sunday. I hope the whole House will join me in offering our sincere condolences to his wife Joy and his whole family. [Hon. Members: “Hear, hear.”] One of the many victims of Russell Brand’s evil and calculated sexual abuse, a woman named Szilvia Berki, was barred by the High Court from speaking to family, friends and even the police about her assault. On top of that, she was ordered to pay £50,000 in legal costs to Brand and his then girlfriend for the injunction, seemingly with the intention of bankrupting her. Will the Attorney General consider the merits of a comprehensive law on strategic lawsuits against public participation that includes sexual abuse, and commission a review into the weaponisation of such injunctions by the rich and powerful that includes enhanced powers for the Solicitors Regulation Authority to regulate the lawyers and law firms who bring them?

I join the hon. Gentleman in paying tribute to his predecessor, John Pardoe. Turning to the question, I commend the bravery and courage of all victims who have come forward. Powerful men should not be able to use the law to silence their victims. Non-disclosure agreements should not be used to obstruct justice. The Government also recognise the profound financial and psychological impact that SLAPPs have on individuals. With the Victims and Courts Act 2026, we will ensure that victims in crime can tell anyone what happened, despite signing an NDA, and we remain committed to introducing further legislation in relation to SLAPPs.
2. What advice she has given to the Government on the potential impact of removing jury trials in certain circumstances on the rule of law.

The Government inherited a justice system on the brink. The record backlogs mean that victims are facing devastating delays for justice. The Government continue to invest in our courts, but vital reforms are needed, too. The Prime Minister and the Justice Secretary have rightly listened to the strength of feeling from victims, the sector and the House and have decided not to establish the Crown court bench division, but we will now act with urgency to implement the rest of our vital reforms, delivering swifter justice for victims with an urgency that was wholly absent from the words and actions of the Conservative party.

The Lord Chancellor has already had to drop the bench division. Will the Solicitor General advise him that ending the right to elect jury trial for burglary and theft—crimes that my Mid Bedfordshire constituents care a great deal about—would damage confidence in justice and that he should drop that, too?

No, I will not. The implication of the hon. Gentleman’s question is that the over 90% of cases that are decided in the magistrates court are somehow of a lesser order. We expect and receive the highest standards of justice in both the magistrates and the Crown court.
Will the Solicitor General outline how this Government are investing in our justice system to bring down the court backlogs created by the Opposition?
We are indeed investing in our courts, which will fund unlimited sitting days, boost legal aid and ultimately speed up justice for victims, and we will continue to do so.
3. What assessment she has made of the potential impact of the proposed requirement for her to give consent for prosecutions for serious troubles-related offences on the Good Friday agreement.

The Good Friday agreement is one of the proudest achievements of any Labour Government, but after many years of bereaved families being let down, this may be our last chance to get this right. In line with the recommendations of the Joint Committee on Human Rights, the proposed amendment is intended to strengthen confidence in decisions to prosecute serious troubles-related offences. Any decisions would be quasi-judicial and made independent of Government, applying established evidential and public interest tests.

The Justice (Northern Ireland) Act 2002 implemented reforms arising from the criminal justice review of 2000, following the Good Friday agreement, and created an independent Public Prosecution Service for Northern Ireland. The Act states: “The functions of the Director shall be exercised…independently of any other person.” Those reforms were key safeguards, ensuring the independence of prosecution decisions free from political interference. Does the Attorney General recognise that requiring her consent for serious troubles-related prosecutions risks rolling back that safeguard, and will she reconsider the provision to protect the independence of Northern Ireland’s justice system and public confidence in it?

I give my hon. Friend the assurance that there will be no political interference in decision making. As I said in my first answer, all decisions would be made quasi-judicially and independent of Government. There is precedent for that approach, with a number of offences for which Attorney General consent is already required. As the Joint Committee on Human Rights said, that approach could add an extra layer of assurance that there is accountability for prosecution decisions in this sensitive area.

The Attorney General will be aware that there are concerns in Northern Ireland about vexatious claims against former members of the security forces. Under what circumstances would she intervene to ensure that there would not be a prosecution? Does she agree that the only circumstances under which that should happen would be the recent emergence of compelling new evidence?

Any decision that I would take would be made quasi-judicially, free from political interference and independent of Government. It does not change the legal tests—the long-established evidential test and the public interest test—and I will apply those without fear or favour and free from political interference.
5. What advice she has given to the Government on reparations for the historic transatlantic slave trade.

The Prime Minister has expressed his sorrow and regret for the pain and suffering of so many millions of people caused by the transatlantic slave trade. He has also made clear that financial reparations are not the right answer. The hon. Member will understand that the Law Officers’ convention means that I can neither confirm nor deny whether I have been asked to advise or have advised on that matter or, indeed, any other.

I am concerned that the idea that Britain has to apologise for slavery may open the door to reparations. I do not believe that Britain has anything to apologise for. It abolished slavery and thousands of British sailors lost their lives in the fight against slavery. When the advice was given—the Attorney General might not be able to tell me what the advice was, but she might be able to tell me what the question was—did the Prime Minister ask how we may be able to defend against frivolous claims for reparations? The British population is not a cash cow for those countries.

I gently refer the hon. Gentleman back to the Law Officers’ convention. We are proud of the role that Britain played in abolishing the slave trade, but we should also acknowledge the harms done when Britain was one of the largest participants in the slave trade. The Prime Minister is clear that this is morally the right thing to do. He has also made it clear that he does not believe that financial reparations are the right answer, but it is absolutely right to commit to a structured, time-bound, inclusive and good-faith dialogue on the transatlantic slave trade.

I may not be an historian, but actions of the past have consequences for the future. Indeed, many generations of families have benefited from the wealth and the brutality of slavery. Everyone in this Chamber has benefited from slavery in one way or another, and to think that we have not benefited shows a level of deception or even of delusion. If countries and communities feel that they need an apology for slavery because they are still being affected by it, I think that is absolutely fine. Would my right hon. and learned Friend agree with me?

I thank my hon. Friend and constituency neighbour for her question. We both have a large Caribbean diaspora in our constituencies and are proud of the role they have played and continue to play in our communities. If we are to meet the challenges of the future, we need to be ready to face up to the past. That is why the Prime Minister has committed to establishing dialogue on the transatlantic slave trade. This will allow us to discuss its history and ongoing legacy, including the question of a formal apology, to which we are open. It is morally the right thing to do, and it also helps us to build relationships with our trusted partners.

In his attempt to fend off the demands to pay reparations for historical slavery, not least from the Back Benchers behind him, the Prime Minister has proposed to work towards an apology for Britain’s historical role in slavery, together with a £40 million infrastructure payment to Caribbean nations. This would be, of course, an apology for something that no one alive is responsible for. Can the Attorney General confirm that this apology approach, linking historical acts with modern Britain, will not actually serve to increase the risk of claims for reparation payments rather than reduce them?

For years, members of the Commonwealth affected by the slave trade have asked for an honest conversation about the legacies of slavery, and it is right that the Prime Minister is not shying away from those conversations. I do not accept that it opens the door to reparations. The hon. Gentleman talked about the £40 million. We are playing our role as a major global economy in supporting the development of partner countries around the world, and supporting Caribbean countries to address climate change will not only promote growth and stability in the Caribbean but benefit the UK by opening opportunities for collaboration.
6. What assessment she has made of the effectiveness of the Serious Fraud Office.

The Serious Fraud Office is delivering results. Over the past five years, the SFO has secured over half a billion pounds for the taxpayer, investigations announced in the last year included suspected criminality worth over £350 million, and two recently charged cases involved potentially 50,000 victims. I know that the right hon. Gentleman takes a legitimate and forensic interest in the important work of the SFO, and I am very happy to talk to him about this any time.

Last week, the Court of Appeal recommended that six victims of the miscarriage of justice in the Libor scandal should have money that was wrongfully taken from them returned with compound interest, yet the Serious Fraud Office appears unwilling to do that. The SFO is not just being ineffective in this; it is being immoral, piling injustice upon injustice. With a strict court deadline this Friday, will the Minister now direct the SFO to follow the express wish of the Court of Appeal, rather than wasting further public money in the courts?

I do not think it is for me to direct the SFO in this matter. As the right hon. Member says, the Court of Appeal handed down its judgment last week—last Friday, I think. It is therefore reasonable, notwithstanding any timetable, that the SFO is still considering the matter. The court declined, as he says, to make a ruling on interest, but there are a number of elements to the case.

Fraud makes up nearly 50% of overall crime, and the Serious Fraud Office is the UK’s agency dedicated to tackling serious economic crime. But it needs powers comparable to those of the National Crime Agency to conduct surveillance and accompany police on searches to keep pace with increasingly complex economic crime and corruption at home and abroad. Its work protects people’s savings and the honest businesses on which jobs and prosperity depend. Will the Attorney General bring forward legislation to give the SFO the powers it needs to investigate these crimes more quickly and efficiently?

This is the first opportunity I have had to answer a question from the new Chair of the Justice Committee, so may I begin by congratulating her on her new position—and on the fact that she is doing a much better job than her predecessor? [ Laughter. ] As evidenced by this question, she is absolutely right that the SFO needs more effective powers to investigate serious economic crime swiftly and effectively. We do keep those powers under review, and we will seek a suitable legislative vehicle to strengthen them for complex investigations in the future.
7. What assessment she has made of the effectiveness of the victim transformation programme.
11. What assessment she has made of the effectiveness of the victim transformation programme.

In September I was pleased to announce the national roll-out of the CPS’s victim transformation programme. That includes an enhanced service for victims of domestic abuse, providing them with a dedicated victim liaison officer who can support them from charge to trial. This is a vital step in improving CPS support for victims and placing them at the heart of the criminal justice system.

My constituent Mark Noke was tragically murdered, and his family described the experience of the eight-week trial as harrowing, not just because of its contents, but because support for them changed day by day. They sat in a shared gallery surrounded and intimidated by the perpetrators’ families, and they had to pay for transcripts and rulings that the defendants got for free. The defendants had accommodation; the bereaved family had none. Will the Attorney General meet me and Mark’s family to discuss how their experience can help shape the bereaved family scheme, and will she ensure that every bereaved family gets one dedicated liaison officer from charge to verdict?

May I start by saying how sorry I am for what my hon. Friend’s constituents have experienced and for the loss of their loved one, Mark? The CPS is strengthening the bereaved family scheme, including providing dedicated victim liaison officers to have a consistent point of contact from charge to trial. Bereaved families deserve consistent, compassionate support throughout the justice process. I would be happy to meet him and his constituents to hear directly about their experience.

As MPs, we hear heartbreaking accounts from constituents who have experienced domestic abuse and the difficulties they face in seeking justice. I welcome the expansion of enhanced support through the victim transformation programme, but victims’ voices must remain at its heart. What steps will the Attorney General take to ensure that the CPS continues to listen directly to victims and use their experiences to improve the support available?

My hon. Friend is right, and I recently visited the CPS in Mersey-Cheshire, where I met victim liaison officers supporting victims of domestic abuse and serious sexual violence. I was struck by the valuable work they do and their passion for ensuring that victims’ voices are heard. If my hon. Friend has not yet visited her local CPS area, I would strongly encourage her to do so to speak to them about the good work they are doing. [ Interruption. ]
Order. Both of you should know better—you are walking between me and the hon. Member who is asking a question.

Every victim of crime deserves clear communication and compassion, not just a postcode lottery. Given that a recent independent evaluation by Crest Advisory highlighted inconsistencies in how the victim transformation programme is being rolled out across different Crown Prosecution Service areas, what steps is the Attorney General taking to ensure that the victims of sexual violence receive exactly the same high standard of dedicated liaison support, regardless of where they live?

Every victim deserves to have their voice at the heart of the justice system, which is why the national roll-out of the victim transformation programme that I announced in September is so important. It will no longer be a postcode lottery, with dedicated victim liaison officers extended from rape victims to victims of domestic abuse, and clearer, more frequent correspondence for all victims. I am determined to ensure that victims are at the heart of our justice system.

Before we come to Prime Minister’s questions, I would like to pay tribute to Sir David Evennett, who died recently. Sir David was the former Member of Parliament for Bexleyheath and Crayford, and before that for Erith and Crayford. He served this House and his local area for more than 30 years. He will be remembered fondly by many colleagues. I sure that Members across the House will want to join me in sending our condolences to David’s family and friends.
Q1. If he will list his official engagements for Wednesday 18 November.

May I add my condolences to the family, friends and colleagues of Sir David Evennett? He was a kind and generous friend to me when I was in this House before, and to many on all sides, particularly those on the Conservative Benches. He will be much missed. This morning I had meetings with ministerial colleagues and others, and—according to ChatGPT—I shall have further such meetings later today.

Sir David Evennett was a member of the Education Committee with me when I was first elected. He was a really kind man and I was very fond of him. I send my heartfelt condolences to his family. May I add that we should pay our condolences to the family of John Pardoe, who passed away this week? He served North Cornwall and the Liberal movement so proudly for many years. Every year, more than 600 people with cancer in south Cumbria have to make debilitating round trips of nearly four hours, every day for weeks on end, to the nearest radiotherapy centre in Preston. We have the worst access to radiotherapy in the whole of England, and therefore tragically many of my constituents die before their time. The answer is obvious: we need to open a satellite radiotherapy unit at the Westmorland general hospital in Kendal. Will the Prime Minister agree to meet me, local cancer patients and clinicians to help us achieve that long overdue investment, so that people who suffer from cancer in south Cumbria can have shorter journeys, but longer lives?

I want to see the end of the postcode lottery in cancer care. I am going to agree with the hon. Gentleman—he and I used to talk about this very issue 15 or so years ago, when I was Health Secretary. I would like to see cancer care more in the community and more satellite units, exactly as he says. I will arrange for a Minister to meet him to discuss this issue. We are investing in new cutting-edge radiotherapy machines in hospitals across England. Perhaps there is an opportunity to do more in his area, and we will look into it.

Q3. I was really proud to organise recently the first ever South West Norfolk farming conference, with more than 70 rural stakeholders meeting near Downham Market. It has been a difficult year for farmers, with rising input costs, wildfires and water scarcity. That has led to food productivity being increasingly unprofitable, and alternative uses for land being proposed, such as AI data centres and ground-mounted solar, tragically on some of the most productive farmland. So with the EU reset and the 10-year plan on the horizon, will my right hon. Friend the Prime Minister commit to tackling those fundamental challenges around farm profitability and commit to domestic UK food production?

I have an idea of how difficult this year has been for our farmers. I visited a farm myself in Truro at the height of the summer. At the time, we confirmed funding for reservoirs on farms to support them with the changing climate that they face. I will be fighting in Brussels on Friday for a new arrangement to improve the Tory Brexit deal that actually will support our farmers and our food producers, but I recognise that we can do more to support farmers and farming, and I will work with my hon. Friend to that end.

May I, too, start by paying tribute to Sir David Evennett? He passed away suddenly yesterday after a short illness. He was a good friend of mine, a good Whip and a great constituency MP, and he will be very much missed. I am sure that the whole House will join me in offering our condolences to his wife Marilyn, his two sons, and all his family and friends. Will the Prime Minister cut welfare in this Parliament?

I will do everything I can as quickly as possible to get the welfare bill down. We received the landmark report yesterday from Alan Milburn, and I say a huge thank you to him, because he has done a great service to this country and particularly to its young people. Finally—a landmark report that will change the way we think about the coming generation and give them the support that they need to get on in life. I hope that all sides of the House will get behind it. Specifically, I have asked the Cabinet to reprioritise spending plans for ’27-28 to put the beginnings of a fund together to support the youth opportunity service, initially delivering 25,000 quality work placements for 16 and 17-year-olds. We are making progress immediately to get the welfare bill down.

I asked the Prime Minister if he was going to cut the welfare bill in this Parliament; it sounds very clearly like he is not. He talks about a landmark report, but he is not planning any savings for 10 years. Those young people are not going to be young in 10 years’ time. Everything that he wants to do takes 10 years. He wants a 10-year plan—which is still not ready, by the way. The NATO defence plan will take 10 years. Now it is going to take him 10 years to make any welfare savings. We cannot wait 10 years: those young people need those jobs now. Working-age welfare alone costs £180 billion a year and is set to rise to more than £220 billion a year because of this Government. As the welfare Secretary told us, every Labour MP just wants to know who they can tax to pay for more benefits. Keir Starmer failed to make welfare cuts, because this Chief Whip, the right hon. Member for Knowsley (Anneliese Midgley), and that First Secretary of State, the right hon. Member for Sheffield Heeley (Louise Haigh), led the rebellion on welfare. Now they are in charge of the Labour party. Is that not more proof that the Labour party is just the welfare party?

The right hon. Lady reveals time and time again, when she comes to that Dispatch Box, why she does not understand this issue, because she only ever stands at that Dispatch Box asking for cuts. That is all she ever asks for. Her shadow Work and Pensions Secretary confirmed on the television that hundreds of thousands of disabled children would lose funding under her proposals. The Milburn report says that, in order to reduce the welfare bill, we have to improve support. Here is where the Opposition really do not understand it: the report also says that the biggest rise in NEETs came between 2022 and 2024. That is because a report by Sir Kevan Collins, commissioned by the Conservatives, recommended major investment in support for young people coming out of the pandemic to prevent them becoming NEET. Some 250,000 people became NEET because the Conservatives failed to provide that support. We will give hope to young people, and we will oppose the cuts-only approach of the Conservatives.

The Prime Minister says that I do not understand—the only person who does not understand is him. He talks about NEETs, but let me clear his confusion up. When we were in government, between 2011 and 2021, the NEETs rate actually fell by 7%. It then went up because of covid. That 7% is more than all of the savings that the Government are going to find to help young people from the Milburn review. We did more during our time in government than the Prime Minister is proposing now. That is a fact. The Prime Minister wants to pretend that he actually understands. What he wants is the vibes of welfare reform without actually doing any welfare reform. We need to bring down the welfare bill because we cannot afford it, but he does not understand. On Sky News yesterday, the Prime Minister actually said that no one would lose money as a result of his welfare changes. Also on Sky News yesterday, Alan Milburn said that there will be some young people “who…get less”, so there seems to be some confusion here. Can the Prime Minister clear it up for us? Who is right?

We are about helping young people into work. We are about giving young people hope and a better life. That is what this whole reform is about, and I need to hear from the Leader of the Opposition today whether she and her party are going to back the opportunity and support guarantee—a legal guarantee—so that young people in this country can have a better life and can have hope. There needs to be some humility from the Conservatives. They left government with almost 1 million young people without any hope for their future; we want to give them a better life. Yes, we do want people to accept the support that is on offer. That is clear and it is in the report, but we will not accept the Conservatives coming to this House time and again saying, “We are going to bring down the welfare bill”, but failing to support our young people. They slashed youth services when they were in government, they cut the education maintenance allowance, and they trebled tuition fees. They took hope from a generation; we will give it back to them.

I am going to cut through all this waffle. The Prime Minister says that he wants to give young people a better life; all he is offering them is false hope, because none of the things he is saying are going to work. He keeps talking about all of the schemes that the Government have. The youth guarantee scheme is a complete and total failure—everyone out there knows it. The Government destroy jobs, they kill businesses, and then they offer the businesses a little money to give young people work placements. It makes no sense at all. We are not offering young people false hope; we are the ones who are offering them a better plan. Yesterday, I spoke to a café owner in Waterloo. He said to me: “I can’t believe the Government thinks I’m not a working person because I employ people.” Earlier, I asked the Prime Minister to clear up the confusion about who would lose out, and he could not do so. Let me tell him who is really losing out: it is people like that man, every single hard-working taxpayer out there struggling with the cost of living who is going to have to pay higher taxes because of Labour’s welfare bill. That café owner did not blame the last Government; he blamed this Government. Since Labour came into office, the cost of hiring a young person has gone up by almost £5,000. The best thing the Prime Minister could do to solve this crisis is to cut the jobs tax for young people. Why will he not do it?

The Leader of the Opposition comes to the Dispatch Box time and again with her selective facts. Did she see in the news yesterday that unemployment is down? There are hundreds of thousands more people in work in this country, and that includes young people. Did she see last Thursday that growth is up over the last three quarters? Actually, they are the best growth figures for a 10-year period if you exclude the bounce back after the pandemic. The fundamentals of the British economy are strong, and they are getting stronger. We will consider the Milburn report in the round. We will look at all of its proposals in detail and bring forward our response next month, but if the Leader of the Opposition is arguing for a cuts-only approach, we will stand against that, because we know that that will not help a generation to move on. We will bring forward an approach based on support and opportunity—that will always be the approach of the Labour party. We know that our approach will work, and we also have evidence that the Conservatives’ approach failed comprehensively.

I think the Prime Minister said the quiet part out loud when he said he will consider the report in the round. That will probably take another 10 years as well. The Government want to have reviews, to consult and to create reports, and then they come here and say, “It’s a landmark report.” No—it is yet more kicking things into the long grass. We do not have 10 years; we need to get jobs now. The cheek of him to say that unemployment has gone down! He does not know why. It is because people have stopped looking for work; they cannot get jobs, so they have moved into claiming benefits and are no longer classified as unemployed, and that is because of this Labour Government. Across Britain, we are watching a lost generation of young people going straight on to welfare because jobs are disappearing. There are nearly 200,000 fewer vacancies under this Labour Government, and the Prime Minister is congratulating himself that unemployment has gone down. Then on Friday, he will, as he said, go to Brussels and sign up to 100,000 more young people coming to our country to compete for those jobs. Where are those jobs supposed to come from?

We do need jobs now, and that requires growth in the economy. We know that over the last decade, when the Conservatives were in government, we had a decade of low growth. Those are the facts; they go quiet, because they know that is a fact. The deal that is on the table will bring growth to the British economy; it will reduce red tape for businesses; it will cut the cost of exporting to Europe; and, critically, it will bring food prices down. M&S says that it will ease pressure on the price of the weekly shop. Asda says that it will reduce costs. Morrisons says the same thing. Right now, when families across Britain are struggling with the cost of the weekly shop, what are those families to make of a Conservative party that used to back business in reducing red tape and to back working families with their costs, but that is now so split over this issue that it cannot stand up for this country and support a deal that will bring growth to the British economy?

Again, I am just going to clear up some confusion for the Prime Minister. [ Interruption. ] Yes, I have to. He said that we do need jobs and that that requires growth. No, the growth is created by the businesses that create the jobs. It is business that creates growth, not Government. Growth comes after the jobs. It does not just happen. After all these years, Labour still does not understand that there is only one way to reduce youth unemployment, and that is to make it easier for firms to hire people. All the Government have done is make it harder and harder for firms to hire people. They are in a mess on welfare, because the same people who led the welfare rebellion against Keir Starmer are now in charge—the same people who think social security is more important than national security. Let us see how they are doing. Today, we learn that energy bills are going up by 26%. Inflation is up, interest rates are up and young people aren’t working. Isn’t the truth that it is the Labour party—and this Labour Government—that isn’t working?

As I said, growth is up and unemployment is down. The right hon. Lady can ask all the self-serving questions that she likes, and she can take a patronising tone, if she wants to, at that Dispatch Box, but this Government are leading on the big issues. We will not let a lost generation be the let-down generation. We are acting to deal with these issues and to face them. And we will—yes, we will—lead on Europe and bring growth to the British economy. This side of the House believes in the next generation; that side wants to throw them on the scrapheap again with more cuts. This side of the House has a vision for growth and a positive working relationship with our biggest market; that side is still stuck in the politics of the past and cannot accept that the status quo that they negotiated is not working. They gave us a decade of drift and division; this side of the House is letting Britain believe again and bringing back hope.

Q5. Tomorrow is International Men’s Day. May I, as someone who is doing his rather small bit for Movember, ask whether the Prime Minister agrees that, as three out of four suicides are by men, we must challenge the idea that men should simply man up and keep worries to themselves without asking for help? Will he join me in paying tribute to the fantastic organisations in High Peak that are working to change that, from Mentell in Glossop and Buxton to Andy’s Man Club in Whaley Bridge, and will he commit himself to taking further action to support these efforts so that we can save more lives in the years to come?

I certainly pay tribute to all those organisations, and I look forward to welcoming Andy’s Man Club into 10 Downing Street later today. We know that suicide is the leading cause of death for men under 50, and we know that the sessions that those organisations put on make all the difference, connecting men of all backgrounds so that they can talk openly in a way that they could not do in the family home or at work. We are launching the first ever men’s health strategy, which will put more funding into the kind of projects that my hon. Friend has mentioned. May I also compliment him on his Movember efforts? He has 12 days to go—it might even turn into a moustache at some point. [ Laughter. ]

May I join others in sending our condolences to the family of Sir David Evennett and to the family of John Pardoe? Halloween may be over, but the Vote Leave zombies are out in force: Boris Johnson, staggering back, denying the enormous damage to our economy and the cost of living caused by the Conservatives’ Brexit deal; and Dominic Cummings and Lord Gove, trying to scare us with a new made-up number, no doubt coming soon to the side of a bus. But British people now see the true Brexit horror—higher taxes and higher bills—and they want change now, so will the Prime Minister ditch the whole trade and co-operation agreement, and get a new deal that works for the British people?

Well, I think we heard from some of those zombies a few moments ago—they were shouting at me. The truth is that they do not like it when we say the truth in this House. The truth is that the Brexit deal that they negotiated was not good enough for Britain. It is just a fact, and the vast majority of the public know that as well. It is really important that we face up to that. They burned bridges with our largest market—old friends and neighbours. They just destroyed all those relationships. Exports are down from their constituencies, and they know that as well. There will be a deal in front of us on Friday, and I am looking for support across the Floor of this House for what we are trying to negotiate. [Interruption.] Yes, I am, because it can bring growth to the British economy. It can lower the cost of the weekly shop. It can get greater collaboration back on immigration. It is time that they faced up to these facts, and I am hoping that the right hon. Gentleman will back us in our efforts on Friday.

I thank the Prime Minister for his answer, but I hope that he will absolutely ditch the trade and co-operation agreement, because it is bad from start to finish. If the cost of living crisis does not convince him that a totally new deal with Europe is needed, surely the security implications of Trump, Putin and Xi cosying up should. Lurking behind their talks in China is the scandal of Nvidia, the US firm accused of shipping $12 billion of advanced AI chips to China. With Donald Trump investing millions in Nvidia and selling shares before news of Jensen Huang’s affair broke, White House corruption is once more in plain sight. Does the Prime Minister accept that the Nvidia scandal is not just a major US security threat but a threat to the whole world, and given that corrupt President Trump will not, can he tell us what steps he is taking to keep Britain safe?

I think we have to have our eyes open to all the threats that are out there, particularly in relation to the issue that the right hon. Gentleman has raised in relation to Nvidia. We have to establish all those facts, and act on them. Can I say where I will be tomorrow when that meeting is taking place in China? I will be in Berlin for a meeting of the coalition of the willing. The thing that we need to do is continue to stand squarely by Ukraine, and that is what this Government will do. On this issue, I pay tribute to both sides of the House, because that is what we have managed to do in the years since the conflict began, and that is the right thing to do. On this issue, let that clear message go out as that meeting takes place in Beijing: this country is squarely with Ukraine. We know who the aggressor is in this situation, and we will not in any way deflect from continuing that support.

Q9. There are currently 35 brain tumour drug trials in the UK. Of these, about 10 relate to glioblastoma, which has an average life expectancy of just nine months and has seen no improvement in treatment for 30 years. Astonishingly, as of today, nobody appears to know how many people are on those trials. The Department of Health and Social Care does not know, and the National Institute for Health and Care Research does not know, or is at least not telling the Department, so may I ask the Prime Minister if he can find out? I suspect that it is less than 1%, or less than 30 of the 3,000 people diagnosed with this terrible illness in the UK in the last year.

My hon. Friend has been a formidable campaigner on this issue, and rightly so. We all remember her sister Margaret with love and affection, and we all support Margaret’s final campaign. My hon. Friend is asking the right questions in this House, and many people are asking the same questions up and down the country. I recently met Archie Goodburn, who is campaigning on these issues, and we all know that Tessa Jowell’s family are campaigning on the same issues as well. As well as understanding how many people are on those trials, we need to galvanise a change here and get a breakthrough, so that more people can access them. The Health Secretary and I, in that meeting with Archie, agreed to appoint a new national brain cancer clinical lead—that is No. 1—and we have said that we will use the G20 next year to see if we can bring a catalyst for change in respect of cutting-edge research on this terrible issue. I look forward to involving my hon. Friend in all of that work.

The Prime Minister has already acknowledged that Brexit has been an unbridled disaster for businesses and communities up and down these islands, but let me contrast the ruthlessness with which he dispatched his predecessor with the queasiness with which he now prevaricates over Keir Starmer’s red lines on the European Union. Rejoining is something that his Back Benchers, in their greater number, would support. It is also something that the more progressive members of his Cabinet, all the Liberal Democrats and even the SNP would support him on. With the parliamentary arithmetic and public opinion behind him, why does he continue to kick this can even further down the road? Why does he not just set out when we are rejoining the EU?

Well, I am leading on Europe, as I have said today, but I will also stick by what I said at the recent by-election, where I said that I would honour the red lines in the Labour manifesto. That is the answer to the hon. Gentleman’s question. We made a clear commitment. That is a contract with the people, and I will honour it.

Q10. With new skilled jobs in manufacturing and aerospace to the left of us, and new nuclear to the right, there are more opportunities within reach of our young people in Clwyd North than ever before, thanks to record investment in north Wales by this Government. But without decent transport links to key sites, our young people are at risk of being stuck in the middle on the north Wales coast. Funding for the new Deeside Parkway station is an excellent start, but does the Prime Minister agree that we must continue investing in Welsh rail so that young people can be connected to good work, wherever they live?

I completely agree that north Wales needs better transport; it is so connected to the north-west of England. The Welsh Labour Government, when in power, created Transport for Wales, which I believe is one of the better rail operators under public control, but the infrastructure is not good enough, and that often leads to delays. I can commit to work with my hon. Friend and her colleagues to improve transport infrastructure across Wales, but particularly in north Wales, where it does need to be better.

Q2. The war in Ukraine has demonstrated that space is an increasingly critical domain—one where operational control is all-important—so can the Prime Minister assure the House that, when procuring future military satellites, he will prioritise British manufacturing jobs, and will he give a guarantee today that any contract will ensure British sovereign control over this vital capability?

The hon. Gentleman is raising a live public procurement, and in the circumstances, I think it is best that I do not comment in detail on what he has said, but I heard the important points that he raised.

Q12. It was the devastating cuts to youth provision by the coalition Government that led me to join the Labour party, yet today the Opposition have proven that they have learned nothing; their only idea is to take more things away from our young people. Whether born in Chelsea or Clayton-le-Moors, every young person deserves the opportunity to thrive. That is why I am driving forward a youth opportunity hub in Hyndburn. Can the Prime Minister please tell me how this Government will ensure that every young person in Hyndburn has the opportunity to earn or learn?

I pay tribute to my hon. Friend, because her youth hub in Hyndburn sounds to me like a forerunner of the Milburn report. I have agreed with the Work and Pensions Secretary that we need to see a much more devolved approach to employment support, and this is exactly the type of facility that we need—a place that people do not fear walking into, as they sometimes do when it comes to Jobcentre Plus, and a place that is going to support them. This is entirely in keeping with what we are trying to do, and I will ensure that she gets support for the youth hub in Hyndburn.

Q4. Brixham is the highest-value fishing port in England, yet local fishers tell me that they can hardly afford to go out to sea any more because of the extraordinarily high cost of fuel. One is spending an extra £18,000 a week for his three vessels. The smaller inshore fleet is being particularly hard hit. Governments across Europe are supporting their fishers. If the Prime Minister wants growth in every postcode, that means growth for our fishing communities, too, in the places that are literally at the end of the road, where job opportunities are scarce and the fishing industry is crucial. Will his Government commit to supporting the fishing industry, so that our inshore fleet can survive this existential crisis due to the high price of fuel?

I was talking about farming before, but I am going to make the same commitment to the hon. Lady: I will also support our fishing industry, and I look forward to having that conversation with it. We have taken action on fuel duty; obviously, it was frozen in the Budget. I know that there is probably more that can be done, but again, it is really important that we focus on what we can do in the here and now. The Budget did provide help for businesses up and down the country, but we know we need to do more.

Q14. I begin by asking the Prime Minister and, indeed, the whole House to join me in congratulating the Welsh rugby team on beating the All Blacks on Saturday, for the first time in 73 years.In Wrexham, the communities of Coedpoeth and Minera have for months had to put up with illegal waste dumping and non-permitted development. There are 16 similar sites across Wrexham county and hundreds across Wales and the UK. Over 1,000 people have already signed my petition to the Senedd calling for action. Those tipping waste simply ignore Natural Resources Wales notices, and the Plaid Cymru Welsh Government have yet to respond. As a former mayor, the Prime Minister knows that when councils, the police and regulators work together, crime does not pay. Will the Prime Minister urge the Welsh Government to give Wrexham council and NRW the stronger powers that they need?

Yes, certainly, I will congratulate Wales on a genuinely historic victory. Perhaps, in return, the Welsh parliamentary Labour party will congratulate England on their fantastic victory in Spain. On the question of powers, I am talking to the First Minister of Wales about pushing power further down in Wales, in a similar way to what we see happening in England. It has to be a model that is right for Wales, but the offer is on the table to work to put power right down into the communities of Wales. I look forward to working with my hon. Friend on that, and with Welsh colleagues across the House.

Q6. The hundreds of my constituents who work at British Steel Scunthorpe greatly appreciate the support that the Government are giving. Looking to the future, though, the 2,000 acre site, which stretches across the Brigg and Immingham and Scunthorpe constituencies, offers great opportunities for investment and future jobs. Could the Government reaffirm that they consider it a priority location for the strategic sites accelerator programme?

I am very keen to pay tribute to the hon. Gentleman, because I know that he has done a really good job on this issue. I hear that from my Parliamentary Private Secretary, my hon. Friend the Member for Scunthorpe (Sir Nicholas Dakin), who has also worked hard on it. We have common cause here, I believe. The hon. Gentleman mentions the strategic sites accelerator, which is backed by £700 million and is open for applications. We would absolutely encourage an application from his area.

My constituent Keaton Slater was just 12 years old when he was killed by a dangerous driver, who then fled to Latvia. His family spent more than two years seeking an extradition. Does the Prime Minister agree that when offenders flee the country and extradition is required before they can face justice, that should be taken into account in sentencing guidance and sentencing decisions?

I understand that this case has been referred to the Attorney General’s Office, and I will ask for an update on it myself. If appropriate, I will raise this with the Latvian Prime Minister when I next see him. I credit my hon. Friend for raising this issue, and if she would like to discuss it further, I would be available for that.

Q7. In August, it was reported that Leicestershire police have been issuing dual identity warrant cards for gender-fluid officers. At a time when women in Leicester East and across the country are rightly demanding basic common-sense protections and single-sex safeguards, this sends entirely the wrong message about operational priorities and public trust. The Government were built on a pledge to halve violence against women and girls, so can the Prime Minister explain why he is yet to reaffirm that commitment, and will he ban these absurd dual identity warrant cards today?

I have said repeatedly that the Government I lead will be relentless in tackling violence against women and girls in every single respect, and the everyday harassment that people are on the receiving end of. I am not aware of the case the hon. Lady raises, but I will look into it.

It was a pleasure to welcome my right hon. Friend to my constituency recently. We sat down with the Single Homeless Project, a wonderful and vital service. We spoke to women with lived experience, and heard about the difficulty identifying women who are rough sleeping, as often their homelessness is out of sight and hidden away. Will the Prime Minister support a dedicated women’s census, so that we can understand the full scale of the issue and ensure that support reaches those who need it most?

Credit to my hon. Friend for the work that she does on this issue and on homelessness. I remember well the meeting we had at the Single Homeless Project. It is an amazing organisation that made the point that women’s homelessness can often go missed and does not get the same attention, so I support what she is saying on a local census. We have a drive to end rough sleeping; that is a personal priority for me. I will make sure that there is the right focus in councils across the country on women’s homelessness as well.

Q8. Meur ras, Mr Speaker. Although I was disappointed that my private Member’s Bill, which puts first homes before second homes, was postponed last week, the campaign for housing justice will continue. Will the Prime Minister meet me and the supporters of the Bill to consider the extreme housing challenges in places like my west Cornwall and Isles of Scilly constituency, and in particular the unintended risk of the recent Budget further rewarding second home owners who holiday-let their properties to obtain multimillion-pound tax benefits—tax benefits, of course, that the Tories do not take into consideration? This is public money that could be far better spent, not least on helping those in particular housing need.

I did ask officials to look seriously at the hon. Gentleman’s private Member’s Bill. It was felt that it was not the best way to address the issue, but we do not disagree with what he is trying to do. I will ensure that the Housing Minister meets campaigners, as the hon. Gentleman requests. We will see if we can come back to the issue with a workable solution.

Further to the very important points made by my hon. Friend the Member for High Peak (Jon Pearce), the last few weeks have shown us that there is a critical need to hold powerful men to account when they abuse their position, and to tackle the manosphere, but also to create and support alternative places for our young men and boys, with humour and love. Will the Prime Minister therefore join me in thanking Suggs from Madness, Rowan Williams, Ella Vaday from “Drag Race”, Richard Herring and Sanjeev Bhaskar for being willing to start that conversation on International Men’s Day, this Sunday, at the Soho Theatre Walthamstow? It will show that it must be love, not hate, that leads the relationship between men and women in the future.

I am more than happy to send that message to all those people, who are brave for stepping forward. We must address this issue of power imbalances in workplaces; in the media industry, as the Culture Secretary is doing; and in our own workplace. There is an obligation on every single Member of this House, as I said, to be relentless in tackling violence and sexual crime against women and girls.

Q11. Habibi is the pseudonym used by a troll on the internet. This individual has been identified as Ben Tait, who has deep connections in the House of Lords. He has smeared and attacked Members in both Houses, as well as prominent public figures. We all enjoy freedoms afforded to us by democracy, but when those freedoms stray into inciting religious hatred against Muslims and Jews, or inciting violence, such as driving a van into a serving MP’s constituency office, every Member should condemn such abhorrent behaviour. I am afraid to say that the shadow Justice Secretary, the hon. Member for West Suffolk (Nick Timothy), unashamedly referred to this account-bearer as “brilliant”. Does the Prime Minister agree with me that we must all condemn, not celebrate, such vile hatred, and will he meet me to discuss measures to stop such online abuse?

The case the hon. Member raises sounds serious. I do not know all the details. It does sound as though there are issues for the Conservative party, although, again, I do not know the full details, but I will ensure that a Minister meets the hon. Member to discuss this.

Since the Law Commission reforms introduced by the Conservative party, licensing authorities no longer know who is driving cabs in their area. This puts passengers at risk, as Baroness Casey identified, and distorts local markets. Given the Prime Minister’s past remarks on the issue of cross-border hire, will he now act to ensure that taxis are licensed in the areas in which they operate?

Yes, I will. This is a matter of public safety—and, actually, of the safety of women and girls. I do not believe it is acceptable that we can have people with licence plates from 100 or 200 miles away operating in an area where the driver cannot be held to account, so the simple answer is yes. This is an issue that I raised as Mayor of Greater Manchester, and I will correct this in this House.

Q13. The e-MERLIN network is the UK’s national radio astronomy facility. Its network of radio telescopes stretches from the Knockin telescope in my constituency of North Shropshire all the way to south Cambridge. Its headquarters are at Jodrell Bank, which has the grade I listed Lovell telescope. I was recently privileged to visit it. Its high-resolution radio imaging is world leading. Sovereign capability in radio astronomy is critical for the UK scientific community, and for national security, given the network’s tracking and observatory capabilities; once lost, they will be lost forever. The network is set to lose its funding in 2028. It would be reckless to lose this capability in an increasingly uncertain world, and it would be vandalism to allow the Lovell telescope to fall into disrepair, so will the Prime Minister commit to finding the money to save it?

As part of a generation of north-west schoolchildren who went on trips to Jodrell Bank, I feel duty-bound to do everything in my power to save that critical infrastructure, which is also part of the heritage of this country. I am with the hon. Lady on this one. We need to find a solution, and I will ensure one is found.

Will the Prime Minister join me in congratulating the England wheelchair rugby league team, which this week became the first men’s team to win the world cup for the third time? As we are celebrating the achievements of our para-athletes, does he agree with me and the Paralympian Richard Whitehead that the achievements of our sportsmen and women with disabilities should never be weaponised against others?

I join my hon. Friend in congratulating the whole of the England wheelchair rugby league team. Back-to-back world championships is a phenomenal achievement. It is a thrilling sport, and I know that Mr Speaker gives it his full approval. I thought the comments by Richard Whitehead deserved a response from the right hon. Lady the Leader of the Opposition. She is not listening, but her remarks were crass and insensitive, and I think she should withdraw them.

Q15. Nearly 10 years ago, brave young women at Oxford University told me that they had been sexually assaulted in their colleges, only to then be silenced by gagging orders supposedly protecting them. These shameful agreements are rightly illegal in higher education, and I commend this Government on extending that ban to workplaces, although I urge them to speed up. But there is a gaping loophole: even with these new laws, freelancers and fans, like those targeted by Russell Brand, can still be silenced, and it has to stop. Will the Prime Minister meet me to discuss how we can extend these protections to everyone, so that the rich and powerful can no longer buy the silence of the vulnerable, anywhere?

I know the hon. Lady has worked closely with the First Secretary on these issues, who speaks highly of the very effective work that she has done. NDAs should never be used to silence victims. Powerful and wealthy people able to do that—it should not be possible. I pay tribute to the women who have come forward. We never want to see powerful men using the law to silence accusers. We have taken action in the Employment Rights Act 2025, but the First Secretary has assured me that we will go further. We will look at freelancers and do exactly what the hon. Lady says.

Olympian Beth Dobbin recently wrote to the Prime Minister about the devastating impact that ME has had on her. Hundreds of thousands of people across the UK live with the heartbreaking effects of ME. Many are left bedbound, with many more left unable to live any semblance of a normal life. But it is an illness that has been overlooked and under-invested in for far too long. Will the Government back Beth’s call for more research funding and take further action to ensure that those suffering with ME get the treatment and support that they need?

The Health Secretary will soon be meeting Beth to discuss her experiences. We will ensure that my hon. Friend is kept updated and thank her for raising Beth’s cause in the House. We are supporting cutting-edge research, including a first-of-its-kind programme to study the genetic factors behind the condition, and we are exploring a clinical trial for potential new treatments. Progress is being made, but my hon. Friend is right—more is needed.

On a point of order, Mr Speaker. Yesterday, the Prime Minister of Mauritius gave his National Assembly a lengthy and detailed account—available online—of recent discussions he has had with the United Kingdom’s Prime Minister and our National Security Adviser on the sovereignty of the British Indian Ocean Territory. He also confirmed that he had received reassurances on the future of the Chagos treaty and the UK Government’s continuing advocacy of it. None of these seemingly extensive discussions, at the Commonwealth Heads of Government meeting and elsewhere, has been reported to this House. Have you, Mr Speaker, received notice from the Government of any intention to make a statement on “reassurances” recently given to Mauritius about the future of the Chagos islands? Can you advise hon. Members how we can ensure that the House is kept properly informed of such developments, or must we continue to depend on tendentious pronouncements in a foreign Parliament to discover our Government’s latest manoeuvres to surrender sovereign British territory?

First of all, I have received no notification of a statement from Ministers. I am sure that Ministers on the Treasury Bench have picked up on what has been mentioned. What I would say is, the Member has been here a very long time. I do not think this is the last we will hear from him, and I know those avenues will be pursued—the carpet will be worn out from him knocking on the door—to ensure that this issue is brought forward. I am sure that the Government will have heard him. Bills presented Powers of Attorney Bill Presentation and First Reading (Standing Order No. 57) Adam Thompson presented a Bill to make provision about lasting powers of attorney; and for connected purposes. Bill read the First time; to be read a Second time on Friday 27 November, and to be printed (Bill 186). Future Generations (Policy Impact) Bill Presentation and First Reading (Standing Order No. 57) Layla Moran presented a Bill to require public bodies to have regard to the impacts of policy decisions on future generations and the sustainable development principle; to require the assessment and measurement of the long-term effects of such decisions; to provide for reports to Parliament; and for connected purposes. Bill read the First time; to be read a Second time on Friday 19 March 2027, and to be printed (Bill 187).

I beg to move, That leave be given to bring in a Bill to make provision about park homes. Residential home parks offer a different way of living: a peaceful setting and beautiful surroundings; usually a garden to call your own; and often a lovely community atmosphere. Around 160,000 people live in mobile homes in England—that is about one and a half times the population of my constituency—but because they are spread across 1,800-plus sites, their needs have barely been spoken about in this Parliament, and they have been exploited and let down by an outdated system in desperate need of reform that is mostly on the side of rogue operators. Residents are being forced to live in unsafe conditions and put up with non-stop non-compliance while enforcement proceedings take too many years to run their course. Legal responsibilities ignored, safety responsibilities ignored, prosecutions ignored, fines ignored, communications from residents ignored—my residents deserve better. Today, I am pressing for the changes that will keep them safe. Our country’s legislation on park homes should be on the side of residents and should make them feel safe; instead, it is on the side of those who would make them feel unsafe. Bournemouth’s best days lie ahead of us, and we are not afraid of a fight. Working together to call for park homes regulation, we are fighting for fairness for everyone. That starts with the residents of Iford Bridge in my constituency, where my constituents have been forced to endure an operator who repeatedly fails to meet basic legal and safety responsibilities. Indeed, so concerned are my constituents in Iford Bridge that they feel reluctant to be named in this Parliament and reluctant to speak on our national public service broadcaster. That cannot be acceptable. Residents of Iford Bridge face an operator who, in 2022, was fined for offences involving failure to comply with a notice; who, in 2024, received a further compliance notice requiring 33 actions; and who, in 2025, following prosecution and conviction for failing to comply again, received a fine of nearly £28,000. And yet in 2026, despite repeated enforcement action, people remain dependent on this operator to manage and maintain their homes and the wider site, while significant concerns persist. I am calling on the Government to provide key changes: a set of stronger powers against persistent offenders, because serious breaches of site licence conditions should have meaningful consequences; a stronger fit and proper person test, because nobody should operate a park home site when they are found to have made repeated and serious regulatory failures in defiance of the standards set directly by this House; a set of stronger local authority intervention powers, because councils need a middle ground between repeated prosecution and licence revocation; proper recognition of flood risk in the regulation and management of park homes, because nobody—particularly the elderly—should be unnecessarily evacuated and put at risk; an end to the unfair 10% charge on sales, because the costs fall hardest on older people, who make up 80% of park homeowners; and action to tackle the complex ownership structures that undermine people’s protections, because nobody should face charges that leave them out of pocket and in fear of the future. I am calling for powers that in many cases already exist for other housing sectors, because everyone, wherever they live, deserves equal protection under the law. My Bill seeks stronger powers against persistent offenders, with two changes in particular. First, a site licence condition breach should be an offence, whereas a local authority must currently serve a compliance notice then pursue action if that notice is breached. Secondly, councils should be given the power to impose civil penalty notices of up to £30,000 as an alternative to prosecution. It should be easier to punish rogue operators so that they do not see the benefit in dodging their res
I inform the House that I have selected the amendment in the name of the Prime Minister. I call the Opposition spokesperson to move the motion.

I beg to move, That this House believes that taxes, regulations governing product and food standards, and migration policies should be set by the UK Parliament, not the European Union; further believes that giving the EU control over these matters will lead to more expensive goods for British citizens and increased costs and regulations on businesses; also believes that UK taxpayers should not be paying to subsidise university fees for EU students at all, particularly while the Government refuses to take action to reduce the cost of Plan 2 student loans for British students; and believes that UK taxpayers should not have to pay any additional money to the EU.
