It is a genuine pleasure to open this debate, not least because as things stand this is the first and only opportunity that Members of this House will have to express a view before the Government prepare to sign away basic areas of British sovereignty at this weekend’s summit and pay Brussels for the privilege. Once again, this House is treated less like a sovereign legislature and more like the readers of a Sunday newspaper, left to piece together the future of our constitutional settlement from carefully curated leaks to the press rather than hearing ministerial statements from the Dispatch Box. The House will know that I always approach these occasions with a spirit of Christian charity towards Ministers. Negotiating with the European Union is never a walk in the park. Even the most seasoned diplomats have occasionally found themselves feeling like an optimistic terrier entering a particularly well-organised kennel. Yet looking at the draft agreement that is currently circulating, one is forced to conclude that this Government arrived in Brussels without a plan, without a compass and with only one overriding strategic objective: to avoid coming home without a piece of paper to wave at the cameras.
Surely the greatest mistake was to give away the principal ask of the Europeans before we had secured anything in return by giving them 12 years’ additional access to our fish for nothing.

My right hon. Friend is clearly right; it is a matter that I will come to very soon. The European Commission could scarcely have dreamt of a more docile negotiating partner. We know that some parts of the leaked draft will have been put there solely so that they could be removed at the summit on Friday, in an apparent win for Ministers. Not even this Government are so completely inept as to agree to not return EU criminals to their home countries at the same as releasing dangerous criminals on to the streets of Britain—that one is clearly not going to be in the final agreement. But there is so much more that, worryingly, looks like it could be. Let us start by examining the price tag of this diplomatic enthusiasm. While Ministers have conjured up an optimistic and, to put it politely, highly debatable projection of economics that might, if the wind is in the right direction and Jupiter aligns with Mars, materialise sometime in the 2040s, the direct costs to the British taxpayer are immediate and eye-watering. They amount to at least £23 billion over the decade ahead, and even that staggering sum excludes the regulatory burden imposed on the 90% of businesses across the length and breadth of our country, particularly small and medium-sized enterprises, that never export a single chicken nugget or wheel of cheese to the European Union yet will be forced to comply with every new directive and regulation that rolls off the Brussels conveyor belt.

The hon. Gentleman is making an interesting case in giving his interpretation of the economic harm that Brexit has done. I am surprised, though, that he is not choosing to talk about the number of businesses that are now not exporting because of the sheer weight of bureaucracy that has been imposed by the Conservative Brexit deal that we so urgently need to get away from. I would be keen to hear his analysis of those figures.

I thank the hon. Lady for her intervention; I will certainly speak later about the need to remove unnecessary bureaucracy. I find it interesting that the hon. Lady is so worried about that number of businesses, which actually is not very big. Every business matters, but it is a smaller number than, for example, the number of businesses in Northern Ireland that have reported that they are no longer trading between Northern Ireland and Great Britain as a result of the Government’s refusal to use the provisions of article 16 of the Northern Ireland protocol.

I commend the shadow Minister on his speech; he is right to highlight the issue of Northern Ireland. When it comes to UK-EU relations, Brussels has prioritised wider diplomatic goals over Northern Ireland. The Windsor framework has institutionalised a democratic deficit, and the Stormont brake is largely illusory. Does he agree that a true partnership requires an end to the diplomatic patch-up and respect for Northern Ireland’s constitutional integrity and democratic voice, which is lost at this moment in time?

I do agree with that, but I also— [ Interruption. ] If the Minister wishes to intervene, he may; otherwise I will continue. The additional burdens that are being imposed on the many businesses that do not trade and have never traded directly with the European Union are on top of the 76 new directives that have already been adopted by the EU since the divergence after Brexit. It is the very definition of a blank cheque—a binding commitment without knowing what the costs will be because we cannot know what the future regulations will be. For Brussels, it may be the gift that keeps on giving, but for so many British businesses it will just be the cost that keeps on rising.

The point my hon. Friend is making is really important. Does he recognise that the UK already has world-class food standards, but under the deal being touted by the Prime Minister, the sanitary and phytosanitary rules would not only apply to exports to the EU but would be applied on British food that is entirely for British consumption? What does that say about our sovereignty?

My hon. Friend is absolutely right. I saw this when I met a major food processor in my constituency a few weeks ago, who spoke about the increasing regulations because they do export to Brussels—sorry, to Paris. [ Interruption. ] The increasing regulations coming out of the European Union— [ Interruption. ] Will the hon. Member for Walthamstow (Ms Creasy) let me finish my sentence? Because that business exports to Paris, it obviously already has to comply with European regulations, but there are growing new regulations with additional costs, such as the specifications for the coating that must be put on pallets for boxes to be piled on. Those burdens have to be met by exporters. It is not right for those regulations to be extended to every other business. The 92% of food and drink manufacturers in the UK that do not trade with Brussels should not have to face those additional burdens.

The shadow Minister is making a powerful case for the need to remove EU regulation. Does he regret that the Leader of the Opposition, when she was Secretary of State for Business and Trade before the general election, failed to remove some 4,000 EU regulations because, as she said, it was a bit difficult?

The hon. Gentleman has a very selective memory of the Retained EU Law (Revocation and Reform) Act 2023. It does not match that of those here who remember the work that the Leader of the Opposition did as Business Secretary to streamline legislation and repeal unnecessary regulation.

To those of us who have sadly lived and breathed this debate for over a decade, it rather sounds as though the shadow Minister has forgotten who invented the border operating model that added hundreds of pounds to a pallet of exports for British exporters. [ Interruption. ] The hon. Member for South Northamptonshire (Sarah Bool) is chuntering from a sedentary position; I was sat on those very Opposition Benches when her Government invented the mess that is the border operating model. Will the shadow Minister at least have the courtesy to apologise to the British farmers and 20,000 businesses who have given up exporting to Europe altogether because of such paperwork?
The hon. Lady always speaks with enthusiasm on this issue. She speaks of her sadness about the ongoing debate while missing no opportunity to try to reopen and prolong the divisions of the past.

On the SPS issue, the European Union has always had it in its power to make that a simple operation. It does so for other importing and exporting countries such as New Zealand, whose vets are trusted to certify that goods meet the European Union’s requirements, and they go right through Rotterdam without being checked. In the negotiations with the UK, the EU chose not to take that approach, even though it had worked for the whole time we were a member. It was the bad faith of the EU that meant that the SPS— [ Laughter. ] Hon. Members may laugh, but the reality is that we will have to give up control and responsibility to get something that the EU has granted to New Zealand for free.

My right hon. Friend is clearly correct: mutual recognition ought to be the way forward. It is worse than he suggests, because the agreement does not take that forward but takes it off the table going forward. The Prime Minister laid down three tests for any deal with the European Union: first, whether it respects Labour’s general election manifesto; secondly, whether it improves on the existing trade and co-operation agreement; and thirdly, whether it passes the Makerfield test by delivering the Brexit that people actually thought they were voting for. On all three counts, this draft agreement is not merely a stumble but a comprehensive, gold-winning failure. Let us take the manifesto test. Labour promised the British people that there would be “no return to the single market, the customs union, or freedom of movement”, yet for whole swathes of our economy, the agreement places Britain squarely back into the single market’s regulatory orbit, requiring dynamic alignment with EU laws over which the House has no vote, no veto and no voice.

The shadow Minister is being ever so generous. The hon. Member for Walthamstow (Ms Creasy) talked about apologising to farmers, but now our farmers will have to take rules, have increased competition from European farmers and have no say, despite us having better welfare and better quality food production. Is that not the case?

My hon. Friend is clearly right. I mentioned the manifesto test, and another part of Labour’s manifesto was about banning the sale of foie gras in the United Kingdom. I am interested in hearing whether the Minister can commit to that still being possible after whatever he agrees on Friday.

May I beg all hon. Members on both sides of the House to look at the reality of what is being said? We talk about having no say, but if we get the deal right and it goes well we will have the opportunity, for the first time in 10 years, to sit around the table with the European Union at which the standards will be set. I have had this conversation with farmers and farmers’ representatives, and they welcome the opportunity that has been denied them for 10 years to shape the standards. Yes, we will not have a final vote, but we will be back there shaping the standards and having a say, which has been denied them for 10 years as a result of the actions of the previous Government. Let us welcome that.

While the hon. Gentleman is doubtless well meaning, I am afraid he is mistaken. We do not have a meaningful seat at that table—we get informed as to what the decision is. There are already forums for exchanges between parliamentarians and Ministers, but those are not part of the formal decision-making process and are not even at the level of the formal processes that Switzerland or Norway have. This is the very definition of legislation by fax machine.

On that very point— [ Interruption. ] It is interesting that Labour Members are getting so excited. My hon. Friend is completely right: the Swiss might be consulted when a bit of legislation will be coming from the European Union, but as soon as the legislative process starts in Brussels and in the European Parliament, they are locked out of the discussions. Even when we were a member of the European Union, we were regularly outvoted on matters of national interest. Now, the Government are taking us to a situation that is even worse than when we were a member.
As I said, no vote, no veto and no voice. The Prime Minister’s second test is whether an agreement improves on our existing deal. On the contrary—

Sorry, I really do need to move on. The agreement fundamentally alters the nature of our relationship with the European Union. Under the trade and co-operation agreement, we co-operated as sovereign equals. Under this draft agreement, we will be contracting out our lawmaking to Brussels, and paying handsomely for the privilege. Of course, the Opposition support sensible agreements to reduce unnecessary friction at the border. Nobody enjoys paperwork for its own sake, and we certainly do not enjoy the cost.

I really do have to make some progress. [ Interruption. ] I have taken a lot of interventions—maybe later. Where administration harms both sides, we should strip it away through bilateral agreements based on mutual recognition between sovereign partners, just as we do and as the EU itself does with trading partners around the world. Sadly, because Ministers signalled from day one that they were willing to surrender legislative autonomy, the European Union realised that it had no need to offer genuine compromises—why meet Britain halfway when Britain is sprinting across the pitch to hand you the ball? The Prime Minister’s recent, rather ham-fisted attempts to reopen the debate on rejoining only weaken our negotiators further. If this agreement goes ahead, the United Kingdom will become by far the largest economy in the world voluntarily to hand control of its laws to an external organisation in which it has zero representation. That is what happens when Ministers negotiate on the touching, if rather naive, assumption that unilateral concessions early on will be rewarded with generosity later. It is a triumph of hope over experience.

Is that not the exact problem? It was the former Prime Minister Baroness May who negotiated away the position of treating the United Kingdom as one unit. She conceded the point that Northern Ireland could be treated differently from the rest of the British Isles. Was not that the fundamental problem?

My hon. Friend knows that I have a number of disagreements with the negotiating strategy at that time. But while it is important to learn from one’s own mistakes, surely it is even better to learn from the mistakes of those who have gone before. Instead, the Government insist on repeating them. It is a triumph of hope over experience. Let us look at what happened earlier in the process. Ministers happily gave away our fishing rights for 12 years in the breezy expectation that British defence manufacturers would be welcomed into the EU’s Security Action for Europe programme. What was the result? We were left with neither the fish nor the defence contracts. That was not bad faith on the part of Brussels; it was simply amateur hour in Whitehall. What of the Prime Minister’s third test—the Makerfield test? If the Prime Minister genuinely believes that these proposals reflect what voters in Makerfield or anywhere else thought they were backing in 2016, I gently suggest that he spends a little more time knocking on doors in his constituency. Had we said to voters on either side of the referendum campaign in 2016 that leaving the European Union meant being bound not only by existing Brussels laws but by every future law that the European Union chooses to pass, does any Member of this House seriously think that anybody would have agreed to that? That is not a reset; that is rejoin by direct debit. Taking back control meant taking back control over our laws, our trade and our money. This agreement gives away control of all three, by signing us up to open-ended commitments and even imposing penalty clauses to stop us withdrawing if the costs are too high. The Minister for Intergovernmental Relations and European Relations has been busy auditioning for the silver screen with his social media videos. I know that the whole House shares his profound disappointment that, despite his best efforts in front of the lens, they still went with Robert Pattinson. In his latest production, the Minister posed earnestly behind a supermarket basket, assuring viewers that his deal would make their weekly shop cheaper. There was just one small flaw in the script: the products that he was waving at the camera were British-produced, British-sold and destined never to leave these shores. Reducing border checks at Calais cannot miraculously lower the price of a Lincolnshire sausage sold in a Lincoln supermarket. [ Interruption. ] Or even a Staffordshire sausage sold in a Staffordshire supermarket. What will affect that producer, however, is being forced to comply with costly new EU directives on goods that will never cross the channel. Far from making the Minister’s shopping basket cheaper, this deal will make it decidedly dearer.

The shadow Minister is very kind, especially as I am not certain this is going the way he wishes it was. Irritatingly, he left out Lorne sausage from Scotland, although I will be the first to concede that the EU market for Lorne sausage was not particularly large after Brexit. My Montrose lobsters, however, were on a truck straight to the EU, and now they only do that once they have been inspected by a vet in west-central Scotland. He talks about abstract points of theory and policy. Will he set out where either his constituents or mine are one bit better off as a result of the Tories’ Brexit?

If the hon. Gentleman wants to see examples of benefits of Brexit freedoms, he only had to look at the Chancellor’s Budget statement a few weeks ago, when almost everything he had to announce was only possible because of the freedoms of Brexit. Finally, there is the question of taxpayers’ money. The Cabinet Office recently launched a rather defensive—

The shadow Minister is very kind. A lot of the debate has focused on food so far. My constituency is home to Borough market, Bermondsey Street and the Roses greasy spoon, next to my constituency office, where they do not sell foie gras. My constituency does more for food in this country than many others, I will wager. The shadow Minister’s deal left Neal’s Yard at Bermondsey market paying £320 a week for produce certification that was not there before. That is damaging British jobs and British produce on a weekly basis. The shadow Minister is clearly not going to apologise today. Is his message to Neal’s Yard and other British producers to suck it up further, or will he congratulate this Government on trying to cut those costs and improve our economy?

I was clear earlier: we should be working with European Union, where there is a mutual benefit, for mutual recognition to reduce those unnecessary barriers. The way to do that is not to impose those same regulations on the 92% of food producers who do not export or import from the European Union, adding their costs to the same level as the exporters; it is to reduce the costs across the board. This is not the right way to do it.

It is tangential, because the company that I am referencing is in Staffordshire. It is a chemical manufacturer that exports to Europe and it will now have to register under a UK REACH regulation and a European REACH regulation. I agree with the shadow Minister about working together where there is an opportunity for mutual recognition that cuts bureaucracy and cost. Why did the Conservatives not do that in the deal that he is defending?

The short answer is that it takes two parties to reach an agreement, and I do not think there was the appetite at that time for that level of trust. We need to build that trust, but the way to do that for mutual recognition and more frictionless trade is not by indicating that we are prepared to sign up to every programme and regulation that the other side adopts. The Cabinet Office recently launched a rather defensive website that featured a “mythbuster”. The website asks: “Will British taxpayers have to pay millions of pounds into the EU budget?” The answer is a brisk no, followed by a mention of the sanitary and phytosanitary deal, the emissions trading linkage and the youth experience scheme. How wonderfully lawyers’ drafting works, as hon. Members will notice the glaring omission from that list: the EU’s internal electricity market. The Minister has previously conceded that he is prepared to talk about payments into EU regional cohesion funds in exchange for electricity market access. Given what his Department’s website is saying, I invite him to stand at the Dispatch Box and give us a straight answer. Will he categorically rule out the UK paying a single penny towards EU regional cohesion funds, levelling up Bratislava instead of Birmingham or Bolton, in exchange for an electricity deal or any other part of the package? The same one-sided generosity infects the proposed return to Erasmus+. To rejoin a scheme where Britain historically paid in twice as much as it got back and which predominantly subsidised EU students coming here, the Government have scrapped the Turing scheme, a global programme that supported more British students, including those from far more from disadvantaged backgrounds, to study in 150 countries around the world at a fraction of the cost. Worse still, Ministers cannot even tell us what Erasmus+ will cost after year one, while reports indicate that they are preparing to subsidise domestic tuition fee status for EU students. His Majesty’s Opposition are crystal clear that our priority should be reducing the burden of student loans to British students, not subsidising continental undergraduates.

I am very pleased that my hon. Friend has come on to this. Does he agree that the Turing scheme was a far more logical attempt to achieve stuff for UK students, as opposed to Erasmus being overwhelmingly, and at a huge cost to the UK Treasury, a benefit for middle-class European students who wanted to come here to do a gap year while studying for a master’s in a humanities subject? That is of no use to UK students. We need to invest in further education, and I suggest reducing the crippling cost of plan 2 loans.

My right hon. Friend is correct. We clearly welcome overseas students to the UK, but they should not present a cost to the British taxpayer. Our scheme should support opportunities for British students to study and get new opportunities abroad. The Turing scheme did that effectively and efficiently. The Erasmus scheme will predominantly fund EU students to travel here.

I really must conclude. Again on youth mobility, instead of seeking a genuinely reciprocal scheme with similar numbers of young people travelling to and from the EU, the Minister looks set to submit to EU demands for a high cap of 50,000 or 60,000 or possibly even more. Just a day after the publication of the Milburn review, and with the Government consigning a lost generation of school and university leavers to a future on welfare, it is incredible that they should be considering allowing so many new visas. Finally, let us look at the Government’s claim on energy bills. Ministers promised dramatic falls in electricity prices from joining the EU internal electricity market, yet we import only around 10% of our electricity from the continent and industry estimates suggest market coupling might shave roughly 0.5% off wholesale costs. Meanwhile, both Energy UK and Fuel Industry UK have highlighted that the real sting in the tail of merging our emissions trading scheme with Brussels will drag UK carbon prices up towards EU levels, imposing between £3.5 billion and £8 billion in additional carbon costs over the course of this Parliament, as well as increasing the cost of fertilisers for our farmers by as much as £100 per tonne. That will push energy bills up, not down, for every household and every factory in Britain. Britain is a proud, independent, innovative nation. We should be trading freely with our European neighbours as sovereign partners, not signing away our laws, our borders and our taxpayers’ money in a frantic bid for a photo opportunity. This is set to be a bad deal, negotiated by a Government without a clear plan. It will not have the public’s support, and it should not have this House’s support either.

I beg to move an amendment, to leave out from “House” to the end of the Question and add: “regrets that the previous Government’s agreement with the European Union imposed new costs, checks and red tape on British businesses and held back exporters; notes the electoral mandate of the Government to seek a closer relationship between the United Kingdom and the European Union that will support economic growth, cut costs and deliver benefits for UK businesses and working people, while respecting the manifesto red lines of no return to freedom of movement, the Single Market or the Customs Union in this Parliament; and supports the Government’s position in seeking to achieve progress towards those objectives at the UK-EU Summit on Friday 20 November 2026.” I would like to thank the Opposition and the hon. Member for Kingswinford and South Staffordshire (Mike Wood) for moving the motion. He suggested that we learn from some of the mistakes made on the Conservative Benches, so if he will forgive me, I will make a little progress before taking interventions, though I look forward to doing so. I want to start by recognising the world we face today, and I think it is important that we start with a sober tone about the challenges facing Europe. When the referendum took place a decade ago, Russia had not launched the full-scale invasion of Ukraine, and global trade and energy supplies were not being used as geopolitical weapons. Since then, we have faced a global move towards more isolationism and protectionism, and there are new challenges to our economy from aggressive over-production. We have heard about the pressures that puts on constituencies right across the land. With war in Europe and the middle east, there are challenges to our security and to the values that we hold: democracy, the rule of law and, indeed, economic openness—a view that has been shared across both sides of the House. A decade ago, some argued that Britain could thrive by pulling up the drawbridge. In today’s world, I believe the opposite is true. A closer, stronger relationship with the European Union is fundamentally in our national interests.

I will give way to the Father of the House in a little while, of course. This is not just about the threats and challenges we face from a more global context, however. It is about the practical consequences of a status quo that we inherited that is not working. The inherited Brexit deal has pushed up the cost of living, making it harder for British families to get by. It has generated a wave of red tape—something that the Conservatives have traditionally been against—driving up costs for British businesses, as our amendment notes. Instead of building up a balanced partnership, the Conservative Government needlessly damaged trust with our closest neighbours. I was grateful to the Opposition spokesperson for acknowledging, as indeed did the right hon. Member for Chingford and Woodford Green (Sir Iain Duncan Smith), that a relationship of trust with the European Union can have very practical benefits indeed. The lack of trust that we inherited has had a material cost to UK exporters and, indeed, to people across this country. I will take an intervention from the Father of the House, but before I do, I want to quickly turn to some of the more outlandish claims from the Conservative spokesperson— [ Interruption. ] There were a few, but let me just deal with some of the most egregious. The first such claim was the suggestion that I am tactically leaking negotiation documents in order to look better. I will leave the negotiating to those on the Conservative Benches; we saw that during the course of the hon. Member’s speech. That is not true, and I will not give a running commentary, whether on leaks or the negotiations themselves. Of course this House will have the opportunity to scrutinise fully the deal that we reach, but as Members would expect, when we are knee deep in the negotiations and with a few days to go, I will not provide a live commentary on them.

The Minister is obviously totally committed to the European project, which he is entitled to be. Many people view this reset as the opening move in rejoining the EU. He is my constituency neighbour in Brexit-voting Lincolnshire. I know he will say that he stands by the Government’s red lines, but what is his personal view of the long-term future? He is a Europe Minister and I would like to know whether he believes, as the Prime Minister does, that it would be in our national interest to rejoin the EU eventually. He is completely honest, and we are going to have an honest debate, so does he think that people will have to accept no opt-outs or rebates, and a full commitment, treaty-wise, to Schengen and the euro? Will he give his own personal view, please?

I am keen to talk to the right hon. Gentleman about personal views in many places, but not as a Minister bound by collective responsibility. We have set out our position very clearly. I am focused on delivering a good deal for the public on Friday, alongside the Prime Minister, who will then deliver a speech about our future options with Europe at a future date.

I am grateful to the right hon. Gentleman, who is another Lincolnshire MP, like the Father of the House, and a Minister whom I both respect and, much more importantly, like. The argument he has made, however, requires further examination. He says that, in a more uncertain and increasingly introspective world, we need to cling to this supranational institution, but these are the arguments that were used in 1972 by the people who betrayed us in the first place. If we look back at Hansard from those times, we see that those people said the world was uncertain, that we lived in an increasingly complex environment and that we had to abandon our sovereignty in order to cope with those uncertainties. Those same arguments were rehearsed again by the liberal bourgeoisie at the time of the Brexit debate, so this is not about a changed set of circumstances leading to an inevitable outcome; it is about a choice that the Government are exercising, irrespective of the will of the British people.

The right hon. Gentleman goes back into a debate that roiled both the Conservative party and the Labour party in the 1970s. He talks of betrayal, and I would just caution him on that. I recognise that this is a very emotive subject but, because our constituents often take a lead from us, let us in this House try to avoid talk of betrayal and traitors, and the sort of antagonism that was such a feature of previous debates. We can legitimately disagree on these questions, and we can do so respectfully, and it is in that tone that I will try to conduct my interventions.
I will of course take two respectful interventions. I think the right hon. Member for New Forest East (Sir Julian Lewis) was first.

I am very grateful to the Minister, and I agree with his point about tone and will try to live up to that. Does he accept that, for many people, the decision to vote to leave the European Union was not primarily about economic arrangements; it was about the fact that the European Union has a stated fundamental aim to create a politically unified united states of Europe, which would dissolve the sovereignty of the member countries? That is the reason I voted to leave. Does the Minister have any reason to believe that the European Union has abandoned that long-term political unification ambition?

Why did people vote in the way they did in 2016? There will be myriad reasons, but I speak from my own constituency experience, and I say this with great appreciation, having taken interventions from many Lincolnshire MPs to ensure that, despite the efforts of my hon. Friend the Member for Stoke-on-Trent Central (Gareth Snell), we do not talk exclusively about Staffordshire today. I am pretty sure that people in Lincoln did not vote to prevent fresh sausages from being exported, or to have hundreds of pages of checks— [ Interruption. ] The right hon. Member for Chingford and Woodford Green complains that the EU introduced such checks. The work that we are engaged in is seeking to improve those circumstances. The question that I was asked is: why did people vote in the way they did? There are myriad reasons. I am confident that on Friday we will deliver a better deal for those who voted for Brexit and the like.

The Government are proposing, in the area of veterinary science and certain aspects of food regulation, to adopt what is called dynamic alignment. That means that, once we have signed up in those areas, if the EU changes its regulations, we in the United Kingdom would automatically have to follow them, regardless of the will of Parliament, in perpetuity. That is true, isn’t it?

I will try to make a little progress and deal explicitly with the key question that the right hon. Gentleman asks me. We can have a lot of discussion around the overall questions of Brexit, but he is right to turn to the arrangements on Friday. Let me try to answer his question directly, make some progress on the summit on Friday and then I will take some more interventions, because otherwise I fear that I will run out of time. On Friday, I intend to reach an agreement that is strongly in Britain’s interests. Any powers to implement any deal that we reach—whether that is in relation to the SPS agreement, the veterinary agreement mentioned by the right hon. Member for Chingford and Woodford Green or the emissions trading scheme agreement, which was also referenced—would obviously come back to this place for Parliament to decide. We have taken— [ Interruption. ]

I look forward to having a debate with the right hon. Gentleman, if we reach an agreement on Friday, about how Parliament might exercise its powers in relation to implementing this agreement. Clearly, as he knows, maintaining arrangements on food safety does of course require alignment, but that is a debate to come after we have signed an agreement, which we have not yet done, at which point of course we would return to Parliament.

As promised, I will make a little bit of progress. I will take a final round of interventions, but let me push on. On Friday we aim to strike important deals to boost our economy, to cut the red tape that has been referenced so many times and to help businesses grow. The deals that we aim to conclude at the summit should add 0.4% to long-term GDP. The agrifood deal should cut costs for businesses and keep costs down in shops by removing post-Brexit checks on food and agriculture exports, which should save UK businesses money every time they sell British goods abroad, while adding up to £5.1 billion a year to the economy. Since 2023, British businesses have had to pay for over 1 million multi-page export health certificates to trade with the EU, and indeed to Northern Ireland. That costs them between £90 million and £210 million—costs that should now fall away with this deal. That should save companies up to £200 more every time they sell British agrifood abroad, £1,200 more when they sell a load of British cheese abroad, and £1,400 more when they sell a shipment of British salmon abroad. Far from increasing costs, as their motion wrongly claims, the Opposition want to vote today to support keeping the status quo, keeping this bureaucracy for British businesses. For Northern Ireland, as the hon. Member for Strangford (Jim Shannon) said, very significant checks were introduced by the previous arrangements. Far from no checks in the Irish sea, we have seen a blizzard of them. This agrifood deal will facilitate the smoother flow of agrifood and plants from Great Britain to Northern Ireland, protecting the UK’s internal market, reducing costs for businesses and improving consumer choice.
For farming and those sectors that may be looking for transition arrangements, is that something being considered as part of the negotiations on Friday?

As I have said, I do not want to provide too much of a running commentary on negotiations, but I can assure my hon. Friend and his constituents in Rushcliffe that I am very conscious of the areas in which the rules have diverged. I do not agree with my Lincolnshire colleague, the hon. Member for Boston and Skegness (Richard Tice), on much, but he was right to say that, in fact, the divergence on food and drink safety rules under the previous Government was relatively limited. Where there were divergences, it is important that there are transition periods and that we ensure that businesses do not end up suffering the cost.

The Minister is being generous with his time and is giving a clear and precise description, without giving away the Government’s negotiation tactics. When I talk to businesses in Harlow, many of which are food producers and distributors, the No. 1 issue they tell me they face is the red tape created by us leaving the EU. Can he reassure businesses in Harlow that whatever negotiations happen with the EU, he will be putting those businesses first and at the heart of everything he does?

Business views are at the heart of this. I want to return to the kind comments of the shadow Minister, the hon. Member for Kingswinford and South Staffordshire, about what was not quite my debut on the silver screen, but I am glad that he watched it so closely. It is worth including what I had in my shopping basket and saying a little bit about particularly business interests in relation to supermarkets, given the close eye the Opposition have on these questions. This is what businesses, including many supermarkets in all our constituencies, have said. Morrisons called an agreement “a leap forward” that would “ease a source of pressure on food prices” and therefore good news for shoppers. Asda has said it “has the potential to significantly reduce costs and bureaucracy both for the fresh produce we import from the EU and the goods we move every day to our customers in Northern Ireland.” I made the mistake of checking social media this morning and saw that the shadow Secretary of State for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs, the right hon. Member for Louth and Horncastle (Victoria Atkins), was straight on to the Union Jacks on the goods in my shopping trolley. At the moment, even goods with Union Jacks can face checks, as we heard in relation to Northern Ireland. There are checks as they go into Northern Ireland, but even more importantly—returning once again to Lincolnshire, as you would expect, Madam Deputy Speaker—fresh meat cannot be exported at all. Welsh shellfish cannot be exported at all. I talked about the additional burdens on cheese. This is a good deal for supermarkets, whether it is in relation to goods with a Union Jack on them or, indeed, those we import.

One of the areas in which the UK has regulatory advantage thanks to Brexit is in the precision breeding of crops, and there are pioneering firms at Norwich research park. Rather than telling them to wait and see what is agreed on Friday, can the Minister confirm that the Government objective is not to agree to anything that would undermine that freedom and advantage?

The hon. Gentleman asks an important question. He is right about precision breeding. Agritech is an important area of British strength, including, once again, in Lincolnshire—I will see how many times I can mention it. We are not leaving the industry in the dark about what our priorities are; we are discussing these questions closely with them. Of course, I cannot broadcast at this stage the details of the negotiation, but I am very conscious of the strengths we have in some of these areas and the importance of protecting them.

There are 1 million young Brits who are not in employment, education or training, and the way to fix that crisis is to put them at the front of the queue for new jobs. Why on earth, then, are the Government proposing to open the doors to hundreds of thousands of young Europeans who will come here and work in our shops and restaurants? Is that not a total and utter betrayal of young people in this country?

I noted the right hon. and learned Lady’s using the language of “betrayal”. Despite saying this before, let me say that I really would encourage everybody to try to be temperate in their tone. We are in discussions about the youth mobility scheme. It is important to listen to what young people themselves would like. Brexit removed a whole host of opportunities from people right across the country. In the interest of time, I am not sure that we can do full justice to Erasmus+, but we are seeking to restore opportunities to young people that have been taken away in a scheme that would be capped and that would have no access to benefits. We are completely committed to tackling the NEETs crisis in the way that Members heard yesterday from the Secretary of State for Work and Pensions, but that should not mean that we do not give opportunities both to our young people and, indeed, to others. I am writing to all MPs today about taking up the opportunities from Erasmus+. Whether Members believe that we should have done Erasmus+ or not, there are institutional opportunities for schools, colleges and youth clubs right across the country. They may not like it, but I really encourage them to ensure that young people in their constituencies make full use of them. These bonds have frayed, and it will require some effort from us all to rebuild them; I encourage Members to take that opportunity up in their constituencies.
I will, and then I will seek to conclude, otherwise I fear the House may be hearing from me forever.

Of course, we know that dynamic alignment will fall under the jurisdiction of the European Court of Justice, for which there can be no accountability, and its purposive interpretations can expand what the Government might feel they have agreed. Would the European Court of Justice jurisdiction also apply to the youth mobility scheme?

I know the hon. Gentleman’s interest in this issue, but I cannot provide a running commentary on negotiations. We do not have to wait very long—I am sure that I will be back in the House shortly and we will be in a position to go through all the details of what we have agreed. I am familiar with his strong and well-expressed views on these questions over many years. We will no doubt be able to have that discussion, but I am not in a position to do so while the negotiations are ongoing.

The Minister is somebody who gets it. He understands the difficulties of Brexit, and the chaos and disaster that it has been over the course of the past 10 years. He understands what it does to businesses and to our sense of ourselves as a nation. What we want to hear from the Government is where they are going to take us with Europe now. We in the SNP want to rejoin the European Union, but the Government have been hot and cold on this for about the last two months. What is their intention? Will we be back in the European Union in the next decade?

The hon. Gentleman asks the question with real charm, but I am going to give him the same answer that I have given before. As he would expect, today I am focused on the negotiations. The Prime Minister will say more in due course in response to all of the questions that have been raised by Members from across the House, and I look forward to that discussion. Our focus is to ensure that our relations with the European Union are fit for the challenges we face now and in the future. Europe is our neighbourhood, it is our home, and it is our closest and largest market. A stronger, deeper relationship is in our interests. After a decade of division, this Government have chosen pragmatism over ideology and constructive partnership over pointless confrontation. Friday’s summit is an opportunity to deliver on our commitment for a closer relationship with our nearest neighbours and largest trading partners, to strike practical arrangements that produce a tangible benefit for British industry, for our businesses and, most of all, for working people across this country. Every proposal that we take to the negotiating table is guided by whether it delivers real improvements in everyday lives in postcodes across the United Kingdom by slashing costly red tape for exporters, protecting our industry, helping us to tackle illegal immigration and strengthening our collective security. That is how we draw a line under the failures of the past, rebuild trust with our closest allies, and deliver lasting prosperity and security for Britain. On that basis, I urge colleagues to support our amendment.

As ever, I welcome this opportunity to debate Britain’s relationship with Europe, but I have to confess to being astonished by the motion before us. Here we have the Conservatives—the chief architects of perhaps the greatest act of economic self-harm in modern British history—presenting themselves today as the defenders of British business and prosperity. The audacity is breathtaking! They promised liberation from red tape, then buried British businesses beneath mountains of it. They promised frictionless trade, then delivered customs declarations, border checks and additional costs. None of this should have come as a surprise. The shadow Minister, the hon. Member for Kingswinford and South Staffordshire (Mike Wood), said that no one has an intrinsic love of paperwork for its own sake. Well, let me take that suggestion and raise him one Surrey banger. And I do not mean a porky white sausage—I mean Michael Gove, my predecessor as the Member of Parliament for Surrey Heath. On 13 July 2020, standing at that very Government Dispatch Box, Michael Gove, my predecessor—thankfully, new ideas have emerged since—spoke about the new customs industry that Brexit would necessitate. He described this emerging industry not as an unfortunate side effect or a necessary evil of Brexit, but—and here is the sheer audacity—as an economic opportunity. Perhaps he was the enthusiastic puppy that the shadow Minister mentioned in his opening statement, because he welcomed the prospect of creating “a totally new industry” here—not just audacious, but absurd. The Conservatives did not eliminate the bureaucracy. They created an entirely new industry to administer it, and they claim it as a success. British business has been paying the cost ever since. Between 2022 and 2025, an estimated £7.7 billion was spent by British businesses, purely in the completion of customs declarations forms in order to trade with Europe.

The other day I met representatives from the cold chain sector, who were highlighting this very point about bureaucracy and checks at the border. The sector is critical for the transportation of pharmaceuticals and food, and yet those businesses are the very ones impacted at our borders every single day. Does my hon. Friend agree that we absolutely must cut this Brexit tape here and today?

I could not agree with my hon. Friend more. Some £7.7 billion has been spent just on the transaction costs of the paperwork itself. I am sure that businesses like the ones she mentions have also had to pay for additional staff in order to administer that paperwork. Earlier this week, I visited Hedley’s, a fantastic logistics firm in west London that now has three members of staff dedicated purely to the administration of customs forms. Those costs represent money that is not being invested in machinery, plant, apprenticeships, innovation or increased wages. That is money being consumed by navigating barriers that the Conservatives themselves created.

While the hon. Gentleman is talking about extra staff for businesses, we should also mention the extra 100,000 to 140,000 civil servants who have ended up coming into the workforce in order to deal with the administrative headache of Brexit. Does he agree that was not a good use of public money?

The full economic cost of the Conservatives’ appalling Brexit deal would take, frankly, an army of actuaries to fully calculate, and I am grateful to the hon. Gentleman for drawing our attention to just another facet of that complex arithmetic.

When negotiating the trade and co-operation agreement, the United Kingdom Government did make an offer to the European Union to have mutual recognition in an SPS agreement—a veterinary agreement based on mutual recognition—on the basis that that was offered and given to New Zealand and to Canada. How does the hon. Gentleman think the EU justifies not offering the same to us?

Sovereignty is a bugger—if that is a parliamentary term, Madam Deputy Speaker—and the EU was clearly exercising its own in that case; it was under no obligation to offer us anything. Frankly, given the level of distrust that the Conservatives had engendered in the entire process, I am not surprised that we got such a poor deal. Research published by the National Bureau of Economic Research estimates that Brexit has left Britain’s economy 6% to 8% smaller than it would otherwise have been, with substantial damage to business investment and to productivity. The resulting economic damage is today costing the Treasury up to £90 billion annually in lost tax revenue. That is almost £250 million every single day.

Since Brexit, the number of lorries and trailers passing through the port of Holyhead in my constituency has fallen by 107,000—a reduction of nearly 22%. Does the hon. Member agree with me that this underlines the need for a closer relationship with the European Union to remove the damaging trade barriers and the economic failure created in constituencies like mine, and will he acknowledge the importance of the port of Holyhead?

I have not spoken to the hon. Lady about this situation before, but I hear exactly the same observations about other port cities in our country as those that she makes about Holyhead, and I fully support her point.
The hon. Member is being very generous with his time. I represent Cairnryan in Dumfries and Galloway, and the ferries there are going like gangbusters.

I presume that most of the trade going from Cairnryan is travelling to Northern Ireland, so the hon. Gentleman will also be aware that when those same customs forms that I mentioned before are not completed properly or have not been adequately registered, then entire truckloads of fresh produce from our supermarkets travelling to Northern Ireland sit there and rot on the very streets that he represents. That is not a proud legacy for him to stand on. Imagine what £250 million of lost tax revenue every single day could do for our hospitals, our schools and our armed forces. The Conservatives promised a Brexit dividend, but they left Britain paying an extraordinary Brexit bill. Now they return to this House with another collection of the same tired arguments. Their motion warns that European product and food standards will make British goods more expensive, but they conveniently ignore the cost of having two sets of standards—the cost of duplicating testing, additional certification and separate compliance systems. The Government estimate that removing unnecessary barriers to food and agricultural trade could benefit our economy by up to £5.1 billion annually. Aligning regulations involves choices and obligations, but so does diverging from them. The Conservatives insist on counting the costs of co-operation, while pretending that the costs of separation do not exist. On migration, Brexit ended Britain’s participation in the Dublin system for returning asylum seekers to other European countries. We surrendered a mechanism for international co-operation, and then discovered that controlling migration in fact requires co-operation with our neighbours after all. Then there is the extraordinary claim about university fees. There are discussions on the possibility of reciprocal arrangements, through which European students could pay domestic fees at British universities, but again, the Conservatives conveniently omit the other half of the equation: British students could enjoy the same rights at European universities—and in many European countries, public university tuition fees for domestic students are negligible or zero. Think of the needed opportunities that could open up for our young people.

Does my hon. Friend agree that while the economic side of the conversation about youth opportunities is important, the issue goes far beyond that? Encouraging young people to travel to Europe and having young Europeans coming and living here creates friendships, lasting ties and a cultural understanding that is so important in a world that has become increasingly unstable since we voted to leave the European Union in 2016. For the stability of our continent, we absolutely must strengthen those ties again.

My hon. Friend speaks about these issues with alacrity and knowledge, and has a history of great involvement with them. I do not know whether we can call the things that she refers to “intangibles”, but if they are intangibles, they are perfectly representative of the people-to-people diplomacy that will secure the peace and security of our continent—the original intention of the scheme when it was founded. We are discussing the future of young people. They are not raw material for another tawdry social media clip of the sort that the Conservative party may seek to present in the aftermath of this debate. Consider the timing of this debate. Britain and Europe’s automotive industries have warned that unresolved changes to the rules of origin could lead to the imposition of £1.8 billion in tariffs in 2027 across trade in both directions, as a result of the ratcheting up of the trade and co-operation agreement. Once again, the Conservatives cannot claim that they were not warned about the dangers to our automotive sector. Long before Brexit was pursued or realised, in In one of the Committee Rooms upstairs, Patrick Minford, one of Brexit’s leading economic advocates, gave evidence to a Committee of this House that made that reality plain. When asked whether leaving the European customs union could mean the collapse of the entire UK car industry, Minford acknowledged that we would have to “run…down” the British car industry; he comparing its fate to Britain’s coal and steel industries. Today, with British manufacturing jobs and investment at stake, the Conservatives are still defending the barriers that have put industry at risk. There is something even more troubling here. While the Conservatives remain consumed by the arguments of 2016, the world around us and them has changed profoundly. Russia’s war against Ukraine has shattered the foundations of European security; China is reshaping global industry and supply chains; and American leadership can no longer simply be taken for granted. Economic strength, technological resilience and national security have become inseparable, and the Conservatives’ motion says nothing about the world in which Britain now competes. That is why the Liberal Democrats have proposed an ambitious growth and defence partnership between Britain and Europe. It would restore Britain’s economic strength by ensuring that we rejoined the single market and negotiated a new, bespoke customs union that removed the barriers holding back British business. This would deepen European defence co-operation, and our collective security would be strengthened through joint procurement and defence production, and through closer collaboration with our NATO allies. Economic strength is national security, and in an increasingly dangerous world, Britain cannot afford to be politically or economically weaker, strategically isolated, or politically irrelevant. That brings me to Labour. The Prime Minister has recently discovered the language of honest conversations about Brexit—or perhaps I imagined that. Recognising the damage is not the same as having the courage to repair it. He wants credit for confronting reality and recognising that the Brexit emperor never was wearing a scrap of clothing, while maintaining the very red lines that prevent any meaningful change. That is not pragmatism. It is timid; it is cowardly; and it is costing us billions. Friday’s UK-EU summit should be an opportunity to transform Britain’s relationship with Europe; instead, Labour’s internal divisions have reduced its ambitions to a desire to repair some of the damage while refusing to confront its causes. It is extraordinary that we still need to explain what Adam Smith understood 250 years ago this year: trade creates shared prosperity; there is no requirement for one nation to lose for another to gain. Our geography has not changed—Dover is still 21 miles from Calais—and our economic futures and security interests remain deeply intertwined. The C

It is a pleasure to follow the hon. Member for Surrey Heath (Dr Pinkerton). This debate has been mainly in two parts. If I may use the phrase, there is a weary familiarity to the conversation taking place on the Conservative Benches about what Brexit meant. I have reflected on this matter over a long time, and the Conservatives remind me of diners who go into a restaurant and order a Brexit, having no idea what it will be. When the dish arrives, they say, “This isn’t what I ordered.” Why is that? Because there is a clear dissonance between the promises that were made and the reality. Their only way to deal with that is to say, “Waiter, waiter! This isn’t what I ordered.” That is what they do, rather than opening up to the fact that the promises that were made have not come to pass. Let me touch on Northern Ireland, which was mentioned earlier. The fact that Northern Ireland has the arrangements that it does was completely predictable, because we ended up with the United Kingdom, which was no longer in the European Union, having one set of rules; Ireland, which was still in the EU, and the rest of the EU having the European set of rules; and an open border between the two entities. Here is the question: how were we going to manage trade across an open border? It was plain-as-a-pikestaff obvious that the only way we could do that, given that the border was open, was by ensuring that goods arriving in Northern Ireland complied with the rules of the EU. Out of that came the Windsor framework. Once again, I pay tribute to the last Government for what they negotiated in the Windsor framework, which made things just about workable. About the only thing that all parties in Northern Ireland agreed on during my time as Secretary of State for Northern Ireland was their welcome for the SPS agreement, which my hon. Friend the Minister spoke about. That was precisely because it will make the movement of goods so much easier. The other debate that we have been having this afternoon is of a very different character, and it is about the way in which the world has changed in the last 10 years. I urge the House to lift up its eyes collectively and look around us at the world in which we live. The public’s view of Brexit has changed quite significantly, in so far as one can tell from the polling that has been done, because the public can see that it has been bad for our economy; the evidence of that is growing all the time. That is not very surprising. If you make trade with your biggest, nearest and most important trading partners more difficult, and make it involve more paperwork and more bureaucracy, do not be surprised if it damages your economy. However, it is also because other things have changed, and we are living in new circumstances. Who would have thought, decades after the fall of the Berlin wall, which was referenced, that Russia would invade Ukraine? Look at the threats we face, including people’s ability to turn up the temperature of freezers remotely and ruin all the food—something that no one appears able to prevent; other types of cyber-attack; the threat to communications; the vulnerability of our cables; hybrid conflict; and the fact that the United States of America, under the current President, has revelled in removing itself from international agreements, and has called into question the long-standing US commitment to the security of Europe. We have seen populism spreading, and I very much regret that the official Opposition in this House are now advocating for our leaving the European convention on human rights. Winston Churchill would not recognise the Conservative party of today, because he supported that, and it is very striking that the former Leader of the Opposition William Hague gave an interview in which he said, “I couldn’t be a candidate for the Conservatives at the next election, because I do not agree with leaving the European convention on human rights.” By the way, doing so would have serious implications for

The right hon. Gentleman is speaking with his customary passion. His reference to the invasion of Ukraine is not relevant, for one good reason, which is that the UK was first to come out in support of Ukraine. Most importantly, though, the NATO framework under which all those countries gathered is about collective defence. The EU is not about collective defence—it is about wholly different issues. I would be grateful if the right hon. Gentleman recognised that.

Obviously, I agree with the right hon. Gentleman about the role and importance of NATO, but we have seen a big change in the attitudes of EU member states to defence and defence spending, which is also reflected here in the United Kingdom. It is possible to argue both that NATO is the bedrock of our defence—it has been since it was created—and that having a closer relationship with the European Union is also important to our defence, including when it comes to purchasing military equipment. That is why progress on the Made in Europe question will be so important for us. I was making the point that working with other countries is not a betrayal, because it is the best way of protecting and advancing the interests of the people who send us to Parliament to represent them. Of course, one of the great political challenges is where we strike the balance between the supranational and the local or devolved. In part, the Brexit referendum had that question at its heart, because people had it put to them, “Would you like to have some control?”. To be frank, if many of my constituents had been asked, “Do you feel you have any control over what is happening in the world out there?”, they would have said, “I don’t have any control at all over what is happening.” However, this is about striking a balance in a more complex world. Co-operating on trade will undoubtedly help our economy; helping our economy will give us growth; and growth is what we need to generate revenues to pay for many of the things that we would all like Governments to do. The agreement that the Government hope to conclude on Friday—and I wish them every success in their endeavours—is a really important first step towards what I hope will be the destination of putting us back in the heart of Europe.

It is a pleasure to follow the right hon. Member for Leeds South (Hilary Benn). It is always interesting to hear his views and perspective. I will start by reflecting on what has been said in this Chamber already, particularly about the changing world that we live in. Over the past decade, not just Britain but the rest of the world has been confronted by the axis of authoritarianism, hybrid warfare and other significant challenges. At the same time, NATO—the bedrock and foundation of this country’s defence—has continued to hold up and be strong, particularly with the transatlantic partnership as well, making sure that as a member of NATO, we are strong when it comes to our defence and security. I do not think we should be conflating some of these discussions and arguments with leaving the EU—conflating Brexit with where we are now and going forward. It is a statement of the obvious that we have to work with our international counterparts. We are a member of Five Eyes, and we have great convening strength around the world. We led the convening when Russia illegally invaded Ukraine—it was Britain that convened other countries in Europe and across the world. We should all be proud of that strong record. Frankly, we have to stop running our country down, because our place in the world is incredibly strong.

The right hon. Lady makes an important point, but does she accept that Europe has a lot of defence equipment to buy to defend itself against threats coming from the east? Defence procurement is a really important aspect of closer European co-operation, so that we can buy and make the defence equipment that we need.

I thank the hon. and learned Member for his intervention. In the unstable world we live in, defence procurement is now vital for us all, but it is not just with the EU; we are competing for resources, including critical minerals, and all sorts of elements that are fundamental to defence and security. We are a Five Eyes country, and those are exactly the conversations that are taking place around the world with Five Eyes partners. Particularly given Russia’s illegal invasion of Ukraine, it is inevitable that those conversations go full circle across the board, and it is right that we have them. Turning to today’s debate on UK-EU relations, I mean no disrespect to the Prime Minister, but when he was seeking election during the Makerfield by-election, he told the country that he would not rerun the debates and arguments about Brexit. However, on the eve of the UK-EU summit, the Minister has today confirmed in his responses to interventions that at that summit on Friday, he will sign agreements on alignment, and then return to this House to rubber-stamp something that the British public have had no say over. There is no legitimate democratic mandate to do that. We should recognise that the previous Prime Minister put this country on the slippery slope back to EU control, with British taxpayers paying the costs. If I can say so in the right tone, Labour Members are flying kites for our paying money to the EU and going back into the EU without having full discussions, and without a mandate to do so. It is important for all Members of this House to recognise that what Labour Members are now proposing, and what was being proposed under their previous Prime Minister, is neither simple nor straightforward. Not only do these agreements take a great deal of negotiation, but they involve trade-offs, some of which we have heard about in interventions from Opposition Members. However, it is also important to recognise that we have to be pragmatic, and through the better use of technology and innovation there are ways in which we can overcome some of the burdens that exist.

The right hon. Lady was trying to make the argument that the current EU-UK summit proposals do not have a mandate, but I want her to reflect on how this Labour Government were elected on a clear mandate for a pragmatic and closer working relationship with the European Union. Will she reflect on, and perhaps correct, her remarks about a mandate? It is the democratic responsibility of this Government to do everything we can to achieve economic growth. I think she might want to refresh her remarks.

Democracy is fundamental. It is part of our values in this country and it is what we all strive for, day in, day out. No one would question that, but Labour does not have the mandate to renegotiate the trade and co-operation agreement and major elements of what came out of Brexit. It is important to reflect upon that, particularly when it comes to issues such as alignment and costs. To be fair to Labour Members, they will have to go back to their constituents and explain all these key areas. They will be trying to wrap it up in Christmas bunting and say that all will be well off the back of a summit, when there are no details on the costs and the implications for British taxpayers more widely and in the long run. Erasmus has been mentioned, but when it comes to migration deals and other aspects, every Member in this House— [ Interruption. ] There is no point shaking heads: we all will be accountable for the implications of the summit, and that is the point about democracy. We should all be proud of that democratic point.

This is not a sophisticated point, but does the right hon. Lady not accept that if we do a deal that makes it easier for us to export food and drink to the European Union, our businesses will do better, they will pay more tax and we will have more income for the national health service, the defence of the country, education and all the things that everybody in this House believes in? Will she therefore tell those businesses in her constituency that are looking to save money, because they export to the EU and it is difficult, that they are wrong?

I speak to those businesses every single week and engage with them every single day. They are under the cosh because of Labour’s regulation and higher taxes. When it comes to being pragmatic and sensible, we should absolutely use technology and innovation, but the fundamental question has to be: at what cost? It is important for all colleagues to recognise that this will be a moment where we will surrender power, sovereignty and decision making back to Brussels. It is important for every single one of us to understand the long-term consequences of that. The Minister for EU relations, the right hon. Member for Lincoln (Mr Falconer) is not in the Chamber right now, and I am sorry about that, because I spent a lot of time debating across the Dispatch Box with him in previous portfolios. He admitted at the weekend that we will be in the room but we will not have a vote. Laws and decisions on our food products going to the EU and those coming into our domestic market will once again be determined by EU regulations and bureaucracy—by EU politicians with no mandate from the British people and, importantly, no accountability to them. The Prime Minister has admitted, in contrast to what he said in the Makerfield by-election, that he wants to go further. I will air a few points to the House about why I disagree with what is being proposed, but I will first give way to the hon. Lady.

The right hon. Lady talks about EU regulations and bureaucracy. Perhaps she would like to have a conversation with John and Nicki Holmyard in my constituency, who now have to have 17 different documents signed by a vet before they can export one load of their top-class British shellfish to the European Union. Often that shellfish gets sent back from the French port, because one of the bits of paper has been signed in the wrong place or something has slipped. I suggest that there is far more bureaucracy and regulation for their business now than ever before. They are hanging on by a thread, and they are desperate for this SPS deal to go through so that their business does not go under, as so many other fish and shellfish-exporting businesses have since the Conservative Brexit deal destroyed them.

First, I would be happy to speak to the hon. Lady’s constituents about this, because my understanding is that shellfish sales have not gone down at all. [ Interruption. ] The information is out there.

As my hon. Friend says, the information is in the Library. The hon. Member for South Devon (Caroline Voaden) should check some of the information out there. I represent a part of the east of England where oysters and other fish products go over to the EU. I want to make a number of points. First, when the Prime Minister sought election in the leave constituency of Makerfield, he said that he did not want to rerun the Brexit argument. One of the debates being rerun is about whether Britain should be in or out of the EU, the customs union, the single market or some variation of them. Those are divisive debates. None of this is straightforward or simple, but such debates will absorb the political capacity and bandwidth of the Government when they could be dealing with so many of the other important issues that this country faces and engaging with businesses. That engagement is not just in terms of the EU, but understanding the challenges that businesses are facing. Those of us who served in previous Parliaments after the referendum—there are probably many more of us on the Opposition Benches than on the Government Benches, although the right hon. Member for Leeds South has spoken—will remember that we were in near paralysis over some of those decisions in the debates that raged. It was undignified. Madam Deputy Speaker, you may recall some of those times, too. They did not put this House in a good light. It led to a breakdown of political trust. Out in the country post-referendum, the public just wanted us to get on with respecting the referendum result and with the job of governing. Taking the country back to that period will not be helpful when we all face so many other big challenges. Secondly, the Prime Minister has no mandate to make this change. He has no personal mandate through his by-election and no mandate—I disagree here with the hon. Member for Cities of London and Westminster (Rachel Blake)—through the Labour manifesto. Those so-called red lines are being blurred and faded every time the Prime Minister and Labour Ministers talk about rejoining. They are speaking about more integration, and there is a distinction. I come back to that mandate from the referendum. We have to reflect on and recognise the lessons from the past. The EU is consistently interested in two key elements: one is cost, which means access to British taxpayer funds; and the other is exerting control over us. It is about rules, regulation and decision making. We heard that with the reset argument under Prime Minister Keir Starmer. My other point is that when the Prime Minister is advancing his case to align with the EU and rejoin, he is making the argument around the British economy, and that is misguided and wrong. Growth in the UK has been higher and stronger than much of the EU since the referendum. Outside of the EU, we were free to rebound strongly through the difficult period of the covid pandemic. We have been free to remove burdensome regulations and costs on British people. Government Front Benchers have an opportunity to provide some assurances about what this move will mean for our domestic economy and trade arrangements. Outside of the EU, we have been free to negotiate new trade deals globally, with new deals and new benefits. Labour Ministers and Members have frequently welcomed those deals. They boast about free trade arrangements around the world, whether those are with India or even the comprehensive and progressive agreement for trans-Pacific partnership. Will the Minister give some assurance to this House about what this new EU deal will mean for these existing trade co-operation arrangements around the world, including with countries in the Asia Pacific, whether that is India or even Japan? We have new signatories to some of these arrangements. What will the alignment that the Government are trying to achieve with the EU mean for some of our positions at the World Trade Organisation?

What my right hon. Friend is discussing is essentially the most important issue, in a way. We have now negotiated many of these agreements—very successfully, by the way—including the trans-Pacific partnership and others, meaning we are open for new foodstuffs, including meats, for export. However, if anything changes and we have to adopt a deal, it leaves us unable to negotiate and re-design deals with those partners. How long does my right hon. Friend think it will be before they then say that we do not have a deal anymore?

My right hon. Friend is spot on. Let me say to the House gently that none of this is a walk in the park. It is complicated. When I was in government I had a different portfolio, but I know about trade and have seen what has happened to my local farmers. Wicks Manor produces great pork products that it sends not just to EU countries but across the world, as far away as the United Arab Emirates and Indo-Pacific countries. It will be asking what this agreement means for those relationships. I want to press the Minister on that. Will the Minister, in her closing remarks, commit herself to providing the full funding model and the assumptions of the costs and benefits that underpin the figure the Government have given, namely an economic uplift of 0.4% of GDP over the long term, including the definition of “the long term”? Will she say what primary and secondary legislation the Government will be introducing as part of their renegotiation and this deal? As for the economic factors, inflation has been a fundamental challenge for this country in recent years. That is obviously due to the Ukraine conflict, energy prices and life post-covid, but we should also reflect that it has been exactly the same for the rest of Europe. Our levels of inflation are not higher than those in the rest of Europe. Claims that rejoining the EU or giving more powers to Brussels would lead to lower prices are therefore not accurate, which is why the modelling is fundamental. I appreciate that the Minister is from the Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office, but in this context we need to see the dynamic modelling from the Treasury, because the claims are not backed up by facts. The economic analyses, predictions and models that are often quoted are subject to huge variability, big caveats and questionable assumptions. For example, the 4% figure from the Office for Budget Responsibility, which is often quoted, is not an OBR forecast; it is an OBR prediction that results from looking at other studies. I think that the Government should examine these details and consider the economic implications and consequences before trying to make assumptions on behalf of British businesses. The Minister for Intergovernmental Relations and European Relations is not in the Chamber now, so I call on the Minister who will sum up the debate to tell us how many of the goods to which her colleague has referred—including the basket of goods that he was holding up on social media—would have their prices changed by the deal that he will be signing this week, and to also tell us whether there will be a risk of higher prices as a result of increased EU red tape. Let me also caution the Government about using the Cabinet Office to promote pro-EU views. Having been in the last Parliament—we have seen how divisive these campaigns can be—I know that that is deeply unhelpful. Ten years ago, just before the referendum, the Cabinet Office produced a booklet that was sent to every household explaining what it felt was the case for remaining in the EU. It suggested, among many other things, that 3 million jobs would be at risk, that a trade deal with the EU could not be delivered, and that our services sector, which is the best in the world, would struggle. It made so many vacuous and false promises and claims that did not materialise, and it actually did a lot to undermine trust in democracy and politics. We do have a free trade deal with the EU, and we have not seen a huge reduction in the number of jobs. The current problems in our employment market have been well debated in the House this week and in previous weeks, including the week following the Budget, but we have to look at the Employment Rights Act 2025 and the costs imposed on businesses through higher taxes and national insurance contribution increases. We have to carry out a sobering check on all this. We should also bear in mind that the value of goods exports to the EU is up by 30%, from £146 billion to nearly £191 billion
