Friend, with both perspicacity and foresight, to anticipate the very reason that my hostility to the European Union has its roots back in the 1970s. Those roots were of two forms. The first was because I believe that in nationhood, we nurture the sense of belonging that nourishes a true sense of worth—so I believe in the magic of nationhood. The second was because I believe that political power is best exercised closest to its effect. When it becomes remote from its effect, it risks at first becoming unaccountable and ultimately becoming corrupt. For those two reasons, I resist the idea of surrendering nationhood to something supranational. I know that that was the ambition of the architects of the European Community. If we look at what Monnet and others said back in the 1950s, before the treaty of Rome, we see that they were under no illusions that this was a common market and a means of perpetuating good trading relationships. They saw it as a political project, and “project” is the word often used to describe it by them and about them.
I will. I am always happy to teach liberals a lesson, as the hon. Lady knows. [ Laughter. ]

We did 10 rounds on this subject last week. The right hon. Gentleman says that he is against supranational institutions. Obviously the subject of this debate is UK-EU relations, but, if we extend his argument, is he also against the United Nations, the World Trade Organisation, the World Health Organisation, NATO and all other supranational organisations in which co-operation happens on a whole range of different issues?

The difference there is in the emblems and totems, the reality of governance and the character of polity. The problem is that the European Union has taken on the function of a polity itself. It is a law-making body. In other words, it exercises governance. Organisations of the kind that the hon. Lady describes—I think particularly of NATO, which I do not think she mentioned—are intergovernmental organisations, in which Governments come together, co-operate and collaborate. Of course, collaboration between nations matters—she and I would agree on a lot of that, actually—but the creation of something that has an anthem, a President, a flag and, more substantially, the ability to make laws that affect this place, irrespective of the will of this Parliament, is of an entirely different nature. I knew that back in the 1970s, and I know it now. That is why, as my right hon. Friend the Member for New Forest East (Sir Julian Lewis) predicted, year by year both my understanding and hostility grew and had their culmination in the magical moment when we voted to leave the European Union in 2016—perhaps the greatest moment of my time in politics.

We have had this idea that somehow the EU is just the same as NATO or any other international organisation all the way through these debates for decades, and I am afraid that it is based on a very fundamental ignorance. The EU is completely different to any other international organisation. It makes laws that are binding on the member states, whether they like it or not, and its courts overrule the courts of the member states. We are putting ourselves in that position through dynamic alignment, which is why it is a breach of the mandate given to the Government. There is nothing about that in their manifesto, and it is a breach of their manifesto commitments.

My hon. Friend, like my right hon. Friend the Member for New Forest East, shows remarkable insight, because I was about to say exactly that. Dynamic alignment is the acceptance of a series of regulations without further consideration here—it is an automatic process. You can believe in that, as many Labour Members clearly do, but if you accept that, you by nature accept the declining influence of this place in altering our destiny.
That is not something I believe in, any more than my neighbour does.

This issue of dynamic alignment is part of the thin end of the wedge that the British people are so concerned about. Nobody asked for a great debate about rejoining the European Union. Does the right hon. Member share my concern that the Prime Minister is using this week’s EU summit as a stepping stone towards trying to rejoin the European Union—as the thin end of the wedge? Turning to immigration, the youth mobility scheme sounds all very fluffy and cuddly, but the previous Prime Minister talked about a youth mobility scheme of 50,000 for a year. Now, we hear it is 100,000 for three years. Where is this going to end? Does the right hon. Member share my concern that it will lead to freedom of movement and mass immigration?

I am grateful to the hon. Gentleman for his intervention. He is my neighbour, and we have worked together on a number of matters. I said at the beginning of my speech that as well as a revelation, I was going to offer an admission to the House. My admission is that I have always rather liked the Prime Minister—I worked with him on matters of national security when I was a Home Office Minister and he was the shadow Home Secretary. One of the things I know about him is that he has a degree of political wherewithal, and the move that the hon. Member for Boston and Skegness (Richard Tice) has identified is a political move. It is more about the Prime Minister’s political strategy than it is about the strategic interests of the British people. He believes that he can unite the middle-class left around a pro-European position. It may indeed end in an even more arch-pro-European position—which, to give some credit to the Liberal Democrats, they are unabashed about. They are prepared to be naked in their advocacy of the European Union, whereas the Prime Minister is not.

I do not want to move my right hon. Friend on to the next bit of his life, but given his comments in support of the Prime Minister, I think he may be going to Downing Street shortly to receive—how can I put it?—a post.

Another honour, maybe. However, I do want to ask my right hon. Friend a question. Towards the latter stages of covid, I was asked by the then Prime Minister to look at how we could change some of the regulations that were imposed on us. I spoke to the scientists from Oxford who developed the first vaccine. When they sat in front of us, they confessed that although they had all voted to remain, when covid happened and they were hunting for a vaccine, they realised just how constrained they had been in developing new medicines when they were in the EU, because of the nature of the controls. We had lifted all of those controls, and they got the first vaccine, and millions of lives were saved as a result.

It is certainly true that a nation alone can be nimbler and more responsive than a nation that is obliged to agree what it does in concert with many others, where there will be differing opinions about both scale and speed. My right hon. Friend is right—that is a good example of how, freed from those obligations, we were able to deal with a pressing problem. That is part of a bigger point, which I referenced earlier when I intervened on the Minister, the right hon. Member for Lincoln (Mr Falconer). Much is made of how the world is changing and how, in this dramatically altered world, we need the security blanket of our connection with the European Union. However, the counter-argument is just as powerful. In a more confusing world, a Government’s ability to act quickly and cut across some of the bureaucracy that is associated with supranational bodies—the nimbleness that my right hon. Friend the Member for Chingford and Woodford Green (Sir Iain Duncan Smith) referred to—is all the more important. In a changed world, a free and dynamic country can be a more effective country.

I invite the right hon. Member for Chingford and Woodford Green (Sir Iain Duncan Smith) to consider correcting the record, because that claim was fact-checked at the time and found to be untrue. Under European law, the UK was permitted to act independently to approve a vaccine in an emergency, and it was made clear—I was a Member of the House at the time and I remember fact-checking Boris Johnson and Matt Hancock when they made that claim—that it was not the case that we were able to accelerate the vaccine because we were outside the EU. We would have been able to do so anyway, because of the exemption for trialling novel vaccines under a specific medical exemption. I refer the right hon. Gentleman to the Full Fact article on that point.

Madam Deputy Speaker, you will have noted that that was more of an intervention on the previous intervention from my right hon. Friend the Member for Chingford and Woodford Green than it was an intervention on me, so I will leave my right hon. Friend and the hon. Lady to sort the matter out between themselves. The bigger point is the one I made about how we perceive our future. I perceive our future as a nation that is outward-looking but sure about the sovereignty of this Parliament, for though the sovereignty of this Parliament may be spoken of blithely, essentially we are talking about the will of the people exercised through this place. The second point that inspired me to oppose the European Union back in those teenage years was the one about power. Here we are directly accountable to the people who elect us. We are answerable in the most palpable way, are we not, to our voters? Every single Member of this House has regular engagement with all kinds of people in their constituencies, with all kinds of opinions, and that is their constituents’ chance to access and influence power. I studied politics at university, and I have studied the EU ever since. One requires virtually a PhD to understand how it works. Many of the people elected to the European Parliament have only a sketchy idea of how it works. We know how laws are made there. It begins with discussion among relatively junior bureaucrats, who then listen to a series of interest groups and lobbying organisations. It is then elevated to a diplomat, who discusses it, plans it and sets it out in rather more detail. By the way, that is long before it gets to anybody who has been elected. Finally, it gets to the MEPs, and they discuss it, usually in some smoke-filled room—well, I guess these days the room would not be full of smoke, so that metaphor is perhaps becoming rather dated. National Governments are reached very late in the process, and their chances to influence EU laws are very limited. The hon. Member for Chelsea and Fulham (Ben Coleman) said he is a fully fledged—he is not shy to admit it—member of the liberal bourgeoisie. In the case of the current arrangements, he also said we will have a chance to shape some of those decisions. The experts— I shudder when that word is used; I never claim expertise in anything, really, and neither should he—will have some influence on this process, but there is a real difference between shaping and deciding.

This is perhaps not a deeply intellectual point, but what is important about this place is the traditions we have, and those are not just the traditions that have pertained for a long time, but those that develop. May I say how grateful I am to the right hon. Gentleman for inventing a new tradition, which is that every time he speaks, he has a go at me? I look forward to it, and I have not been let down.

I detect just a touch of paranoia in the hon. Gentleman. He knows that I am a soft-hearted soul, and I think he was pricking at my soft heart in the hope that I will be kinder to him in future. The key thing is to understand how dynamic alignment works. It is true, as Labour Members have said, that this agreement that the Prime Minister will reach may slash some of the post-Brexit checks imposed thereafter by the European Union, which may make things easier for some of our exporters, of which food producers are a good example. In return, however, the Prime Minister will agree to align permanently—“in perpetuity” was the phrase used earlier—with EU regulations on food and farming. This process means that the UK will have to adopt new EU regulations in areas as soon as they are passed by Brussels, with no vote on them. I will come in a second to the House of Lords Committee that has already been mentioned, but in essence that will mean scores, perhaps hundreds, of new regulations affecting British businesses, about which we will have no say in this place. That House of Lords Committee said that the deal would mean “significant volumes of EU legislation”, and heard evidence that complying with farming laws alone “might generate at least 780 pieces of in-scope EU law a year”. I am not going to second-guess a distinguished Committee of the House of Lords, but even if that were an overestimate, the principle remains that many additional regulations will be imposed on this country, with Parliament having no say. Much has been said about mandates and Makerfield. Let us be clear about the polling. A recent survey in Makerfield about who should decide UK economic policy on 10 different issues, ranging from medicine approval to state aid, showed that in every single case a clear majority of people there said that the policy should be determined by the UK Government alone. The British people may have bought some of the liberal elite’s propaganda about Brexit per se, but when it comes to deciding where laws should be made and how those making them should be held to account, they are pretty clear that that should happen in this country, in this sovereign Parliament. Let me now draw my remarks to a close, as I know you will want me to, Madam Deputy Speaker. The truth—and I think we can speak it in this private place, can we not?—is that a large proportion of the British establishment resented the EU referendum result from the very beginning, and did all in their power, funded by greedy plutocrats, to try and stop it. The greedy plutocrats, of course, benefited from the cheap labour that came across from Europe, and thank God that ended. Now they hope—exactly as the hon. Member for Boston and Skegness described—that this is the beginning of a process that will reverse that. In contrast, I say this: the referendum result was an expression of the will of the people. I will end with George Orwell, if I may. He said of that very left-wing intelligentsia at the time of the last war that they took their tastes from Paris and their instructions from Moscow. We might substitute that with “instructions from Brussels and Strasbourg.” I take the polar opposite view. I believe that this nation should be governed by Britons chosen by other Britons to do so. I believe in the national interest and the common good—first, foremost, forever.
Back Benchers are now on a five-minute speaking time limit. I call Matthew Patrick.

This debate is giving me déjà vu. The Tories have brushed off their Brexit playbook and are replaying their best hits, but sadly—I think sadly—they have a very limited number of new things to say. Let us be clear: Brexit has caused real damage to this country. It has hurt livelihoods. It has created a status quo that is not good enough and simply must change. I am grateful to the Prime Minister for opening up the debate on how it can change, but I believe that if we are to have a debate worthy of this topic, we need to show a bit of humility. We need to make some concessions, perhaps even change our minds, because few topics entrench views and divide our country into camps—leave and remain—quite like this one, and I think it is dangerous when an issue generates maximum emotion and minimum reflection. Cards on the table: I campaigned for remain in 2016, but my learning did not stop on 23 June. My instinct was that being in the EU was a good thing, but we would survive outside it. We are a strong country and I believed we could get by. For what it is worth, I still have faith in our country. I still think that we are a great country and that we can weather storms, but the question that debates like this bring me back to is this: do we not have higher ambition for ourselves than to be able to roll with the punches? Do we not see the problems facing our country, many of which are global in nature, as needing a joined-up response? They include climate change; conflicts that spark humanitarian crises and block trade, causing prices to skyrocket, economies to suffer, and the flow of irregular and illegal immigration; the race towards artificial intelligence and all that it brings; a culture change that is being ushered in by atomised and addictive algorithms; and the issues that flow from that culture change, such as a falling birth rate, buoyant populism, and dangerous levels of Islamist and extreme right-wing terrorism. The issues go on, and they run deep. I am left asking myself, why add to our problems by failing to address the wrongs before us? It is not just about trade, but about our power to confront the global problems threatening us. At the same time, let us not kid ourselves that a panacea awaits us at the end of a road marked “rejoin”. That binary thinking—that one side is good and virtuous and the other stupid and ruinous, which is an accusation thrown at one another by both camps—has stopped us listening to the reasonable dissenting voices of those who also want the best for our country. Some Brexit commentators have pointed out that the world has changed since 2016. Well, this is not a moment for those who campaigned for remain simply to say, “We were right all along; let’s repent, let’s rejoin and let the good times roll.” First, the public will have a thing or two to say about that, and secondly, I believe those commentators are right. In 2016 we argued about trade. Today our challenges are greater and the stakes higher. We have full-scale war in Europe, an increasingly brazen and hostile Kremlin, and an unpredictable America. Commentators are right to say that the world has changed and that it is a harsher place than it was 10 years ago, as the right hon. Member for Witham (Priti Patel) said, but they do not recognise that a harsher world ups the price of standing alone. The motion before us is no better, because it ignores the realities and leans back on arguments that serve the Tory party, rather than the country. We might ask, should we rejoin? For me, it is not that simple. I felt uneasy when those advocating for Brexit argued that the status quo was so bad that we should simply jump to something else. That argument ended with a debate about whether the status quo was good, not what change looked like. Those of us who saw then, and see now, the value of the European Union and our role within it would do well to remember that half-argument. In fact, we should ask ourselves, what does this club offer us and what d

I represented the south-west of England and Gibraltar in the European Parliament for 10 years, and I have seen my fair share of rules and regulations written in Brussels and imposed on the United Kingdom. While we were members of the EU, we did at least have a say in how those were drafted, even if, rather too often, we ended up with compromises that we would not have chosen for ourselves. What the Government are now proposing in relation to food standards is worse than what we had during our membership of the EU, because we shall be a rule-taker, with no ability to amend the rules. I want Britain to have the closest possible trading relationship with the European Union, consistent with the result of the referendum. That means trading with the EU but not being subject to EU laws, paying into the EU budget or coming under the jurisdiction of the European Court of Justice, and that is precisely where the Prime Minister’s approach is going horribly wrong. A reduction in trade barriers is a good thing. We want our farmers and growers to sell their goods more easily on the European market, and we want to enjoy the good products that Europe has to offer us. That could be achieved by the UK and the EU recognising one another’s standards while remaining sovereign jurisdictions. Mutual recognition is a simple solution, yet regrettably something to which we know the EU would never agree. The EU has always demanded more. Its aim is that Britain accepts its regulatory framework and follows its laws, however unsuitable they may be. Its aim since 2016 has always been to drag us back within its regulatory orbit. This deal also means that, whenever there is a dispute about the contents of those laws, it is the European Court of Justice that will decide the outcome. The British people voted in 2016 to ensure that laws affecting this country would be made in this Parliament by representatives elected by the British people. They voted to restore accountability and democratic control, based in the UK. Subjecting ourselves once again to external laws and courts undermines that principle and moves us away from what was promised. The consequences are particularly concerning when it comes to the innovation and technology we have developed since leaving the EU. Britain is a world leader in gene-editing technology. Gene-edited crops can be made more resistant to disease, they require fewer pesticides, and they can withstand drought and changing climate conditions. They are a vital tool in helping farmers to produce more food while reducing costs and environmental pressures. This is exactly the kind of innovation Britain should champion. It is regrettable that the EU sees the hazard in everything. It always takes a more restrictive approach, focusing on potential hazard, rather than a more intelligent, risk-based approach to technological advance. If regulatory alignment means limiting our freedom to develop and deploy these technologies, we risk sacrificing one of the most significant opportunities created by Brexit. Labour Members should ask themselves: why would we voluntarily constrain our ability to innovate when the benefits to our farmers, consumers and food security could be so substantial? The Food and Drink Federation has said that some 400 regulations would need to be amended to facilitate an SPS agreement. These regulations will, of course, apply to the 92% of businesses that do not export to the EU in any event. CropLife UK says that any SPS deal would cost our farmers £800 million in the first year alone. The Government are happy for British businesses to foot the bill, while having no influence over how those rules are made. Of course, each time the UK joins a part of the single market, the EU will demand a payment from British taxpayers to pay for the privilege. Do we believe that laws affecting British farmers, businesses and consumers should be made here in Westminster or in Brussels? I believe that Britain can be a successful outward

I am all for improving relations with our international partners. I am all for ensuring we have the very best relationships abroad, be it in trade, security, or cultural and social ties. Those relationships are important with European allies, and they are important with the US and so many other countries all around the world. Indeed, Britain is a global leader in international relations, in soft power and in understanding its key strategic place in the world of international politics. But what the Prime Minister is seeking to do this week is not that; it is far more significant, and it relates to the institution of the European Union. By his own admission, he is seeking to fundamentally reset and open up an ongoing debate about the relationship between the United Kingdom and the EU—a debate that was fundamentally settled when previous Governments delivered the will of the people as expressed in a referendum. It is slightly unclear to me, and I think to those of us on the Conservative Benches, quite what the endgame is and what the Prime Minister’s intentions are. I suspect it is probably unclear to many of those on the Labour Benches. Indeed, the Prime Minister’s intentions are probably fairly unclear to the Prime Minister himself, given the amount of different messages he has sent out in the course of the last few months. But he has been very open to the possibility of rejoining the EU one day. He has ruled out rejoining the single market, the customs union and free movement in this Parliament—only in this Parliament. This Parliament may have less than a year to run if he presses the button on a general election next year. Even if the Parliament is a full five-year term, there are little over two and a half years left. So the Prime Minister is absolutely paving the way for a wider debate on re-entering key institutions of the EU and possible future membership. I suspect he may well be seeking to frame the next general election on in/out EU membership negotiations, and I think that is a fundamentally damaging prospect not only because I think our future is best outside the EU, but because that debate has been settled. Even among remainers, both in this place and in the country at large, I sense a serious reluctance to go back to the divisive politics of Brexit negotiations. Even for those who voted to remain back in 2016, I suspect the majority do not want this place and our politics to be distracted for years to come by the same old arguments that divided parties, divided communities and divided families. My worry is that the Government will become so distracted by this that they will fail to do what they were elected to do: to improve the lives of people up and down the country. I do worry that the Prime Minister is seeking to put up a deliberate smokescreen for his failure, and his predecessor’s failure, to deliver the change the people wanted. Having failed to run a successful narrative that it was all the previous Government’s fault—indeed, the former Prime Minister lost his job because of a failed narrative—the current Prime Minister is struggling for a new narrative that it is all Brexit’s fault that the current Government are failing to tackle all those things that are within their power to tackle: the ballooning welfare bill, the stalling economy, the cost of living, and energy prices. They can tackle those things today, regardless of the relationship with Europe. I suspect that it is their failure to do so that they are trying to mask with this bogus argument about whether we should rejoin the EU or its institutions.

I thank Members on both sides of the House for a very lively debate this afternoon. On Monday at the Lord Mayor’s banquet, the Prime Minister said: “The people voted for change and it has not happened. It has come down to that crucial word: control.” So how exactly does this reset offer control to the British people? Does agreeing to subsidise the tuition fees of students from the EU offer young British people greater opportunities for their education? Does paying Brussels to deal with illegal migration policy without any returns deal offer greater control of our borders? Does linking the EU emissions trading scheme, potentially pushing up UK carbon prices by over 40% in some cases, allow businesses and households greater control over their costs? This does not grant the British people more control over their future. We do know from all the leaks surrounding these negotiations that this is a deal that will hurt British farmers. It is a deal that will hurt British students by subsidising tuition fees for those from the European Union. The first-year cost of the Erasmus membership will be a massive £570 million in 2027-28. Staggeringly, this is a one-year membership and it factors in a 30% discount, at a cost still 50% higher than when we left the European Union. It is also a deal that increases the cost of emissions, which invariably will lead to higher inflation. The inability of Energy Ministers to answer questions about these consequences at yesterday’s Question Time suggests that there is a substantial bill coming. This Government simply do not want to tell us how much it will be.

My hon. Friend will know that in the last year that we were members of the EU, it cost us about £17 billion. That was the price of membership then, so it is inconceivable that, now that we are not a member, the EU would not want to charge us something for the arrangement that the Prime Minister is hoping to make.

My right hon. Friend has pre-empted my next point exactly. Analysis of this draft deal from our party has suggested that the country could face a £23 billion bill over the next decade as a result of this botched negotiation. That is completely unacceptable.

In this detailed analysis that the hon. Gentleman has undertaken, has he attempted to quantify the benefit to British business, which will then do far more trade and pay more tax, which we can then use for the NHS, policing, education and combating crime, or has he somehow left that out of his equation?

I thank my old sparring partner from Hammersmith town hall for his contribution. We used to disagree then and we disagree now. As was alluded to by my hon. Friends, many businesses will face increased costs, particularly farming businesses, which will really struggle with the impact of the deal. Every negotiating stance we have heard represents a loss of control for British people. And in exchange for what? For more money going from the British people to the European Union. Should we be surprised? Well, no—because, as the Prime Minister of the Czech Republic said when asked by a journalist if they would welcome the UK back: “Yes, of course. We need more money.” This is what the EU does: it works in its own interest and it rightly sees this Labour Government as an incredible opportunity. Nobody should be surprised. It is like welcoming Dick Turpin into your carriage; you cannot be shocked when he asks you to hand over of all your money. We have heard some really excellent contributions from the Opposition Benches this afternoon. My right hon. Friend the Member for Witham (Priti Patel) started off proceedings and got into an interesting discussion about shellfish. As the Member of Parliament for the lobster capital of Europe, I am delighted that we still land 300 tonnes of lobster every year, most of which is exported to the European Union. My hon. Friend the Member for Dumfries and Galloway (John Cooper) and my right hon. Friend the Member for Chingford and Woodford Green (Sir Iain Duncan Smith) highlighted the trade deals that have been done since we left the European Union. The comprehensive and progressive agreement for trans-Pacific partnership is a fantastic opportunity for this country, opening markets in countries from Mexico to Malaysia. The trade deal with India is another wonderful opportunity for the United Kingdom, and deals that we are currently negotiating, such as the Gulf Co-operation Council deal—about which middle eastern countries are incredibly excited—could be ripped up before they are even signed as a result of this negotiation. My hon. Friend the Member for Harwich and North Essex (Sir Bernard Jenkin) highlighted Britain’s world-leading AI industry and how it could be impacted by European regulation as part of this negotiation.

I raised this issue not because it is part of the Government negotiating position: I was pushing them to go further. Let me ask the hon. Gentleman how he would deliver digital sovereignty. This is really important. The EU has chokepoints with ASML in the Netherlands. The EU has purchasing power in relation to AI. This Government are working really hard to deliver more of that, but we do not have it at the moment. How would the hon. Gentleman deliver that sovereignty over AI? He does not have any answer.

I certainly would not be adopting the EU’s position, because industry here is far more advanced in our development of AI. We should be proud of that and should do nothing to put it under threat. My hon. Friend the Member for South Northamptonshire (Sarah Bool) highlighted farming, dynamic alignment and the real threat that we face; ninety per cent of farming businesses in this country do not export to the EU, and a future Conservative Government will not be bound by a bad deal. She also highlighted the fact that Ministers have failed repeatedly to give evidence to the Environment, Food and Rural Affairs Committee—

The hon. Gentleman raises the point made by the hon. Member for South Northamptonshire (Sarah Bool) about Ministers not attending the Select Committee in the Lords, but perhaps he could tell her about the letter sent by Sir William Cash in May 2023, which was critical of the actions of one former Trade Minister, which he described as “unacceptable”, adding that they “suggested a deeply concerning approach to scrutiny” from the then Government. Could he perhaps let the hon. Lady know that that Trade Minister is now the leader of the Conservative party?

The former Member for Stone has expressed many strong views over the years, and I always respect what he has to say. The point is that we are engaged in an important negotiation that will impact British farming; the Committee offered a private hearing to the Minister responsible for the negotiations, and that was repeatedly turned down. That is not the way to do scrutiny in this place. My right hon. Friend the Member for South Holland and The Deepings (Sir John Hayes) took us on something of a journey through recent European political history. I hope that the kind invitation that he gave to Madam Deputy Speaker to join him in Lincolnshire will be extended to other colleagues who want to talk at length about, perhaps, the treaty of Rome, or other such matters relating to the European Union. My hon. Friend the Member for Bridgwater (Sir Ashley Fox) gave us a fantastic insight as a former Member of the European Parliament. It is important that we hear from those on the Conservative Benches with that sort of experience when we discuss these matters. My hon. Friend the Member for Isle of Wight East (Joe Robertson) talked about Britain’s place in the world, and how important it is for our sovereignty that we can project soft and hard power when necessary.

What does the hon. Member make of the Thames Valley chamber of commerce’s statement that the paperwork caused by the Brexit deal is holding back our local exporters? Does he agree that the Conservative party cannot claim to be the party of business when it refuses to listen to businesses on the subject of the EU?

Unfortunately, a lot of problems relating to exports are due to EU intransigence. I worked closely on this matter before I was elected to this place, and I can assure the hon. Lady that when there are Dutch authorities insisting on the use of red biros and French authorities using blue biros, it is farcical. All of this could have been resolved, without any sort of reset, with a simple negotiation on easing trade frictions and digitising systems, so that our brilliant British produce is not held up at the border. I will give another example. The vet who works at the port of Rotterdam finishes at lunch-time on a Friday, so when the port authority decides to check a lorry load that comes in after that time, it is left until Monday morning. That seems absolutely farcical, and it is the fault of not this Government, but the European Union for the rules that it insisted on putting in place.

Does my hon. Friend agree that the EU is in breach of its obligations under the World Trade Organisation agreement to facilitate trade? The EU has those obligations, but it does not seem like they apply to it.

My hon. Friend speaks with great knowledge on these matters. The WTO plays a very important role in facilitating trade right across the world, and the EU regularly finds itself in conflict with it, which says something about the way that the EU operates.

I thank my hon. Friend for raising the point about how the EU behaves. I have such a strong sense of déjà vu. During the original negotiation period, every time that the EU was obstinate, stubborn and difficult, Labour Members sought to blame the Conservatives for that, instead of getting behind this country and standing up to that sort of behaviour.

My hon. Friend is quite right. The spirit in which those negotiations were entered into was, I fear, unnecessarily adversarial, and unfortunately that has meant that issues that it should have been easy to resolve have not been resolved in recent years. Since the Labour Government were elected, there has been a sinking feeling across this country that Labour is a party with no solutions to the big problems facing our society. For instance, in response to the recent Budget, the OBR said that it expects no growth in real earnings in 2027 or 2028, alongside a slight fall in real household disposable income in the near term. Meanwhile, Labour’s plans to bring down welfare spending are set to take over 10 years. Labour could probably produce another five 10-year plans in that time, and we would still be nowhere near funding the defence requirements of this country. Why does that matter? Because this reset does not address the problems that require structural change in the United Kingdom. It is at best a diversion; more likely, it will result in giving away the powers that are needed to deliver changes, and that the UK requires. It does not provide the money that we need to fund defence, or reduce the costs that this Government have imposed on businesses. This is not the difficult debate that the Prime Minister claims it is. It is a distraction started by a former Prime Minister with no new ideas and continued by a Prime Minister with no new solutions. The Prime Minister has reached for the “Now That’s What I Call Brexit” playbook, preferring to play the old hits than to provide the solutions that we need to make the UK a dynamic country, capable of meeting the challenges of this fast-moving and dangerous age. The reset is the embodiment of that mindset; we are giving away control over student finance, migration, border security, and product and food standards, all for the privilege of paying the EU more money. To those who say that the Conservatives are merely prolonging this debate, I say this: if the Government supported this motion, they could bring this debate to a close and make it clear that any future negotiations will be conducted on a generally neutral basis, in the interests of both the EU and the UK. In rejecting the motion, it will be clear that the Government would rather look to the past than the future. The reset is an acknowledgment that we are not going to forge a new relationship based on British confidence and success, but will instead enter a new era in which the EU calls the shots, and we simply ask, “How much?”.

I am grateful to the Opposition, to the hon. Member for Kingswinford and South Staffordshire (Mike Wood) for moving the motion, and to all right hon. and hon. Members from across the House who have contributed their views. I am also grateful for the opportunity to respond on behalf of the Government. This has been a long debate, in which we have heard views from across the House. The hon. Member for Kingswinford and South Staffordshire took us on a journey, mentioning a plethora of British sausages, and reminding us that my right hon. Friend the Minister could double up as Bond. The Opposition have rehashed many of the arguments of 2016, reminding me of a saying: they were the future once. It struck me how many Members have, in their own words, reiterated what the Prime Minister said earlier this week: “The hard Brexit we were given is not good enough for Britain.” The British people voted for change and control, and they simply did not get what was sold to them by the Tories. Our economy has suffered, our businesses still face red tape, and our young people have had, and are having, their futures stifled. This Government are convinced that only a strong UK-EU relationship will deliver the opportunity, growth, security and change that the British public have asked for. Nobody voted for a change that hurts British trade and undermines our national security. What we are doing this week—this is what the Prime Minister aims to do when he travels to Brussels on Friday for the second UK-EU summit—is delivering on the key ambitions set out last year by striking important deals that will strengthen our economy for the British people. We are striking important deals on food and drink; emissions trading; linking our energy systems; opportunities for young people and youth experience; and, crucially, furthering our co-operation on defence, security and migration. The SPS and emissions trading agreements will add up to £9 billion a year to the UK economy by 2040. These deals will boost the UK’s economy, cut costs, cut red tape and provide opportunities to young people—the next generation—who have been denied these vital opportunities since Brexit, when the Opposition failed to negotiate them. The UK and EU will also discuss a shared approach to protecting our economic security to ensure that we do not unintentionally harm each other, and instead tackle shared economic challenges together. Policies that disadvantage UK and EU businesses will not make our economy stronger and our countries more secure. The safety and security of the British people is at the heart of everything that the Government do. As my right hon. Friend the Minister said, when the referendum took place a decade ago, Russia had not launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine; we had not witnessed hostile attacks on European soil; and global trade and energy supplies were not being used as geopolitical weapons.

The Minister mentions Ukraine, which we have talked about today. Not having the arrangements with the EU that the Prime Minister is seeking in absolutely no way dampened our ability to work with Europe on Ukraine. We have been able to work together, and stand up strongly for Ukraine, under existing arrangements. What is so bad about them?

The hon. Gentleman makes my point. True European security and competitiveness are best achieved when like-minded and trusted partners work together to bolster everything that we are talking about, from supply chains to defence, competitiveness and economic security. My right hon. Friend the Minister is continuing to work around the clock with his EU counterparts, so that we can conclude important agreements at the summit. Members in the Chamber will have heard my right hon. Friend set out robustly the Prime Minister’s and Britain’s ambition for this upcoming summit and negotiations. This Government respect the conventions of this House, but I will remind Members that this Labour Government were elected on a Labour manifesto to deliver for the British people. We were elected with a clear mandate to make Brexit work, deepen ties with Europe and tear down barriers to trade, and that is exactly what we are doing. The UK Government will bring forward primary legislation next week to implement the agreements. They will be ratified by Parliament, and Parliament will scrutinise the legislation in full, in the usual way.
I have a very simple request. We have heard this figure of £9 billion bandied around endlessly. Could the Minister tell us how that breaks down?

The right hon. Gentleman will know that I am a Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office Minister, and that those are breakdowns that the Treasury can provide. I can certainly get him a written answer on that. Members will understand that I cannot provide a running commentary on these negotiations, and the House would not expect me to, but once the summit has concluded, the Government will, at the earliest opportunity, update the House on what has been delivered and the impact that the measures will have. As the Prime Minister has set out, any deal must pass three tests. First, it has to be consistent with our manifesto and our red lines. Secondly, it has to improve the Brexit deal to bring it closer to what people thought they were getting in 2016. Thirdly, it has to pass the Makerfield test—produce real improvements in the everyday lives of people who live in areas of the country that have felt neglected for too long. As the Prime Minister said on Monday in his Mansion House speech, along with the Makerfield test, there is a London test to ensure that this deal supports an even more successful capital city. That means reducing red tape and the cost of doing business, and helping with the cost of living and the price of the weekly shop, as seen in my right hon. Friend the Minister’s video. Rumour has it that he was looking for the cornflake cookies in M&S, but actually he was there on behalf of us all, to make this case. If the deal delivers all this, as the Government believe it can, it will easily pass the Makerfield test and the London test, and we will agree it.

I will make some progress. The agreements that will be announced at the summit should not be the ceiling of our ambition. It is very clear that the status quo is not working. Our Prime Minister has been bold. He has said the quiet part out loud—that Brexit has done more harm than good. As a country we are ambitious to go further. We must restore higher growth and greater prosperity. Our ambition extends beyond Friday’s UK-EU summit. We will begin by evaluating all options for the future and opening a national discussion on these options. This will take time, and we will present those options and our assessment of them. That will inform decisions in the next Parliament. At every stage, the British people will be in charge. A number of issues were raised by opposition Members. Time is short, but I will try to run through them in turn. The hon. Member for Surrey Heath (Dr Pinkerton)—the good doctor—took us through a list of Surrey bangers. It turns out he was talking about his predecessor. He also referred to rejoining the single market and the customs union. I gently remind him that this Labour Government were elected on a manifesto commitment not to join the single market customs union. At Friday’s summit, the Government will pursue those gains that we believe are in the UK’s national interest, while respecting the red lines laid out in our manifesto. The Prime Minister is clear that Brexit has damaged our economy, that we are facing a more dangerous world, and that we need a closer relationship with Europe. The right hon. Member for Witham (Priti Patel) asked a number of questions in her 20-minute speech. I do not have time to run through all of them, but let me say this on trade with other countries: the UK continues to respect our international obligations and will continue to pursue our trade deals globally. This evening, I am hosting a UK-India reception in Lancaster House to celebrate those trade deals, and I have offered her an invitation. The SPS agreement is fully consistent with our international obligations. On recent free trade agreements, our membership of the CPTPP will not need to be renegotiated. We will bring forward the European partnership Bill to implement the deals agreed with the EU, starting with the SPS and the emissions trading agreement. I remind everybody that Parliament remains sovereign, and this Bill will not change that. Both Houses will have the ability to scrutinise it in full. I made diligent notes on the colleagues who took part in the debate. I wish that I could go through them, but, alas, I am running out of time, so let me conclude. At Friday’s summit, the Government will cement the progress made so far and inject renewed pace and ambition into our future relationship with the EU. At the heart of that is the young people who did not get a say but whose futures are being determined by what is happening now—I think of my own young constituents in Stratford and Bow. The important deals that we strike will pay off for businesses and families and support growth. They will cut back on paperwork and ease pressure on prices. Our position is clear: it is through our partnership with the EU that we will deliver real results for the British people. Question put (Standing Order No. 31(2)), That the original words stand part of the Question.
I inform the House that Mr Speaker has selected the amendment in the name of the Prime Minister. I call the shadow Secretary of State.

I beg to move, That this House, for reasons of energy security, economic growth and jobs, calls on the Government to commit to developing the Rosebank oil field as soon as is practicable and to support domestic energy production. Talk about timely—this debate, an important debate in its own right, has been put in stark relief by news breaking this morning; news that, regardless of how frequently we hear of yet another company exiting the UK oil and gas sector, is no less shocking, no less worrying for workers and no less illustrative of the utter destruction being wrought on our world-leading sector and our energy security by this Government. EnQuest, a British-based, London-listed energy company, is to become the latest in a long and expanding list of companies pulling out entirely from the North sea, explicitly blaming the hostile investment environment and high-tax regime cultivated by this Government. There is no hiding from it: the Government’s policies on oil and gas are hanging a “closed for business” sign over our North sea. I know the Minister will claim that their North sea policies are pragmatic, that they want to “manage the future of that basin” and that, by maintaining a windfall tax of 78% and legislating to ban all new licences, they are showing global climate leadership. Let me be clear: EnQuest is not pulling out of oil and gas. It is moving its operations and focusing its investment on south-east Asia, where it sees “greater potential to deploy capital, build scale and deliver sustainable long-term growth.” This Labour Government did say they wanted growth in every postcode—I did not know that meant postcodes in Kuala Lumpur. This Government are not showing climate leadership. It might not have dawned on them yet, but they should turn around because no one is following. No one in the world that has an oil and gas basin is pursuing the same course as this Government. The USA is not. Canada, Mexico and countries in the middle east are not. Nor are Australia or Norway, or across Asia and South America. Even our own overseas territories, the Falkland Islands, are not. We now have the utterly farcical sight of the former Secretary of State for Energy Security and Net Zero and now Foreign Secretary, the right hon. Member for Doncaster North (Ed Miliband), signing off on the development of a new oil field in the British South Atlantic, and the Attorney General at an international tribunal defending the exploitation of that field by the Falklands, at the exact same moment that the Government they serve are bringing in a total ban on new exploration in the North sea. It is utterly unbelievable. You could not make it up, Madam Deputy Speaker, except it is actually happening. This Government have clearly been captured, in part, by an extremist green lobby whose sole purpose is to kill what remains of our oil and gas sector. That lobby cares little about the jobs and livelihoods of the men and women being made unemployed or who are choosing to move overseas. They do not give a damn about the communities—communities that I represent and that they are destroying in the process. A few weeks ago, we saw a rare demonstration of common sense from this Government when, after months of unnecessary dither and delay, they finally approved Jackdaw. That was indeed a welcome decision, and for the men and women who work in Britain’s oil and gas industry, it was a glimmer of hope in the darkness that their jobs might have a future. Approving Jackdaw unlocked 40 million barrels of oil and gas, bolstering Britain’s energy security, and gas from that field is flowing into the British gas grid as we speak. The British people are hoping that somewhere in this Government we can eke out just a little bit more common sense, because beneath the waves, 130 km off the Shetland Islands, lies yet more opportunity to deliver for the British people, a shot in the arm for our economy and the means to protect thousands of British jobs.

Did my hon. Friend notice, as I did, that Gary Smith of GMB described the Department for Energy Security and Net Zero as the “Department for P45s”? It is putting people out of work and not reducing the amount of oil and gas we consume by as much as one drop.

As ever, my right hon. Friend hits the nail on the head. We are still using gas to heat over 80% of homes in this country. British industry relies on gas to ensure that it can function. It is not that we are using less gas; it is just that we are using more imported gas from overseas, either through pipelines from Norway, or in the form of liquefied natural gas from the United States and elsewhere. It is no surprise that Gary Smith of GMB has described this Government’s energy policy as “batshit”. The opportunity that is open to us is Rosebank. That field, if allowed to proceed, could help Britain turn the corner, reindustrialise, grow and become more energy secure, utilising what is on our doorstep, just as other countries are doing and just like our North sea neighbour, Norway. It is in our best interests—it is in the interests of our economy, our jobs, our security and our climate.

The shadow Secretary of State knows that the energy security argument for Rosebank is extremely weak, because the vast majority of our oil is exported. He talks about Norway: it is on an energy transition, but the great tragedy for Scotland, and for Aberdeen specifically, is that Governments in this place and in Holyrood have failed to invest in that energy transition. Is that not the case? Does he not regret that his Government did nothing about that transition?

I am glad I took the hon. Gentleman’s intervention, because it underlines the complete ignorance in parts of the Labour party when it comes to debate about our energy policy. Some 65% of the oil that is generated from the North sea comes back into Britain as refined product, so we are talking about thousands of jobs in Aberdeen and across Scotland. Given that he is a Scottish MP, I am surprised that he is using that argument. When it comes to debates about the economy and our security, there is no better or quicker way to produce revenue, to secure jobs and to ensure our security moving forward that approving the field, getting rid of the ban on licences, getting rid of the energy profits levy and getting Britain drilling again. That does not have to come at the expense of a transition. If we talk to all the companies based in Aberdeen and just outside Aberdeen, we hear that the very workers this Government will be relying on to deliver new clean technologies are relying on jobs in oil and gas right now.

I will not. The very technologies that are being used right now in the North sea to export oil and gas are the same technologies that we will need to deploy offshore floating wind at scale, of which I believe the hon. Gentleman is very much in favour.
Will the shadow Secretary of State explain, in the constrained financial times in which people find themselves, by how much Rosebank will reduce bills for consumers?

The hon. Lady knows that Rosebank will generate around £500 million a year in tax receipts, which is money that this country desperately needs. That money could be used to cut taxes on the hard-pressed British people, if this Government were so minded. The opportunity we have is Rosebank. That field, if allowed to proceed, could help Britain turn the corner, reindustrialise, grow and be secure once again, utilising what is on our doorstep, just as other countries are doing. Anyone who has a grasp on reality and the challenges we face as a country understands that simple fact. It is common sense to use our own resources. Rosebank is projected to produce around 69,000 barrels of oil every day at peak, which is roughly 10% of anticipated oil output from the UK continental shelf.

In Northern Ireland, 68% of households use heating oil to warm their houses, and 39% of people in Northern Ireland are in fuel poverty. Here is a golden opportunity to address some of the issues for constituents not just in Strangford, but across Northern Ireland and across this great United Kingdom. Today, in this debate, we have a chance to put things right and ensure that my constituents, and all constituents, can get some benefit from the Rosebank field.

The hon. Gentleman is absolutely right. I know that Members across parties see the benefits in exploiting what we have in our own basin. I also know that Members of all parties who want to see a sensible, pragmatic approach to managing the North sea moving forward do not understand why, in the midst of an energy crisis, this Government are choosing to ban licences and maintain a punitive 78% tax on companies operating in the North sea. We have seen just today companies pulling out yet again from their operations here. Under this Government, we have seen a dramatic slide in refining capacity, demonstrated by the closures at Grangemouth and Lindsey. Sadly, our demand for diesel can no longer be met by domestic processing, but Britain is among the most significant contributors of crude oil to the European market, with 65% of it coming back into the UK. That is barrel upon barrel of British oil keeping this country moving. We can choose to get what we need while we need it from our own seas, or we can buy from jurisdictions further afield, such as America or the middle east, with all the additional costs and emissions brought by shipping it to Britain. There is no escaping the reality that we will be using oil for some time, so let us back Britain. What happens to the oil that does not come back to Britain? Those barrels of oil are used in Europe and displace oil that could have been brought from places elsewhere, such as Russia. Every single barrel of oil that comes from Rosebank is a barrel of oil that does not fuel Putin’s war machine. Last month alone, Russian oil producers earned almost $21 billion. That money will buy the bombs and bullets that are being used in Europe, in Ukraine, right now. I hope—in fact, I know—that most of this House would much rather as much oil bought in this world as possible should be bought from nations that are not actively trying to do harm to Britain and its allies. Although Rosebank is about security, it is also about jobs—the thousands of jobs either directly or indirectly reliant on an industry that is on the brink. Those jobs are held by the talented, dedicated and highly skilled individuals that we need for the future, and whom this Government desperately need if they want to deliver anything close to their own energy goals. Despite that, at a time when we need to protect jobs and prioritise our energy security, this Labour Government have introduced legislation to ban Britain from benefiting from our own resources. The ban on new drilling is putting job security and investment on the line. You do not need me to tell you that, Madam Deputy Speaker, because Ministers in the Department already know it. In fact, the official impact assessment of the Government’s ban on new oil and gas licences estimates that it will cost the British economy £73 million a year and decimate more jobs. That was signed off by the hon. Member for Rutherglen (Michael Shanks)—the Minister sitting opposite me. He is fully aware of the damage that this Government’s policies will inflict, yet his Department and his Government are ploughing on regardless. The Secretary of State was all too keen to come to Aberdeen when the Government wanted to make the announcement about Jackdaw. I presume that, when their ban on new licences passes, she will be just as keen to look those same people—my constituents—in the eye and explain why they are worth less than a steel worker, who is in an industry that this Government are expending vast sums of money and huge effort on to protect. We know that almost one in five Labour Members have signed a letter telling the Government to block Rosebank—maybe the Foreign Secretary is considering adding his name to it. They are not helping us to tackle climate change, but they are threatening to destroy thousands of jobs, weaken our energy security and turn away billions of pounds of investment—specifically, £24.3 billion of much-needed investment into Britain over the Minister’s lifetime. The uni

I beg to move an amendment, to leave out from “House” to the end of the Question and insert: “notes that the previous Government was subject to judicial reviews in relation to oil and gas consenting decisions; further notes that the Rosebank oil and gas development is currently subject to a consenting decision and is a quasi-judicial matter; recognises that it is essential that the Government ensures that any decision is taken in full accordance with the relevant legal requirements and is legally robust, and that any predication of the decision will only compromise this; and welcomes the Government’s commitment to update Parliament in the first instance on the outcome of any decision.” For years, workers in the North sea have powered Britain. They have provided the gas that has flowed into our homes and the oil that has been the foundation of our economy, at considerable personal risk and in conditions that few others have to face at work. At the outset of this debate, in which I know strong feelings will be expressed by Members on all sides of the House, it is important that we can unite around this point: we owe a debt of gratitude to those workers, past and present, and to those who will continue to provide us with oil and gas for decades to come. Let me begin with the Government’s position and the regulatory status of Rosebank, because clarity matters in this debate. Rosebank is subject to a live regulatory process—a process that the Conservatives know about all too well, having experienced it themselves four years ago. The Energy Secretary must decide whether to agree to the grant of consent or reject it. Once her decision is made, the North Sea Transition Authority must then take the final decision. That process is rigorous for a reason: the project’s environmental effects must be considered and weighed alongside all other relevant factors, including any wider benefits to the country. The decision made must take account of the facts and be in line with the applicable law. Parliament is, of course, entitled to debate the future of the North sea and the choices facing our energy system, but I cannot offer commentary on the merits of an individual application. Any decision must be taken in full accordance with the relevant legal requirements, and if I were to prejudge that decision, it would only further compromise the process.

The Minister says that he cannot comment on the decision that the Government are going to take, but can he at least set out a timetable for when the decision will be made? The industry and my constituents are waiting for that decision, and so far it has just been kicked down the road.

As the hon. Gentleman knows, there is a significant amount of evidence to be considered. The Secretary of State is considering it, and the decision will be made in due course, taking account of the amount of time it takes to consider the evidence; that is the right thing to do in a process like this one. I am sure that in this debate, some Members will point to the recent decision on Jackdaw—as the hon. Member for West Aberdeenshire and Kincardine (Andrew Bowie) has done—and ask what it means for Rosebank. The answer is that each case must, and will, be decided on its own facts. In making her decision, the Energy Secretary considered various factors, including the project’s environmental effects; its expected contribution to security of supply, employment, infrastructure and the economy; and the UK’s legally binding carbon budgets. She assessed that Jackdaw would not prevent the UK from meeting those budgets or achieving net zero by 2050.

Could the Minister confirm to the House that Rosebank is expected to average 12 kg of carbon dioxide per barrel of oil produced, which could be reduced to as little as 3 kg if it was fully electrified, compared with a global average of over 30 kg for oil production? The production that is planned there is actually remarkably green. Could he confirm that, on a technical level, those numbers are correct?

The right hon. Gentleman knows that I cannot be drawn on those details while, as I have just set out, there is a live regulatory decision. Jackdaw is expected to increase domestic gas production by around 6% at its peak, safeguard hundreds of jobs, and add billions to the UK economy. However, we should not exaggerate what one field can do; Jackdaw will not remove our dependence on imports, and it will not set the price of gas, which is determined on international markets. That distinction matters. Serious energy policy means acknowledging the contribution that existing oil and gas production can make during the transition, while being equally honest that no single field can insulate families from global fossil fuel shocks. That brings me to the Government’s wider approach. Our objective is a managed, orderly and prosperous transition for the North sea—one that supports workers and communities, strengthens energy security and, importantly, meets our climate commitments. The heatwaves, floods and extreme weather of recent years are affecting homes, businesses, food systems and public services now. At the same time, repeated fossil fuel shocks have shown how quickly events overseas can reach household bills here.

The Minister may not be able to comment on the determination by the Secretary of State, but can he confirm whether the views of elected representatives and of the British people are able to be taken into account by the Secretary of State? It is interesting that 65% of Labour voters across the country want this decision approved.

The hon. Gentleman will know that there were two consultations, and I wonder whether he submitted anything to either of them. I will gladly give way if he wants to tell me what he submitted. No? I will just assume that he did not bother.

I need to make progress. Climate security and energy security are not competing objectives, but point in the same direction: less exposure to fuels whose price we do not control and more clean power produced at home. To achieve that, we need an orderly transition that protects energy security today, while investing in the cleaner, more secure energy system of tomorrow. Oil and gas will remain part of our energy mix for decades as we build the cleaner system that will replace them. We are not turning off the taps. Millions of barrels of oil will continue to flow from the North sea, and existing fields will continue to be managed for their lifetime. At the same time, we must face the reality that North sea production has fallen by around three quarters since 1999. Britain has been a net importer of energy since 2004. [ Interruption. ] As the shadow Secretary of State chunters from a sedentary position, he will remember that when his party was in government, 75,000 jobs were lost in the North sea in a decade. We cannot and will not make the same mistake. More licences to explore new fields would not change that long-term decline and would not determine prices in a global market.

I thank the Minister for giving way, because he has brought up what we did in government. I will tell him what we did when we were in power, in the face of a global oil price collapse in 2014-15. We introduced a policy of maximum economic recovery from the North sea. We cut taxes on North sea production. We made the North sea the most investable basin in the world for oil and gas production. His Government are deliberately, through policy, driving down an industry. This is not a global price collapse or a global issue for the oil and gas industry. This is a made in Britain crisis—a made by the current Foreign Secretary crisis—that only this country is enduring, because the Government’s policy to ban licences and to stick with the EPL is creating issues. Does the Minister not agree?

The shadow Secretary of State will not be surprised that I do not agree with what he said. We can look at the evidence of what happened when his party was in government: 75,000 jobs lost. I heard no response from him about the loss of jobs during his time as an Energy Minister. The Energy Independence Bill, which was introduced to the House recently, delivers on both climate security and energy security. It ends new licences to explore new fields and introduces transitional energy certificates, so that production can take place in already explored areas on or next to existing fields, linked back to existing infrastructure. That is a practical policy, giving certainty to industry where activity supports existing fields, and a clear limit where new exploration would take us in the wrong direction. We should be candid about that choice. New exploration cannot restore the North sea to its peak. It cannot end imports or guarantee lower bills. Building clean, home-grown power gives us greater control, because the wind, solar and nuclear power we produce here is not priced by events beyond our shores.

Are we not at risk of swapping one set of vulnerabilities in relation to oil and gas and a country like Russia with another set of vulnerabilities in relation to a country like China, given its dominance of critical mineral supplies and solar panel manufacturing? We will be just as insecure, just in a different way.

We are already investing in supply chains in this country for critical minerals, and the hon. Gentleman knows that is what we are doing. The transition will succeed only if it works for the people who have powered this country for generations. That means that North sea workers need a genuine stake in what comes next, with investment, training and good jobs in the places where they live. The clean energy jobs plan sets out how employment, supported by clean energy industries, is estimated to grow hundreds of thousands of jobs by the end of the decade. The number supported by clean energy industries could almost triple in Scotland and at least double in Wales, Northern Ireland and almost every region of England. Those opportunities are already becoming real. [ Interruption. ] The hon. Member for Broadland and Fakenham (Jerome Mayhew) says that is fantasy; it is happening right now, right across the country.
No, allow me to make progress. I have already given way a number of times.

The transition is happening. Just this week, I visited RWE in my constituency. A young man who undertook an apprenticeship with RWE is now a technician, and, with various shift allowances, is earning £85,000 a year. These are good jobs, they are long-term jobs, and they are happening in places like Great Grimsby and Cleethorpes.

I am always happy to give way to my hon. Friend, and she has made an important point. The effect of these industrial jobs is being felt throughout the country, not least in the north-east of Scotland, where floating offshore wind and other opportunities are being made real.

No, thank you; I need to make progress. Sumitomo has opened the UK’s first high-voltage direct current subsea cable factory at Port of Nigg, creating more than 200 direct jobs. Two major offshore wind projects off Norfolk have reached final investment commitment, unlocking £12 billion of investment, supporting nearly 2,500 jobs, and generating enough power for the equivalent of about 3 million homes. A fair transition cannot mean managing the decline of one industry and simply hoping that another will turn up. It means building the next industries deliberately, with workers and trade unions at the table, and fairness must be measured locally, not just nationally. It means a fabrication contract won in Britain, a training place available before a worker has to transition, and a port community seeing the benefit of the infrastructure that it hosts. It means listening to workers when they say what will make a move realistic: pay, travel certification and job security, rather than assuming that a headline number is enough.

No, thank you. Since July 2024, more than £110 billion of private investment has been announced for the UK’s clean energy industries. The new energy wealth fund will begin with a £2 billion injection, and will link future North sea revenues to investment in renewable and low-carbon energy. That is how we turn today’s national asset into tomorrow’s energy security.

That is a really important point, is it not? The Conservative party would have us believe that the only way in which to drive economic growth in this country is to drill every last drop from the North sea. The reality is that we have burgeoning green energy in this country, and we need to support that, because it will ultimately deliver the jobs for young people, in Bracknell Forest and across the country, that we so badly need.

I agree, and I know that my hon. Friend is committed to making sure that those opportunities extend to his constituents in Bracknell and to those right across the country. This debate is sometimes presented as a choice between climate action and energy security, or between existing workers and new industries. It is not. The serious course is to manage the North sea responsibly, maintain the oil and gas that we need during the transition, and build the clean power that will reduce our exposure to volatile international markets. It is to uphold a lawful process on Rosebank, explain the Jackdaw decision honestly, and invest in the people and places that will deliver the next chapter in this country’s energy story. This is a practical, credible and fair plan. It means lower exposure to fossil fuel shocks, greater control over our energy, good jobs across the country, and a clear path to our climate goals.

The Conservative motion states that, for three reasons, “energy security, economic growth and jobs”, the House should commit itself to Rosebank “as soon as is practicable”. I listen to Conservative Members, and I ask myself why the party that spent the last decade failing to deliver on the real trilemma of energy affordability, energy security and sustainability finds it so hard to look at the evidence and change course. Why would its Trumpian “drill, baby, drill” approach succeed with this one oilfield when hundreds of new licences did not? I will focus on those three claims, and I will also focus on the elephant in the room in the Conservatives’ motion: the climate impacts of the burning of the oil from the field, the very reason their own original consent for Rosebank was found to be unlawful.

Does the hon. Member not understand that if we produce more oil and gas in this country, it does not mean that we will burn more? It just means that we will import less oil and gas from other nations that have a higher carbon footprint than us.

I will definitely come on to that point. The head of the International Energy Agency has said that new fields, such as Rosebank, will not change that much for UK energy security, and that Britain will remain a price taker. We will still be exposed to the rollercoaster of volatile fossil fuel prices. The oil from Rosebank will be sold to the highest bidder—I do not think that any Members question that. We participate in a global market, in which prices are set internationally, regardless of where the oil is extracted or how much is imported. We know that, because we are part of the global market. We Liberal Democrats recognise that the UK will continue to require North sea oil and gas to be part of our energy mix for years to come, and so does the Climate Change Committee. Much of the reason why is that, as the shadow Secretary of State said, we should have been following dual paths: we should have continued with the extraction of oil and gas over the past decades, but also accelerated reducing our reliance on them. Instead, we have had years of maximising oil and gas extraction. Unlike the examples that the Conservatives brought forward—countries such as Norway—the Conservatives failed to turn those resources into a long-term plan for energy security and transition.

The hon. Lady refers to the Climate Change Committee. Its estimate, as we work towards net zero by 2050, is that the UK will still need 13 billion to 15 billion barrels of oil before then. As we are going to use oil, even if we follow the Climate Change Committee’s advice, does she not agree that it would be better if it was produced in UK waters, using UK men and women, who pay tax to the UK Exchequer?

The Climate Change Committee looks at that. As I have said, we agree with the committee on the abatement curve. We need an energy mix, and we will need oil and gas, but the committee says that that does not necessarily mean that we have to open up new fields, and that we have to consider the climate impacts. It says that the best way to stop importing is to drive up electrification in our country. I will come back to that, because that is where the Conservatives doubled down on policies that left Britain exposed. The Conservatives scrapped insulation schemes, blocked onshore wind and cancelled the Lib Dem policy of zero-carbon homes. By contrast— [Interruption.] We did; we started with renewable energy and decarbonisation, which is starting to deliver the energy security that we need. Since the start of the Hormuz crisis, through record-high UK wind and solar generation, we have avoided the need for gas imports worth £5.9 billion. Analysis from Carbon Brief shows that the 15 GW of wind and solar capacity secured in the latest renewable energy auction will avoid the need to import 78 liquefied natural gas tankers every year by 2030. Every wind turbine, solar panel, heat pump, battery storage facility and small modular reactor will make Britain less dependent on volatile international energy markets and more secure in an uncertain world.

As the hon. Lady knows, we will nonetheless be net importers for years and years. I challenged the Minister on this issue, and I was surprised that he could not answer. Rosebank is expected to produce a maximum of 12 kg of CO 2 per barrel. The global average—in other words, the amount for imports—is 33 kg, and that is before it is brought here. It is madness not to produce low-emission domestic oil and gas, rather than importing much higher-emission and more polluting fuel from elsewhere. I would have hoped that the logic of that was irrefutable, even for a Liberal Democrat.

That was debated in the Supreme Court case. We have to account for cleaner production. I am so glad that Conservative Members agree that we should all have zero tolerance for methane venting and flaring, and should make sure that our production is as clean as Norway’s. How clean is the oil that goes on to the international market, or into the international pool? The Supreme Court judgment was about how we deal with our collective scope 3 emissions globally, and I will come on to that later. On economic growth, the Conservative party has, in the face of the evidence, stopped claiming that giving consent for this new oilfield will bring down bills, which is good. There are arguments about economic growth, and it will indeed be important to carefully scrutinise tax arrangements. Let us look at the net fiscal revenue from oil and gasfields, and make sure that, as we do have to depend on some, this truly does support and strengthen our economy.
