The shadow Secretary of State, the hon. Member for West Aberdeenshire and Kincardine (Andrew Bowie), said proudly that the previous Conservative Government cut taxes repeatedly. Under the maximisation policy, they handed out generous reliefs and allowances to the big oil and gas companies to incentivise new production. However, let us be honest: under that regime, net tax revenues from North sea oil and gas fell below zero in both 2015-16 and 2016-17, meaning that the Treasury paid the industry more than it received back. We are also looking at decommissioning costs. This is a maturing basin, and as 93% has already been drilled, it is quite normal that there will be more cost for decommissioning the rigs. In fact, His Majesty’s Revenue and Customs projects that we will need almost £11 billion of taxpayer support to help decommission North sea infrastructure. That involves jobs too—that is just the reality—but let us talk about net fiscal revenue. As we have heard, £500 million could come in tax, but £440 million was paid out last year alone for decommissioning, so let us just be honest about the net fiscal revenue.

Does the hon. Member not understand that the Rosebank floating production, storage and offloading unit is already there? It is in place, waiting to be given the go-ahead. Even if it does not go ahead, the Government will probably still have to pay decommissioning costs for that asset, which has generated no tax revenue.

As I understand it, the Supreme Court judgment said that this could go ahead, but at the producers’ own risk. However, taxpayers are also paying for it, as the hon. Member said. As everybody has said, we have cross-party consensus on jobs. The oil and gas workers have powered Britain’s economy for generations. They have literally kept the lights on, and still do. They deserve certainty about their future from a Government who are willing to back that future. The shadow Secretary of State did not respond to the evidence showing that 75,000 jobs had been lost, despite hundreds of new licences being given. It is just the reality that this is a declining basin. We need to look at the transition out of this, and to support the workers who sustain the sector. A new field on its own will not reverse the long-term trend. I felt I could not speak here without having visited Aberdeen. This summer, I spent a lot of time in Scotland, talking to oil and gas workers, those in the supply chains and various organisations. Having heard those voices gives me some legitimacy. I also met new apprentices in all these sectors. One of them had not had many chances. Given that we have just had the Milburn review, this is quite relevant. He did not think there was much of a future for him, but he told me what he thought about his new future. He is now in the second year of his apprenticeship and earning £22,000, and in the fourth year of his apprenticeship he will be on £34,000. He said that he is now doing welding, just like his grandad, and he knows he has a high-skilled, high-paying future ahead of them. I asked him what he wanted me to do. He said that when people say that they will scrap the net zero economy and rip up the contracts that he is looking for, I should look them in the eye and tell them that they will not take away his future. I have just done that, as I told him I would. The Liberal Democrats continue to call for a just transition commission that puts workers and communities at the heart of the energy transition, because no community should be left behind. I will move on to the climate. I questioned the Opposition’s arguments for Rosebank in their motion. I turn to the missing element in their motion—the wider environmental consequences following the Supreme Court’s Finch judgment—and to the Government’s amendment, which says that any decision must be “legally robust”. This House has a responsibility to consider what the decision means for our climate commitments and future generations. We heard the Minister talk about the record heatwaves, wildfires, drought and avoidable deaths this summer.
On Rosebank, the hon. Lady talks about the consequences of the climate heating. What percentage contribution will Rosebank make to the global warming of this country?

I heard the most fantastic response to that on a radio programme. On the 0.1% difference it will make, the very British response was, “When I take my dog to the park and it has a poo, I don’t say, ‘That’s only 0.1% of the poos in this park.’ What I do is pick it up, and I expect everybody else to pick up theirs, because that is what we do collectively. We lead by example.” Just this week, we heard of the incredible amount of concern in all our constituencies and across all parties, following the “People’s Emergency Briefing”. We must be honest with the public. Now that we have the Finch judgment, the full climate impacts of oil and gas production can finally be properly assessed. Rosebank’s projected scope 3 emissions are around seven times greater than those associated with Jackdaw, and are equivalent to roughly a quarter of the UK’s sixth carbon budget. The Supreme Court Finch judgment does not provide a definitive road map for resolving tensions between economic development and climate goals, but it does require explicit recognition of the climate impact, and legal decisions that align the UK’s approach to fossil fuels more closely with our climate objectives. When I say “climate objectives”, I am speaking to the Government Front Benchers. I ask, with respect, that we are not gaslit on—
Order. May I respectfully suggest to the hon. Lady that she has now spoken for as long as both the shadow Secretary of State and the Minister? She needs to conclude her remarks.

We can approve all new oil and gas fields and probably stay within our net zero targets, because they do not consider scope 3 emissions. Let us be honest with the public when the Government say that we can do this and meet our net zero carbon targets; scope 3 emissions are not within them. There must be mitigations. That is what I would like to say. The Liberal Democrats say that Rosebank does not bring greater energy security and does not address our climate commitments, so it should not be approved.
With an immediate four-minute time limit, I call Torcuil Crichton.

Thank you, Madam Deputy Speaker. Time is short, and I am still reeling from that metaphor too far from the Liberal Democrats. I am very proud to be part of a Government who are committed to the change to renewables. This great movement—the transition from oil and gas to renewables—is what this first-term Labour Government will be best remembered for. That transition is already well under way. Some 52% of our electricity last year was supplied by renewables. I am glad to note that the legacy of Tom Johnston and the hydro boys made a contribution to that; 2% came from the dams in the highlands that were opposed by the nimbys of their day, the landlords who wanted to use the glens for sport, rather than for clean energy. We are not there yet; I realise that. We are on a mission, and we are heading in the right direction. There are, thanks to the Conservatives, only 121,000 jobs in oil and gas, both in the supply chain and directly. There are now 145,000 jobs in the renewables sector. That shows not only that the energy mix is right and the transition is getting under way, but that the transition of jobs is happening at pace and pragmatically. It has to happen at pace, but also at a sensible pace. The movement to renewables is a process. It cannot be a perilous drop that leaves the workforce, the skills and the supply chain behind. I say that as much to my own side as to the other. We cannot afford to abandon these communities and the workforce that powers our economy like previous Governments abandoned the coal communities in the last century. The truth is, as everyone acknowledges, that we will require oil for decades to come; that is an unavoidable fact. That is why I support this pragmatic transition, utilising our own oil and gas production rather than importing it, supporting skills and jobs as we move the workforce away to that new renewable sector. But we should be clear-eyed about this: Rosebank, which we are dealing with tonight, is already licensed, although legally snarled up thanks to the previous Government’s SNAFU, and is already part of the transition. Its refusal has become something of a totem for those who would rather offshore our carbon footprint and their environmental conscience, and its approval has been something of a talisman for the industry that predicts economic disaster if it does not go ahead. We must not pretend that Rosebank’s approval will either save or end the North sea story, however. It is true that it would support 580 well-paid jobs throughout its lifetime, with £24 billion in economic activity downstream and directly, and, along with Jackdaw, would provide £3.8 billion of tax revenues in 2034. Those are significant benefits. But the North sea, as people have said, is a declining basin with over 70,000 jobs lost under the last Government. However, as I said earlier, transition is not the same as abandonment. This Labour Government should not be switching off the North sea, and that is why the energy wealth fund announced by the Chancellor to channel revenues directly from Rosebank and Jackdaw into renewable infrastructure and jobs access is so welcome. I note, too, the mercy SNP amendment calling for tax revenues from Rosebank to be used exclusively in Scotland, a policy sent by fax machine from 40 years ago. It is a slogan.

Does my hon. Friend agree that it is worth reflecting on the fact that the oil industry supports jobs and the economy not only in the area of Aberdeen and not only in Scotland, but across the whole UK?

My hon. Friend is absolutely right. The map of North sea employment shows only two postcode areas in the UK that do not have a direct jobs connection to the industry. This is not a parochial issue, and it is not an Aberdeen issue; it is a nationwide economy and supply chain issue affecting every constituency and every MP.
I will give way. Because it is a Wednesday, we might learn that the Scottish National party has a new policy on Rosebank.

Not for the first time, the hon. Member is missing the point. It is not about where the jobs are. The oil and gas industry, he might like to know, is not a UK endeavour; it is a global endeavour with people moving across the entire world to deliver it. On the point of the SNP’s amendment, he might like to explain to his constituents why all of the oil and 90% of the gas is in Scottish waters but under his Labour party’s plan he wants Scotland to gift 92% of that revenue to the rest of the UK, and he does it with a straight face?
Order. Mr Doogan and all Members should pay heed: please make interventions brief as we are very short on time.

I thank the hon. Member for Angus and Perthshire Glens (Dave Doogan) for that reasoned intervention, and only turn to ask him what happened to that other national wealth fund: the £700 million national wealth fund that the SNP Government were to make out of the ScotWind licences—licences that they were ready to sell for £70 million but then became £700 million when the Crown Estate in England set up its sale. That £700 million has not been turned into the national wealth fund, as promised: half of it has gone in day-to-day Scottish Government spending. It is not there, and neither is the publicly owned national energy company that the SNP promised us a decade ago.

I think we have just heard an audition for the next production of “The Cheviot, the Stag and the Black, Black Oil” from the SNP. Might my hon. Friend also comment on the fact that not only are we failing to see SNP policies, but we do not have nuclear jobs in Scotland either?

That is another policy that the SNP opposes, which does not make any sense in the modern day. What makes sense is that, as long as this country requires oil and gas, it should be produced domestically. We should carry on with domestic production in the North sea—that makes sense to me, to my constituents who work in the sector and to constituents across the country. We have been fortunate in Scotland to have struck gold twice: first in the North sea with oil, and now with the wealth of wind, onshore and offshore. We need to harness and build on the success of both, using the supply chains and skills that we have developed over decades to create jobs for the next decade. That is why I believe Rosebank should be approved—

I am extremely grateful to speak in this debate. I feel a bit of déjà vu, because last week I attended a Westminster Hall debate on this same issue, and I listened as the same wrong-headed ideological arguments were trotted out time and again by Rosebank’s opponents. I did not find a single one of their objections convincing. These worn-out illogical arguments are based on a fundamental misunderstanding of the oil and gas industry and UK energy security, and not one of them outweighs the enormous benefits that Rosebank could bring not just to Aberdeen but to the whole of the UK—as we heard earlier, it means jobs right across the country. I will spend my time in this debate countering some of those myths and explaining what Rosebank would really mean to people in my constituency. The first argument I hear is that Rosebank would worsen climate change. What utter, utter nonsense. We all know that we will be using oil and gas for many years to come. The Department for Energy Security and Net Zero admits that, and even the Climate Change Committee admits that. We know that oil and gas produced in the UK is better for the environment than imports from overseas. That may sound perverse, but it is actually true.

Given the truth of what my hon. Friend is saying, I wonder if he has any idea why the Government want to legislate to ban new oil and gas licences? It is bad not only for this country, not only for tax revenues, not only for the worker, but for the environment.
My right hon. Friend is absolutely correct. I have no idea why the other side wants to ban these things. It is completely illogical.

Might it have something to do with the fact that, across the globe, fossil fuel companies have already been given the go ahead to extract—and therefore burn—enough fossil fuels to create seven times the carbon emissions that would keep our planet within safe warming limits?

I really am tired of hearing this. It is absolute nonsense that we will rely on imports from elsewhere, while at the same time constituents of mine in Aberdeen South are losing their jobs because of some of the nonsense that we are hearing from Labour. Shutting down domestic production is nothing more than greenwashing: outsourcing production so that our hands look cleaner, without reducing consumption at all. This is plain common sense, and something that recent polling shows that the majority of people in this country—even the majority of Labour voters—instinctively understand. But it is something, as we have just heard, that certain Labour Back Benchers seem completely unable to grasp. The second argument is that Rosebank will not increase our energy security because crude oil is sold on the open market. It is true that crude oil is sold on the open market, but green activists often conveniently forget to mention where it goes next. From Rosebank, it will probably go to Rotterdam, and then the majority of that product—65%—ends up back in the UK. By strengthening that security of supply, Rosebank can play an immediate role in both the UK’s energy security and that of wider Europe. Now, as Labour Members are all friends with the EU, surely they should be trying to help it with its energy security. That brings me on to the economic argument. Rosebank would be an enormous revenue raiser for the Exchequer. The green zealots have even managed to turn that on its head, by trying to claim that Rosebank will take money from the Treasury instead. They have got that completely wrong. Huge amounts will flow to the Treasury for the Government to make political choices with. They can reduce our borrowing, spend it on welfare or even spend it on reducing people’s energy bills if they so wish. That would be their choice. No other country would shoot themselves in the foot and make themselves poorer, as we seem to be doing. Another argument I hear is that the investment should be made in renewables and not Rosebank. The investment in Rosebank is private money, and a huge amount has already been spent. As I said earlier, the floating production, storage, and offloading vessel is there—it is all ready to go. To deny permission now would be complete madness and would stop so much of the tax revenue that would come in. It is not an argument of oil and gas versus renewables. We need both. We need an energy mix. This debate also gives us the opportunity to see whether other parties back our oil and gas workers. We are firmly on the side of those workers, but what about the SNP? The hon. Member for Perth and Kinross-shire (Pete Wishart) has been absolutely clear that Rosebank should not go ahead, but when the First Minister in Scotland was asked about his position seven times at First Minister’s questions last week, each time he could not get off the fence to answer the straightforward question. Obviously, the murky legacy of Nicola Sturgeon still has huge influence over the First Minister. As for Labour, the Prime Minister has promised us growth in every postcode, a pragmatic approach to oil and gas, and a stop to deindustrialisation. Well, this is their chance. This is the Government’s chance to back the industry. Voting against Rosebank tonight would be a slap in the face of all the workers who work in harsh environments to keep our houses warm, our transport moving and our hospitals working. It would be turning their backs on the trade unions who call for no ban without a plan. Rosebank should be the easiest decision on Labour’s to-do list. Approving Rosebank is better for jobs, better for our economy, better for our energy transition and better for the environment. I urge the Prime Minister and the Energy Secretary to show some backbone and some leadership, face down their Back Benchers and make the sensible decision to approve this field as soon as possible.

I am aware of the time, so I will keep my remarks fairly brief. I will begin by mentioning a constituent who contacted me recently. She told me that she had borrowed money from her parents to top up her heating oil tank. She did not contact me for a lecture about the climate; she simply wanted to know whether anyone in this House would help to keep her family warm. That is the approach I want to take to Rosebank today: not whether it sounds strong, but whether it helps my constituency. The Opposition motion speaks of security, jobs and growth, which are very good words, but I do not believe that Rosebank earns them. Nine tenths of what lies under the seabed is oil, and most of it would be headed abroad; the company itself expects those buyers to be across the water in Europe. Who would it warm? It would not warm my constituent. Some 13,500 homes in my constituency are heated with oil, and not one of them would see a lower bill due to Rosebank. The price of oil is set on the global market. Drilling off Shetland will not lower prices for my constituents in the Allen valleys, Slaggyford and Knarsdale. Let me be plain about who is letting down my constituents close to home. In April, the Government gave Northumberland county council £5 million, including nearly half a million purely for heating oil. My hon. Friend the Member for North Northumberland (David Smith) recently submitted a freedom of information request to the council about where that money had gone. By 21 September, only a third of applications had been paid out—just a touch over £36,500, or about £320 a household. The Morpeth Conservatives’ explanation for the rest was that the other households could not show they were vulnerable enough or on a low enough income. They are content for families in my constituency to still be rationing heat in January because they sit just above the line it has set. Of course, I would like to see more support for the houses on heating oil, but the feigned concern for rural communities to mask the fact that nothing was done for off-grid households for 14 years under the Conservatives should not obscure the fact that this Government have taken action when it was needed.

The hon. Gentleman is most generous. I am sure that he will want to correct the record. The intervention when I was Energy Minister was much more generous for those in rural areas—and, in fact, all across the country—than the rather paltry sums he has just identified. I am sure he will want to correct the record straightaway, because I know he is one of the most straightforward Members of this House.

I would ask the right hon. Gentleman to write to the leader of Northumberland county council and ask him to get the money out of the door and into my constituents’ accounts, where it is needed, because that is what motivates me today. I am a bit concerned that Opposition Members are asking the House to approve a new oilfield, and naming families in my constituency who are struggling with fuel poverty, when the help that has been promised from the council has failed to reach those families. We will not fix fuel poverty in rural Northumberland by drilling off Shetland; we will fix it by getting money out of county hall and into the tank. No one should be talking down offshore workers; we have leant on them for decades. But in the 10 years to 2024, employment in the North sea fell by more than half, with new fields still being signed off. Rosebank offers around 500 UK jobs, on average, but the main vessel was built in Dubai. That is 500 jobs set against more than £50 billion of clean energy investment, hunting for welders, electricians, engineers—the same trades that need a just transition and a manifest commitment to that transition. I have already touched on this point, but I want briefly to return to it: the money. Shell is a partner in Rosebank, and it has posted £8.1 billion of profit for a single quarter. Giving a green light to Rosebank is to accept profits when our constituents have to count their pennies, crippled with worry about the little oil left in the tank just as we come to winter. Our children will get the carbon bill. Over its life, that one field will release roughly 70% of what the entire UK emits in a year. I do support domestic energy—turbines on our coasts, panels on our roofs, proper insulation for the stone houses in the Allen valleys—energy that is made here, owned here and out of the reach of any foreign dictator. We promised no new licences. I urge the Government again to reject Rosebank. We are not obliged to go along with the terms of this motion today.
I commend the hon. Gentleman for his brevity, but sadly there will now be a three-minute time limit. I call Graham Leadbitter.

I will speak to the SNP’s amendment, which strikes directly at the heart of five decades of Westminster’s economic failure. It establishes an unshakeable principle: if the Rosebank oilfield is approved by the UK Government, every single penny of resulting taxation must be ringfenced to serve the people of Scotland and directly fund a renewable transition. For 50 years, the Treasury has treated Scotland’s natural resources as a bottomless cash cow to plug short-term London Budget deficits, costing Scotland at least £1 trillion, according to the Chancellor. We need only look across the North sea to Norway, with its £2 trillion sovereign wealth fund, to witness the staggering scale of generational wealth that has been stolen from the communities of Scotland by successive Westminster Administrations. The SNP’s approach to Rosebank and our North sea resources is grounded in a pragmatic parallel track transition. We must responsibly manage domestic production while accelerating the deployment of renewables at pace, where Scotland already leads Europe through offshore wind. Licensing and consenting decisions remain entirely reserved to the UK Government and are quasi-judicial in law, but for as long as our economy requires hydrocarbons for domestic heating, heavy transport and industrial feed stocks, decisions must be made on a rigorous, evidence-led, case-by-case basis, measured strictly against our statutory net zero targets and national energy security.

Does the hon. Gentleman accept that the logical conclusion of geographically ringfencing tax income from every industry right across the UK ringfencing would be no Barnett consequentials for Scotland? What does he think the impact of that would be on his constituency?
I do not accept that premise. As somebody who clearly campaigns for Scottish independence, I am not going to agree with that ever.

Does my hon. Friend agree that it is paradoxical that we are a nation that is so rich in energy, whether it is oil, gas, renewables or any other source, yet in Scotland we pay among the highest bills in Europe for our energy?

I agree entirely; it is an absolute disgrace that that is the case. Scotland has demonstrated clear climate leadership. The Scottish Government have halved greenhouse gas emissions since 1990 and demonstrated true international moral leadership, committing £36 million to climate justice, including £10 million for loss and damage to vulnerable nations on the frontline of climate change. Yet we must confront the staggering hypocrisy running through Westminster’s energy policy. The UK is projected to rely on oil and gas for years to come. If the UK Government simply shut down domestic extraction, while national demand remains unchanged, we will not reduce global emissions by a single gram; we simply offshore our responsibilities. Instead of using domestic supplies extracted under strict environmental standards and strong trade union oversight, the UK will increasingly import liquified natural gas, with far higher production and shipping emissions, alongside crude oil from foreign nations such as Libya. Shutting down domestic fields only to import hydrocarbons from countries with lax environmental safeguards and appalling records on workers and human rights is not climate leadership; it is moral cowardice and environmental outsourcing of the worst kind. Finally, we must confront the looming cliff edge facing our energy workforce. The Conservative party spent years bellowing “Drill, drill, drill” without building the renewable bridge, merely pushing that cliff edge further away. Now Labour’s blunt exploration bans and punitive energy profits levy threaten to push our communities straight over that cliff edge, repeating the devastating industrial destruction inflicted by Margaret Thatcher. The energy transition institute at Robert Gordon University has warned that north-east Scotland risks losing over 18,000 jobs by 2035 because clean energy job creation is failing to match the pace of oil and gas decline. The GMB union has made it crystal clear that, without a real bridge, “There is no transition…There is only a cliff edge.” The world-class subsea engineering and marine skills held by our offshore workers are the precise foundation needed to power the renewables revolution. Not only would it be morally wrong, but we simply cannot afford to throw those workers on the scrapheap. The majority of Scots want energy powers to be in Scotland and to ensure that Scotland’s energy wealth is placed where it belongs: in Scotland’s hands.

The one thing that I agree with Conservative Front Benchers on is that this is a timely debate. Although some Members might have gone a wee bit further from Rosebank and into a broader debate, I welcome the focus on Grangemouth and the damascene conversion we saw yesterday when Conservative Front Benchers backed my calls for quicker state intervention at Grangemouth. But, just to set the record straight, the announcement of the refinery closure was in November 2023, and it was called a “commercial decision” by their Government, as my constituents recognise. As we have gone a bit broader, I implore the Minister to continue to lobby the Treasury for a quicker introduction of a carbon border adjustment mechanism so that we can protect our refining sector throughout the United Kingdom and stimulate the market for biorefining. I support the Government’s approach, especially because it rightly reaffirms that consenting decisions will be taken through the settled licensing process, as seen under successive Governments by the Secretary of State on the merits of the application. Any decision must not fall foul of the legal requirements that the previous Conservative Government rode roughshod over when the initial application was approved. The judicial review’s decision was based on material grounds that are still relevant as the Secretary of State reconsiders the decision, such as the initial information disclosed in 2022 about the carbon emissions throughout its lifetime being 45 times lower than what are applied today. Because of the legal process, not a single drop of oil has been extracted to date. As the North sea basin has been depleting, 75,000 North sea jobs were lost while licensing was occurring. Collectively, we in this House must square with the public that the future opportunities of kids going through colleges, apprenticeships and university courses in the energy sector and supply chain today will be in the renewables sector. Some hon. Members seem sympathetic to that argument but, purely for political expedience, are calling on the Government to cut ourselves off today from our existing domestic supply. The Green party’s amendment states that the Government can “commit to not developing the Rosebank oilfield” tonight, implying that we can simply bypass the legal process that the Minister has articulated and reject Rosebank without a second thought. That is a blunt approach that would be available to the Government only if we were to adopt the position of revoking existing oil and gas licences, as the Scottish Greens committed to in their manifesto in 2024. Let us be clear that I did not stand on—and this Labour Government did not win an election on—a manifesto to revoke oil and gas licences, cut off existing domestic extraction, and directly and aggressively accelerate the market attrition of job losses that has characterised the past 12 years for the North sea. I caution any hon. Members against seeking to echo that extreme and impractical position. I come to the SNP amendment, which I welcome as a misplaced improvement to the representations that the First Minister made on Jackdaw to the Labour Government. In the letter that the First Minister sent to the Prime Minister on 21 October, he said that he wanted the Labour Government’s energy wealth fund to be reserved for the north-east of Scotland, seeking to exclude from eligibility in the process—
Order. It might be helpful to hon. Members if I point out that only the amendment in the name of the Prime Minister has been selected.

I very much appreciated the remarks of the hon. Member for Falkirk (Euan Stainbank) and agree with much of what he had to say. I have seen Aberdeen over the years as a visitor, and it has pained me to see its ups and—more particularly—its downs. There is no doubt that the high-quality jobs in the frame here would galvanise that great and fine city. Unlike the made-up jobs we heard about yesterday, these are real jobs, paying good money: welders, electricians, construction workers and all the associated jobs that fall from those high-paid occupations. That is what is at stake. I am staggered that the Government should even consider simply waiving those. The other reason why I think the Government will make the right decision on Rosebank is because of lobbying on their side. Tony Blair has said that the Government’s energy strategy is “doomed to fail”. Gary Smith, the general secretary of the GMB, has said that the Government must approve Rosebank. He characterises the Government’s current position as “economic madness” and “a disaster for many working people”. He says that the Department for Energy Security and Net Zero is “basically the ministry for P45s”, and famously, he said that the Government’s position is “batshit crazy”. I am not particularly worried about what Gary Smith says, but there are 250 Labour parliamentarians who should be. The GMB has the biggest Labour parliamentary membership of any trade union. It supports many Labour Members of Parliament, and I think I am looking at some of them right now.
Does my right hon. Friend agree that Gary Smith expresses his views on the policy so much better than the Ministers on the Front Bench, however reputable they may be?

Yes, I do. However, in the spirit of non-partisanship with which I started my remarks, I hope very much that the Minister for Energy, who is chuntering from a sedentary position, will listen to people such as Mr Smith and his former leader Tony Blair, because on this they are talking sound good sense in the interests of people.

I declare an interest—as set out in my entry in the Register of Members’ Financial Interests—as a member of the GMB, and I offer the right hon. Gentleman membership of the GMB, seeing as he is such a great fan of Gary Smith.

I feel that we ought to have a hands-up from Labour Members who are members of the GMB, just to clear the air. Suffice it to say that, on the Treasury Bench, views appear to be rather different. The last Energy Secretary said that Rosebank was “climate vandalism”. His successor posted, “We will #StopRosebank”. Tony Blair and Gary Smith are plainly on the right side of the argument being waged on the Labour Benches. We know that if we do not exploit Rosebank, investors across the board, not just in this industry, will give up on Britain.

No, not unless the hon. Gentleman wants to explain the Liberal Democrats’ quest for net zero by 2045—but even then I will not give way. The situation sends a message that Britain is not serious about growth. We know that net zero by 2050 will make us colder and poorer, at a cost of an estimated £695 billion to avoid a rise in global temperature by the end of this century—by 0.0037°C, based on UN figures. We know that listening to the Liberal Democrats on this matter would consign our constituents to living in caves. The Government’s position appears to be predicated on climate leadership. That is just hopelessly naive—the sort of naiveté we have heard in relation to their negotiations on the European Union. To suppose that we are in the position of being in Yalta in 1945, in Shenzhen this year, is pathetic when we are not in the line-up. Countries are not listening to the UK as they once did; they do not look to the UK for leadership. The leadership that Ministers construct in relation to arguments such as this is a complete illusion. We can lead on oil and gas—that is a matter of fact— and we can lead on the export of oil and gas technologies. I saw that as a trade envoy. Yet those countries no longer look to us for leadership on those matters because we are closing down our domestic industry, we have canned the use of UK export finance for oil and gas, and we are quietly killing off the North sea. That will not do. It is not leadership; it is an abrogation of our responsibilities, and I hope the Minister will think again.

I start by thanking the oil and gas workforce, who have given this country decades of service. Thank you to the engineers, the technicians, the crews who spend weeks at a time offshore and the entrepreneurs who built their British-owned businesses in the supply chains of the oil and gas giants, a few of whom I met recently when the Energy Security and Net Zero Committee visited Aberdeen. Those people deserve better than what they have been offered by the Conservatives this afternoon. This has sadly become a debate where people are used by the Opposition as political footballs for point scoring. It is therefore our responsibility to remind the Conservatives about their appalling record when they licensed everything and protected nobody. During their tenure, employment in offshore oil and gas halved. Over 100,000 jobs were lost under the Conservatives, while permissions were handed out without any consideration of the impact on our climate or of the future strategic resource that is the North sea. The truth is that the Conservatives never took those jobs seriously. They ignored the warnings and they did not have any plan for workers. The results speak for themselves. I wanted to comment on the impact on the climate and on taxation, but in the limited time I have, I will focus on jobs, because that is where this argument lies. Consenting will sustain some jobs in the short term—potentially around 500 over the lifetime of the development—but those are sustained jobs, not created jobs. We must recognise that over 100,000 people are still working in the industry and that they need protection and support, but a declining basin is still declining, whatever this House decides this afternoon. How we support workers through the transition should be the laser focus of this House, not arguing over a single consent, and I am proud that this Labour Government have started that work. The North sea future plan establishes the North sea jobs service, giving oil and gas workers end-to-end support into other energy sectors, backed by the transition training fund and an expanded skills passport. Importantly, our trade unions sit on that North sea future board, ensuring that the voice of workers is at the heart of decisions—something that the Conservatives never did when they were in power. This is what a plan looks like: developed with industry and with workers, and delivering for the good of all. On the topic of energy security, the broader point that we cannot underplay is that this is a strategic resource. It is a finite resource that becomes more valuable as global supply tightens, so it is imperative for our long-term energy security that we do not extract that oil now, at the bottom of the tax cycle, and sell it abroad. The question for the House should be: do we sell off this reserve on the cheap and leave the workforce stranded, or do we keep the resource in hand and focus on building a diverse, vibrant energy industry that everyone wants to work in? That is what I would support.

On behalf of the Greens, I have tabled an amendment to the Opposition’s motion on Rosebank because, frankly, it is based on myths and misinformation. In this speech, I aim to bring some clarity and accuracy to the debate. On energy security, Rosebank is mostly an oilfield. In January 2024, Conservative Government Ministers admitted that most of the oil extracted from Rosebank would be sold on the international market, not to UK customers. We also know that, whether or not new drilling goes ahead, the UK will still be almost completely dependent on imports to meet our energy needs by 2050. Rosebank’s minimal gas reserves have the potential to reduce UK annual gas import dependency by just 1% on average, and that would be if none of the gas was sold overseas, so it is likely to be even less than that. The idea, then, that Rosebank will improve UK energy security simply does not stack up. In the last decade, the number of jobs supported by the UK oil and gas industry has more than halved, and that is even though the Conservative Government approved hundreds of drilling licences in that period. We know that 93% of viable— [ Interruption. ] Those on the Opposition Front Bench might want to listen to this bit. We know that 93% of viable oil and gas reserves in the North sea have already been extracted, so jobs there will continue to decline. That is geology, not politics. Therefore, surely the best thing we can do for those workers is ensure that they are supported, with a fully funded transition programme, to access good-quality green jobs.

I will not, because of time. On the economy, the economic case made by the Opposition is equally spurious. I have one number for them: £258 million. That is the estimated net loss to the UK Treasury if Rosebank goes ahead—[Hon. Members: “Rubbish!”] That is right: approving Rosebank will not bring in money to the Treasury. It will lose it. Meanwhile, the companies behind Rosebank would earn £1.5 billion in profit based on the long-term average oil price of $70 a barrel.

I will not because I only have a few moments left. On energy bills, gas is what is driving up the cost of energy. It sets the price of electricity 98% of the time. Anyone claiming otherwise is not being honest with the public. I have one final point to debunk. The right hon. Member for Beverley and Holderness (Graham Stuart) kept mentioning that oil from the UK is only 12 kg a barrel. He neglected to mention the amount emitted by burning that oil, which is around 430 kg, dwarfing the irrelevant number of how much it costs to produce it.

As someone who represented north-east Scotland for three terms in the Scottish Parliament and who was based in Aberdeen, I know how important the oil and gas sector is to that great city and to communities across Scotland, including my own in Glenrothes and Mid Fife. The North sea is a mature basin for oil and gas production, so we have to get the transition to renewables jobs and production right. It is an uncomfortable fact for the Opposition that tens of thousands of jobs in the North sea were lost on their watch and that we are debating the future of Rosebank in this Chamber because their handling of the decision process led to it being successfully challenged in the courts. It is this Government who are taking the right approach over what is a quasi-judicial matter. Jackdaw is finally going ahead now because the decision was made in the right way and it was the right decision. If after due process, Rosebank is approved too, I also believe this will be the right decision, because the key question for the UK and for Scotland, including the north-east of Scotland, is how we build the bridge to increased jobs and production in renewables from oil and gas. That is why Ministers have rightly and repeatedly said that oil and gas will play a role in our energy mix for decades to come. The skills of the workers in the oil and gas industry will be crucial if we are to have the skilled workforce we need in our renewables sector in the future. Collectively, Rosebank and Jackdaw will provide more than 3,500 jobs at peak construction and are worth a total of £28.7 billion to the UK economy. That could make a massive contribution to the energy wealth fund, which will allow us to make a significant investment in major new renewable projects in the future, many of which will undoubtedly be in Scotland given all the natural renewable resources we have. I will give some credit to the Opposition today: they have been clear in their views on whether Rosebank should proceed or not. It is regrettable that the Scottish Government, on such a key matter of energy policy, are not clear on that. For all the reasons I have set out and more, I believe the argument is compelling to continue with a pragmatic approach and proceed with Rosebank, but it is of course essential on this occasion that due process is followed, that we get this decision right and that the decision can proceed. That is why I support the approach the Government are taking on this vital question—not just for Scotland, but for the whole of the UK energy industry.

Until I came to this place, I thought oil rigs were installations surrounded by the sea, but it seems they are instead islanded by misinformation. Many myths are ingrained and presented as fact by the left: Mrs Thatcher gave away UK oil assets so friends could get tax cuts and build conservatories; a Norway-style sovereign wealth fund would today be worth £1 trillion—not so. Riches pour into the Treasury coffers in tax receipts from North sea oil. The left did not howl when it paid the welfare bill. Those receipts helped to fund defence properly—something that today’s Chancellor might wish to consider. The trillion-pound wealth fund is based on the idea that no withdrawals were made—is that credible? Spendthrift Labour lives from paycheque to lottery win. Rosebank is another target for inaccuracy. Its gas content is dismissed as trivial. In fact, fed in through the west of Shetland pipeline, it could support 2% of domestic usage. Yes, its oil will likely head for the continent as we lack the refining capacity here in the UK, so that may not directly affect bills here, but it is axiomatic that having greater supply will bring overall bills down. Crucially, tapping new sources of oil such as Rosebank does not drive up demand. It simply covers existing demand, reducing the need to import from unreliable sources further away and produced with a greater carbon footprint.

Does my hon. Friend agree that if Rosebank does not go ahead, we will get the oil anyway from the same basin via Norway? The only difference will be that Norway will get the jobs and the Treasury receipts.

My right hon. Friend is absolutely correct. It is insane that we are going to import from the very same basin. Yes, it is a declining basin, but it must be borne in mind that Rosebank is to the west of Shetland, in waters that were until recently thought to be uneconomic. This declining basin actually may have a future, if it is allowed to have one. Let us be clear too that Rosebank going ahead will generate wealth for the country. I cannot believe the suggestions that it will somehow cost us money—that is an absolute nonsense. The talk is of just transition to renewables, but we cannot say to today’s bright young technicians and engineers, “There are good jobs for you in renewables in 10 years’ time.” They have bills to pay and families to feed right now. There is good news on renewables: Japanese titans Sumitomo Electric opened the UK’s first high-voltage subsea cable manufacturing facility at the Port of Nigg in the Cromarty freeport. Those cables are crucial for offshore wind farms, but it should be noted that the freeport was opened in the face of fierce opposition from the SNP, overcome by huge efforts by the then Secretary of State for Scotland, Alister Jack, now Lord Jack of Courance. The Sumitomo deal was announced under that same Conservative Government—so, please, no claims that the Conservatives are anti-renewables. We Conservatives know that this country needs a mixed scorecard on energy generation, including renewables, nuclear and, yes, oil and gas. This is a time for realism. Net zero was never about ceasing to use any fossil fuels. We need them, we will continue to need them, and practicality says that we should utilise our own resources, not Vladimir Putin’s.
With an immediate two-minute time limit, I call Jonathan Brash.

I will attempt to be brief, Madam Deputy Speaker. It is no secret that I support the Rosebank approval. I said so in the Westminster Hall debate last week—the Minister heard me then and he can hear me again now. I support it because I believe that approving Rosebank passes what I call the British worker test: it is good for energy security, it is good for jobs and it is good for communities, including mine in Hartlepool, where there are jobs that rely on it. What I am sick to death of is the politicisation of our energy security, whether by people in Reform UK, who would destroy renewables jobs at steel mills, cable companies, solar or wind companies in my constituency, which has one of the biggest clean energy economies in the north of England, or by the Green party, whose leader sat on a panel with me in the north-east and said quite happily that he would cancel the new nuclear deal for Hartlepool, costing us 2,500 jobs—and apparently he wants votes in the north-east! It is very much a case of clowns to the left of me and jokers to the right. I like the hon. Member for West Aberdeenshire and Kincardine (Andrew Bowie), but I have to say: this motion is a farce. We know full well that no decision taken at the end of this debate will have any impact on the quasi-judicial decision that the Secretary of State has to take. We know why the Conservatives have chosen this topic for debate—it is for their social media clips. I can guarantee there will be Conservative commentary on social media tonight, saying that MPs have voted to block Rosebank, when they know that is not true. I am in favour of Rosebank, but this motion is a farce and, frankly, I do not want any part of it.

We are blessed in this country because oil and gas is treasure—it is our own energy treasure. The idea that one would not extract our energy treasure is nothing short of gross financial negligence. We should be extracting and using every last barrel and every last drop, like any other sensible major nation. We seem to be the only major nation that thinks it is a good idea to ban the extraction of this treasure. Of course the Secretary of State should approve the Rosebank application. Let us look at some of the numbers: over £20 billion of GDP into our economy, 3,500 jobs during the construction, and 800-plus jobs during its operation, including over 125 apprentices at a time when we are worried about jobs for young people. These are great opportunities. Some say that it makes no difference, because the product is going to be exported to be refined overseas. Wrong! Sixty-five per cent comes back to the UK. Others say it will not bring the bills down. Wrong! Because of the billions of pounds of tax revenue that will be generated, the Government will then have political choices. They could, for example, reduce VAT on energy bills, which would bring those bills down. On every level, we absolutely should approve Rosebank. It is ironic that the Foreign Secretary is approving oil and gas extraction exploration in the Falkland Islands at a time when his colleague in the Cabinet may think of not approving Rosebank. That is absolutely absurd, illogical and negligent. I urge the Government and the Secretary of State to do the right thing and approve Rosebank.

Some 75% of the energy that the UK uses every day comes from oil and gas. The Government need to ask themselves one very simple question: do we believe that the UK should use the oil and gas resources that we are so lucky to have on our doorstep, and benefit from the world-class skilled workforce that we have built up over generations, or are they happy to allow a key UK industry to decline, jobs to disappear and investment to go elsewhere? That is the decision for the Government on Rosebank and the wider North sea. As we have heard from the contributions of Conservative Members, we are in full support of our oil and gas sector. My hon. Friend the Member for Aberdeen South (Douglas Lumsden) spoke about its importance for the skilled workers in his constituency and the wider domestic production that it supports. My right hon. Friend the Member for South West Wiltshire (Dr Murrison) spoke about the sensible voices that are usually so revered by Labour Members, and why they are not being listened to this time. My hon. Friend the Member for Dumfries and Galloway (John Cooper) spoke about the tax revenues brought in by the industry over decades, and the true investment that has given rise to throughout the UK. Rosebank represents a significant opportunity for not just north-east Scotland, but the entirety of the UK, and the Government—or the Treasury, at least—know that. Why else would the Office for Budget Responsibility have included the tax receipts from Rosebank in its forecast? Last month, when the Government approved Jackdaw, they rightly celebrated its importance for jobs and energy security. Jackdaw’s gas goes directly into the UK grid and is enough to cover 6% of our needs, but with Rosebank, that figure would increase to 10%. At a time when global and European gas stocks are low and supplies are disrupted, Rosebank’s additional gas should not be written off. To those who have said time and again that the oil will be exported, let me say that, as we have heard many times, some 65% of that oil will be refined abroad and will come back to the UK as products that we use every day. It is naivety bordering on madness to think that just because we do not approve Rosebank, we will suddenly stop using diesel, jet fuel, asphalt on the roads and petrochemicals. We would just import more and more from further and further away. When the strait of Hormuz was blocked this year, was anyone really wishing that we were more reliant on oil from the Gulf? I certainly was not, but that would be the result of blocking Rosebank. If Jackdaw is good for Scottish jobs, why is Rosebank not? Can the Minister explain that? If Jackdaw is good for investment, why is Rosebank not? If Jackdaw is good for the UK’s energy security, why is Rosebank not? The Government cannot take a victory lap for approving one field while refusing to accept the same arguments for the other. Approving Jackdaw was welcome, but approving Rosebank is the obvious next-but-not-final step. The Government’s approach to our oil and gas sector is nothing short of an ideologically driven disaster. More and more companies are leaving; another company left today. Production is falling, investment is going abroad and 25,000 jobs linked to the oil and gas sector have been lost since the general election. That is 1,000 jobs every single month. If 1,000 jobs a month were being lost in the automotive sector, steel manufacturing or any other major sector, would the Government be so relaxed? Would they be happy watching investment leave, businesses scale back and skilled workers going to find jobs overseas? Would Labour Back Benchers— 75 of them and counting, apparently—be pleading with the Government to keep making things worse? Of course they would not, but the oil and gas sector and its jobs are apparently just not as important as others to Labour. Despite grand but meaningless words from the Government about “a pragmatic approach to the North Sea”, growth in every postcode and reindustria

I thank all hon. and right hon. Members who have participated in today’s wide-ranging debate. I will not repeat the metaphor that the hon. Member for South Cambridgeshire (Pippa Heylings) employed, but Members who were not in the Chamber for that should read it in Hansard. She also made an important point about climate leadership. As always, my hon. Friend the Member for Na h-Eileanan an Iar (Torcuil Crichton) talked about the sensible pace of the transition; he always brings Tom Johnston and the hydro boys into the debate, and he is right to do so. The hon. Member for Moray West, Nairn and Strathspey (Graham Leadbitter) harked back to the 40-year SNP story of “It’s Scotland’s oil”. We have been waiting almost as long for the SNP’s energy policy; we still have no clue whatsoever what its policy is. I want to pick up on a point made by the right hon. Member for South West Wiltshire (Dr Murrison). I often respect his contributions in the House, but I think he made a completely misjudged comment when he suggested that workers in the renewable sector were a fiction. I have met many of them; they are doing incredibly important work across a whole range of sectors, and I do not think we should trivialise them in the way he did.

The Minister is absolutely mischaracterising what I said. I was referring to the made-up jobs that the Secretary of State for Work and Pensions announced as part of the Milburn review yesterday. I hope he will correct the record.

I apologise if I misunderstood the right hon. Gentleman’s point, but those are also not made-up jobs. They are real jobs for young people, giving them a future in this country, and the Conservatives should back that. This debate about the future of the North sea is important. These issues matter, because behind every headline and every policy argument are workers, families and communities that have powered this country for generations. We owe them our thanks, as well as a serious discussion about their future. The North sea has never just been a source of hydrocarbons; yes, it has produced energy for half a century, but it has also sustained communities, supported hundreds of thousands of jobs and generated billions in revenue for the country. It is one of our greatest concentrations of engineering skill, industrial capability and energy expertise. It is something we should be proud of, and we should work to make sure that it has a long-term future. As serious as this debate is, I want to make it very clear that we should not in any way prejudice a live regulatory decision that has not yet been made. The right hon. Member for Beverley and Holderness (Graham Stuart)—who was in the Chamber for much of the debate, but is not here now—made that point for me very well when he told Parliament in 2023 that “it would be neither appropriate nor helpful” for Ministers to provide “a running commentary on a live application” —[ Official Report, 28 June 2023; Vol. 735, c. 131WH.] before the regulators had reached their decisions. He was right. I will not undermine the regulatory process that is under way by discussing the merits or demerits of the Rosebank project today. Turning to the wider debate on the North sea’s future, some have argued today that the choice is simple—we should either drill every last drop, or abandon hydrocarbons in the North sea immediately. The truth is that neither of those propositions is credible. We have to strengthen our energy security, protect consumers from fossil-fuel price shocks and redouble our efforts to tackle irreversible climate change, but even on the most ambitious pathway, the reality—I accept it is perhaps an uncomfortable reality for many—is that we will continue to need oil and gas for decades to come. At the same time, it is also true to say that we have been a net importer for more than 20 years, so it is simply fantasy to pretend that domestically produced oil and gas can ever be the whole answer. The North sea remains an enormous national asset, but two things can be true at once. While the North sea is enormously valuable, it is also a declining basin. The answer is not to turn off the taps or to drill every last drop, but to manage the transition, invest in workers and build what comes next as part of an orderly and prosperous energy transition, instead of the drift and delay that cost thousands of jobs and left Britain even more exposed over the past 14 years. For decades, the North sea has helped to power Britain. Its workers have built world-class engineering, project management and offshore expertise. We should be proud of that record, but pride cannot become a mask for denial of what has been staring us in the face for decades. Production began declining more than 25 years ago. It is more than three quarters below its 1999 level. The UK became a net importer in 2004. A third of the workforce has left the industry in the past decade. New licences take years to move from award to production, and only a small fraction ever do. They would not reverse the basin’s natural decline, end imports, or determine prices on the international market. There is a bigger picture. We have seen again and again what dependence on fossil-fuel markets that we do not control means for families and businesses. When conflict disrupts supply, the price shock lands on doormats around the country. We do not set the international price of oil and gas; we pay it. We should not pretend that Britain can drill its w
Does the Minister not understand that we need to protect these jobs, and that part of protecting the oil and gas jobs that we will need for the transition is approving proposals like Rosebank?

I have already explained why I will not comment on that project. If the hon. Gentleman is interested in it, he will want the process to complete properly, and I will not interfere in it. I speak regularly to people across the industry, and I will be in Aberdeen again tomorrow, doing exactly that. Many have spent decades building skills that are the envy of the world. Their future should matter to everyone in this House, not just because they built that past prosperity, but because they are a critical part of how we build for the future. This debate comes down to a choice, but not the false choice that the Opposition have presented us with today. Nobody in the House can change the simple facts about the North sea, but we can invest in the industries that come next, and we can strengthen our energy security in the process. We choose to act to shape the future, not simply to be passengers—not turning our back on the North sea, but backing the North sea with a future worthy of its past. Question put (Standing Order No. 31(2)), That the original words stand part of the Question.

On a point of order, Madam Deputy Speaker. I seek your advice on how I might request that the Minister for Border Security and Asylum correct the record on claims made during yesterday’s debate. In speaking about my new clause 62, the Minister said: “I do not accept that the country has a duty to let domestic abusers, shoplifters and sex offenders settle” —[ Official Report , 17 November 2026; Vol. 793, c. 829.] New clause 62 would have frozen the suitability requirements as they stood when a person entered the skilled worker route, and under this the Home Secretary would therefore have the power to exercise her discretion to refuse leave on the grounds of criminality. I am sure it was not the Minister’s intention to suggest that my amendment provided a duty to let sex offenders settle in Britain. I would be grateful, therefore, for your advice on how the Minister might be asked to correct the record.

I thank the hon. Member for notice of his point of order. Ministers’ contributions in the Chamber are, of course, not a matter for the Chair, but he has placed his concerns on the record and the Treasury Bench will have heard him. Should it be necessary for the record to be corrected, there are, of course, established mechanisms for doing so.

I am grateful for the opportunity to raise an issue that underpins a huge amount of political discussion and discourse in Britain today: the regulation of free-to-air television news, the responsibilities of our television broadcasters, and the ability of the public to distinguish between journalism, political campaigning and outright conspiracy-theorising nonsense. I want to begin by making something absolutely clear. I believe passionately in a free press. I believe in robust journalism, in challenging interviews, in broadcasters holding politicians to account, and in people having access to a wide range of opinions. Indeed, in just the last couple of days I have given interviews and comment to a dozen or so outlets on a range of topics, and I have been challenged by all of them—so much the better for ensuring that contested and controversial issues find a reasonable and balanced way forward, underpinned by truth. I also believe that we have a responsibility to protect something that has served this country remarkably well for generations: the principle that television news—news underpinned by the spoken word and by visual images beamed into our homes—should be accurate, impartial and worthy of the public’s trust.

Does the hon. Member agree that safeguarding our public service broadcasters is vital as we navigate our way through the changes facing the BBC? Welsh language news provision is prepared by the BBC for S4C. Does he agree that this provision should be ringfenced?
I am increasingly concerned about the way in which the BBC is managing the cuts, and I fully support what the hon. Lady has said.

I commend the hon. Gentleman for bringing forward this debate— I spoke to him beforehand. It is a really important issue, so I am grateful to him for letting me intervene. In Northern Ireland, trusted free-to-air news from BBC Northern Ireland and UTV is a vital lifeline for our rural and older communities, who rely on impartial, locally grounded journalism. Does he therefore agree that as viewing habits shift online, regulation must protect universal access to regional news, and guarantee that Northern Ireland’s distinct voice is never ever sidelined?

Regional news is of paramount importance, and we should do everything we can to protect it. There is a reason why Britain has historically treated newspapers and the print media and television news differently. Our newspapers have always been free to take political positions: The Guardian can support the Lib Dems; the Mirror can support Labour; The Telegraph can support Reform UK. Readers understand that. They know what they are buying. Television news, however, was developed under a different settlement. That settlement, to my mind, is informed by the principles of no less an authority on free speech than John Stuart Mill, one of the founding fathers of English liberty. He wrote persuasively on this topic, and with the House’s indulgence, I wish to quote some of his words. Mill wrote: “opinions lose their immunity, when the circumstances in which they are expressed are such as to constitute their expression a positive instigation to some mischievous act. An opinion that corn-dealers are starvers of the poor, or that private property is robbery, ought to be unmolested when simply circulated through the press, but may justly incur punishment when delivered orally to an excited mob assembled before the house of a corn-dealer,”. I heartily concur with Mill on that. In a modern-day context, it appears to me that the point at issue is whether television news, and by extension online provision of news in the same context, is more like the printed word or like something “delivered orally to an excited mob”. Is it more like being printed in a newspaper, or more like being spoken at a rally during the 19th century? Given the immediacy of the spoken word, and the passion aroused by visual imagery, I think that the question needs only to be put to be answered. It is obvious why television news is regulated to be impartial in a way that newspapers are not. Broadcasters were given access to a powerful medium, reaching directly into millions of homes on the understanding that news would be presented with due accuracy and due impartiality. That settlement has helped to ensure that British broadcasting has been respected around the world. However, in recent years something has changed. We are seeing the emergence of television channels increasingly resembling the hyperpartisan cable news networks of the United States—channels built around political identities, confrontation, dividing lines and manufactured controversy, where the lines between reporting the news in the interests of the public good and generating controversy in the interests of clicks and shares have been blurred. According to Ofcom, it helps to keep an eye on the TV, yet it appears that in the past decade Ofcom has taken its eye off the ball when it comes to broadcast standards and impartiality rules. Any organisation wishing to operate on television is subject to Ofcom regulation, which exists to protect the public from harm. Section 5 of the broadcasting code covers impartiality and accuracy, yet we are repeatedly seeing just criticism of Ofcom for not enforcing the provisions within the code. Take a comment from a news broadcaster this July in a discussion about the covid pandemic, who said: “There is no evidence that the vaccine saved a single person. There is no empirical evidence that it saved a single human being.” That strikes me as being as far from accurate, trustworthy or protecting the public from harm as possible. It is materially misleading. I think it is fair to say that these falsehoods are a harm to the public, yet insufficient action is being taken. Another example, from February, is about an interview with the US President that had been broadcast on a UK channel. This was criticism levelled at the time: “If there were ever a case that merited investigation for the broadcast of potentially misleading material and a failure to meet due impartiality requirements, this was it. This was a test case for how Ofcom regulates broadcasters on due impartiality. It has

Does my hon. Friend agree with me that journalism itself is a profession that is grounded in all the things that we hold dear, such as impartiality and professionalism, and that the blurring of the lines between what is a professional journalist and what is an entertainer in the media industry at the moment is not helpful? Journalism and broadcast journalism are something to be cherished and protected. Does he agree that when Government are looking at this, they should make sure that the impartiality of journalism is protected and that we celebrate what journalists bring to our democracy?

I agree entirely, with the one caveat that some of these people are neither journalistic nor entertaining. Last month, in a hearing of the Digital, Culture, Media and Sport Committee, the chair of Ofcom, Sir Ian Cheshire, suggested that someone should “set up a left-wing version of GB News.” First, this appears to be an implicit admission that Ofcom has granted a licence to an explicitly right-wing channel, despite its multiple protestations to the contrary. Even more seriously, it also suggests that Sir Ian either does not understand or is ignorant of the law governing impartiality on Ofcom-licensed channels. That law is enshrined in the Communications Act 2003, which gives Ofcom a statutory duty to ensure that “news included in television and radio services is presented with due impartiality”. The Act spells out precisely what that statutory duty entails: impartiality requirements apply to all programmes dealing with “matters of political or industrial controversy”, and “matters relating to current public policy.” The discrepancy between Sir Ian’s comments to the Digital, Culture, Media and Sport Committee and the wording of the Act is obvious. I wish to finish by putting a few specific questions to the Minister. First, do the Government remain committed to the principle that free-to-air TV news should be subject to due accuracy and impartiality, regardless of the political perspective of the broadcaster’s owners? Secondly, what assessment has the Department made of Ofcom’s ability to address patterns of partiality across a broadcaster’s output, rather than considering individual programmes in isolation? Finally, will the Minister consider engaging with Ofcom about the wider implications of increasingly partisan television broadcasting, including whether further research into public expectations and trust is needed? I want to end where I began. My point is not about silencing voices with which we disagree. It is about ensuring the impartiality of news in a medium that is recognised as having the power of the spoken word and the power of the visual image. I do not want a Britain in which every political tribe has its own TV news channel, its own version of events, and pretends to its own set of facts. I want a country where people can disagree about politics while retaining some confidence in the information on which those disagreements are based. I think that is worth protecting. I hope the Minister will agree that the principles that have underpinned British broadcasting for generations remain just as important today as they have ever been.

I congratulate my hon. Friend the Member for Southport (Patrick Hurley) on securing this important debate. I would like to pay a special tribute to him for the work he has done in this area. We often use the tragic circumstances of the Southport attack as an example of where local media came to the fore. During that crisis, there was an amount of misinformation and disinformation circling. It gave us all hope that local people turned to local news outlets to make sure that they were reading the truth and what was accurate. I pay tribute to the Stand Up For Southport journalists, who recently received money from our local news fund, which forms part of our local news strategy, as well as to the Southport Visiter and BBC North West for the role they played for local people. I think that gives us hope that we do journalism, particularly local journalism, very well in this country. The UK has a long tradition of TV acting as a source of impartial and trustworthy news. In response to the question posed by my hon. Friend, I can confirm that the Government remain committed to ensuring that free-to-air TV news is duly accurate and impartial. Free-to-air TV news plays a vital role in supporting a healthy information environment, and we rely on our broadcasters to interrogate power, explain complex global events and help to build a shared understanding of the world, which then strengthens social cohesion and democratic participation. Now more than ever, the need for trusted news is essential to our democratic and cultural life. This includes our public service media providers, which remain among our most trusted news sources. Research shows that audiences who rely on public service news are more likely to correctly identify important factual information, to have higher levels of trust in institutions and to be less polarised. That is because the truth and facts matter. A key pillar of audience trust in TV news is its regulation by Ofcom. Under Ofcom’s broadcasting code, which my hon. Friend has mentioned, news on licensed TV services must be reported with due accuracy and presented with due impartiality. In undertaking this role, Ofcom carries out its duties independently of Government. However, that does not mean that the Government and this House should not scrutinise and take action through the democratic process where it believes that audiences and businesses should be better served. I understand that there are concerns about the effectiveness of Ofcom’s regulation of specific news broadcasters, and some have criticised Ofcom’s speed and willingness to act. On that point, my hon. Friend asked about Ofcom’s ability to assess patterns of potential partiality across a broadcaster’s output. I think it is important for me to be clear that the Government are committed to a free, independent and plural media. My hon. Friend mentioned that as well. I understand his concern, but Ofcom’s legislative duties do not require it to take a view of partiality across a broadcaster’s entire catalogue. It is important that broadcasters are free to determine their own editorial output. Nevertheless, they must still ensure that due impartiality is maintained. When considering these matters, Ofcom is able to assess a series of editorially linked programmes to see a wider picture. My hon. Friend asked whether Ofcom has the necessary powers and resources to act promptly and effectively, whether the Government will engage with Ofcom about the wider implications of increasingly partisan television broadcasting, and whether further research into public expectations and trust is needed. I recognise the importance of the regulator being equipped to act effectively in all the areas that it regulates—concerns have been raised on that point in the House in recent weeks—especially when we are in a fast-moving developing media environment. Through our media Green Paper, we are considering whether Ofcom has the right tools and powers around broadcasting regulation. We
1. How experts for the public control taskforce will be recruited.

We are exploring how greater public control can ensure that our essential services—housing, water, energy and transport—run in the interest of those who use them. The taskforce is committed to hearing diverse perspectives. I am driving the taskforce, which is supported by civil servants, drawing on expertise across central, regional and local government, business, civil society and academia, and its work will inform the 10-year plan that will be published next month.

I welcome the Government’s plans for a taskforce to help deliver public control to essential services such as water. It is vital that key organisations that represent the public’s views on the matter are represented on the taskforce. Will the Minister clarify whether campaign organisations, including Windrush Against Sewage Pollution and Ilkley Clean River Group, which have a great deal of knowledge of the sector and have campaigned for many years on the issue, would be involved in the taskforce in any meaningful way?

I am grateful to my hon. Friend for his long-standing campaigning on this issue. I pay tribute to the organisations he mentioned: Windrush Against Sewage Pollution and Ilkley Clean River Group. I know that the Parliamentary Secretary, Cabinet Office, will be happy to meet them to discuss the issues that they campaign on.
2. What steps her Department has taken to tackle issues impacting the civil service pension scheme.
5. What steps her Department plans to take in response to Capita not meeting June and August deadlines for clearing the backlog of civil service pension scheme cases.
10. What steps she is taking to ensure the accountability of Capita for its performance in the administration of the civil service pension scheme.
11. What estimate her Department has made of the length of time for Capita to clear outstanding civil service pension scheme cases.
12. What steps she is taking to support pensioners impacted by Capita’s management of the civil service pension scheme.
17. What steps she is taking to support civil servants and bereaved family members to access civil service pensions.

Capita’s performance on the pension scheme has had unacceptable impacts on people who have dedicated years of their working lives to serving this country and they deserve better. We are using the most stringent commercial levers, including requiring deliverable plans and withholding payments under the contract, which was signed under the last Government.

Joseph Cassidy from Buxton in my constituency has given 40 years of public service in the military, police and civil service, yet two days after he took voluntary retirement last year, he was told that the principal civil service pension scheme had somehow miscalculated his lump sum by 30%. Twenty months later, he is still yet to receive an outcome to his complaint or a redundancy payment, leaving his family under immense pressure and without an apology. Will the Minister set out what steps the Department is taking to hold Capita to account and get such long-standing cases resolved, so we can give public servants like Joseph the comfort and security they deserve in retirement?

I am very sorry to hear of Mr Cassidy’s poor experience. If my hon. Friend writes to me, I will ensure that his case is investigated. Capita is being held to account against the progress of its backlogs, and the access that we now have in the Cabinet Office to Capita’s data allows us to challenge its performance in greater detail.

Despite raising these issues with Ministers in the Chamber and in writing, unfortunately I still, on a weekly basis, have constituents who are being let down by Capita: for example, Mrs Gillian Stollery who lost her husband earlier this year, whose bereavement case is still six-months outstanding; or Mr Stephen Hill, who served in the prison service for 20 years and applied for his pension in November last year.
