Local authorities do have planning powers to limit the proliferation of HMOs, and we will keep the regulation of HMOs under review. I understand the frustration of the hon. Gentleman’s constituents. I am not sure that people would necessarily jump to some of the conclusions that he jumps to in these matters, but we keep these matters under review.

This year, Steve at the Neptune, volunteers and Derby punters have pulled together and raised a whopping £36,744 for the poppy appeal. They are a credit to our city, and their efforts remind us that no community is complete without its local pub. Will the Leader of the House join me in congratulating everybody at the Neptune on their brilliant fundraising work? Does he agree that we must protect our local pubs, which are the heartbeat of our communities?

Yes, I do. I join my hon. Friend in congratulating Steve and all the volunteers and customers of the Neptune on raising an extraordinary amount of money for the poppy appeal. As my hon. Friend says, great community pubs are the cornerstone of our towns. They bring people together to tackle isolation and serve as hubs for local communities—and long may they continue to do so. The Government are not just praising them; we have brought forward support for hospitality in the Budget, and I am sure that we will look at what further actions we can take to ensure that pubs continue to flourish in the future.

It is Restorative Justice Week, which has the theme of rebuilding communities, repairing connections and building peace. In my experience, restorative justice is a powerful tool that helped my family heal after I was attacked in my home. It puts the victim at the heart of the criminal justice process. Does the Leader of the House agree that restorative justice should be available to every victim of crime, where deemed appropriate, and can he assist me in pushing for a cross-Government review to maximise its potential to help victims and cut reoffending?

The Government agree with the hon. Member that victims should be at the heart of the criminal justice system. If he wishes to raise those points directly with Ministers, I will help to arrange a meeting with them.

I greatly welcome the Prime Minister’s ambition of devolving by default the powers and investment that this Labour Government are spreading out from Whitehall and Westminster into local communities, where they should be, but can the Leader of the House give a gentle nudge to departmental colleagues to ensure that non-mayoral strategic authorities receive those powers as the rule and not the exception?

My hon. Friend and all his Cornish colleagues are powerful advocates for their region, and I pay tribute to him and each and every one of them for that. We are seeing the biggest transfer of power, funding and responsibility away from Westminster in a generation to ensure that local decisions are made by local people. But this is a process, and it will continue. Not every part of the country is in the same place, as he suggests. In the meantime, I am sure that Departments will want to ensure they give due regard to where resources should be spent, not least in areas like his. I hope that Ministers have heard what my hon. Friend has said.

I will give the Leader of the House a brief respite from Brid Town—perhaps we can return to their heroics at a later date. I want to cover an altogether more serious subject—something I hope the Leader of the House will agree with me on—which is that it is now over five years since Sir Chris Whitty’s report on health in coastal communities. Its implementation was delayed by covid. I know that the Leader of the House’s constituency shares the same challenges as mine in towns such as Bridlington and Hornsea, so could he persuade the Health Secretary to give a statement to the House updating us on the implementation of the recommendations of that incredibly important report?

I will do that. I will go away and talk to colleagues about what might be said in response to that. But I gently point out that at the end of covid, the then Government commissioned the Collins report, which suggested that £6 billion should be spent to tackle the real problems that face young people in particular. Not a penny was spent on that, so I think we need to be clear about the promises that were made, and the Milburn report addresses that directly.

Collette Gallacher was murdered in 1986 on her way to school. Her murderer is due for parole again next year. Since being in prison, he has changed his name. The family will not be advised of the name change as the presumption is not to inform them to protect the rights of the murderer. Would the Leader of the House agree with me and my campaign for Collette’s law that families of victims should automatically be advised of a name change of a convicted criminal to protect the rights of the victims and not those of the perpetrator?

My hon. Friend raises a very concerning case on behalf of his constituents. He is right that we need to do everything we can to protect victims of violence against women and girls, which is why we introduced a requirement for registered sex offenders to notify the police in advance of any intended change of name. I accept that that is not exactly what he is referring to. I understand that the family are meeting the relevant Minister in the new year, but I will make sure that the Minister has heard his representations made here today.

Yesterday I tabled early-day motion 1226, calling for a national register of asylum accommodation. [That this House believes that the use of public money to provide asylum accommodation must be subject to proper transparency and scrutiny; recognises the need for accurate information about houses in multiple occupation and other residential properties used for this purpose; calls on the Government to establish and maintain a comprehensive national register of such properties, recording their addresses, ownership, accommodation providers, occupancy, public cost, planning status and compliance with applicable licensing requirements; further calls for accommodation providers to be required to keep those records up to date; urges the Government to ensure that relevant local authorities and constituency hon. Members have access to the register and are notified before properties are brought into use; and also calls for the publication of quarterly figures by ward and local authority area showing the number of properties, residents accommodated and associated expenditure.] In Runcorn and Helsby and across the country, homes that local families could otherwise live in are being used to house asylum seekers. When I asked the Home Office over a year ago how many HMOs in my constituency were being used for this purpose, I was told that it would cost too much to give me that figure. My constituents deserve to know, ward by ward, how many homes are being used to house asylum seekers and how much it is costing them. Will the Leader of the House ask the Home Secretary to make a statement on whether the Government will establish this register?

There have been opportunities to raise this directly with the Home Secretary, not least during the remaining stages of the Immigration and Asylum Bill. I will take away what the hon. Lady says, because I understand that there is often concern in communities and a need for as much clarity as possible. But as an MP representing a constituency where rumour of HMOs very recently caused violence that made the national headlines, I think there is an element of public safety here. We have to balance what information local people have against the need to keep the community safe, because there are people out there who, once they get information, will stir it up, cause trouble and put people’s lives at risk, and that is not acceptable.

Understanding, not division; light, not darkness. Last Sunday, I was proud to again join the Sunderland Inter Faith Forum’s walk of friendship, featuring Christian, Muslim, Buddhist, Sikh, Hindu and Quaker contributions. They say that hope happens when we walk together in peace, so will the Leader of the House join me in thanking the organisers for their important work, and will he consider a debate on the importance of interfaith work in supporting community cohesion?

With some irony, my hon. Friend follows the previous question with one that offers hope. He is a strong advocate for community cohesion not just in his area but across the country, and I pay tribute to him for that. I join him in thanking all those involved in the Sunderland Inter Faith Forum’s walk of friendship for the important work they do in encouraging interfaith dialogue. Should he seek an Adjournment debate or a Westminster Hall debate, I am sure that he and other Members will be able to share stories of hope from their own constituencies.

The Prime Minister has rightly talked about growth in every postcode, but the people of Peasedown St John are not feeling that at the moment because the West of England combined authority has cut a key local bus route, which means they are struggling to get to their jobs and to the Sulis hospital. Will the Leader of the House help me to secure a meeting with the relevant Minister to discuss how we can ensure that the funding the Government have given to combined authorities reaches people who do not necessarily live in the big cities of those areas, like those living in the Somer valley?

The hon. Lady raises a very important point—it is one that is referred to in the Milburn review—about people getting into work but also ensuring that the transport is there. She will know that my right hon. Friend the Prime Minister is, quite rightly, somewhat obsessed with this. I will take that back to the relevant Minister, but I hope the local authority that she refers to has heard what she said and can restore services to people who need them in her area.

I welcome the news that the Government have called on Google to take down Russell Brand’s YouTube account in the wake of his conviction, but that simply does not go far enough, because his podcast can still be seen on other streaming platforms such as Spotify, Amazon and Rumble, which is deeply disturbing for his victims. This issue also extends to the likes of LinkedIn, as in the case of Naomi Timperley and Brad Burton, who were victims of a convicted criminal who used LinkedIn and other methods to stalk them and try to make their life a living hell. Will the Leader of the House work with me to urge Ministers to bring in regulation and perhaps legislation to ensure that these tech platforms are acting based on not just how they feel about something but what the law dictates they must do, so that victims see justice when criminals are locked away?

To be clear, the request was to take down the specific video, which is clearly appalling. The matter is being investigated urgently, and we expect further action to be taken if he is found to have broken the rules. We have taken some steps on online safety, but my hon. Friend raises a perfectly legitimate concern. Should she wish to speak to Ministers about it, I will help to arrange a meeting.

It is reported today that the Secretary of State for Energy Security and Net Zero is encouraging her Labour colleagues to lobby against the Rosebank oilfield development. We are constantly being told that the decision on Rosebank is quasi-judicial, so there should be no lobbying. Does the Leader of the House believe it is still appropriate for the Secretary of State to make the decision if she is behind attempts to lobby against the proposal?

The hon. Gentleman should not believe all the rumours that may swirl on these matters. It is a quasi-judicial decision, and I am sure that my right hon. Friend the Secretary of State will make it in the right way.

My residents still face huge challenges getting driving tests. One constituent, Andrew, logged on to the booking system at 6 am on Monday only to find 12,500 people ahead of him in a 70-minute queue. When he finally got to the front of the queue, there was no availability for tests within a 50-mile radius. The Government are rightly determined to help young people into education, training and employment, but in areas like Aylesbury and the villages, where we have very limited public transport, that often depends on young people being able to drive to college or work. Will the Leader of the House make time for us to further debate the issue and progress it?

My hon. Friend has been an assiduous campaigner on this matter, and I absolutely sympathise with those affected by the long wait for tests. As she said, we are taking action—we are stamping out test reselling and limiting changes to bookings and locations to stop bots—but there is further work to be done, and I will make sure that she gets an update from the relevant Minister on what further steps are planned.

As we have heard, it is national Road Safety Week. One of the worst accident blackspots in the midlands is the Llynclys crossroads in my constituency, on the A483 between Welshpool and Oswestry. I am pleased to say that a complete redesign of the junction to create a roundabout, which I fully support, has been included in the national safety programme as part of road investment strategy 3, but the certainty of that funding has been put into question by changes to defence investment. The safety programme is critical, so will the Leader of the House ask the Transport Secretary to make a statement, or perhaps arrange a meeting for me with the relevant Minister to impress upon him the importance of this change?

The hon. Lady is right to press the case for her constituents in the way that she does. I will take it up with the relevant Minister and see whether we can get that meeting so she can make the case that she wants to make.

I warmly welcome the Government’s £2.5 billion youth guarantee package. However, discussions of youth employment and financial independence must not exclude those affected by the student loans system. Student loans remain one of the greatest barriers to young people achieving financial security, imposing a seemingly insurmountable financial burden on them for the majority of their working lives. Will the Leader of the House help to ensure that appropriate attention is given to that unfair system, which so desperately needs reform?

My hon. Friend is right to praise the Government’s youth guarantee package, and I join him in doing so. We are taking action by capping maximum interest rates at 6% for plan 2 and plan 3 loans, and reintroducing maintenance grants. However, we continue to look for ways to make the system even fairer for students, who I have to say were let down in a big way by the previous Government. We want to make the system fairer for students, graduates and, indeed, taxpayers, in a financially sustainable way, but I will make sure that Ministers have heard his concerns.

Will the Leader of the House join me in paying tribute to Lady Elizabeth Godsal MBE, who sadly passed away last week? Lady Elizabeth gave decades of service to local institutions, including 26 years as the high steward of Wokingham. She was a vice-lord lieutenant of the Royal County of Berkshire, high sheriff of Berkshire in 1990, chief president of St John Ambulance, chairman of the board of visitors of Reading Prison, patron of Girlguiding Royal Berkshire, and a former president of the Wokingham Society. Lady Elizabeth made an exceptional contribution to Wokingham and will be greatly missed.

I certainly join the hon. Gentleman in paying tribute to Lady Elizabeth. She sounds like one of those very busy people who we meet as we go about our civic roles. They are not only busy but live exceptional lives, and we should pay particular tribute to the contribution that they make to society. I join him in paying tribute to Lady Elizabeth and all the other people out there who are making a similar contribution.

I declare an interest as a member of GMB. Recently, Jo Taylor, in my High Peak office, celebrated 25 years of working for Labour Members, which is a tremendous achievement. Jo has dedicated her career to making the everyday lives of people better and protecting their rights. Now is a good time for us to look to protect the rights of all staff like Jo, which is why I am backing GMB’s “One Parliament One Employer” campaign. The Independent Parliamentary Standards Authority writes the contracts, sets the job descriptions and the pay bands, and pays the salaries, yet the legal liability sits with 650 individual MPs. Will the Leader of the House join me in congratulating Jo on her 25 years of public service, and make time in Government time for a debate on making Parliament the single employer for its staff?

My hon. Friend is right to recognise the incredible work done by our staff, both in Westminster and across the country. I join him in paying tribute to Jo and thank her for all her hard work over the years. There are a range of views on this topic. I note, Mr Speaker, that the Speaker’s Conference did a great deal of work on this matter in the last Parliament, and I am sure that the issue will continue to be a matter of debate. Should my hon. Friend want to press his case with House officials, then I will help him to arrange those meetings, and I will see what we can do about finding some time to arrange a debate on these matters, because it is an important question.

The Department for Education’s keeping children safe in education accreditation scheme is voluntary and does not automatically apply to permanent online-only schools. Ofsted visits only those providers who choose to join it as a quality assurance body, rather than under the usual inspection regime. As of August 2026, only 17 providers in England are accredited. Safeguarding children should not rely on whether their education provider opts in, so will the Leader of the House ask the Education Secretary to look again at bringing all full-time and part-time online education providers within a statutory framework?

The hon. Lady is absolutely right that safeguarding should never be an option. I have to confess that I do not know enough about this subject to give her any more of a response than that, except to say that I will take it up with the Secretary of State for Education and see what further plans there are to address what is a very important matter.

The Sair Inn is a characterful old pub in my constituency and has been a great asset to the local community for many years. I recently visited after it was recognised as one of the best pubs in the UK by The Daily Telegraph, and enjoyed an excellent pint with Jim, the landlord and owner. It is not the only pub that has been recognised in my constituency: the Royal Oak in Upperthong was given the same accolade. Will the Leader of the House join me in congratulating both the Sair Inn and the Royal Oak, and recognise the great work of the landlords and excellent staff at both pubs?

I will indeed join my hon. Friend in congratulating Jim and the Sair Inn, as well as the Royal Oak and its publican, on being recognised as among the best pubs in the United Kingdom. I have said it before and I will say it again: local pubs are the beating heart of our towns and villages. We are committed to supporting them, including through cutting business rates, and there was help in the Budget. They have gone through a tough time—7,000 closed during the period of the last Government. We are doing everything we can and looking at what more we can do to ensure our pubs thrive, because if they thrive, it helps our communities to thrive.

The wonderful Evington Road in my constituency already has two gambling shops, and a third gambling arcade has been proposed. Families are already feeling the financial squeeze, and there is practically nothing for young people to do, yet the gambling outlets keep coming. Will the Leader of the House make time for a debate on the spread of gambling premises in communities that are the hardest hit financially?

The hon. Gentleman is right to raise the state of our high streets because this Government care very deeply about that and share his concern about the proliferation of gambling shops. The Chancellor referred to this matter in his Budget and the action that we intend to take. This sounds to me like the sort of issue that the hon. Gentleman might want to raise in an Adjournment debate or a Westminster Hall debate, because I am sure that colleagues on both sides of the House will want to express similar concerns and hear from the Government on what more we intend to do about it.

Ayrshire Cancer Support, based in my constituency, delivers essential transport for people affected by cancer. Alongside that, it has dedicated support for children living with the disease and supports parents through treatment. Next year, I will be doing a 23-mile kilt walk as a way of raising awareness of its vital work. Will the Leader of the House join me in commending the staff and volunteers at Ayrshire Cancer Support on all their hard work? Will he consider donning a kilt and joining me on the walk?

I certainly join my hon. Friend in thanking Ayrshire Cancer Support for all its hard work, and I wish her every success in her kilt walk. I will certainly give her suggestion some consideration, but I would be hard pushed to decide which Campbell tartan kilt I would wear—there are so many. On a serious point, she will know that the Government are committed to taking action on cancer, and we have published our national cancer plan to end the cancer postcode lottery. At a local level, it is so important that she pays tribute to local people and gets involved in that work, and I wish her well on her kilt walk.

As it stands, China projects itself as a country of great freedom, but the fact of the matter is that the truth is very different. Back home, we would say that butter would not melt in his mouth, but the fact is that President Xi is involved in suppressing human rights, denying religious liberty and ensuring that people are tortured and killed because of their faith. I want to ask the Leader of the House about one example. Will he ask the Foreign Secretary to make a statement on the reported death of Rahile Omer? She was a Uyghur Muslim who was detained at the age of 14 and later sentenced to 12 years’ imprisonment after reportedly being punished for praying during her detention in Konasheher in Xinjiang province. What representations are the Government making to urge the Chinese authorities to clarify the circumstances of her death, release medical evidence and prison records, and protect Uyghur Muslims from detention and punishment for peacefully practising their faith and praying?

The reports of Rahile Omer’s death in custody are very distressing, to say the least. We stand firm on human rights, including standing against China’s repression of people in Xinjiang and Tibet. We continue to raise these issues directly with the Chinese authorities and other international partners. I will ensure that the Foreign Secretary hears the hon. Gentleman’s concerns. As ever, he makes a very important point in a very responsible way, and I will ensure that he gets an update on what this Government are doing to hold the Chinese authorities to account.

I recently visited Hednesford nursery school to toast its success, because a recent Ofsted inspection saw it achieve an incredible three areas at “strong” standard and three areas at “exceptional” standard. That makes it the highest-rated school in Staffordshire, the highest-rated nursery school in the country and, we believe, one of the highest-rated schools overall across the UK. Having seen the incredible work done by nursery manager Dawn Freeman and her team, that feels correct. Will the Leader of the House join me in congratulating the team at Hednesford nursery school? Can we have a debate on the vital importance of high-quality early education?

I join my hon. Friend in congratulating Dawn Freeman and the entire team at Hednesford nursery school on their exceptional achievement, which is certainly something to be proud of. I hope that the whole House will join me in paying tribute not only to their work, but to all the teachers, educational support staff and nursery workers across our constituencies. We truly appreciate their hard work.

At the weekend, it was announced that Lomond Radio in my constituency is to be awarded the King’s award for voluntary service. What started as a small lockdown project in 2020 has grown into a brilliant local radio station powered by more than 50 volunteers who provide local news, support charities and community groups, and give a platform to local talent across West Dunbartonshire and beyond. Will the Leader of the House join me in congratulating everyone involved—both on air and behind the scenes—on receiving the highest award presented to voluntary groups in the UK, and in wishing Lomond Radio every success for the future?

I certainly join my hon. Friend in congratulating the team at Lomond Radio on their vital work and all the volunteers who provide the services he describes. As he says, the King’s award is a considerable achievement, and I congratulate them on that. We are committed to supporting local radio and have launched our local media strategy, increasing community radio funding. At the end of the day, however, local radio depends on volunteers and the fantastic service they provide.

This week, the BBC released a podcast called “Chasing Mr Sunshine”, which is a deep dive into how a dodgy grifter called Liam Kavanagh managed to siphon vital public funds away from Thurrock council, aided and abetted by Sean Clark, the then finance director. It cannot be right that the closest these people have ever come to answering questions about putting my constituency in such dire straits is through BBC reporters’ efforts in chasing them down at their homes. Will the Leader of the House allow a debate in Government time about how we can hold to account public officials who so diabolically fail in their duty to the people they serve, so that we might finally be able to hold them to account?

My hon. Friend is absolutely right to raise that matter. As she says, it cannot be right that this information has to be dragged out by others; it should be out in the open for all to see. That debate is going on in government, and if my hon. Friend wants to know where our thinking on that has got to—or to raise this matter further, if necessary—I suggest that an Adjournment debate or Westminster Hall debate would be the way to do so.

Constituents in Truro and Falmouth who live on a park home site have reached out to me because the owner has not allowed them to have individual water meters. During the drought over the summer, they have been trying to conserve water, and they do not feel this is fair. Would the Leader of the House be able to either make space for a debate in Government time on this issue, or ask the relevant Minister to speak with me about whether they plan to review the rights of park home residents in relation to billing arrangements for water and other utilities on residential park home sites?

I am sure that situation must be very frustrating for my hon. Friend’s constituents. I understand that the rules around park homes and their residents are quite complex, but one of the Ministers responsible for these matters, the Minister for Housing and Planning, is sitting on the Front Bench and has heard what my hon. Friend has said. I am sure that if she catches him outside the Chamber, he would be more than happy to meet her.

Businesses at Lancing’s Chartwell business centre are losing customers after hundreds of them have received unfair fines of £100 due to poorly rolled-out automatic number plate recognition enforcement by One Parking Solution. As well as damaging those businesses, it has had a dangerous knock-on effect, with children at risk of injury from heavy goods vehicles on the neighbouring road. Will the Leader of the House join me in calling on One Parking Solution to work with me and the affected businesses to fix this problem as soon as possible, and will he grant time in this place for Members to debate how we can more effectively hold parking management companies to account?

My hon. Friend is a great advocate for businesses in his constituency, which will undoubtedly have been negatively impacted by what he describes. We are cracking down on unfair private parking charges through our new strengthened private parking code of practice, giving drivers the right to challenge those unfair charges. However, I hope One Parking Solution has heard his words today and that a swift solution can be found. I hope it respects my hon. Friend’s position as a Member of Parliament and offers him a meeting to work on how it can put this right. He is doing his best on behalf of his constituents, and One Parking Solution should listen to what he says.

The Holy Trinity night shelter in Bishop’s Stortford provides much-needed support and stability to those who are most in need in our community. It is no exaggeration to say that its work changes lives. I was delighted to see those who run the shelter awarded a King’s award for voluntary service last week. Will the Leader of the House, and the whole House, join me in congratulating Dave, Michelle and all the volunteers at the night shelter, and in thanking them for their hard work?

I am sure that the whole House will join me in congratulating Dave, Michelle and all the volunteers at the Holy Trinity night shelter on a very well-deserved King’s award, which, as I have said, is a very high and prestigious award. I am sure that it means a great deal to them and to the whole community. As my hon. Friend will know, ending rough sleeping is a top priority for the Government and the Prime Minister, and the valuable work of such shelters does not go unnoticed. I pay tribute to the work of people in my hon. Friend’s constituency and across the country, as we bear down on that intolerable problem.

We now come to the Select Committee statement on behalf of the Education Committee. Helen Hayes will speak for up to 10 minutes, during which no interventions may be taken. At the conclusion of the statement, Members may ask questions on the subject of the statement; they should be brief questions, not full speeches.

I am grateful to the Backbench Business Committee for granting time for this statement on the Education Committee’s fifth special report, “Reading for Pleasure: Government Response”. Select Committee work is a privilege. We hear hard evidence about systems that have failed and opportunities that have been lost. However, scrutiny is not only about finding fault, but about finding what works and ensuring it travels further. This inquiry gave us that chance, and it offered something that is rarer than it should be in public policy: joy. Witness after witness in our inquiry described reading as something that brings joy to life. Former children’s laureate Frank Cottrell-Boyce told us that in education, we can teach children all the steps, “but the important thing is that they dance.” He urged us to encourage policymakers to “prioritise the pleasure before you get into the learning”. The children we spoke to, including at our World Book Day roundtable, told us that reading helps them “escape from stress”, lets them “enter a whole new world full of new adventures”, and makes them feel “free”. I am sure that every one of us in this Chamber can remember a first book that did that, a torchlight under the covers, a library card, or a character who inspired us or made us feel less alone. Matilda found her refuge in the village library; Alice followed a rabbit down a hole and never looked back. Millions of children have since picked up a book and found a whole world that they had not known existed. That is what our report is about. Reading for pleasure is not an optional extra to be squeezed in once the serious business of education is done. The evidence was remarkably consistent: children who read for pleasure do better at school, develop stronger language and communication skills, enjoy better wellbeing, build empathy and understand the world more deeply. One witness described it as a form of preventive medicine. When we published, I said that if a miracle medicine that improved educational outcomes, built empathy and widened horizons existed, we would want every child to have it. Reading for pleasure comes remarkably close and costs a fraction of the price of any medicine. Yet too many children are missing out—and not at random. Children from disadvantaged backgrounds, children with special education needs and disabilities, and teenage boys are the least likely to fall in love with reading. A child’s chance of finding a book they love should never depend on how many books are on the shelves at home, or on the postcode of the nearest library. That is why, in the early years, joy must lead the way. As Frank Cottrell-Boyce put it, no parent says to a child, “When you’ve learned the offside rule, then I’ll play football with you.” We should not make children earn the pleasure of a story. Our report asked for a national reading guarantee: regular opportunities for every child, whatever their background, to enjoy books, stories and shared reading from birth through to adulthood. We called for stronger support for libraries, better access to books and a long-term strategy to reverse the decline in reading for pleasure. We were clear that that cannot rest on schools alone; it would take families, communities, libraries, charities and Government pulling in the same direction. In the Government response, Ministers have embraced the central importance of reading for pleasure and accepted our underlying ambition. I welcome the support for local areas through Best Start family hubs, and I welcome the National Year of Reading and its encouragement for schools to share best practice. I pay tribute to all the organisations involved in the National Year of Reading. I also welcome the work to explore how successful primary school reading culture programmes might be taken into secondary schools, and I welcome the early results. More than 2 million children have taken part in National Year of Reading activities, and there are encouraging signs that childr
Mr Swallow, you seem to have some special privileges. [ Laughter. ]

I thank Mr Speaker for delivering my opening speech for the International Men’s Day debate that is to follow this statement. It is testament to how important he knows the issue is. On reading for pleasure, will my hon. Friend join me in paying tribute to the immense legacy of Dolly Parton and all she did to support children’s literacy? Our report highlighted the work of the Imagination Library. I am sure that she will join me in welcoming the funding for charities, including the Imagination Library, in the Budget.

I thank my hon. Friend for his question and for the contribution he made as a member of the Select Committee to our inquiry on reading for pleasure. I join him in paying tribute to the late, great Dolly Parton. It is due to her work that every child in my constituency has access to books from birth through her Imagination Library. It has been a transformative programme for millions of children. All of us owe her a great debt of gratitude for that work.

I thank the Education Committee and its Chair for their contribution. As the grandfather of six children, I am very aware of the importance of books. When I was small, we had maybe one or two books, whereas today’s child has maybe a dozen or 20 books. The hon. Member for Bracknell (Peter Swallow) referred to Dolly Parton. In the world we live in, partnership and how we can do things together is incredibly important. Dolly Parton’s Imagination Library has donated 7 million books to the United Kingdom, and I think almost 300,000 to London alone and 300 million across the world. Is there not an opportunity here to work with the Imagination Library to collectively and collaboratively do something that can benefit all our children? Dolly Parton wanted that, the hon. Member for Dulwich and West Norwood (Helen Hayes) wants that, and so do I.

The hon. Member is right about the need for partnership. Books and literature are the product of creativity. It takes creativity across the whole infrastructure of reading to get the best out of it for every child, and that does involve partnership working. It also involves infrastructure and frameworks from the Government into which that creativity can flow. We called for both of those things in our report.

I want to take this opportunity to welcome the Select Committee’s report and to draw attention and give thanks to Cheshire’s school library service. Not every area still has access to such a service, but my area does. I had the great pleasure of visiting it recently, so I just wanted to highlight for my local schools that it is still there and we absolutely must make use of it. Lastly, I would just like to say a huge thank you to my father, on International Men’s Day, because he took me to the library when I was child, as I take my children now. Truly, reading has been one of the greatest pleasures of my life and that is thanks primarily to him.

I thank my hon. Friend for that lovely tribute to her father. I take this opportunity to extend that tribute to every parent who opens up for their children the whole universe through books. One of the things we call for in our report—we are delighted that the Government have accepted this recommendation—is a real focus on making reading for pleasure an essential strand of the work of Best Start family hubs, so that parents and carers, from the earliest stages of a child’s life, understand just how precious that gift is and also how accessible it is. As Frank Cottrell-Boyce told us, you can read with your child in a book that does not have words in it. Literacy need not be an automatic barrier to sharing the pleasure of bonding with your child in the earliest stages. I join her in paying tribute to school library services, where they still exist. They are a precious resource and play an important role in unlocking the pleasure of reading for so many children.

I thank my hon. Friend and the Committee for their work, and all who contributed to the report. As a former teacher, I have campaigned for decades for children to discover the joy of reading. In Portsmouth we have our very own Dolly Parton in James Ralls from the Victorious Festival. Alongside his wife Terri, he like Dolly has championed children’s love of books, even paying anonymously all children’s overdue library fines—he believes that if you love a book that much, you should keep it. Will my hon. Friend thank James and Terri for all their work not only on the Victorious Festival but in doing what they do for the children in our city? Will she let me know how the Committee will ensure that reading for pleasure becomes a lasting priority, so that every child has the chance to fall in love with books?

I thank my hon. Friend for her question and for her tribute to James and Terri for everything they do—it is a huge and generous gift to my hon. Friend’s city, and a great blessing, I am sure, to so many children in Portsmouth. Through our report, we set out, based on the evidence, what we believe the infrastructure looks like to ensure that that love of reading can be extended to every child across the country. I think for all members of the Committee who were a part of the inquiry, that became a burning passion—if it was not already, it certainly was by the end of our inquiry. This is certainly an area the Committee will continue to pursue and we will continue to hold the Government to account on going even further than they are already.

My hon. Friend the Member for Bracknell (Peter Swallow) might be Mr Speaker’s favourite, but— [ Laughter. ] I’m just saying. I thank the Education Committee and its Chair for all their work on this really important issue. Books teach us so much. I have recently learnt that you should not invite a tiger in for tea, however polite that tiger might be, that you should never feed chocolate cake to a hungry caterpillar, and more importantly, that a stickman is definitely not a stick. I have not got Harlow into this question, so I apologise. Does the Chair of the Education Committee agree that reading to our children can and should start from day one, and that we also need to encourage parents to get off their phones and into a good book?

My hon. Friend is right that reading for pleasure should start from the earliest days, weeks and months of life, because it is also a precious opportunity for parents, grandparents and carers to bond with their children—the evidence is really clear on that. Everybody can enjoy the pleasure of those children’s stories, which help all of us to unwind and connect with our babies and children. It is a precious thing. My hon. Friend is also right to say that this is an effort that involves everybody, and that it is for parents to model good behaviour to their children with regard to phones.

On a point of order, Madam Deputy Speaker. At Prime Minister’s questions yesterday, the Prime Minister told the House that UK exports have gone down since the UK left the EU. However, UK exports in our last full year of membership totalled £723 billion; last year, that figure rose to £913 billion, an increase of £190 billion, or 26%. Even adjusted for inflation, that is still an increase of 2%, so perhaps the Prime Minister might wish to return to the House and correct the record.

The hon. Member will know that Ministers, not the Chair, are responsible for the accuracy of the words that they use in the Chamber. Those on the Front Bench will have heard his concerns, and if a correction is needed, I am sure that one will be forthcoming.

On a point of order, Madam Deputy Speaker. Mine is not a tedious one, unlike the one from the hon. Member for Bridlington and The Wolds (Charlie Dewhirst). Over a number of months—maybe a year now—I have been raising the case of Dr Hussam Abu Safiya, who was the director of the Kamal Adwan hospital in Gaza, which was bombed. He was then arrested by the Israelis in December 2024. He has remained in prison since. I have just met the representatives of the family. There are now real concerns from those who have visited him—his lawyers, because the Red Cross are not allowed to visit—about his life. There is an opportunity, if the Israelis are willing to undertake it, to allow him to go to a third country, if they do not want him to go back to Gaza. However, we are now fearful that he will not survive. I have contacted the Foreign Secretary, and I ask that those on the Treasury Bench take the message back that this is a matter of urgency now and there needs to be action fast.

The right hon. Member knows that this is not a matter for the Chair. Further advice is available from the Table Office, but as he pointed out, the Front Bench have heard, and they will no doubt ensure that the message gets through to the right Department. Bill Presented Commonhold and Leasehold Reform Bill Presentation and First Reading (Standing Order No. 57) Secretary Angela Rayner, supported by the Prime Minister, Secretary Alex Norris, Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh, Secretary Stephen Kinnock, Secretary Matthew Pennycook, Ian Murray, and Justin Madders presented a Bill to make provision about commonhold land; to prohibit the grant or assignment of certain new long residential leases of flats; to amend the Leasehold and Freehold Reform Act 2024 in relation to the prohibition of the grant or assignment of certain long residential leases of houses; to make provision about leasehold enfranchisement and the right to extend a long residential lease; to make provision about ground rent; to make provision about administration charges; to make provision about gigabit-capable broadband connections in leasehold premises; to make provision about advice concerning estate management matters; to make provision about remedies in connection with breach of covenants of long residential leases; to make provision about estate rent charges and similar sums; and for connected purposes. Bill read the First time; to be read a Second time tomorrow, and to be printed (Bill 189) with explanatory notes (Bill 189 - EN).

I beg to move, That this House has considered International Men’s Day 2026. I thank all colleagues for being here today on International Men’s Day for this important debate, I thank the Backbench Business Committee for granting it, and I thank Mr Speaker for helping to get my speech into my hands. I am honoured to be opening the 11th Backbench Business debate to mark IMD. Since 2015, Members across the House have used this debate to highlight persistent issues facing men and boys in this country in the spirit of bipartisanship, from mental health to parental leave, missing only a single year—2019 —because of a general election. This might be International Men’s Day, but what we talk about in today’s debate affects each and every one of us. We still see gender disparities in almost every walk of life, whether that be in outcomes at school, progression in the workplace, or caregiving and responsibilities at home. When fathers are unable to take more than two weeks of paternity leave, it is not only men who suffer, but their partner, who has to shoulder the lion’s share of caregiving while, in many cases, recovering from the physical challenge of giving birth, and their child, who is deprived of vital time with their father in those crucial first weeks of life. When boys, particularly those from disadvantaged backgrounds, leave school without the qualifications they need to get on in life because the education system has failed to meet their needs, the impact is not confined to their future, but shows up in the welfare system, in our mental health system and, too often, in our criminal justice system.

I commend the hon. Gentleman for introducing this debate. He is absolutely right to underline the issue of mental health. The stats in Northern Ireland are incredible: we face a devastating mental health crisis among our men, with official figures showing that nearly eight in every 10 suicide deaths are male. Suicide remains the leading cause of death for men under 50; too often, stigma and silence prevent our young men from reaching out before it is too late. Does the hon. Member agree that the Government must work closely with the Northern Ireland Executive and grassroots community groups to deliver accessible, targeted mental health support so that no young man feels he has to suffer alone?

I do. I thank the hon. Member in particular for raising the important role of community groups, such as Andy’s Man Club, which works tirelessly in Bracknell and across the country to provide an opportunity for men to share their mental health challenges in a way that works for them. I also pay tribute to the fantastic men’s shed in my constituency, which again works to provide men with a place to share how they are feeling that day, often in a way that does not centre and focus on mental health, but that still includes it as an important part of its function. The voluntary sector does so much to support the health services in this country, and we can never thank them enough for that. When men feel that they are not being heard and disengage from seeking help, the tragic impacts of that disengagement can, and all too often do, reverberate out, affecting and impacting those around them. Confronting what it means to be a man in this world means confronting issues that go right to the heart of some of the most serious and difficult challenges we are grappling with as a society. I want to acknowledge that we are having this debate at a time when we are again asking questions about how cultures of misogyny and violence against women and girls continue to be perpetrated, particularly among those with power and influence in our society, but also behind closed doors in households across the country and, as we are increasingly seeing, online. International Men’s Day gives us an important opportunity to be very clear: a world in which we do not seriously reckon with both what it currently means and what we want it to mean to be a man or a boy today is a world that fails us all. We should not be mealy-mouthed in calling out violence against women and girls and sex-based crimes. We can, and should, tackle these issues head-on. Of course, we should also recognise and commit to supporting the male victims of domestic violence and sexual assault; these are men’s issues, too, and we need to be honest about that. But whatever difficult topics we discuss in today’s debate, International Men’s Day is also an opportunity to celebrate the many positive contributions that the men in our lives make. Last year’s debate saw many Members doing so with that purest of things: the dad joke. Not to be outdone, I have asked my own dad for his very best, or should I say worst, examples. I stand ready to take an intervention on this one, if anyone happens to know the answer. Can anyone tell me why the French have only one egg for breakfast?

Absolutely. I will let the Minister for Intergovernmental Relations and European Relations know that he can use that at tomorrow’s summit. I know personally the importance that a male role model can have. Like many men, my dad worked long hours to support our family, but when my mum died when I was a teenager, he took time away from work to finish raising me, and to support me through that loss. That is something for which I will always be grateful. I recognise the privilege we had as a family that allowed him to do that. Not all fathers can be there for their families in times of need, even if they want to be. That is especially true at birth. We know that a father’s presence in the first few months after childbirth is indispensable. Greater involvement by a father in a child’s life improves a child’s cognitive and emotional outcomes, and it is linked to lower levels of post-partum depression in partners and better mental health for fathers. That is without mentioning the wider benefits for the economy and improvements to gender equality in the workplace. Why, therefore, do around a third of men take no leave at all when their baby arrives? Statutory paternity leave is not long enough and does not pay enough. By failing to give men the security that they need to be with their family at the start of a child’s life, we are locking them out of the most important job they will ever have. We are also reinforcing gender roles that we claim to have left in the past, and the inequalities that they entrench. This is a question of equality. Office for National Statistics analysis shows that mothers lose around £65,000 in earnings in the five years after the first birth. Let us be completely clear: what locks men out of care-giving locks women out of the workplace. We cannot expect to make progress on one without recognising its relationship to the other. I pay tribute to the many people who are campaigning on this issue for their tireless work, including many Members across this House, the Dad Shift, and many other organisations. I also welcome the Government’s announcement of a new paternity allowance for self-employed dads. With the parental leave review due to conclude soon, I urge the Government to go further and set out a clear route to improving statutory paternity leave and delivering real equality. Empowering men to take the time to be active, present fathers is a structural issue that affects us all and, crucially, we can change it. Young people do not look only to their parents for role models, and I welcome the Government’s national youth strategy, which recognises that every young person should have a trusted adult outside their home. It sets out steps to make that a reality, including by embedding youth workers and professionals in new young futures hubs, and empowering local leaders to provide the support that the young people they work with might need. I take this opportunity to thank all the adult volunteers across Bracknell Forest and the country who work so hard to provide opportunities and support for our young people, including in the cadets, scouting groups and sports clubs. I pay particular tribute to one youth worker in Bracknell Forest for his years of dedication to boys and girls in our community. Gareth runs The Wayz, a youth club that recently celebrated its 60th year supporting young people in Bracknell, making it almost as old as our town. Gareth actually went to The Wayz as a young person, and he has dedicated his life to supporting some of the most vulnerable, hard-to-reach young people in our community. Every time I see him, he tells me about a new project to reach more kids and offer them support. There are Gareths in every town in Britain, working tirelessly to support young people and to be that trusted adult.

The hon. Gentleman has referred to a number of organisations, and we congratulate them all, but there are a couple that he has not spoken of: the Boys’ Brigade and the Campaigners, which are found in my constituency of Strangford and across Northern Ireland. Those Church-oriented and faith-based groups ensure that young people are given the leadership and encouragement that they need. Does the hon. Member recognise that, too?

I am happy to recognise that; it is so important. I have frequently made the point that we need a range of opportunities for young people to engage with youth services, because what is right for one will not be right for another. It is so important that we take a holistic approach. That is why it is so fantastic to see the Government’s enrichment entitlement for young people. Not everyone will be lucky enough to have a man at home whom they can trust and turn to, but they should be able to look to someone like Gareth, or other inspiring leaders in the wider community.

As my hon. Friend knows, like him, I used to be a teacher. I will not comment on where I ranked among teachers in Harlow, but Madam Deputy Speaker was kind about that earlier. I was 22 years old when I became a teacher, and I found it daunting that young men in my class saw me as a father figure; I certainly did not feel ready to be that. Does he agree that it is important that as well as having male teachers as role models, we have role models in the community? I will quickly plug groups in Harlow, including the sea cadets and the air cadets, that provide that leadership—that parental substitution, I might say, but perhaps that is unnecessary—in the community.

My hon. Friend is so right. I want to focus a little on teachers, because they have an important part to play. Only about 24% of teachers in England are men. The shortfall is particularly acute in early years and primary education, which is a time when growing numbers of boys and young men turn to social media and the manosphere for role models. If we do not want young, often vulnerable, men turning to the Andrew Tates of this world when they are feeling isolated, we need male role models in schools, youth services and the community—leaders who can give them a different perspective on what it really means to be a successful man. With Alan Milburn’s report fresh in my mind, it is important to highlight that more young men than women are not in education, employment or training, and that outcomes at school for boys, particularly white boys, continue to lag behind those of girls. Boys are also more likely to be excluded from school, and the review’s interim report found that exclusion was a strong predictor of becoming NEET. These are complex issues, but if we do not want young men who are feeling vulnerable or isolated to disengage from their education or turn away from the world and towards the seductive and easy answers of the manosphere, we must face up to these challenges and do whatever it takes to ensure that school speaks to and engages boys. Between family, schools and local youth groups and clubs, we can build a safety net that ensures that every young man has somewhere to turn and someone to look up to. Landmark longitudinal research by the Australian Institute of Family Studies found that more than one in three Australian men commit intimate partner violence in their lifetime. It also found that men who felt strongly that they had a quality relationship, marked with affection, with a father or a father figure during childhood were 48% less likely to report ever having used intimate partner violence. Men who reported high levels of social support were also less likely to report using intimate partner violence. Men with moderate or severe depressive symptoms were 62% more likely to use it than those without such symptoms. Violence against women and girls is a men’s issue, a health issue, and something that we as men, and as politicians, can prevent, but not if we do not have the right role models for young men, and the right support to enable men to be those role models. There is another difficult truth that we have to confront: suicide remains the leading cause of death for men under 50 years old. While the suicide rate for women has almost halved since 1985, for men it has reduced by only 7%. There is a wider context, too: men in the UK have a lower life expectancy than those in many OECD countries, and are more at risk of heart disease, cancer and substance abuse. I welcome the men’s health strategy—the first of its kind. It is a real step forward in recognising that there are issues in men’s health that require attention, and in setting out a clear plan to address them. It is important to highlight that the strategy explicitly recognises the relationship between challenges for men’s mental health and their physical health, and the impact that can have on those around them. It draws wider connections to ongoing plans and projects across Departments, including the NHS 10-year plan and the national youth strategy, as well as legislative changes, including the Employment Rights Act 2025. In this context, I welcome the announcement this morning that the Government will convene a summit on men and boys in the new year, which will ensure that we continue to draw together the work being done across Departments to deliver on this important mission. That is exactly the holistic view we need to take, so I thank the Government for their work up to this point, and urge them to outline a comprehensive men and boys strategy as quickly as possible. Preparing for this debate was complex, in part because of the wide range of issues t

I thank my hon. Friend the Member for Bracknell (Peter Swallow) for securing this debate, and commend him on his fantastic speech. International Men’s Day is an opportunity to celebrate men and recognise the contribution they make to our families, workplaces and communities, but also to confront some uncomfortable truths about men’s health. Speaking of uncomfortable truths, my eldest daughter recently broke and asked me to stop telling dad jokes. I told her that I completely understood where she was coming from, that it was an important issue that I was determined to do something about, and that I therefore asked for a judge-led statutory inquiry, which I fully expect to report at some point after her 18th birthday. In the meantime, I am attempting to do my bit for Movember. At Prime Minister’s questions yesterday, the Prime Minister offered hope: I still had 12 days to grow a proper moustache. As he delivers growth in every postcode, I will do my best to deliver a little bit more growth in mine. While the ’tache may be failing to live up to expectations, it is at least achieving its purpose of getting people to talk about men’s health. As I said yesterday at PMQs, three in four people who take their own lives are men. Suicide remains the leading cause of death for men under 50. We cannot and should not accept this. Last International Men’s Day, the Government took the important step of publishing a men’s health strategy for the first time. It is important recognition that men’s health needs a proper, co-ordinated response. The £3.6 million investment in neighbourhood-based suicide prevention for middle-aged men is particularly welcome. Support does not always begin in a doctor’s surgery or mental health clinic; sometimes it begins in a room where men feel comfortable and able to talk. Sometimes it begins on a football pitch, and sometimes it begins over a cup of tea. We are very fortunate in High Peak to have some fantastic organisations that allow for exactly that. Mentell in Glossop and Buxton provides safe, confidential spaces for men to talk. I have seen for myself that the men’s shed in Whaley Bridge provides another way of tackling isolation and bringing people together. I am also particularly pleased that the Minister and the Prime Minister this morning took Andy’s Man Club into 10 Downing Street. I saw this support for myself when I joined one of Buxton FC’s mental health kickabouts last year. Men of all ages and abilities get together for a game of football before heading to the clubhouse for a cup of tea, a biscuit and a chat. Thanks to some very charitable defending, I was even kindly allowed to score a couple of goals. There are many stresses and strains, changes and turning points in our lives that can affect our mental health—debt, insecure work, relationship breakdown, gambling, alcohol, loneliness and housing insecurity, to name but a few. I want to focus on one change that is particularly personal to me: becoming a dad. I remember how overwhelming it was when we had our first daughter. Of course, you want to be there, be involved and do your bit, but you are also trying to work out how to be a dad, how to support your family, and how to navigate all the changes that come with that. If I were asked, I would say that becoming a dad is the best thing I have done and will ever do. But I will be honest, if I were to be asked the same question most nights at 2 am when my two-year-old is point-blank refusing to accept that night time is when we sleep, I might give a rather unparliamentary reply. Whether it is your first child or third child, becoming a dad brings enormous joy, but it can also feel like an overwhelming responsibility. Suddenly there is a little person who depends on you for absolutely everything. Priorities change overnight, and new things have to be learned that are not always easy. Finances come under pressure, which is all the more difficult during a cost of living crisis. What I have found is tha

I thank both of the speakers so far, particularly my hon. Friend the Member for Bracknell (Peter Swallow), who gave such a great big overview of International Men’s Day. To start, I will say that, probably like a lot of men, this is a day that has passed me by throughout most of my life. This is not a day that necessarily has the same degree of awareness around it as International Women’s Day. I do not mean that in the way that some very annoying reply guys on the internet say, every International Women’s Day, “When is International Men’s Day?”—it is today; it just passes us by and does not have the same amount of awareness around it. Since becoming an MP, however, the issues facing men in our communities—in my community in Sittingbourne and Sheppey and across every constituency in the country—have really come to the fore. On the Women and Equalities Committee, we have also looked into things such as the manosphere, and the roles, responsibilities and part that men play in violence against women and girls, in the perceptions of women and men online, and in our communities. We have also done some work looking at parental leave around the world and how that impacts. This year has also given me the opportunity to reflect a bit on myself: what it means for me to be a man, the experience of that and how, in the end, being a man is something you just are—if you are a man. You just have it, but it is also something you have to work at. There are challenges to understanding what it is to be a man in the world and what it is to be a man for you. That is true for any adult of any gender: you have to work out who you are and not take on everyone else’s definitions of who you are and who you might be. For men, there are other people’s definitions of masculinity and what that looks like, and other people’s definitions of how you should respond and behave in a society. The core point of that came when I realised I was gay at the age of 11. It hit me as a bit of a bolt from the blue—an instant realisation—and several things flowed from that straightaway. One was about fatherhood. As the eldest child in a large Catholic family, I had always expected to be someone who had kids of my own. Suddenly, there was a realisation: I will not have a female partner, I will not marry a woman and it is very unlikely that I will have children of my own. There was no expectation at the time that gay people would be able to adopt. That came a lot later in my life, at a point when neither I nor my husband were able to take that on. That was quite a big blow; it was quite a big shock. I absorbed it at the time, like a lot of teenagers—well, some teenagers—would, but it has had impacts and it has affected the whole of my life. It has also affected the way that I approach manhood and what being a man is. The other thing that came with that experience was that, at that time, most of the social expectation for gay men was about being effeminate—the sort of Larry Grayson-type presentation of what a gay man would be. That is a great and a fantastic way to be, but it is not quite me. Although I was useless at football and a lot of those sorts of boys’ activities, I was a very geeky boy and I loved stuff like science fiction and transport—other boy activities. Those are all things you have to work out. What does it mean to you as you approach manhood and, as you then progress into adulthood, what are the responsibilities that you take on? How do you avoid the toxicities of manhood that are out there? My response was: I am just me, but I am a bloke and I will be a bloke. On an incidental note, that is why I very much understand how trans people know that they are trans. I know that I am not trans; I am a gay man. It really is just automatic; it does not even take any thinking. If we reflected a little on that in the whole debate around trans and non-binary people, most of us would think, “I never even thought of that.” I had to think of that at that age and that gives m

Thank you, Madam Deputy Speaker. I congratulate my hon. Friend the Member for Bracknell (Peter Swallow) on securing this important debate. My hon. Friend the Member for Sittingbourne and Sheppey (Kevin McKenna) mentioned people who complain about International Women’s Day. They say, “When’s International Men’s Day?” That happens so often, especially in this House. We are always getting criticised. Where are they? There is not one person on the Opposition Benches for International Men’s Day. [ Interruption. ] I mean on the Back Benches, not the Front Bench. They complain about International Women’s Day and other things for women. They talk about men as though they care about them, but they do not care enough to come to the Chamber and participate in this debate. That is a disgrace, and I hope that their constituents are watching. International Men’s Day was formally inaugurated by a lecturer, Dr Jerome Teelucksingh, in Trinidad and Tobago. Dr Teelucksingh was driven to promote positive role models. The theme for 2026 is supporting men and boys, and there is nothing more important than ensuring that we are leading on that. Men, especially young men, sometimes feel isolated—as though the world does not belong to them or they are lost in the world. It is important for us, as politicians, not to use the insecurity of young men to get them angry. That is the playbook of Reform Members especially: getting young men angry. What do they do with that anger? They use it for their own personal gain. They do not accept or acknowledge that they are having an effect on young men’s mental health. It is important that we set the political agenda, and doing so through this debate is fundamental. Being a man includes protecting women and girls. Real men protect women and girls, and we should teach that. Real men cry. There is all this stuff about keeping calm and carrying on, not accepting that real men cry. Men are criticised or called wusses and all sorts of other things. Real men cry, and that is okay.

My hon. Friend is giving a powerful speech; it is important that we hear voices like hers in debates such as this. My constituent, Leo Shepherd, is a victim of domestic violence, and he has a powerful one-man show that talks about that. Does she recognise the importance of role models, such as Leo, talking about their experiences and encouraging other young men who have been victims of violence to come forward?
Order. The hon. Member is so experienced that she knows better than to use the words “you” or “your”, because she is speaking through the Chair.

I apologise, Madam Deputy Speaker. I congratulate Leo on the work that he is doing. We must recognise that men also suffer from domestic abuse and domestic violence. Real men wear pink. I have seen some say online that real men do not wear pink. Real men can wear whatever colour they please. Real men talk about their feelings. Real men are woke. I read an article about a Member saying that the new James Bond is going to be all woke. Who cares? Woke is a good thing. When I was a child, my dad was 8 feet tall to me, and when I became an adult, he was still 8 feet tall. I would fix cars with him. He would take me to A&E when I was suffering from period pains, and was being sick and having cramps. He explain to the doctors and nurses, “My daughter is suffering from really bad period pains.” He was not ashamed to talk about periods. That is a real man. On 1 June 2026, the Mayor of London launched a £1 million fund to call on society to act on a lost generation of young men. That is an important fund, and we need to ensure that we activate it. We cannot afford to lose a generation of young men. We need them to be participants, good participants, in society. Research has shown that 15% of Londoners think that young men and boys do not have enough positive role models, and 55% of men say that they face pressure to meet societal expectations related to being a man. That rises to 71% among men aged 18 to 24. Londoners are nine times more likely to say that social media is harmful and harmful to their mental health. We have to get a grip on social media. The algorithms are there to promote an environment of continuous scrolling and of bubbles, such that if someone hates women, they will be put in circles where other people hate women and will think that that is the norm. We have to get a grip on social media and algorithms. In Brent, we have several men’s clubs that tackle how to parent. We have a scheme in which barbers have positive conversations—they have a captive audience when they are cutting hair. That is an innovative way to interject positivity into everyday life. We have heard about suicide in men. In 2022 to 2024, 73% of suicides were, very sadly, men, and suicide remains the leading cause of death in men under 50 years old. These are men who say that they do not know what to do, or that they do not know how to carry on. That is something of an emergency. This Government have done a great deal to acknowledge men and to ensure that we have legislation that showcases the role that men play. That is important. Women live longer than men—it is a fact. We sometimes make light of that when we see some of the stuff that men get up to, especially on social media—we think, “No wonder women live longer.” But it is not just about living longer. Older men often have worse health outcomes, and we have to tackle that. This goes back to men being told to suffer in silence. They do not have to suffer in silence. If they are ill, they should go to the GP. If they have a pain, they should go to the GP. Because men are sometimes reluctant to go to the GP, they get diagnosed later, and so they have worse health outcomes. In Brent, male life expectancy at birth is 80 years old, and for women it is 85 years old. Across London, men do slightly better, at 80.5 years old, and women do slightly worse, at 84.7 years old. The charity Mind reports that 33% of men say that their job has a negative impact on their mental health, that 43% of men regularly feel worried or low, and that young black men are around three times more likely to present as a suicide risk than young white men. The Government’s men’s health strategy is vital when it comes to cancer. The incidence of cancer is higher in males than in females. We have to say to men, “It’s okay to talk about your mental health and your physical health.” It is still a fact—it has not changed—that a woman is killed every three days by a male partner or male former partner. We need men to call this out. The
Because they are shellfish. I am available for after-dinner speeches.
Real men do wear pink, as the hon. Member for Wimbledon (Mr Kohler) can attest to. I call Samantha Niblett.

Thank you for calling me, Madam Deputy Speaker, as I furiously update my speech with the latest names suggested to me of brilliant men in my constituency who deserve recognition, but I will start at the beginning. I rise to mark International Men’s Day and, in particular, to pay tribute to some of the remarkable men and groups that have been nominated by people across South Derbyshire for the positive difference they make to our communities. A personal mention for me is Ian Bottrill, who we sadly lost earlier this year. He was my agent in the general election, but he was also my friend. I and many across our community miss him dearly every day, especially those at Sharpe’s Pottery where he was a trustee and those at Swad in Bloom where his personal contribution was so valued. Before moving to south Derbyshire, he dedicated years of his life as a teacher inspiring many and as a councillor, including as leader of Warwickshire county council. I want to give a special mention to the wonderful Antony and Roger Cobley. They have spent a lifetime caring for others, and they still do. They dedicated their lives and careers to nursing and were the first gay couple to foster and change the lives and fortunes of boys whose future was not hopeful based on their start in life. Their ongoing commitment to their sons and their families is wonderful, as we would expect from all good fathers, but they are not just good fathers; they are amazing fathers. Back to some of the people who were recommended by my community, I asked local people to put forward the names of men who they felt deserved recognition, and this is just the tip of the iceberg—it really is. The response was a powerful reminder that across our towns and villages, there are men quietly doing extraordinary things, men who give their time, compassion and energy, and often their own personal experiences, to help others. One name that came up time and again was Alex Garner, who co-founded and runs Our Little Angels. Alex provides invaluable support to families experiencing miscarriage and the devastating loss of a baby or child. His personal compassion, alongside his fundraising efforts, has touched many lives. Supporting families through unimaginable grief requires a special kind of strength, and Alex deserves enormous recognition. Adam Foster, the owner of Nomad Tattoo & Co in Swadlincote, was also nominated repeatedly. Adam uses his business and influence to raise money for good causes, including fundraising connected with hospital dermatology services in Birmingham children’s hospital. He demonstrates how local businesses can be a force for good. I want to recognise Adam Stretton, a military veteran and the head coach and owner of Fight Station in Church Gresley. Through his work supporting men’s mental health, veterans and those facing serious personal challenges, including through a men’s release and recharge programme, Adam is helping men find connection, support and a way forward when life becomes difficult. There are many others whose contributions deserve to be acknowledged. Stephen Morley—I know Stephen personally; he is such a lovely man—owns Swadlincote Electrical and Solar Supplies and will frequently send me a message on LinkedIn just checking that I am okay. He was praised for his work supporting our local community, including frequent and generous donations to South Derbyshire CVS food bank. Graham Knight, who I know personally, too, as a fellow Labour party member, has dedicated nearly 40 years to running Moira Replan. Moira is just outside my constituency, but has certainly served those who live in it. He has served his local community. People have a lot of time and love for Andy Dawson because of the time he has dedicated to parish council work, rugby and charity fundraising, but he is one of those people who does not make a fuss about it, rolls up his sleeves and just gets on with it.
